title: The Return of the Urban River

passage_json.title: The Return of the Urban River

paragraphs.text: In the nineteenth century, dozens of small rivers that ran through European and North American cities were covered over. Engineers of the period treated them as drains rather than as waterways, and the treatment was thorough. Culverts of brick, and later of concrete, carried the water underground, and streets, markets, tenements and railway yards were built on top of them. The logic was straightforward. A buried river could not flood a warehouse, it could not be used as an open sewer by the households along its banks, and it could not spread the smells that city dwellers of the time associated with disease. Municipal engineers were rewarded for burying rivers, and the more ambitious the burial, the greater the reward. For roughly a century the decision looked sound. Seen from the present, it looks like one of the most expensive mistakes in the history of urban engineering.

The reversal of that policy is known as daylighting. A daylighting project removes part of a culvert, excavates the original channel and returns a river to the open air, usually along with a footpath, some planting and a strip of public space. The best known example is the Cheonggyecheon in Seoul, where an elevated motorway carrying about 168,000 vehicles a day was demolished in 2003 and a 5.8-kilometre stream was uncovered beneath it. Smaller schemes have followed in Zurich, Sheffield, Yonkers and Auckland. Most of them involve only a few hundred metres of channel, and most cost less than the flood defences they were designed to replace. There are now more than a hundred completed projects worldwide, although the definition is loose enough that the figure should be treated with caution.

Hydrologists give three reasons for the change of heart. The first is capacity. A culvert sized for the rainfall of 1880 cannot carry the rainfall of 2030, and when it fills, water backs up into basements, car parks and streets. An open channel can be widened, and the land beside it can be allowed to flood harmlessly. The second reason is temperature. Water in a buried pipe absorbs heat from the pavements and buildings above it, and arrives downstream several degrees warmer than it should be, which suits very few native fish. The third reason is access. A river that nobody can see is a river that nobody defends, and the political cost of polluting an invisible watercourse is close to zero.

The ecological results have been measured, and they are encouraging rather than spectacular. Surveys of the Saw Mill River in Yonkers recorded eleven fish species in the uncovered reach within four years, where the culverted section had held two. Invertebrate populations recovered more slowly, and in some reaches they have still not reached the levels found upstream. Birds arrived almost immediately, but the species that appeared first were generalists such as gulls, mallards and pigeons rather than the specialists that conservationists hope for. Ecologists now argue that a daylighted river should be judged as a corridor connecting larger areas of habitat, and not as a habitat in its own right.

The economic argument has proved easier to make than the ecological one. Property values beside the Cheonggyecheon rose by about 30 per cent in the decade after the stream reopened, roughly double the increase recorded elsewhere in central Seoul over the same period. Small businesses along the corridor reported heavier foot traffic, and the city recovered part of its costs through higher land taxes. Cities have accordingly learned to present daylighting as regeneration rather than as conservation, and the language of their funding applications has changed to match. That shift is pragmatic, but it carries a risk: a project sold on property values will be designed for property values.

Not every scheme succeeds, and the failures are instructive. Where a buried river still receives untreated runoff from roads, uncovering it exposes residents to the pollution instead of removing it, and two British projects were abandoned at the design stage for precisely this reason. Where the surrounding land is privately owned, the negotiations can outlast the political term of the council that began them. And where a channel is uncovered without room for the water to spread, the result is a concrete trench with a stream at the bottom of it: visible, tidy and ecologically almost worthless.

None of this argues against daylighting. It argues for doing it properly. The lesson of the last twenty years is that a river is not a pipe with better public relations. It is a system that needs width, shade, gravel and time, and the cities that provide those four things end up with a working river. The cities that provide only a view end up with an expensive ornament. The distinction matters, because the next generation of projects will be judged against the promises made for this one.

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century an electricity grid worked on a single unforgiving principle: generation had to match demand at every instant. There was no reservoir in the system and no margin for hesitation. Operators met the morning surge by starting more turbines and the evening collapse by shutting them down, and the whole apparatus of dispatch, pricing and reserve capacity grew up around that requirement. Storage was not unknown, merely uneconomic. A kilowatt-hour held in a battery cost many times a kilowatt-hour burned in a boiler, and because coal and gas could be stockpiled cheaply in solid or liquid form, the fuel itself was the storage. The principle held for a hundred years because the technology of the day offered no alternative to it.

Wind and solar generation broke that arrangement, not by being unreliable but by being uncontrollable. A gas plant can be told what to do; a solar farm can only be told to stop. As the share of variable generation rose above roughly a fifth of supply in several regions, operators began to face a problem they had never had to price: surplus. In 2022 California curtailed about 2.4 million megawatt-hours of solar and wind output, electricity that had been generated and then deliberately discarded because there was nowhere for it to go. Curtailment on that scale is not merely wasteful. It undermines the economics of the next wind farm, because a generator paid only for what the grid accepts cannot count on selling what it makes.

The obvious answer was already in place, and had been for decades. Pumped hydroelectric storage moves water uphill when power is abundant and releases it through turbines when power is scarce, and it still accounts for the overwhelming majority of the world's installed storage capacity, around 90 per cent measured by energy. Its efficiency is respectable, typically between 70 and 80 per cent, and its working life is measured in generations rather than years. What it cannot do is go anywhere new. A scheme needs two large reservoirs at different heights, close together, on ground that will hold water, and near enough to a transmission line to be worth connecting. Sites meeting all four conditions are rare, and most of the good ones in Europe and North America were developed before 1990.

Lithium-ion cells solved the siting problem by being indifferent to terrain. Between 2010 and 2023 the price of a lithium-ion pack fell by roughly 85 per cent, and grid batteries stopped being demonstration projects and became ordinary infrastructure. Speed is their distinctive quality. A battery responds in milliseconds, which makes it excellent at the tasks a grid needs performed instantly: smoothing frequency, covering the seconds after a fault, shaving the sharpest peak of the evening. What it does badly is endure. Most grid batteries are built to discharge for two to four hours, because the cells are the expensive part and adding hours means adding cells.

Two to four hours is ample for a sunny grid and useless for a still, overcast week in January. The industry calls this the duration problem, and it has produced an unusually diverse set of candidate solutions, none of them yet dominant. Flow batteries hold their energy in tanks of liquid electrolyte, so capacity can be increased by buying a larger tank rather than a larger stack. Compressed air systems use caverns or insulated vessels. Thermal schemes heat crushed rock, molten salt or graphite blocks and convert the heat back to electricity days later, accepting a poor round-trip efficiency in exchange for very cheap materials. Iron-air cells rust and un-rust a metal that costs almost nothing. The logic behind all of them is the same: once storage has to last for days, the cost of the material matters more than the elegance of the chemistry.

Technology, however, is no longer the binding constraint. Storage sits awkwardly in electricity markets that were written for generators and consumers, and a device that is sometimes one and sometimes the other can find itself charged twice for the same connection. Some regulators still classify a battery as a generator, which brings obligations designed for power stations; others cap the number of services a single asset may be paid for, so that a battery providing frequency response is barred from also earning from arbitrage. These rules were not written maliciously. They were written before the thing they now govern existed, and rewriting them is slower work than building the hardware it applies to.

What follows from all this is a change in the way a grid is described. The traditional question, how many megawatts can this system supply, is being displaced by a harder one: for how many hours can it supply them? A network with abundant generation and four hours of storage is not a decarbonised system; it is a system that works until sunset. The value of the next increment of storage depends entirely on how long that increment lasts, and this is why the least glamorous technologies, the rusting iron and the hot gravel, may in the end matter more than the cells that arrive in shipping containers.

difficulty_rationale.note: Each paragraph carries a qualified claim, a figure and a consequence in the same three or four sentences, and the subject is a constraint rather than an object, so nothing can be pictured.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Four unlike technologies are described in one sentence each and then collapsed into a single principle that arrives only in the last clause.

question_groups.instructions_extra: There are more headings than paragraphs, so you will not use them all.

options.text: Rules written for a different machine
A technology abandoned too soon
Geography sets the limit
A new question for planners
Opposition from communities near new sites
A principle that held for a century
Fast, cheap and short-lived
Storing heat in ordinary homes
The problem created by supply that cannot be controlled
Why extra hours change the priorities

teaching.strategy: Six of these seven paragraphs announce their job in the first or the last sentence. Say each job in six words before you open the list, then place C and F first: both name a single obstacle explicitly, so they are the two you will be sure of.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, so nothing narrows the search. Every paragraph must be read at least twice.
teaching.watch_out: Three headings name a technology or a problem that a paragraph genuinely mentions in passing. Mentioning is not the paragraph's job.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.evidence_quote: The principle held for a hundred years because the technology of the day offered no alternative to it
questions.explanation: Paragraph A is about the century-long rule that generation must match demand, which heading vi paraphrases.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The principle held for a hundred years
paraphrase_link.note: 'A hundred years' in the text becomes 'a century' in the heading; nothing else changes.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph states one rule, explains why no alternative existed, and dates its survival. A heading naming the rule and its duration covers all three; every other candidate covers one detail.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph says storage was 'not unknown, merely uneconomic', which reads as a good idea passed over.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing was abandoned. Storage was never adopted, and the paragraph explains why it could not have been.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about matching supply to demand, and uncontrollable supply is the obvious problem with that.
distractors.why_wrong: Uncontrollable supply arrives in the next paragraph. Here, generation is entirely controllable and that is the point.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that dates a rule and explains why nothing displaced it wants a heading about the rule, not about what came after.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence_quote: not by being unreliable but by being uncontrollable
questions.explanation: Paragraph B's controlling idea is that renewables are uncontrollable rather than unreliable, and that this creates surplus.
questions.trap_note: Heading ii is tempting because curtailment sounds like abandonment, but nothing in paragraph B is abandoned.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: not by being unreliable but by being uncontrollable
paraphrase_link.note: An adjective inside a not-X-but-Y contrast becomes the heading's relative clause.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's controlling sentence rejects one explanation and asserts another, then spends the rest of its length on the consequence of the one it asserts. The heading has to name that consequence's cause.

distractors.why_tempting: Curtailment means output that was made and then thrown away, which feels like something being given up.
distractors.why_wrong: What is discarded is electricity, not a technology, and the paragraph argues the technology is expanding.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about priorities changing as renewables grow, and this heading promises exactly that.
distractors.why_wrong: Extra hours are never discussed here. That argument belongs to the paragraph about multi-day storage.

teaching.reusable_rule: In a 'not X but Y' opening, Y is the heading. X is there only to be eliminated.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence_quote: Sites meeting all four conditions are rare
questions.explanation: Paragraph C explains that pumped hydro works well but cannot be built in new places, because four geographical conditions must coincide.
questions.trap_note: Heading v also concerns sites, but the passage mentions no public opposition anywhere.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Sites meeting all four conditions are rare
paraphrase_link.note: Four physical conditions become the single category 'geography'.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph praises the technology for three sentences and then names one obstacle, which occupies the rest of it. The heading has to name the obstacle, because the praise is there to make the obstacle matter.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is entirely about the difficulty of finding sites, and objections from neighbours are the difficulty most readers expect.
distractors.why_wrong: Nobody objects anywhere in this passage. The four conditions are height, proximity, ground and a transmission line.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Most of the good ones were developed before 1990' suggests a technology that stopped being built.
distractors.why_wrong: It stopped because the sites ran out, which is the heading already keyed, not because it was given up.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a paragraph opens with praise and closes on a limit, the limit is the point. Praise is set-up.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence_quote: Most grid batteries are built to discharge for two to four hours
questions.explanation: Paragraph D covers a collapsing price, millisecond response and a short discharge time — fast, cheap and short-lived.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A battery responds in milliseconds
paraphrase_link.note: Three properties spread across the paragraph are compressed into three adjectives.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph makes exactly three claims about one technology: the price fell, the response is instant, the discharge is brief. Only a heading carrying all three fits, and the third is the one most candidates drop.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends on hours, and hours are what the duration argument is about.
distractors.why_wrong: Here the hours are a stated limitation. The change in priorities they produce is argued in the next paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: Terrain is named in the first sentence, so a reader still holding the geography idea places it again.
distractors.why_wrong: Terrain appears precisely to say it no longer matters, which is the opposite of a geographical limit.

teaching.reusable_rule: A three-part heading needs three supports in the paragraph. Count them before you accept the fit.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence_quote: once storage has to last for days, the cost of the material matters more than the elegance of the chemistry
questions.explanation: Paragraph E argues that stretching storage from hours to days changes what designers optimise for.
questions.trap_note: Heading viii picks up 'heat crushed rock' from this paragraph, but the thermal schemes described are grid-scale, not domestic.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Why extra hours change the priorities
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: once storage has to last for days, the cost of the material matters more than the elegance of the chemistry
paraphrase_link.note: A conditional clause plus a comparison becomes a 'why' heading about a change of priority.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph lists four technologies and then says what they have in common, and the common factor is a change in what designers optimise for. The heading must name the change, not the technologies.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Heat crushed rock, molten salt or graphite blocks' is the most concrete image in the paragraph, and heat storage sounds domestic.
distractors.why_wrong: Every scheme here is grid-scale. Homes are not mentioned anywhere in the passage.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens on the two-to-four-hour limit, which is the heading's 'short-lived'.
distractors.why_wrong: That clause is a bridge from the previous paragraph. This one is about what happens beyond those hours.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph lists examples and then states what they share, the shared principle is the heading.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence_quote: They were written before the thing they now govern existed
questions.explanation: Paragraph F is about market rules designed for generators and consumers, which storage does not fit.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Rules written for a different machine
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: They were written before the thing they now govern existed
paraphrase_link.note: A time clause becomes a prepositional phrase, and 'the thing' is glossed as 'a different machine'.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's first sentence removes technology from the argument and every sentence after it describes a regulatory misfit. A heading about hardware or geography contradicts the opening.

distractors.why_tempting: Regulation and local objection sit close together in most readers' picture of new infrastructure.
distractors.why_wrong: The obstacles described are classification and payment rules, and no community appears in the passage.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does describe something being rethought, and a new question is a plausible label for that.
distractors.why_wrong: The new question is asked in the final paragraph, about duration. Here nothing is being reframed, only misapplied.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph opens by ruling out one explanation, no heading naming that explanation can be correct.

questions.prompt: Paragraph G
questions.evidence_quote: for how many hours can it supply them?
questions.explanation: Paragraph G replaces the traditional megawatt question with a question about duration, which is heading iv's 'new question'.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is being displaced by a harder one
paraphrase_link.note: 'A harder one' is a pro-form; the heading restores the noun it stands for.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph replaces one measure with another and then says what follows from the replacement. The heading must name the replacement itself, which the paragraph states as a question in its own words.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does argue that duration changes what matters, which is very close to a change of priorities.
distractors.why_wrong: That argument was made two paragraphs earlier about materials. Here the subject is how a whole system is described.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who has not yet placed the market-rules heading may put it here, since both paragraphs sound conclusive.
distractors.why_wrong: No rule, regulator or market appears in this paragraph.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that literally asks a question is handing you its heading. Take the question, not its answer.

questions.prompt: A grid battery reacts within {{gap}}, which suits tasks that must be done instantly.
questions.evidence_quote: A battery responds in milliseconds
questions.explanation: Paragraph D gives the battery's response time as milliseconds and links it to instant tasks.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A battery responds in milliseconds
paraphrase_link.note: 'Reacts within' for 'responds in' is a two-word swap that defeats a keyword search on 'responds'.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'within', which needs a unit of time, and only one such unit is attached to a battery's reaction anywhere in the passage.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Within' feels singular, so the plural marker is dropped in transcription.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage writes the plural, and completion answers are copied character for character.

distractors.why_wrong: That is the length of the event the battery covers, not the speed at which it reacts.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two time units in neighbouring sentences do different jobs. Match the one that measures the verb in your gapped line.

questions.prompt: Where storage has to last for days, what matters most is the cost of the {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: the cost of the material matters more than the elegance of the chemistry
questions.explanation: Paragraph E concludes that for multi-day storage the cost of the material outweighs the elegance of the chemistry.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: what matters most is the cost of the
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the cost of the material matters more than the elegance of the chemistry

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'the cost of the', a phrase the passage uses once, so the answer is the singular noun it governs there.

distractors.why_tempting: Four different substances are named in the paragraph, so the plural feels right for the sense.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage generalises them into a singular noun, and that is the form to copy. This plural was accepted earlier and has been removed.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other abstract noun in the same clause and it is the one most readers remember.
distractors.why_wrong: It is what the passage says matters less, so it fills the wrong half of the comparison.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a summary inverts a comparison into a not-X-but-Y frame, the gap takes the side the text ranked higher.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'the cost of the' before the gap fixes a singular uncountable noun.

options.text: Long discharges shorten the working life of the cells.

paragraphs.text: Almost every object in a modern museum is accompanied by a small rectangle of printed text, and almost no visitor gives it a second thought. The label seems as native to the gallery as the parquet floor beneath it. It is in fact a comparatively recent arrival, and few visitors think of it as an invention at all, still less as the most argumentative object in the room. A label decides what a thing is called, which century it belongs to, whose name is attached to it and, by omission, what about it need not be mentioned. Every one of those decisions is contestable, and the history of museums is in large part a history of quarrels about them conducted in a typeface too small for anyone to notice.

The earliest ancestors of the label belonged to the world of the private cabinet, where an inscription served the collector rather than the public. The change came with museums that admitted strangers. When the painter Charles Willson Peale opened his museum in Philadelphia in the 1780s, charging twenty-five cents for admission, he arranged birds and minerals in Linnaean order and attached written descriptions intended to instruct visitors who had no tutor to accompany them. Peale's assumption, that a paying stranger could be taught by reading, was a radical one, and it established the original purpose of the label: to stand in for a knowledgeable companion who was not there.

By the end of the nineteenth century that purpose had acquired a determined opposition. The aesthetic movement in museums held that a painting communicates directly, and that anything placed between the eye and the canvas is an obstruction. Benjamin Ives Gilman, secretary of the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, gave the argument its most durable formulation and its most quoted phrase when he wrote in 1916 about museum fatigue, the peculiar exhaustion produced not by walking but by the effort of stooping, reading and straightening again in front of object after object. Gilman was not wrong about the fatigue; anyone who has finished a large exhibition with aching shoulders and no memory of the last four rooms has felt it. His conclusion, that the remedy was to remove the text, has worn less well.

A third position avoided the quarrel by moving explanation out of print altogether. From the 1880s Wilhelm von Bode arranged the Berlin collections into period rooms, setting paintings among the furniture, textiles and panelling of their own century so that the ensemble would supply the context a label otherwise had to state. The technique was influential and is still in use, but it substitutes one authorial voice for another rather than removing it: a room assembled by a curator is an argument about the past no less than a paragraph written by one, and it is harder to disagree with precisely because it does not announce itself as a claim.

Interpretation expanded rapidly after the middle of the twentieth century. Audio guides arrived in the 1950s, didactic panels grew from a paragraph to several hundred words, and museums built departments to produce them; by the 1990s the wall text in a large institution was as likely to have been drafted by an education department as by a curator. Attendance figures were cited to justify the expansion, and the implied argument, that more explanation yields more understanding, has been repeated ever since with remarkably little evidence. Studies of visitor behaviour suggest that the average time spent in front of a labelled object is measured in seconds, and that long panels are frequently begun and rarely finished. If interpretation is judged by whether it is read, a great deal of it fails.

The political turn came later, and it changed the subject. In 1971 the Canadian museologist Duncan Cameron asked whether a museum was a temple or a forum: an institution that pronounced, or one in which disagreement took place. Once the question had been put in that form, the label became visibly a piece of authorship rather than a statement of fact. Recent disputes about collecting histories have made the point unavoidable. A bronze acquired in 1897 can be described as acquired, purchased, removed or looted, and the four words commit a museum to four different positions; several institutions have rewritten thousands of labels for this reason alone, and the rewriting is not a matter of accuracy but of admission.

None of this amounts to an argument for fewer words on the wall. It is an argument against a particular pretence, the pretence of neutrality, which invites visitors to mistake an interpretation for a description. A label is not a caption; it is a compressed argument, made by identifiable people, on evidence that is sometimes thin. Museums that acknowledge as much lose nothing that matters and gain a reader who is able to disagree with them. What the visitor is owed, in the end, is not less text but visible authorship: a sentence that says who is speaking, and on what grounds.

difficulty_rationale.note: Four positions are set out in sequence and the writer endorses part of each while refusing the conclusion each draws, so the stance shifts inside single sentences rather than between paragraphs.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: One sentence concedes an opponent's diagnosis and the next rejects his remedy, so a reader tracking approval alone will record the wrong verdict.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A, then the first sentence of G. A states the subject and G states the verdict; everything between is the argument.
skim_plan.skip: The dates and institution names in B, C and E. Note where they sit and read them only when a question sends you back.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer of the passage?

teaching.strategy: Before each statement, ask whose view it reports: the writer's, a named figure's, or a named figure's that the writer rejects. Three of these five hang on that distinction, and the passage marks it with concessive verbs rather than with names.
teaching.order_note: In passage order. Question 30's evidence lies below question 29's, so never search upwards.
teaching.watch_out: The writer agrees with part of two positions he goes on to reject. Partial agreement is not endorsement, and it is not refusal either.

questions.prompt: The writer believes that most visitors have never considered that the museum label was invented.
questions.evidence_quote: few visitors think of it as an invention at all
questions.explanation: Paragraph A states that few visitors think of the label as an invention, which is the writer's own claim about visitors.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: most visitors have never considered that the museum label was invented
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: few visitors think of it as an invention at all
paraphrase_link.note: 'Few think' becomes 'most have never considered' - the same quantity from the other end of the scale.

teaching.decision_rule: The claim is the writer's own, made in his voice with no attribution, and its quantifier matches: 'few think' and 'most have not considered' cover the same population. Nothing is added beyond the text.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens by saying almost no visitor gives the label a second thought, which reads as a stronger claim than the statement makes.
distractors.why_wrong: Understating a claim the writer makes is not contradicting it, and here the two quantifiers agree anyway.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Invented' appears as a noun, not a verb, so a reader scanning for the verb finds nothing and reads the paragraph as being about typography.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Think of it as an invention' is the same proposition with the word class changed.

teaching.reusable_rule: A quantifier at one end of a scale licenses its mirror at the other end. Both express one claim.

questions.prompt: The writer considers Gilman's complaint about the effect of reading in galleries to have been groundless.
questions.evidence_quote: Gilman was not wrong about the fatigue
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly concedes that Gilman was right about the fatigue, while rejecting his proposed remedy.
questions.trap_note: The writer does reject Gilman's conclusion, and readers often transfer that rejection to the diagnosis as well.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Gilman was not wrong about the fatigue
paraphrase_link.note: 'Not wrong' is a concession; 'groundless' is a rejection, and the two cannot both stand.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer states the opposite of the statement in five words and then rejects a different thing, the remedy. Because a specific sentence denies the statement, the key is NO rather than NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends by saying the conclusion has worn less well, and a reader tracking the writer's overall attitude to Gilman records disagreement.
distractors.why_wrong: The disagreement is with what Gilman proposed, not with what he observed. The observation is conceded in its own sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'groundless' never appears, and the writer's verdict is carried by a double negative that is easy to read past.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Was not wrong about the fatigue' is an explicit verdict on exactly the thing the statement calls groundless.

teaching.reusable_rule: A writer who concedes a diagnosis and refuses a remedy has taken two positions. Check which one the statement is about.

questions.prompt: The writer thinks von Bode's period rooms explain an object better than an audio guide does.
questions.evidence_quote: The technique was influential and is still in use
questions.explanation: The passage discusses period rooms and audio guides in separate paragraphs and never ranks one against the other.
questions.trap_note: Both devices are described as ways of supplying context, which invites a comparison the writer never makes.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed twice and the ranking is not: no sentence states that one device explains better than the other, and none states the reverse. Both verdicts fail, which leaves NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage says the room supplies context a label would otherwise have to state, which reads as a claim of superiority over other methods.
distractors.why_wrong: It is compared with a label in its own paragraph. The statement's comparison is with a device introduced later and never set beside it.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer criticises period rooms for hiding their own authorship, and criticism feels like a denial of superiority.
distractors.why_wrong: That criticism is about visibility of the argument, not about how well the object is explained, and it names no rival.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two methods described in separate paragraphs have not been ranked. A ranking you can construct yourself is one the writer did not make.
teaching.nearest_text: The technique was influential and is still in use, but it substitutes one authorial voice for another rather than removing it

questions.prompt: The writer doubts the assumption that additional explanation produces additional understanding.
questions.evidence_quote: has been repeated ever since with remarkably little evidence
questions.explanation: Paragraph E calls the argument that more explanation yields more understanding an implied one repeated with remarkably little evidence.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: doubts the assumption that additional explanation produces additional understanding
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: has been repeated ever since with remarkably little evidence
paraphrase_link.note: 'Remarkably little evidence' is how the writer expresses doubt; the doubt itself is never named.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer calls the argument implied, says it has been repeated with remarkably little evidence, and then supplies findings against it. That is a stated position, not an inference, so YES.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph reports that attendance figures were cited to justify the expansion, which reads as the writer supplying support for it.
distractors.why_wrong: He reports the justification and then undercuts it. The reporting verb belongs to the museums, not to him.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer never says 'I doubt', and readers who require a first-person marker for a YES treat the paragraph as neutral reportage.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Remarkably little evidence' and 'a great deal of it fails' are evaluations in the writer's own voice.

teaching.reusable_rule: An evaluative adverb in an otherwise factual sentence is the writer speaking. Doubt does not need the word doubt.

questions.prompt: The writer maintains that a museum loses authority when it admits who wrote its labels.
questions.evidence_quote: Museums that acknowledge as much lose nothing that matters
questions.explanation: Paragraph G argues the opposite: a museum that admits its labels are authored loses nothing that matters and gains a reader who can disagree.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: loses authority when it admits who wrote its labels
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Museums that acknowledge as much lose nothing that matters
paraphrase_link.note: 'Lose nothing that matters' is the direct denial of 'loses authority', with the condition unchanged.

teaching.decision_rule: The final paragraph states the outcome of admitting authorship, and the outcome it states cannot hold at the same time as the statement. A specific sentence denies it, so NO.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage concedes that a label's evidence is sometimes thin, which sounds like an admission of weakened authority.
distractors.why_wrong: That clause describes the labels, not the effect of admitting who wrote them, and the very next clause states the effect.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'authority' appears nowhere, so a keyword reader finds no sentence about it.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Lose nothing that matters and gain a reader who is able to disagree' answers the question in different words and answers it flatly.

teaching.reusable_rule: A gain-and-loss sentence at the end of an argument is a verdict. Read both halves before deciding what the writer thinks is at stake.

teaching.strategy: Each stem names a kind of content rather than a topic: a bodily effect, a sum of money, a definition. Decide what shape of sentence would carry it, then sweep the paragraphs for that shape instead of for a keyword.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a description of a physical experience, and only one sentence in the passage lists physical actions. Paragraphs that discuss visitors elsewhere describe their behaviour, not their bodies.

distractors.why_tempting: It reports how long visitors spend in front of an object and whether they finish reading, the passage's other paragraph about visitors.
distractors.why_wrong: Those are measures of attention and time, not of physical effort.

distractors.why_wrong: The setting is described, not any effect on the visitor's body.

questions.prompt: a mention of the sum charged for entry to a museum
questions.evidence_quote: charging twenty-five cents for admission
questions.explanation: Paragraph B gives Peale's admission charge of twenty-five cents.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the sum charged for entry to a museum
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: charging twenty-five cents for admission
paraphrase_link.note: 'Charging for admission' becomes the noun phrase 'the sum charged for entry'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a figure of money attached to entry, and exactly one figure of that kind appears in the passage. Every other number in the text is a date or a word count.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other paragraph carrying numbers about museums, including several hundred words and a decade.
distractors.why_wrong: None of its figures is a price, and admission is not mentioned there.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem naming a unit of measurement turns the search into a scan. Hunt the shape of the answer, not its meaning.

questions.prompt: the writer's own definition of what a label is
questions.evidence_quote: it is a compressed argument, made by identifiable people
questions.explanation: In paragraph G the writer defines a label as a compressed argument made by identifiable people, as against a neutral caption.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the writer's own definition of what a label is
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A label is not a caption; it is a compressed argument
paraphrase_link.note: A two-part definition, what it is not and what it is, compresses into one noun.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a definition given in the writer's own voice. Only one sentence uses the defining copula with no attribution, and it appears in the paragraph where the writer states his conclusion.

distractors.why_tempting: The first paragraph does say what a label decides and what it does by omission, which reads like a definition.
distractors.why_wrong: It lists the label's effects, which is a description of behaviour rather than a statement of what the thing is.

distractors.why_tempting: The four alternative words for one acquisition look like a definition exercise.
distractors.why_wrong: That passage defines four positions a museum may take, not the label itself.

teaching.reusable_rule: A definition is an X-is-Y sentence with nobody credited. If a name is attached, it is a reported view, not the writer's own.

options.text: Charles Willson Peale
Wilhelm von Bode
Benjamin Ives Gilman
Duncan Cameron

teaching.strategy: Four people are named across four different paragraphs, and one of them is not needed. Read each statement for the action it describes - holding a view, posing a choice, arranging a room - and match the action, since all four figures share the same subject matter.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, and one name is never used. Locate all four names in the passage before you match anything.
teaching.watch_out: Two of the four arranged their displays deliberately. The difference is whether the arrangement replaced the text or supported it.

questions.prompt: He held that written information stood between the visitor and the work itself.
questions.evidence_quote: anything placed between the eye and the canvas is an obstruction
questions.explanation: The aesthetic objection that text obstructs the eye is the position Gilman formulated in paragraph C.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: written information stood between the visitor and the work itself
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: anything placed between the eye and the canvas is an obstruction
paraphrase_link.note: 'Anything placed between' narrows to 'written information'; 'eye and canvas' widens to 'visitor and work'.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement describes a position rather than an action, and the passage attributes exactly this position to one figure, naming him as the person who gave it its most durable formulation.

distractors.why_tempting: He is the figure most associated with written descriptions in the passage, so a reader matching on 'written information' lands on him.
distractors.why_wrong: He attached the descriptions. Holding that they obstruct is the opposing view.

distractors.why_tempting: He removed explanation from print, which looks like acting on the belief that text gets in the way.
distractors.why_wrong: He moved the explanation into the room rather than objecting to explanation itself, and the passage says his method substitutes one voice for another.

distractors.why_tempting: He is the figure who most directly challenges the museum's authority, and challenging authority sounds like challenging its text.
distractors.why_wrong: His question is about what kind of institution a museum is, not about whether text should be present.

teaching.reusable_rule: In a features group, several names may share the topic. Match the position held, not the subject discussed.

questions.prompt: He described the museum's choice as one between two opposed public roles.
questions.evidence_quote: asked whether a museum was a temple or a forum
questions.explanation: Paragraph F attributes the temple-or-forum question to Duncan Cameron.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: asked whether a museum was a temple or a forum
paraphrase_link.note: Two metaphors are glossed as the category they belong to: opposed public roles.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement describes posing an alternative, and only one figure in the passage is credited with asking a question at all. The others are credited with arranging, writing or holding views.

distractors.why_tempting: He is the figure most often quoted in the passage and he too framed an opposition, between looking and reading.
distractors.why_wrong: He argued for one side rather than putting a choice, and his subject was text, not the institution's role.

distractors.why_tempting: His museum admitted paying strangers, which is a claim about the museum's public role.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage credits him with an assumption about teaching, not with a question about what a museum is for.

distractors.why_tempting: His period rooms are described as an argument about the past, and an argument implies a position on the institution.
distractors.why_wrong: The argument the passage attributes to him is about historical context, and he is never said to ask anything.

teaching.reusable_rule: Verbs distinguish attributed views more reliably than nouns. Posing a question, arguing a case and arranging a display are three different claims.

questions.prompt: He made the arrangement of the rooms themselves carry the explanation.
questions.evidence_quote: so that the ensemble would supply the context a label otherwise had to state
questions.explanation: Paragraph D credits von Bode with period rooms in which the ensemble, not the text, supplies the context.
questions.trap_note: Peale also arranged his displays deliberately, but by Linnaean classification supported by written descriptions.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: made the arrangement of the rooms themselves carry the explanation
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: so that the ensemble would supply the context a label otherwise had to state
paraphrase_link.note: 'The ensemble would supply the context' becomes 'the arrangement carries the explanation'.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement requires that the arrangement replaced the text, not merely accompanied it. One figure is credited with exactly that substitution, in a purpose clause.

distractors.why_tempting: He also arranged his collection deliberately, in Linnaean order, so both figures organised their displays on a principle.
distractors.why_wrong: His arrangement was supported by written descriptions; it did not carry the explanation on its own.

distractors.why_tempting: He wanted the text removed, and removing the text leaves the room to do the explaining.
distractors.why_wrong: He proposed removing the explanation altogether rather than relocating it into the arrangement.

distractors.why_tempting: Both figures are treated as changing how a museum speaks to its public.
distractors.why_wrong: He reframed the museum's purpose in print; he is never described as arranging anything.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where two figures did similar things, the discriminating detail is usually what each one kept. Look for what was replaced, not what was added.

layout.title: The argument of the passage

The writer's objection is not to explanation itself but to the pretence of {{39}}, because every label selects, omits and argues.
What visitors are owed, on this account, is not less text but visible {{40}}.

teaching.strategy: The summary covers the last part of the argument only, so read paragraphs E and G and nothing else. Fix the word class of each gap first: all three take a singular abstract noun, which means the bank must be sorted by meaning rather than by grammar.
teaching.order_note: All three answers sit in the last three paragraphs, in order. Locate that stretch once.
teaching.watch_out: Five of the eight bank words are abstract nouns that fit every gap grammatically. Grammar eliminates nothing here.

bank_analysis.why_wrong: Conservation is a museum activity the passage never discusses, and it is not the pretence the writer objects to.
Fatigue is the passage's own word, but it names Gilman's objection, not a department that drafts text.
The passage discusses rooms and arrangements, never buildings, and architecture is not what visitors are said to be owed.
Collecting histories raise questions of ownership, but the closing sentence asks for the identity of the writer, not of the owner.
The writer never asks for simpler labels; he explicitly refuses the argument for fewer words.

questions.explanation: Paragraph E says wall text was as likely to come from an education department as from a curator, so the bank word is 'education'.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: as likely to have been drafted by an education department as by a curator
paraphrase_link.note: 'Written' for 'drafted' is the only change, and the comparative frame is copied whole.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: It is an argument against a particular pretence, the pretence of neutrality
paraphrase_link.note: 'An argument against' becomes 'objects to', and the appositive naming the pretence is left in the gap.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer criticises long panels that are rarely finished, so a case against complexity is easy to construct from the passage.

paraphrase_link.note: The summary reproduces the closing frame exactly, so the only work is choosing the bank word the passage already used.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits inside the passage's own final phrase, so the answer is whichever bank word the text puts there, and only one bank word makes the closing sentence's demand coherent with what precedes it.

paragraphs.text: Few technologies have changed what people eat as quietly as refrigeration. A shopper in a northern European city can buy Peruvian blueberries in February. Kenyan beans arrive in March, and New Zealand lamb is on sale all year round. Almost none of these journeys are visible on the label. The system that makes them possible is usually called the cold chain. It is an unbroken sequence of chilled rooms, insulated lorries, refrigerated ships and supermarket cabinets. Together they keep perishable food within a narrow band of temperature, from the field to the plate. Break one link and the whole chain fails. A pallet of fish that spends four hours on a warm loading bay may look perfectly fresh. It will still spoil days earlier than it should.

The idea of moving cold around the world is older than the electric age. In 1806 a Boston merchant named Frederic Tudor cut blocks of ice from New England ponds. He loaded them onto a ship and sailed for the Caribbean. His first voyages lost money, but by the 1830s he was selling ice in Calcutta, packed in sawdust and shipped halfway across the planet. Mechanical cooling arrived later. In 1882 the sailing ship Dunedin carried frozen mutton from New Zealand to London. A coal-powered compressor kept the cargo solid, and most of the meat arrived still saleable. That single voyage rearranged the economics of farming in the southern hemisphere. Within twenty years, refrigerated shipping had turned distant pasture into a supplier for European cities.

A modern cold chain is less dramatic and far more precise. Perishable goods are divided into temperature bands, and each band has its own equipment. Fresh fruit, vegetables and dairy travel chilled, usually between zero and four degrees Celsius. Meat and fish for long storage are frozen to minus eighteen degrees. That figure is agreed internationally, because the enzymes that spoil food become almost inactive there. Bananas are a special case: they are shipped at thirteen degrees. That is warm enough to avoid chilling injury, yet cool enough to delay ripening until the fruit reaches a ripening room near its market. The containers are known in the trade as reefers. Each one is an insulated box with a small refrigeration unit at one end and sensors that log temperature every few minutes. When a shipment is rejected, that log is usually the evidence.

The economic consequences reach much further than the supermarket. Cold storage allows a farmer to sell when prices are good rather than when the crop happens to ripen. That shifts bargaining power away from traders. It also allows countries with warm climates and cheap land to compete in the winter markets of richer regions. Kenya's vegetable exports, Peru's asparagus and blueberry industries and Chile's fruit trade all grew on the back of refrigerated freight. In each case the crop existed long before the export boom. What changed was the ability to deliver it to a distant buyer in the condition that buyer expected.

Where the chain is missing, the losses are severe. The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that about fourteen per cent of the world's food is lost between harvest and the retail shelf. A large share of that loss happens in hot regions with little cold storage. In parts of South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, farmers often sell tomatoes or milk within hours of harvest. They accept whatever price is offered, because the alternative is to watch the produce spoil. Every tonne lost also wastes the water, fertiliser and labour that went into growing it. That is why some economists describe cold storage as the cheapest form of agricultural investment available.

The chain has an environmental bill of its own. Refrigeration consumes electricity. The gases that circulate inside the machinery are also potent greenhouse agents. The chemicals used today replaced an earlier generation that damaged the ozone layer. They trap far more heat per molecule than carbon dioxide does, and they leak. The Kigali Amendment, agreed in 2016, commits its signatories to using far less of them over the coming decades. That has pushed manufacturers towards ammonia, carbon dioxide and hydrocarbon refrigerants. Efficiency helps too. A well-maintained reefer with clean coils and neatly stacked cargo uses noticeably less power than a neglected one.

The most interesting developments are now happening at the small end of the system. Solar-powered cold rooms, some no larger than a shipping container, are appearing at market sites in Nigeria and India. Farmers there rent space by the crate rather than buying a machine they cannot afford. In my view this is where public money should go. Adding another link at the top of an already sophisticated chain delivers only marginal gains. Giving a first cold room to a village that has never had one can lift a whole season's income. The cold chain, in other words, is not finished, and its remaining gaps are also its greatest opportunities.

difficulty_rationale.note: Short declarative sentences carrying a high count of figures, temperatures and trade terms. Nothing is syntactically hard, but almost every sentence adds a fact a later question can turn on.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Three temperature bands and one exception are stated in four short sentences, so the numbers must be held together to be compared.

skim_plan.skip: The country names in paragraph D and the refrigerant names in paragraph F. They are illustration, and no question asks you to list them.

teaching.strategy: Five of these seven paragraphs open with a sentence that states their whole job, so read first sentences before anything else and place A, E and F first. Then use the three headings left over to check the paragraphs you were unsure of.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, so the search is never bounded. Read every paragraph before committing to any heading.
teaching.watch_out: Three unused headings name something the passage does touch: taste, engineers and subsidies. None of them is ever the subject of a paragraph.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.evidence_quote: Break one link and the whole chain fails
questions.explanation: Paragraph A defines the cold chain as an unbroken sequence and stresses that a single failed link ruins the result, which heading iv paraphrases.
questions.trap_note: Heading vii is tempting because temperatures are mentioned, but the precise bands are set out in paragraph C, not here.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Break one link and the whole chain fails
paraphrase_link.note: A conditional in the text becomes the heading's claim that the technology works only as a whole.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph defines a system and then states the property that makes the definition matter: it fails entire. A heading naming any single component describes an item on the list, not the claim.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph says the food is kept within a narrow band of temperature, which sounds like precise limits for goods.
distractors.why_wrong: The bands themselves are set out two paragraphs later. Here the narrow band is one clause inside the definition.

distractors.why_tempting: The last two sentences describe a pallet of fish spoiling, which reads as what happens when the chain is absent.
distractors.why_wrong: That example is a broken link inside a working chain. The absence of a chain altogether is a different paragraph.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that defines something and then names its critical property wants a heading about the property, not about the parts.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence_quote: The idea of moving cold around the world is older than the electric age
questions.explanation: Paragraph B is a short history of the earliest shipments of ice and frozen meat, which is exactly what heading viii describes.
questions.trap_note: Heading i also fits the New Zealand trade, but paragraph D is the one that generalises about markets for warm countries.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The idea of moving cold around the world is older than the electric age
paraphrase_link.note: 'Moving cold around the world' compresses into 'cargoes of cold', and 'older than the electric age' licenses 'first'.

teaching.decision_rule: Every sentence in the paragraph dates an early shipment, and the paragraph ends where the practice becomes ordinary. A heading naming a market or a policy needs a claim the paragraph does not make.

distractors.why_tempting: The last sentence says distant pasture became a supplier for European cities, which is exactly a new market for a warm country.
distractors.why_wrong: That is one consequence stated in one clause. The generalisation about warm countries is the following paragraph's whole subject.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is full of ships and voyages, and a heading naming shipping is the nearest available match.
distractors.why_wrong: No subsidy, grant or public payment appears anywhere in the passage.

teaching.reusable_rule: A single closing clause is not a paragraph's subject. Check whether the point is developed or merely reached.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence_quote: Perishable goods are divided into temperature bands, and each band has its own equipment
questions.explanation: The paragraph lists the specific temperature each category of goods travels at, matching 'precise limits for different goods'.
questions.trap_note: Heading ii mentions frozen food, but taste is never discussed anywhere in the passage.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Perishable goods are divided into temperature bands, and each band has its own equipment
paraphrase_link.note: 'Divided into bands' becomes 'limits', and 'goods' is carried over untouched.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph assigns a specific figure to each category of food and explains one exception. A heading has to name that assignment; naming the equipment or the food quality names a supporting detail.

distractors.why_tempting: Frozen food is discussed here at minus eighteen degrees, and taste is what most readers associate with freezing.
distractors.why_wrong: Taste is never mentioned in the passage. The reason given for minus eighteen is enzyme activity.

distractors.why_tempting: Containers, sensors and logs all appear, which reads like a system working as a whole.
distractors.why_wrong: That claim was made in the opening paragraph. Here the equipment is listed to show how the bands are maintained.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph gives a different figure for each of several categories, its heading is about the figures, not about the machinery that produces them.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence_quote: It also allows countries with warm climates and cheap land to compete in the winter markets of richer regions
questions.explanation: Paragraph D is about warm-climate producers gaining access to distant winter markets, which heading i states directly.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: countries with warm climates and cheap land to compete in the winter markets of richer regions

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph names who gains from the technology, and the gain it develops over four sentences is access to distant markets. A heading about losses or about scale describes other paragraphs.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph's last sentence says the crop existed before the export boom, which sounds like describing what happens without cold storage.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes what was missing before, in order to name what changed. The absence of a chain is the subject two paragraphs later.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about small producers gaining, which is close to small installations having large effects.
distractors.why_wrong: No installation is described here at all. The size of the equipment is the final paragraph's subject.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where several paragraphs share a topic, the heading follows the claim each one makes about it, not the topic itself.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence_quote: Where the chain is missing, the losses are severe
questions.explanation: The whole paragraph describes what happens in places that have no cold storage, which heading vi summarises.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: What happens when the chain is absent
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Where the chain is missing, the losses are severe
paraphrase_link.note: 'Missing' becomes 'absent' and nothing else changes - the cheapest link, and still not findable by keyword.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's opening sentence states a consequence and every sentence after it quantifies or illustrates that consequence. Nothing else is developed.

distractors.why_tempting: South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa are warm regions, so a heading about warm countries seems to fit the geography.
distractors.why_wrong: Here those regions lose crops rather than gain markets. The gain is the previous paragraph's claim.

teaching.reusable_rule: A conditional opening sentence usually is the heading. Read it, then check that the rest of the paragraph only elaborates it.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence_quote: The chain has an environmental bill of its own
questions.explanation: Paragraph F is about energy use and refrigerant gases, so the atmospheric cost in heading ix is its controlling idea.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The price paid by the atmosphere
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The chain has an environmental bill of its own

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph names two costs, electricity and refrigerant gases, and then a treaty and a technical response to both. Every sentence belongs to the environmental account.

distractors.why_tempting: The treaty commits its signatories to a change, and a reader may hear a commitment as a subsidy programme.
distractors.why_wrong: The commitment is to use fewer of the gases. No money changes hands anywhere in the passage.

distractors.why_tempting: The last sentence contrasts a well-maintained unit with a neglected one, which implies somebody has to do the maintaining.
distractors.why_wrong: Maintenance is offered as a way to cut power use. Nobody in the passage is said to be in short supply.

teaching.reusable_rule: An implication you can draw is not a subject the writer took up. Headings match what is said, not what follows from it.

questions.prompt: Paragraph G
questions.evidence_quote: The most interesting developments are now happening at the small end of the system
questions.explanation: Paragraph G argues that tiny solar cold rooms produce the largest gains, which is what heading iii claims.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The most interesting developments are now happening at the small end of the system
paraphrase_link.note: 'The small end of the system' becomes one adjective; the large effect comes from the last two sentences.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph sets a small intervention against a large one and states which returns more. A heading has to carry both halves of that contrast, and only one candidate does.

distractors.why_tempting: Farmers are said to rent space rather than buy machines they cannot afford, which suggests missing local capacity.
distractors.why_wrong: What they lack is money, not trained people, and training is never mentioned.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph describes villages that have never had a cold room, which is a chain that is absent.
distractors.why_wrong: That absence is the setting for the argument, not its subject. This paragraph is about what to do next.

teaching.reusable_rule: A heading with two halves needs both supported. Confirm the second half before you accept a strong match on the first.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.

teaching.strategy: Two of these four turn on comparing figures that sit in one paragraph, one on a time reference, and one on how widely a claim is being made. Mark the number or the quantifier in each statement before you search.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, and the four answers run B, C, C, E. Never search above the previous answer.
teaching.watch_out: The two temperature statements are answered by comparing numbers, not by matching words. Every content word will match either way.

questions.prompt: Frederic Tudor made a profit on his earliest shipments of ice.
questions.evidence_quote: His first voyages lost money
questions.explanation: The passage says his first voyages lost money, which contradicts the statement.
questions.trap_note: He did later sell ice profitably in Calcutta; the statement is about the earliest voyages only.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: made a profit on his earliest shipments
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: His first voyages lost money
paraphrase_link.note: 'Lost money' is the direct opposite of 'made a profit', and 'first voyages' matches 'earliest shipments'.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed, the passage states the outcome of exactly those voyages, and the stated outcome is the opposite of the statement. That is a quotable contradiction, so FALSE.

distractors.why_tempting: A later sentence has him selling ice in Calcutta by the 1830s, and a reader taking the paragraph as one success story records profit throughout.
distractors.why_wrong: The later trade is a different period. The statement is about the earliest voyages, and those are said to have lost money.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'profit' never appears, so a reader hunting the word finds nothing and treats the finances as unreported.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Lost money' reports the finances directly and settles the question in three words.

teaching.reusable_rule: A time expression in the statement is a filter. Confirm the outcome for that period, not for the story as a whole.

questions.prompt: Bananas are transported at a lower temperature than fresh dairy products.
questions.evidence_quote: they are shipped at thirteen degrees
questions.explanation: Bananas travel at thirteen degrees while dairy travels between zero and four, so the banana temperature is higher, not lower.
questions.trap_note: Both figures are in the same paragraph, so a careless reader may match the keywords without comparing the numbers.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: at a lower temperature than fresh dairy products
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: they are shipped at thirteen degrees
paraphrase_link.note: The statement turns two figures into a comparative, and the comparative it forms runs the wrong way.

teaching.decision_rule: Both figures are given in the same paragraph, so the comparison is checkable and it comes out the other way round. A reversed comparison is contradicted, not unmentioned.

distractors.why_tempting: Both nouns and both temperatures appear within three sentences, so every content word matches and the sentence feels confirmed.
distractors.why_wrong: Thirteen degrees is above the zero-to-four range, so the comparison is the wrong way round.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage never compares bananas with dairy in a single sentence, so a reader who requires an explicit comparison finds none.
distractors.why_wrong: Both figures are stated in the same paragraph, which is all a numerical comparison needs.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two figures stated in one paragraph make the comparison checkable. Only comparisons that need a fact from outside are unverifiable.

questions.prompt: Refrigerated containers record the temperature of their cargo at regular intervals.
questions.evidence_quote: sensors that log temperature every few minutes
questions.explanation: 'Log temperature every few minutes' is a direct paraphrase of recording at regular intervals.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: record the temperature of their cargo at regular intervals
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: sensors that log temperature every few minutes
paraphrase_link.note: 'Every few minutes' becomes 'at regular intervals'; 'log' becomes 'record'.

teaching.decision_rule: Every element is supported: the container, the recording and the regularity. 'Every few minutes' is a stronger claim than 'regular intervals', so nothing in the statement outruns the text.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Every few minutes' is vague, and a reader who wants regularity to mean a fixed interval may treat vagueness as a denial.
distractors.why_wrong: A repeated action at short intervals is a regular one. The passage does not restrict the wording any further.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Regular intervals' appears nowhere and 'reefer' is the passage's own noun, so the sentence looks like new information.
distractors.why_wrong: The clause about sensors is in the same sentence that names the containers.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement weaker than the text is still supported. Only a statement stronger than the text can fail on scope.

questions.prompt: Most of the food lost between harvest and the shop is lost in South Asia.
questions.evidence_quote: A large share of that loss happens in hot regions with little cold storage
questions.explanation: The passage says a large share of losses occurs in hot regions and names South Asia as one of them, but never says most losses happen there.
questions.trap_note: Keyword match without meaning match: 'a large share' of hot regions is not the same claim as 'most' in one named region.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the food lost between harvest and the shop
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: lost between harvest and the retail shelf
paraphrase_link.note: 'The retail shelf' becomes 'the shop'. The link is exact; what is attached to it is not.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the specific claim - that one named region holds the largest share - is neither stated nor denied. The passage assigns a large share to a category of regions and names two of them.

distractors.why_tempting: South Asia is named in the next sentence and belongs to the category the proportion was assigned to, so the two facts merge.
distractors.why_wrong: 'A large share' spread across hot regions is not 'most' concentrated in one of them.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph seems to spread the losses over two regions, which reads as a denial that any single one dominates.
distractors.why_wrong: Naming two examples of a category does not rank them, so there is no sentence to contradict the statement.

teaching.reusable_rule: A proportion attributed to a category says nothing about how it divides between the instances of that category.
teaching.nearest_text: A large share of that loss happens in hot regions with little cold storage.

paraphrase_link.note: The passage's participle becomes a full passive in the stem; the noun after 'packed in' is untouched.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Blocks of ice' is the paragraph's most prominent noun phrase and sits two sentences earlier.
distractors.why_wrong: It names the ice itself, not what the ice was packed in.

distractors.why_tempting: The next clause is about shipping, and packing goods for a voyage suggests the vessel.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage distinguishes what the ice was packed in from what it travelled on.

teaching.reusable_rule: When the stem reuses a preposition from the text, the answer is the noun that preposition already governs.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'packed in' before the gap wants a single uncountable material noun.

questions.prompt: Some economists call cold storage the cheapest available form of {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: the cheapest form of agricultural investment available
questions.explanation: Paragraph E ends with this exact phrase; two words fit the limit.
questions.trap_note: 'Cold storage' itself is not the answer — the gap needs what the storage is an example of.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the cheapest form of agricultural investment available
paraphrase_link.note: 'Available' moves in front of 'form', which is why the phrase will not be found by matching word order.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'form of', so it takes the category that cold storage is an example of, and the passage supplies that category in a two-word phrase within the limit.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the subject of the sentence and the thing being praised, so it is the noun phrase the reader has in mind.
distractors.why_wrong: It is what the category contains. A gap after 'form of' needs the class, not the member.

distractors.why_tempting: One word is safely inside a two-word limit and the sense reads naturally.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage's phrase is two words, and dropping the modifier loses the part that identifies the class.

teaching.reusable_rule: A gap after 'kind of' or 'type of' asks for a category, so the answer is never the thing being classified.
