paragraphs.text: In 2016 a professor of urban planning in Paris, Carlos Moreno, gave a name to an old intuition. He called it the ville du quart d'heure, the quarter-hour city. In such a district the ordinary business of life, work, shopping, schooling, healthcare, exercise and entertainment, can all be reached from home within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle. The phrase spread with unusual speed. Anne Hidalgo made it a central plank of her successful re-election campaign for the mayoralty of Paris in 2020. Within three years, variants of the idea had been written into planning documents in Milan, Melbourne, Portland and Bogota. What makes the concept unusual is not its novelty but its unit of measurement. Planners have traditionally counted distance in kilometres or in floor space; Moreno proposed counting it in minutes of walking.

For most of urban history, proximity was not a policy but a constraint. Before mechanised transport, a city could grow only as far as its inhabitants could walk in a working day. Functions were therefore piled on top of one another: workshops beneath flats, markets in the street, schools around the corner. The twentieth century deliberately dismantled that arrangement. The Athens Charter of 1933, drafted by the architects of the modern movement, argued that dwelling, work, recreation and traffic should each be given their own zone. Municipal codes across Europe and North America duly separated them. The results were legible, hygienic and, in the judgement of most planners working today, deeply inefficient. Separating functions guarantees that every errand becomes a journey.

The evidence that shorter journeys are achievable is stronger than sceptics assume. Travel diaries collected in European cities show that a surprisingly large share of car trips are short. In several French and Spanish surveys, close to forty per cent of journeys made by car covered less than three kilometres. That is a distance most adults can cycle in ten minutes. Barcelona's superblock programme, which closes selected residential streets to through traffic and hands them back to pedestrians, has been studied more carefully than most such schemes. Monitoring in one central district recorded a fall of roughly a quarter in nitrogen dioxide concentrations. It also found a marked increase in the number of people lingering in the street rather than passing through it.

Whether such districts can be created deliberately depends on arithmetic that planners know well. Local services survive only where enough customers live within walking range, and retail geographers put rough numbers on this. A single bakery needs roughly 1,500 households within a four-hundred-metre walk to remain viable; a pharmacy needs about 4,000 people; a two-form primary school draws on some 3,000 dwellings; a health centre is normally planned for 10,000 residents and is therefore shared between neighbouring districts. Below those thresholds no amount of enthusiasm will keep a shop open. This is why the quarter-hour city is, in practice, an argument for moderate density as much as for mixed use, and why it is far harder to retrofit into low-density suburbs than into the nineteenth-century blocks where the idea was born.

The most serious economic objection comes from the study of agglomeration. Cities are productive, economists argue, precisely because they are large: a big labour market allows unusual skills to find unusual employers, and firms benefit from a deep pool of suppliers and rivals. Anything that encourages workers to search for jobs only within walking distance of home risks shrinking that market into a collection of villages. Defenders of the concept reply that nobody proposes abolishing the metro, and that the aim is to remove the obligatory journey rather than the chosen one. I find this response persuasive as far as it goes, though it does concede that the quarter-hour city works best as a layer on top of good public transport and not as a substitute for it.

A second objection is harder to answer. Improving a neighbourhood raises the price of living in it. Studies of new parks, tramlines and traffic-calmed streets repeatedly find that rents rise faster in the immediate vicinity than in comparable districts nearby, a pattern now widely labelled green gentrification. The households most dependent on local services, those without cars, with young children or with limited mobility, are also the households least able to absorb a rent increase, and they are frequently the ones who move out. Unless a city builds or protects affordable housing at the same time as it plants trees, the quarter-hour district it creates will be enjoyed largely by people who moved in after the improvements were made.

None of this makes the idea worthless; it makes it a test of administrative seriousness. The cities that have done best have started with the buildings they already control. Paris opened school playgrounds at weekends as neighbourhood squares, on the reasonable grounds that a city already owns them. Milan converted parking bays into small plazas street by street, measuring footfall before and after each change. What distinguishes these programmes from slogans is that they publish their numbers and abandon what fails. Counting a city in minutes is a useful discipline, but only if somebody is actually doing the counting.

difficulty_rationale.note: The second half is built as objection, reply and partial endorsement, and the writer's own position sits inside a subordinate clause rather than in a topic sentence.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: An economic objection, a defence of the idea and the writer's qualified acceptance of that defence are compressed into the paragraph's last two sentences.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. Its last two sentences name what is unusual about the idea, and one question asks precisely that.
skim_plan.skip: The list of cities in paragraph A and the four catchment figures in paragraph D. Note that the figures are there and come back for them.

teaching.strategy: Each stem names a kind of content: a year, a set of figures, a claim, a measurement, an example. Two paragraphs carry numbers and two carry measured findings, so decide what the numbers are counting before you commit a letter.
teaching.order_note: Not in order. Do this group first anyway, because locating these five teaches you the passage for everything after it.
teaching.watch_out: Two paragraphs report a measured change. One measures air, the other measures rents, and both use a proportion.

questions.prompt: a reference to the year in which the idea became part of an election campaign
questions.evidence_quote: successful re-election campaign for the mayoralty of Paris in 2020
questions.explanation: Only paragraph A links the concept to an election, and only it gives the year 2020.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the year in which the idea became part of an election campaign
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: successful re-election campaign for the mayoralty of Paris in 2020
paraphrase_link.note: A named campaign with a date becomes the abstract 'the year ... an election campaign'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem requires a year and an election in the same sentence. Only one paragraph contains an election at all, and it dates it.

distractors.why_tempting: It names two cities acting on the idea, and municipal action is easily read as political adoption.
distractors.why_wrong: Those are administrative programmes with no election and no year attached.

distractors.why_tempting: It carries the passage's other prominent date and a document that changed policy across two continents.
distractors.why_wrong: That document is a planning charter, not a campaign, and it belongs to a period before the idea existed.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a stem names two things at once, search for the rarer one. Dates are rarer than topics and cheaper to scan for.

questions.prompt: figures for the number of homes that a particular kind of shop requires nearby
questions.evidence_quote: A single bakery needs roughly 1,500 households
questions.explanation: Paragraph D is the only place where catchment figures for individual services are given.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the number of homes that a particular kind of shop requires nearby
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A single bakery needs roughly 1,500 households
paraphrase_link.note: 'A particular kind of shop' is the category; the text supplies the instance, and 'households' answers 'homes'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a figure attached to a retail unit. Only one paragraph gives catchment figures at all, and only one of its four figures is attached to a shop.

distractors.why_tempting: It carries the passage's other set of proportions, including a percentage of car journeys.
distractors.why_wrong: Those measure travel behaviour, not the population a business needs.

distractors.why_tempting: It is about housing and who can afford to live in a district, which sounds like a claim about homes.
distractors.why_wrong: It concerns rents and who moves out, and it gives no figure for anything.

teaching.reusable_rule: Match the unit the stem asks for. A paragraph full of numbers is not the answer unless the numbers count the right thing.

questions.prompt: the claim that the size of a city's labour market explains its productivity
questions.evidence_quote: a big labour market allows unusual skills to find unusual employers
questions.explanation: The agglomeration argument in paragraph E ties productivity to the size of the labour market.
questions.trap_note: Paragraph D also uses numbers about people, but they concern shop catchments, not productivity.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the size of a city's labour market explains its productivity
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Cities are productive, economists argue, precisely because they are large
paraphrase_link.note: A because-clause becomes a noun phrase with 'explains', so matching 'labour market' alone will not find it.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a claim about why cities are productive. Only one paragraph makes a causal claim of that shape, and it attributes it explicitly.

distractors.why_tempting: It also connects population size to whether something can survive, and its figures are about people.
distractors.why_wrong: Those figures explain whether a shop stays open, not why a city is productive.

distractors.why_tempting: It defines the idea in terms of work and reaching a workplace, which touches the labour market.
distractors.why_wrong: It lists work as one of several activities. Productivity is never mentioned there.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem containing 'explains' or 'because' is looking for a causal sentence. Scan for causal connectives, not for the topic nouns.

questions.prompt: measured evidence of an improvement in air quality
questions.evidence_quote: a fall of roughly a quarter in nitrogen dioxide concentrations
questions.explanation: Paragraph C reports the monitored fall in nitrogen dioxide after the superblock scheme.
questions.trap_note: Paragraph F also reports measured change, but it is about rents rather than air.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Monitoring in one central district recorded a fall of roughly a quarter in nitrogen dioxide concentrations
paraphrase_link.note: A named pollutant falling becomes the category 'improvement in air quality'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem requires both measurement and air. Two paragraphs report measured findings, and only one of them measures something in the atmosphere.

distractors.why_tempting: It reports studies that repeatedly find a measured change, in the same grammatical shape.
distractors.why_wrong: What is measured there is rent, and the district's environment is the cause rather than the finding.

distractors.why_tempting: It says one city measured footfall before and after each change, which is measurement of a scheme's effect.
distractors.why_wrong: Footfall counts people, not air, and no result is given.

teaching.reusable_rule: When two paragraphs share a sentence shape, discriminate on what is being counted. The shape is the decoy.

questions.prompt: an example of a city making use of property it already owns
questions.evidence_quote: Paris opened school playgrounds at weekends as neighbourhood squares
questions.explanation: Paragraph G gives the playground example and states the reasoning that the city already owns them.

distractors.why_tempting: Closing streets to traffic and handing them to pedestrians is also a city reusing what it controls.
distractors.why_wrong: Ownership is never mentioned there, and the paragraph is offered as evidence rather than as an example of method.

distractors.why_tempting: It describes a city government adopting the idea, so any municipal action seems to belong here.
distractors.why_wrong: It records political adoption of a concept, not a use made of any particular property.

teaching.reusable_rule: An example matches only if the stem's stated reason is the reason the text gives. Similar actions with different justifications are different items.

paragraphs.text: In 1971 the economist Herbert Simon made an observation that has aged unusually well: a wealth of information, he wrote, creates a poverty of attention. Information was then expensive to produce and cheap to ignore; half a century later the ratio has inverted, and the scarce resource in any media system is no longer the article, the broadcast or the film but the finite quantity of human notice available to receive it. Once attention is understood as scarce, it acquires the ordinary properties of a scarce good. It can be measured, priced, traded and hoarded, and the institutions that trade in it come to organise themselves around its supply. That, rather than any particular technology, is the development this article is concerned with.

The structure of an attention market is easy to describe and easy to misunderstand. A commercial broadcaster or website does not sell programmes to viewers; it sells access to viewers to advertisers, and gives the programmes away as the inducement. Economists call such an arrangement a two-sided market, and its defining awkwardness is that the party whose experience is being shaped is not the party paying the bill. A newspaper that loses subscribers loses revenue directly and knows it within a month. A platform that irritates its users loses revenue only at one remove, through a slow decline in the inventory it can offer, and may not detect the damage for years.

What has changed across the past century is less the structure than the resolution of the measurement. Nineteenth-century newspapers sold circulation, a blunt figure counted in thousands of copies and audited annually. Commercial radio, having no copies to count, invented the audience survey and with it the rating, an estimate of the households listening during a quarter-hour block. Early web publishers inherited the page view, then discovered they could record how long a page stayed open. The algorithmic feed completed the sequence: each individual impression is now auctioned separately, in the fraction of a second between a request and a response, against a profile assembled from previous behaviour. Attention that was once sold by the thousand is now sold by the instance.

Finer measurement is not the same as better measurement, and here I part company with much of the industry's own commentary. What a system counts is what it is able to count cheaply, and time-on-page, scroll depth and click-through are cheap. None of them distinguishes absorbed reading from an abandoned tab, and none captures whether a reader was persuaded, informed or merely detained. Because the counted quantity became the traded quantity, editorial and design decisions drifted towards whatever the counter rewarded: the headline that provokes rather than describes, the autoplaying sequel, the notification timed for the moment the user was about to close the application. The metric did not merely describe the product; over two decades it substantially rewrote it.

The consequences for the individual are widely discussed and, in my judgement, unevenly evidenced. The most robust findings concern interruption. Laboratory work on task-switching consistently shows that returning to a demanding task after a diversion costs measurable time and accuracy, and that the cost rises with the complexity of the work interrupted. Studies of screen use before bed are similarly consistent in showing displaced sleep, although the mechanism is disputed and the effect is modest. Claims about permanent damage to the capacity for concentration are far weaker, resting largely on self-reported questionnaires and on samples in which the direction of causation cannot be established. Sceptics are right to insist on the distinction; they are wrong to conclude from it that nothing is happening.

Policy has begun to move, mostly by way of design rules rather than prohibitions. Several jurisdictions now require that services aimed at children switch off autoplay and recommendation by default, on the principle that defaults are the true regulation of behaviour. Others have obliged platforms to offer a chronological feed as an alternative to a ranked one. Subscription funding, once assumed to be the preserve of the specialist press, has proved viable for a wider range of publications than expected, and it realigns the incentive at least partially towards satisfaction rather than duration. What I find least useful is the advice industry that has grown up alongside the problem, urging individuals to undertake digital detoxes. Asking a reader to out-engineer a system designed by thousands of engineers is not a strategy; it is an abdication.

The more productive framing treats attention as something closer to infrastructure than to a private appetite. Roads, water and clean air are all things that individuals consume privately but that only collective rules can keep usable, and attention has begun to look the same. That does not require nostalgia for the era of three television channels, which was neither varied nor accountable. It requires the unglamorous work of deciding which defaults are acceptable, which measurements should be auditable, and which practices are simply not for sale. Attention will remain the scarcest thing in the media economy. The open question is whether its price is set by the people who supply it or only by the people who buy it.

difficulty_rationale.note: The subject is a market rather than an object, and the writer alternates between reporting a position and grading the evidence for it, sometimes inside the same sentence.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Three bodies of evidence are ranked by strength in five sentences, and the ranking, not the findings, is what the questions turn on.

teaching.strategy: This writer marks his own voice with first-person phrases and with evaluative adjectives, and marks reported views with a named group. Decide whose claim each statement is about before you look for it; three of the five turn on that alone.
teaching.order_note: In passage order down to question 30. Question 31 returns to the paragraph that answered question 29, so check backwards on the last one.

questions.prompt: More detailed measurement has improved the way attention is valued.
questions.evidence_quote: Finer measurement is not the same as better measurement
questions.explanation: The writer opens paragraph D by denying that finer measurement is better measurement.
questions.trap_note: Paragraph C describes the increase in resolution neutrally; the evaluation only arrives in paragraph D.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: More detailed measurement has improved the way attention is valued.
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Finer measurement is not the same as better measurement
paraphrase_link.note: 'Finer' becomes 'more detailed'; the passage's denial of equivalence is exactly what the statement asserts.

teaching.decision_rule: The claim is the writer's own and he denies it in the paragraph's opening sentence, then spends the paragraph on what finer counting did instead. A specific sentence contradicts the statement, so NO.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous paragraph tracks measurement becoming steadily more precise and reads as a story of improvement.
distractors.why_wrong: That paragraph is descriptive. The evaluation arrives one paragraph later and reverses the reading.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'valued' never appears, so a reader hunting for a sentence about valuation finds none.
distractors.why_wrong: Pricing and counting are the same operation here, and the writer states directly that finer is not better.

teaching.reusable_rule: A neutral history followed by a verdict is two paragraphs doing different jobs. Take the verdict from the one that evaluates.

questions.prompt: The evidence for the effects of media use on individuals varies in quality.
questions.evidence_quote: in my judgement, unevenly evidenced
questions.explanation: 'Unevenly evidenced' is the writer's own judgement that the evidence is of mixed quality.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: in my judgement, unevenly evidenced

teaching.decision_rule: The writer marks the claim as his own judgement, and the rest of the paragraph ranks three bodies of evidence from robust to far weaker. Both the claim and its support are in his voice.

distractors.why_tempting: He calls one set of findings robust and consistent, and a reader who stops there records a claim that the evidence is uniformly good.
distractors.why_wrong: The same paragraph calls another set far weaker, which is the variation the statement describes.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Quality' is never used of evidence, and the ranking is carried by adjectives spread over four sentences.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Unevenly evidenced' states the proposition in three words before the ranking begins.

teaching.reusable_rule: An adverb attached to the word evidence is a grading, and grading evidence is itself a stated position.

questions.prompt: Advising individuals to cut their own screen use is an inadequate response to the problem.
questions.evidence_quote: Asking a reader to out-engineer a system designed by thousands of engineers is not a strategy

teaching.decision_rule: The writer names the advice least useful and then rejects its central recommendation in his own voice. The statement restates that rejection without strengthening it.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph reports several policies the writer treats favourably, so a reader tracking approval across the paragraph records a positive verdict.
distractors.why_wrong: Those are design rules imposed on services. The advice to individuals is the thing he separates out and rejects.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Inadequate' appears nowhere, and the rejection is delivered as a metaphor rather than as an assessment.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Not a strategy' is an assessment, and 'least useful' precedes it in the same paragraph.

teaching.reusable_rule: A metaphor in the writer's own voice still states a position. Do not require an evaluative adjective before recording one.

questions.prompt: Television was better when audiences had only a few channels to choose from.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Television was better when audiences had only a few channels
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: which was neither varied nor accountable

teaching.decision_rule: The writer names the era and then denies it two qualities in the same sentence, inside a relative clause. That is a specific contradiction rather than silence, so NO.

distractors.why_tempting: The era is raised only because it is the obvious point of comparison, and mentioning it suggests it is being held up as a standard.
distractors.why_wrong: It is raised in order to be refused: the writer says his argument does not require nostalgia for it.

distractors.why_tempting: The verdict sits in a subordinate clause after a comma, which is exactly where a reader scanning for the writer's opinion stops looking.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Neither varied nor accountable' is as explicit a verdict as the passage contains.

teaching.reusable_rule: A writer's verdict often sits in a relative clause rather than a main one. Read past the comma before deciding.

questions.prompt: It devised a new way of estimating its audience because it had nothing physical to count.
questions.evidence_quote: Commercial radio, having no copies to count, invented the audience survey
questions.explanation: Radio had no copies, so it created the survey and the rating instead.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: because it had nothing physical to count
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: having no copies to count
paraphrase_link.note: 'Copies' widens to 'nothing physical', and a participle becomes a because-clause.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement gives a reason as well as an action, and only one medium in the paragraph is credited with inventing a measure because it lacked something countable.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the medium that did the counting of physical objects, so the word 'count' points straight at it.
distractors.why_wrong: It had copies to count, which is precisely what the statement says the answer lacked.

distractors.why_tempting: It also devised a new measure, and its measures were not physical either.
distractors.why_wrong: It inherited a measure rather than devising one, and the reason given for its innovation is capability, not absence.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a statement gives an action and a reason, both must match. The same act done for another reason is a distractor.

questions.prompt: Its audience figure was checked once a year.
questions.evidence_quote: a blunt figure counted in thousands of copies and audited annually
questions.explanation: Circulation, the newspaper's measure, was audited annually.
questions.trap_note: The quarter-hour block belongs to radio ratings, not to newspaper audits.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: audited annually
paraphrase_link.note: One adverb becomes a prepositional phrase, and 'audited' becomes 'checked'.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement fixes a frequency, and only one measure in the paragraph carries a stated frequency of verification. The other frequency in the paragraph belongs to a block of listening time, not to a check.

distractors.why_tempting: Its measure is defined by a quarter-hour block, so the paragraph attaches a time unit to it too.
distractors.why_wrong: That block is the window being measured, not the interval at which anything is verified.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the medium described in the most temporal detail, down to the fraction of a second.
distractors.why_wrong: That fraction measures how fast an auction happens, and nothing about it is checked yearly.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where several options carry a time expression, ask what each expression measures. Frequency of checking and duration of measurement are different claims.

questions.prompt: It made the duration of a visit recordable for the first time.
questions.evidence_quote: then discovered they could record how long a page stayed open
questions.explanation: Early web publishers moved from the page view to recording how long a page stayed open.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: made the duration of a visit recordable for the first time

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: each individual impression is now auctioned separately

teaching.order_note: All three answers are in the opening two paragraphs, in order. Locate that stretch and never leave it.
teaching.watch_out: Two bank words describe the opposite pole of the right idea. Fitting the grammar is not fitting the argument.

bank_analysis.why_wrong: Delay describes how slowly the platform notices, not what happens to the space it has to sell.
Abundant is true of the information in the same sentence, and it is the opposite pole of what attention becomes.
Regulators appear only in the policy paragraph, and they are not a party to the two-sided market described here.
A surge is a rise, and the passage describes the advertising inventory shrinking rather than growing.
Cheap describes information in the past, before the ratio inverted, so it fills the wrong half of the contrast.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a wealth of information, he wrote, creates a poverty of attention

teaching.decision_rule: The gap completes a claim whose two halves are opposed, so the bank word must be the negative pole. The passage supplies the term in its own words one sentence later.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the correct word for the other half of the sentence and the reader has just read it applied to information.

questions.prompt: In a two-sided market the audience whose experience is shaped is not the {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: the party whose experience is being shaped is not the party paying the bill

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the audience whose experience is shaped is not the
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the party whose experience is being shaped is not the party paying the bill
paraphrase_link.note: 'The party paying the bill' compresses to a single agent noun, which is the whole of the item.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'is not the' and the passage's sentence ends with a noun phrase in exactly that slot. The bank word must name that phrase in one word.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about a market and its awkwardness, and regulation is the obvious third party in any market description.
distractors.why_wrong: No regulator appears until the policy paragraph, and the sentence names only two parties.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph's next sentences are about how slowly damage is detected, so delay is prominent nearby.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a bank task compresses a phrase into one word, that word almost always names a role rather than an action.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'is not the' before the gap fixes a singular countable noun naming a role.

questions.prompt: A platform learns of user dissatisfaction only through a gradual {{gap}} in the advertising space it has to sell.
questions.evidence_quote: through a slow decline in the inventory it can offer
questions.explanation: The inventory is the advertising space, and the passage says it declines slowly.
questions.trap_note: Option B, delay, describes the platform's slow detection rather than what happens to the space it sells.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a slow decline in the inventory it can offer
paraphrase_link.note: 'Slow' becomes 'gradual' and the noun after it is the answer, unchanged.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between an adjective of speed and 'in the advertising space', which is the passage's own frame, so the answer is the noun that frame already governs in the text.

distractors.why_tempting: It fits the frame grammatically and reads naturally after 'gradual'.
distractors.why_wrong: It names an increase, and the passage says the platform loses revenue as the space it can sell shrinks.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence is genuinely about something being slow to happen, and the platform may not detect the damage for years.
distractors.why_wrong: The slowness belongs to the detection. What happens to the space is a reduction, not a wait.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a summary keeps the text's adjective, take the noun that adjective already modifies rather than one that merely fits.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'a gradual' before the gap fixes a singular countable noun.

teaching.decision_rule: The question quotes a predicate the passage uses once, so the answer is the subject standing in front of it, and no other noun in the paragraph occupies that slot.

distractors.why_tempting: It opens the paragraph and is what the policy actually consists of, so it is the noun most readers have in mind.
distractors.why_wrong: The principle is stated about defaults specifically, and the question quotes that principle.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the concrete thing being switched off and sits inside the same sentence as the principle.
distractors.why_wrong: It is one of the features governed, not the category the passage calls the true regulation.

questions.prompt: What does the writer compare attention to, rather than to a private appetite?
questions.evidence_quote: closer to infrastructure than to a private appetite
questions.explanation: Paragraph G opens by framing attention as closer to infrastructure.
questions.trap_note: Roads, water and clean air are examples of infrastructure, not the answer itself.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: rather than to a private appetite
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: closer to infrastructure than to a private appetite
paraphrase_link.note: The question copies the second half of the comparison and asks for the first, which fixes the answer's slot exactly.

teaching.decision_rule: The comparison has two terms, the question supplies one, so the answer is the other. Only one noun stands on the other side of 'closer to'.

distractors.why_tempting: The very next sentence lists three things of this kind, and examples are easier to see than a category.
distractors.why_wrong: They illustrate the category rather than naming it, and the question asks what attention is compared to.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the phrase that carries the argument's conclusion and sits in the same sentence as the examples.

paragraphs.text: Roughly one worker in six across the industrialised economies is on duty at some point between midnight and five in the morning. Hospitals, ports, bakeries and power stations have always run through the night, and in the past thirty years distribution warehouses, call centres and data centres have joined them. Night work is not a curiosity at the edge of the labour market; it is an ordinary condition of employment for many millions of people. What has not changed is the body that turns up to do it. Human physiology developed in a world where activity followed daylight, and it has proved stubbornly reluctant to be reorganised by a rota.

That reluctance has a physical address. A small cluster of cells sitting just above the point where the optic nerves cross acts as the body's master clock. Left to itself, it runs on a cycle of a little over twenty-four hours. Because the cycle is not exactly a day, it has to be reset, and the signal that does the resetting is light reaching the eye. Almost every other system takes its timing from that clock: body temperature, digestion, the release of hormones, and alertness itself. Core temperature falls to its lowest point in the small hours and climbs again through the morning, and alertness follows the same curve. This is why the hardest stretch of a night shift is rarely the beginning of it.

A worker coming off a shift at six in the morning must then sleep in the half of the day the clock has prepared for waking. Sleep taken in the morning is on average about two hours shorter than the same worker's sleep at night. It also holds less of the deep stage that the body restores first when rest is scarce. Some of the reasons are environmental. Daylight leaks around curtains, deliveries arrive, children come home from school, and the telephone assumes the household is awake. But the clock is the larger obstacle. It is issuing instructions to warm up and pay attention at the very hour the worker is trying to go under. The deficit accumulates across a run of nights and is only partly repaid on rest days.

The consequences show up in the work itself. Reaction times lengthen, attention narrows, and tolerance for monotonous checking tasks falls away. Operations that keep detailed error logs report that mistakes cluster between two and six in the morning. They cluster again towards the end of any shift longer than ten hours. The pattern is not spread evenly through a run of duty. It is heaviest on the first two or three nights, before any partial adjustment has occurred. It is heaviest again after a rest break has put the clock back where it started. No schedule yet designed removes the effect; the better ones only move it.

Rota design is therefore a matter of choosing which cost to pay, and two decisions dominate. The first is direction. A rota that moves a worker forwards, from mornings to afternoons to nights, asks the clock to run slightly long. That is the direction it drifts in anyway. By contrast, a rota that moves backwards asks it to run short, and workers adapt to that arrangement noticeably less well. The second decision is speed. A slowly rotating rota gives several weeks of nights and allows a partial adjustment. The price is leaving the worker permanently out of step with everyone at home. A fast rotation of two or three nights never allows adjustment at all, but it also never lets a large deficit build.

Employers have a modest toolkit and a mixed record with it. Bright light through the first half of a night shift is now common, on the reasoning that it delays the nightly fall in temperature and pushes alertness later. Controlled napping is permitted at a growing number of sites, usually inside a fixed window before three o'clock and rarely for longer than half an hour. Hot food at night, transport home for workers who would otherwise drive, and quiet rooms at the end of a shift all appear in modern agreements. An interval of eleven hours between consecutive shifts was written into the standard rota agreements in the 1990s. It is the one measure that has survived every later revision.

Two things complicate every conclusion in this field. The first is that people differ. A minority whose internal clock naturally runs late, evening types in the usual shorthand, report finding the night shift less punishing than morning types do. The difference survives when age and length of service are taken into account. The second is that the workforce selects itself. Those who cannot tolerate nights tend to leave within a year or two. A survey of workers currently on nights is in effect a survey of the survivors, and it will understate how hard the arrangement is for everyone else. Both facts point the same way: the useful question is not whether night work suits people, but which people, and on what rota.

difficulty_rationale.note: Everything in the text is concrete and the vocabulary is everyday, which holds it at band 6. What lifts it above band 5 is that each paragraph states two or three qualified claims and leaves the link between them to the reader.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Two independent choices, each with a benefit and a matching cost, are set out in one paragraph with no signposting between them.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It tells you the subject is a body meeting a timetable.
skim_plan.skip: The list of industries in A and the list of workplace measures in F. Both are examples, and any question that needs them will send you back.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below. There are more headings than paragraphs. Paragraphs F and G are not included.

options.text: A body clock that resists rescheduling
Sleep taken at the wrong hour
Designing a rota the body tolerates
Night work as an ordinary condition
The general health of modern workers
The hours when errors tend to cluster
Why freight is moved after dark
What employers have tried, and missed

teaching.strategy: Say each paragraph's job in six words before you open the list. Place D and E first: both begin with a sentence that states the whole paragraph, so they are the two you will be sure of, and each placement takes a heading out of play.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, so nothing brackets the search. Every one of the five paragraphs has to be read.
teaching.watch_out: Three headings name something a paragraph genuinely contains. Containing is not the same as being about.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.evidence_quote: Night work is not a curiosity at the edge of the labour market; it is an ordinary condition of employment for many millions of people.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A exists to correct an assumption. It gives the scale, lists the industries, and then states its point directly: night work is not marginal but normal. The last two sentences add the complication the rest of the passage takes up.
questions.trap_note: The industries in the second sentence are illustration, not subject.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Night work as an ordinary condition
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: not a curiosity at the edge of the labour market
paraphrase_link.note: The paragraph makes the claim by denying its opposite; the heading states it straight.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's controlling sentence is a not-X-but-Y about how common night work is. Only a heading about its ordinariness matches that shape; the rest name things the paragraph merely lists.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage as a whole is about what night work does to the body, so a health heading feels like the right register.
distractors.why_wrong: Paragraph A says nothing at all about health. It counts workers and names industries.

distractors.why_tempting: Ports, warehouses and distribution centres are all in the second sentence, and freight is what they move.
distractors.why_wrong: They are examples of places that work at night. The paragraph never asks why any of them does.

teaching.reusable_rule: A list inside a paragraph is evidence for the claim around it. Head the claim, not the list.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence_quote: That reluctance has a physical address.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B answers the question left hanging at the end of A: why will the body not simply be reorganised? Its answer is a clock that has to be reset by light and that sets the timing of everything else. Temperature and alertness are given as evidence of the clock's reach.
questions.trap_note: The night shift is named in the last sentence, but as an illustration of the alertness curve.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: That reluctance has a physical address
paraphrase_link.note: The paragraph's opening noun, 'reluctance', becomes the heading's verb, 'resists'.

teaching.decision_rule: The first sentence names what the paragraph will locate, and every sentence after it describes that thing. A heading has to name the clock, not one of the systems the clock controls.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends on the hardest stretch of a night shift, which sounds like the hours when things go wrong.
distractors.why_wrong: Errors are not mentioned here at all. Paragraph B explains the alertness curve; paragraph D reports what happens on it.

distractors.why_tempting: Hormones, digestion and body temperature are a list of bodily systems, and a health heading covers all of them.
distractors.why_wrong: They appear as things the clock times, not as a subject in themselves, and nothing here is about workers' health.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph opens by naming what it is about to locate, that sentence is the heading in disguise.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence_quote: must then sleep in the half of the day the clock has prepared for waking
questions.explanation: Every sentence in paragraph C is about sleep that happens at the wrong time: how much shorter it is, what wakes the sleeper, and why the clock is a bigger obstacle than the noise. The final sentence says the shortfall is not made up later.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Sleep taken at the wrong hour
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the half of the day the clock has prepared for waking
paraphrase_link.note: A whole clause explaining what makes the hour wrong is compressed into the words 'the wrong hour'.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's subject is the sleep, not the clock: the clock enters only as one of the reasons the sleep fails. A heading naming the clock would head paragraph B instead.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph says outright that the clock is the larger obstacle, so the clock looks like the point being made.
distractors.why_wrong: It is named as the strongest of several causes of a failure. The failure, not the cause, is what the paragraph is about.

distractors.why_tempting: Deliveries arriving is one of the interruptions listed in the middle of the paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: The delivery is noise outside a sleeping worker's window, and the paragraph never discusses when goods are moved.

teaching.reusable_rule: A cause named inside a paragraph does not become its subject, however emphatically it is named.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence_quote: mistakes cluster between two and six in the morning
questions.explanation: Paragraph D moves from the body to the work. It names the effects on performance and then locates them twice: at particular hours of the clock, and at particular points in a run of duty. The closing sentence says no rota removes them.
questions.trap_note: The last clause mentions schedules, which belongs to the next paragraph's subject.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The hours when errors tend to cluster
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: mistakes cluster between two and six in the morning
paraphrase_link.note: One noun is swapped and the time span becomes 'the hours'; the verb is the passage's own.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's whole second half answers the question 'when?'. A heading naming a time band matches that; a heading naming a remedy matches only its final clause.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends by saying no schedule removes the effect, and a reader who stops on that sentence has just read about rotas.
distractors.why_wrong: That clause is a bridge into paragraph E, which is where rota design is actually discussed.

distractors.why_tempting: 'The better ones only move it' sounds like a verdict on what employers have attempted.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing employers do is described here. The measures they take are listed two paragraphs later.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph's last clause often points forward. Test a heading against the middle of the paragraph, not the end.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence_quote: Rota design is therefore a matter of choosing which cost to pay, and two decisions dominate.
questions.explanation: The paragraph sets out the two variables a rota designer can move, direction and speed, and gives the benefit and the matching cost of each. It reaches no single recommendation, which is why its heading names the task rather than an answer.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Rota design
paraphrase_link.note: A noun phrase in the text becomes an -ing form in the heading; the content word is unchanged.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph is organised as choice, option one with its cost, option two with its cost. A heading naming the act of choosing fits; a heading naming what employers provide does not, because nothing here is provided.

distractors.why_tempting: Rotas are set by employers, so a heading about what employers do covers this paragraph in a loose sense.
distractors.why_wrong: This paragraph sets out a design problem. What employers put in place is paragraph F, and no verdict is reached here.

distractors.why_tempting: Every trade-off here is ultimately about the health of the person on the rota.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph never uses a health measure. Its terms are direction, speed, adjustment and being out of step.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph lays out options and refuses to choose, its heading names the choice, not a winner.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the notes below with words taken from the passage.

layout.title: Reducing the strain of night work
lines: Bright light early in the shift is meant to delay the nightly fall in {{6}}.
Short periods of {{7}} are allowed at many sites, but only before three o'clock.
An {{8}} of eleven hours between shifts became standard in the 1990s.
Evening types find night work less {{9}} than morning types do.

teaching.strategy: Three of the four answers are in paragraph F and the fourth is in G, so read those two paragraphs once and stay inside them. Fix each gap's word class from the word in front of it first: one wants a noun after 'in', one a noun after 'of', one a singular noun after 'An', one an adjective after 'less'.
teaching.order_note: All four come from the last two paragraphs. Locate that section once, then work down it.
teaching.watch_out: Notes drop the words that carry the relationship. Line one says what the light delays, not what the light is; a word that is true of paragraph F but fills the wrong slot scores nothing.

questions.prompt: Bright light early in the shift is meant to delay the nightly fall in {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: it delays the nightly fall in temperature and pushes alertness later
questions.explanation: Paragraph F gives the reasoning behind bright light: it delays the nightly fall in temperature. The note keeps the passage's own frame, 'the nightly fall in ___', so the answer is the noun that already follows it.
questions.trap_note: Alertness is in the same clause, but it is what the light pushes later, not what it delays.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the nightly fall in temperature
paraphrase_link.note: The note reuses the passage's prepositional frame word for word, which is what makes the gap findable by shape.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'a fall in', so it takes a measurable quantity, and the clause names exactly one thing that falls.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other noun in the same clause and the one the whole measure is aimed at.
distractors.why_wrong: The sentence says the light pushes alertness later and delays the fall in temperature. Two verbs, two objects.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the subject of the sentence and the first content word a scanner meets.
distractors.why_wrong: The light is the cause, not the thing that falls, and it also makes the note's sentence meaningless.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a note reuses a preposition from the text, the gap takes the word that already sits after it.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'the nightly fall in' before the gap wants an uncountable noun naming a measurable quantity.

questions.prompt: Short periods of {{gap}} are allowed at many sites, but only before three o'clock.
questions.evidence_quote: Controlled napping is permitted at a growing number of sites, usually inside a fixed window before three o'clock
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says controlled napping is permitted at a growing number of sites inside a window before three o'clock. The note replaces 'permitted' with 'allowed' and 'controlled' with 'short periods of', and leaves the activity in the gap.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is permitted at a growing number of sites
paraphrase_link.note: 'Permitted' becomes 'allowed' and 'a growing number of' becomes 'many', so no content word survives the search.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'periods of', so it needs an activity noun or an -ing form, and only one activity in the section is measured in periods.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the shortest form of the word and reads naturally after 'periods of'.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage writes 'napping'. A completion answer is copied in the form the text uses, and 'nap' is not that form.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the obvious word for what happens in a nap and the topic of the whole passage.
distractors.why_wrong: It does not appear in paragraph F at all, and an invented synonym scores zero even when the meaning is right.

teaching.reusable_rule: Never improve on the text's wording. The mark is for the form on the page, not for the meaning you carried away.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'periods of' before the gap wants an -ing form or an activity noun, not a verb.

questions.prompt: An {{gap}} of eleven hours between shifts became standard in the 1990s.
questions.evidence_quote: An interval of eleven hours between consecutive shifts was written into the standard rota agreements in the 1990s
questions.explanation: Paragraph F dates the eleven-hour rule to the 1990s and calls it an interval between consecutive shifts. The note turns the passive 'was written into the standard rota agreements' into 'became standard' and leaves the noun in the gap.
questions.trap_note: The passage never says who wrote the rule into the agreements.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: was written into the standard rota agreements in the 1990s
paraphrase_link.note: A passive with no agent becomes an ordinary verb; the date is the only word the two share.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'An' and 'of eleven hours', so it must be a singular countable noun beginning with a vowel sound that can be measured in hours.

distractors.why_tempting: The whole phrase is what the sentence is about, and copying more feels safer than copying less.
distractors.why_wrong: The limit is one word, and the words after the gap are already printed in the note.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Agreements' is the nearest noun to the date the scanner used to find the sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: The agreements are where the rule was written down; the rule itself is the interval.

teaching.reusable_rule: The article in front of a gap fixes both number and first sound. Use it to reject three candidates before you search.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'An' before the gap forces a singular noun starting with a vowel sound.

questions.prompt: Evening types find night work less {{gap}} than morning types do.
questions.evidence_quote: report finding the night shift less punishing than morning types do
questions.explanation: Paragraph G reports that evening types find the night shift less punishing than morning types do. The note replaces 'the night shift' with 'night work' and keeps the comparative frame intact.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: finding the night shift less punishing
paraphrase_link.note: 'Night shift' becomes 'night work', so the sentence cannot be found by matching that noun.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Less' before the gap and 'than' after it force a gradable adjective, and the section offers only one adjective describing how the shift feels.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the natural everyday word for the idea, and 'how hard the arrangement is' appears later in the same paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: That phrase belongs to the sentence about surveys, not to the comparison between the two types. The comparison uses a different adjective.

distractors.why_tempting: A learner who has located the right word may write the noun out of habit.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Less ___ than' takes an adjective. The noun makes the line ungrammatical and the mark is lost.

teaching.reusable_rule: A comparative frame fixes the word class before you read anything. Decide adjective or noun first, then search.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'less' before the gap and 'than' after it require a gradable adjective.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage?

teaching.strategy: Underline the comparison in each statement before you go near the text: three of these four make one thing bigger, harder or better than another. Then find the sentence where the passage makes, or conspicuously fails to make, that same comparison.
teaching.order_note: In passage order. Question 11's evidence is below question 10's, so search the band between them and stop at the next answer.
teaching.watch_out: The passage compares many things. It does not compare all of them, and one statement here asks about a comparison the writer never makes.

questions.prompt: A night worker's daytime sleep is typically shorter than the sleep the same worker gets at night.
questions.evidence_quote: Sleep taken in the morning is on average about two hours shorter than the same worker's sleep at night
questions.explanation: Paragraph C makes exactly this comparison and quantifies it: morning sleep is on average about two hours shorter than the same worker's sleep at night. The statement drops the figure and keeps the ranking, which the passage has already stated.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: shorter than the sleep the same worker gets
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: shorter than the same worker's sleep at night
paraphrase_link.note: A possessive becomes a relative clause and a figure becomes a plain comparative; nothing is added.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage states the comparison itself, so no reasoning of the reader's own is needed, and 'typically' is no stronger than 'on average'. Every part of the statement is supported, which is what TRUE requires.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'typically' appears nowhere in the passage, so a reader hunting for it finds only a figure and concludes nothing general is claimed.
distractors.why_wrong: 'On average' is the passage's own generalisation and does the same work as 'typically'.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is a catalogue of everything that goes wrong with day sleep, so a reader skimming for a verdict expects to be contradicted somewhere.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the paragraph denies the length comparison; the paragraph makes it in its second sentence.

teaching.reusable_rule: A hedge in a statement is safe when the text hedges just as firmly. Compare the two hedges, not the two topics.

questions.prompt: Mistakes made in the small hours cost more to put right than mistakes made during the day.
questions.evidence_quote: Operations that keep detailed error logs report that mistakes cluster between two and six in the morning
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says when mistakes happen, and how they bunch within a run of duty. It never says anything about what any mistake costs to correct, at any hour. The passage discusses frequency; the statement asks about expense, and the two are never joined.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the paragraph is emphatic about night-time errors, and its emphasis feels like a claim about their seriousness.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Mistakes made in the small hours
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: mistakes cluster between two and six in the morning
paraphrase_link.note: The subject matches perfectly, which is exactly why the item is dangerous; the predicate does not.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the specific claim, relative cost of correction, is neither stated nor denied anywhere in the passage. No support and nothing to quote as a contradiction is the NOT GIVEN condition.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens by promising consequences, which reads like a preface to what night errors cost.
distractors.why_wrong: The consequences it then lists are slower reactions and narrower attention, not money. Cost never appears.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph says the pattern is not evenly spread, which a reader may take as a denial that night errors are special.
distractors.why_wrong: That sentence is about when in a run of nights errors fall, not about expense. There is no sentence to point at.

teaching.reusable_rule: Matching the subject of a statement is not matching the statement. Check the predicate before you decide anything.
teaching.nearest_text: mistakes cluster between two and six in the morning

questions.prompt: Workers cope better with a rota that moves backwards through the shifts than with one that moves forwards.
questions.evidence_quote: a rota that moves backwards asks it to run short, and workers adapt to that arrangement noticeably less well
questions.explanation: Paragraph E ranks the two directions explicitly. A forward rota asks the clock to run long, which is the way it drifts anyway; a backward rota asks it to run short, and workers adapt to that noticeably less well. The statement reverses the ranking the passage gives.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial arrives in a third sentence, after two that only describe the forward rota.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: cope better with a rota that moves backwards
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: workers adapt to that arrangement noticeably less well
paraphrase_link.note: 'Adapt less well' is 'cope worse', and the statement then swaps which direction gets it.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage makes the comparison and gives it a direction. The statement makes the same comparison in the opposite direction, so the two cannot both be true, which is FALSE and not NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'cope' never appears, and the ranking arrives only in a third sentence, after two describing the forward rota.
distractors.why_wrong: The third sentence says workers adapt to backward rotation less well. That is the ranking, written out.

distractors.why_tempting: The forward rota is described as asking the clock to run long, which sounds like the more demanding request of the two.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage calls running long the direction the clock drifts in anyway, which makes it the easier request, not the harder one.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a statement reverses a comparison, read on until the text ranks the two things. The ranking is often a sentence late.

questions.prompt: Surveys of people currently on night shifts give too favourable a picture of night work.
questions.evidence_quote: A survey of workers currently on nights is in effect a survey of the survivors, and it will understate how hard the arrangement is for everyone else
questions.explanation: Paragraph G explains that people who cannot tolerate night work leave, so a survey of current night workers samples only those who stayed and will understate the difficulty. Understating the difficulty is the same claim as giving too favourable a picture.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: understate how hard the arrangement is
paraphrase_link.note: Understating a difficulty and overstating an ease are the same proposition seen from opposite ends.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage states the consequence in its own words and hedges nothing about it: the verb is 'will understate'. The statement adds no quantity and no cause, so there is nothing left unsupported.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Favourable' does not appear, and the sentence is buried at the end of a paragraph that opens by talking about individual differences.
distractors.why_wrong: The proposition is stated in full, in other words, in the paragraph's second half.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph's first half says some workers genuinely find nights easier, which reads like a defence of night work against the charge.
distractors.why_wrong: That is a claim about a minority of individuals, not about what surveys show. The two halves of the paragraph make different points.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement that shares no vocabulary with the text is not evidence of silence. Read for the proposition, not the words.

paragraphs.text: The nutrition table on the back of a food package is a triumph of completeness and a failure of communication. It lists everything a regulator has asked for, in a format that rewards a reader who has brought a calculator and several unhurried minutes. Neither is present in a supermarket aisle. Work carried out in stores puts the time an ordinary shopper spends on a single packaged item at a few seconds, and much of that goes on the picture and the price. A label that demands arithmetic inside that window is not really a label. It is a document.

Front-of-pack labelling was invented to fit the window rather than the regulation. Two families of scheme now compete for the space. Schemes of the first kind are called interpretive, because they do the judging for the shopper: a colour, a grade or a star converts the numbers into a verdict. Schemes of the second kind are reductive. They repeat a small selection of the same figures on the front of the pack and leave the judging exactly where it was. Manufacturers have generally preferred the second family and public health bodies the first, and the reason for each preference is not hard to guess.

The panel that most shoppers now meet is a compact grid, and every element in it has been argued over. Along the top runs a portion strip, a narrow band stating the quantity that all the figures beneath it describe. Below the strip sit four nutrient cells, one each for energy, fat, sugars and salt, in that fixed order. The order is not decorative, because shoppers read the leftmost cell most reliably. Each cell except the first carries a colour ring around its figure, green, amber or red according to the amount per hundred grams. Energy is left uncoloured, since no threshold for it commands general agreement. Running under the four cells is a reference bar giving each figure as a percentage of an adult's daily intake. A small corner mark in the lower right identifies the scheme that awarded the colours, and it is the only part of the panel carrying a brand.

What such a panel achieves is easier to measure in a laboratory than in a shop. Asked to rank three products by their sugar content, shoppers given an interpretive panel are both faster and more accurate than shoppers given a reductive one, and the gap is widest among those who left education earliest. What happens to actual purchasing is a harder question with a smaller answer. Trials that follow real baskets through real tills report shifts of a few per cent in the categories where a red mark is common, and nothing measurable at all in categories where it is rare. Ashfield, who has reviewed this literature twice, argues that the effect is genuine but modest, and that expecting more of a label was always unreasonable.

The larger effect may not be on the shopper at all. A red mark on the front of a package is a commercial fact, and manufacturers have answered it by changing what is in the package. Reformulation of this kind is unglamorous and cumulative. A little less salt goes into a sauce each year; a sweetener is substituted in a drink; a portion is redefined so that a figure falls below a threshold. Where a scheme has been in place for a decade, the average salt content of the affected categories has fallen by more than the shift in what shoppers choose. The label, in other words, has worked mainly by embarrassing the producer rather than by informing the buyer.

Three limits are built into the design, and no amount of colour will remove them. The first is that a label describes a package while a diet is made of many packages. A product that earns a green mark can be eaten in quantities that no scheme was designed to bless. The second is the portion. Because the figures on the front refer to a stated serving, a manufacturer who shrinks the stated serving improves the panel without touching the recipe, and the practice remains legal in most places where these schemes operate. The third is coverage. Loose fruit, bread from a counter and every meal eaten away from home carry no panel at all, and in many countries those account for a larger share of what people eat than the packaged goods that do.

The argument has therefore moved from design to compulsion. Where a scheme is voluntary, the products most likely to earn a poor grade are the products least likely to carry the scheme, which hollows out the comparison the label exists to make. Norland, who advises several trade associations, maintains that a mandatory scheme would penalise small producers who cannot reformulate and cannot afford the testing. That objection deserves a reply rather than a dismissal, though it is worth noticing that it is an argument about who bears a cost, not an argument that the labels fail to work. What the evidence will not support, from either side, is the claim that a panel on the front of a box can do the work of a food policy.

difficulty_rationale.note: The subject is concrete but the claims are not: most sentences are about what a measurement can and cannot show, and the writer keeps separating an effect from the thing it is usually credited to.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Three unrelated limits arrive in one paragraph, each stated once, and the third is the only one with a figure attached to it.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It sets up a contrast between a complete label and a usable one.
skim_plan.skip: The naming of the four cells in C. You will be sent back to that paragraph anyway, and reading it twice slowly is cheaper than reading it once now.

rewordings: with almost no time to spare

rewordings: makes the assessment on your behalf
reaches a verdict for the reader

paraphrase_families.passage_form: changing what is in the package
rewordings: revising the make-up of a product
puts a better face on it

hinge_words.why_here: It sizes the purchasing effect that question 22 asks you to characterise.
It is the word that makes one achievement primary in question 23 and the others secondary.
It licenses 'legal' and blocks 'illegal wherever' in question 25's second option.
It separates what the writer accepts from what the writer declines, which decides question 26.

mineable.meaning: reach the verdict instead of the reader
measured against a fixed weight, not a portion
how much a grown person should have in a day

question_groups.instructions_extra: Label the diagram below with words taken from the passage.

layout.title: The front-of-pack panel
layout.alt: A nutrition panel: a narrow bar on top, four boxes in a row, a band beneath them and a small badge bottom right.

teaching.strategy: Every name is in paragraph C and nowhere else, so read that paragraph once from the top and match its order to the picture: it describes the panel downwards, from the band at the top to the mark in the corner. Do not start from the diagram.
teaching.order_note: All four come from one paragraph, which describes the panel from top to bottom. Read it once in that direction.
teaching.watch_out: You already know roughly what a food label looks like, and that knowledge will supply names the passage never uses. Only the paragraph's own words score.

questions.prompt: the narrow band running across the top of the panel
questions.evidence_quote: Along the top runs a portion strip, a narrow band stating the quantity that all the figures beneath it describe
questions.explanation: Paragraph C names the top element and then explains it in apposition: a portion strip, which states the quantity that everything below it refers to. The name comes before the explanation, which is the pattern the whole paragraph follows.
questions.trap_note: The word 'portion' also appears in paragraph F, where it names a limit rather than a part of the panel.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the narrow band running across the top
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a portion strip, a narrow band
paraphrase_link.note: The passage gives the name and then its description; the label gives the description and asks for the name.

teaching.decision_rule: The label points at a position, and only one sentence in the section describes something at that position. Its name is the noun phrase before the comma, not the description after it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the distinctive word in the phrase, and one word feels safer than two under a two-word limit.
distractors.why_wrong: The part is called a portion strip. 'Portion' alone names what the strip states, not the strip.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the passage's own wording and it sits immediately after the name.
distractors.why_wrong: That phrase is the description the passage supplies to gloss the name. Copying the gloss instead of the name is the standard loss here.

teaching.reusable_rule: In an appositive, the name comes first and the explanation second. Copy the name.
teaching.grammar_cue: The label wants a noun phrase naming a part, so a two-word compound noun, not a description.

questions.prompt: the coloured circle drawn around the figure in a cell
questions.evidence_quote: Each cell except the first carries a colour ring around its figure, green, amber or red according to the amount per hundred grams
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says each cell except the first carries a colour ring around its figure. The ring is green, amber or red depending on the amount per hundred grams, which is why the first cell, energy, has none.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the coloured circle drawn around the figure
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a colour ring around its figure
paraphrase_link.note: 'Circle' for 'ring' is the only change, and it is enough to defeat a search for the label's own words.

teaching.decision_rule: The section describes only one element that surrounds something else, and the label points inside a cell rather than at the whole cell, which rules out the cell's own name.

distractors.why_tempting: The label sits inside one of the four boxes, and that box does have a name two sentences earlier.
distractors.why_wrong: The label points at the ring around the figure, not at the box containing it. The two are named separately.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the single content word a scanner picks up from the sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: Colour is what the ring carries. The part is the ring, and the passage names it in two words.

teaching.reusable_rule: A leader line points at one object, not at the object containing it. Fix what is being pointed at before you search.
teaching.grammar_cue: The answer is a two-word noun phrase; a single adjective cannot be a label.

questions.prompt: the strip beneath the four cells giving a percentage
questions.evidence_quote: Running under the four cells is a reference bar giving each figure as a percentage of an adult's daily intake
questions.explanation: Paragraph C places a reference bar under the four cells and says what it does: it restates each figure as a percentage of an adult's daily intake. Position and function are both given in one sentence.
questions.trap_note: Two elements in the panel are described as running across it, so position alone does not identify this one.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: beneath the four cells giving a percentage
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: under the four cells is a reference bar giving each figure
paraphrase_link.note: 'Beneath' for 'under' is the whole disguise; the rest of the label is the passage's own wording.

teaching.decision_rule: Two elements run horizontally across the panel, and only the lower one is described as giving a percentage. The function in the label settles which of the two is meant.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other horizontal element and it also states a quantity that the figures depend on.
distractors.why_wrong: The portion strip sits along the top and names a serving; this bar sits under the cells and gives percentages.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the noun phrase nearest the word 'percentage' in the sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: The daily intake is what the percentage is calculated against, not the name of the part of the panel.

teaching.reusable_rule: When two parts share a position, the function named in the label is what separates them. Search on the function.
teaching.grammar_cue: The label names a component, so the answer is a noun phrase, not a percentage or a quantity.

questions.prompt: the small identifier printed in the lower right of the panel
questions.evidence_quote: A small corner mark in the lower right identifies the scheme that awarded the colours
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph C names a small corner mark in the lower right and says it identifies the scheme that awarded the colours. It is also described as the only branded element on the panel.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: in the lower right identifies the scheme
paraphrase_link.note: The position phrase is copied straight from the text, which is what makes this the easiest of the four to locate.

teaching.decision_rule: Only one element is placed in the lower right, and the label asks for its name rather than for what it identifies.

distractors.why_tempting: It is what the mark identifies, and it is the noun the sentence goes on to talk about.
distractors.why_wrong: The scheme is the organisation behind the colours. The part of the panel is the mark that names it.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence ends by calling this the only part of the panel carrying a brand.
distractors.why_wrong: That clause explains why the mark is unusual. It is not the passage's name for the element.

teaching.reusable_rule: A label asks what a part is called, never what it stands for. Copy the name, not its purpose.
teaching.grammar_cue: The answer names an object, so a noun phrase; a word for an organisation cannot label a printed element.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the sentences below with words taken from the passage.

teaching.strategy: These four run top to bottom through the passage, so answer them in a single pass and never search behind you. Decide first what each gap must be: a plural noun of time, a technical adjective, an abstract noun, and a two-word noun phrase.
teaching.order_note: In passage order. Question 20's answer is below question 19's, so start each search where the last one finished.
teaching.watch_out: Two of these gaps sit in sentences that are the writer's summary, not the passage's wording. Look for the proposition, then copy the word the passage uses for it.

questions.prompt: Studies in shops suggest that a shopper gives a single packaged item only a few {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: puts the time an ordinary shopper spends on a single packaged item at a few seconds
questions.explanation: Paragraph A reports work carried out in stores that puts the time spent on one packaged item at a few seconds, most of it on the picture and the price. The sentence in the question restates that finding without changing the quantity.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: a shopper gives a single packaged item
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the time an ordinary shopper spends on a single packaged item
paraphrase_link.note: 'Spends on' becomes 'gives', which is enough to hide the sentence from a search for the verb.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'a few', so it takes a plural countable noun, and the passage measures this quantity in only one unit.

distractors.why_tempting: The same paragraph says the back label needs several unhurried minutes, and that noun is closer to the top of the paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: Minutes are what the back label demands. Seconds are what the shopper actually has.

distractors.why_tempting: A learner who has located the right word may still copy it in the singular.
distractors.why_wrong: 'A few' forces the plural, and the passage writes the plural. A dropped ending is a dropped mark.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two quantities in one paragraph usually belong to two different things. Check which one the sentence is about.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'a few' before the gap forces a plural countable noun.

questions.prompt: Schemes that turn the figures into a verdict for the shopper are called {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: Schemes of the first kind are called interpretive, because they do the judging for the shopper
questions.explanation: Paragraph B divides the schemes into two families and names them. The first kind is called interpretive because it does the judging for the shopper, converting the numbers into a verdict; the second kind, reductive, leaves the judging to the reader.
questions.trap_note: The other family is named in the same paragraph, three sentences later.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: turn the figures into a verdict
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: converts the numbers into a verdict
