teaching.decision_rule: The claim is about quantity only, and the passage states the quantity result without hedging it. The hedge in the sentence attaches to a different claim, which the statement does not make.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence ends by saying something is unclear, and a reader who takes that hedge to cover the whole sentence sees no firm claim.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Though whether they produce better ones is unclear' hedges the quality. The count is asserted plainly before it.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is a list of limits, so a reader expects its final sentence to report a failure rather than a gain.
distractors.why_wrong: The limit is the supervisor's position, not the remedy. The remedy is reported as producing more submissions.

teaching.reusable_rule: A hedge attaches to one clause, not to a whole sentence. Check which half of the claim it is guarding.

paragraphs.text: Screening is not the same activity as medicine, although it deploys identical instruments. A doctor treating a patient is responding to a complaint. A screening programme approaches individuals who have registered no complaint at all and offers them a test. That reversal alters the ethics of everything which follows. The person who is invited was, until the letter arrived, well. If the programme is properly designed, a minority of those invited will be spared a serious illness, while a considerably larger number will undergo anxiety, further tests and occasionally treatment for no benefit. Every screening programme therefore begins by creating patients out of the healthy, and the entire justification of the enterprise is that it creates fewer than it saves.

A programme is a pathway rather than a test, and the pathway has the same shape wherever it is run. It opens with an invitation, sent by post or message to everyone inside a defined age band. The width of that band therefore determines the scale of the programme. The person who accepts attends for a first test, selected because it is cheap, quick and tolerable rather than because it is accurate. The result is then read against a threshold fixed in advance, not judged case by case. Anyone whose result crosses the line is recalled for a second and more precise investigation, and it is that investigation, rather than the first test, which produces a diagnosis. Everyone else returns to the routine schedule and is invited again at the next interval.

The arithmetic governing a screening programme is the arithmetic of rare events, and it is deeply counter-intuitive. Assume a condition affects one person in a thousand, and assume the initial test is accurate ninety-five times out of a hundred. Among a thousand individuals invited, the test will correctly identify the single affected person. It will also designate about fifty unaffected people as requiring a second look. A positive result in somebody who does not have the condition is called a false positive, and in this example the false positives outnumber the true ones fifty to one. Nothing is defective in the test itself. How many positives prove to be real depends far more on how common the condition is than on the precision of the instrument, and no laboratory improvement modifies that relationship.

Overdiagnosis is the harder concept, and the one programmes have been slowest to communicate. It does not denote a mistaken diagnosis. It means the correct identification of a real abnormality that would never have caused symptoms in that person's lifetime, because it grows too slowly, or ceases to grow, or the person dies of another cause first. Nobody can establish which individual case is which, so everybody detected is treated, and every treated person is subsequently counted among the lives the programme saved. The outcome is a statistic that improves as overdiagnosis increases. Brackenfield, who has examined several long-running programmes, calls this the central measurement problem of the field.

A second illusion operates in the same direction. Suppose a disease is detected five years earlier than it would otherwise have been, and nothing about its course is altered. The person will still die on the same day, but the interval between diagnosis and death will be five years longer. Survival measured from the moment of diagnosis therefore improves without a single life being extended, an artefact known as lead-time bias. The only measure immune to it is the death rate across the whole invited population, set against the death rate in an equivalent population that was never invited. Establishing that figure requires a controlled trial lasting a decade or more.

Who receives the letter is a decision about arithmetic rather than about fairness, and it is the decision the public finds hardest to accept. Programmes define an age band and an interval because both the frequency of the condition and the utility of the test vary with age. Extending a band downwards incorporates people among whom the condition is rarer, which reduces the proportion of positives that are real and raises the number of healthy people harmed. Contracting the interval has a similar consequence. Requests to widen the criteria are therefore almost always requests to increase the harm, and they are rarely interpreted in those terms.

The response to all this has been a shift of tone rather than a revision of policy. Invitation letters used to instruct; they now inform. The letter sets out the benefits and the harms in the same type size, presents the figures for a thousand people rather than for one, and states plainly that attending is a voluntary choice. Sandmouth, who assisted in rewriting several of these documents, maintains that the shift is genuine but incomplete, because the letter still arrives unsolicited, and an unsolicited offer conveys a recommendation whatever its wording says. That objection is legitimate, and it has no obvious remedy.

difficulty_rationale.note: Three of the seven paragraphs explain a counter-intuitive statistical idea in ordinary words, and each one has to be held in mind for the next. The vocabulary is easy and the reasoning is not.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It defines a term by first ruling out the thing everyone assumes it means, then explains why the resulting error is invisible in the figures.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It states the one fact everything else depends on: the person invited is well.
skim_plan.skip: The worked numbers in C on a first pass. Read the sentence before them and the sentence after them, and come back for the arithmetic only if a question needs it.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct heading for each paragraph from the list of headings below. There are more headings than paragraphs. Paragraphs A and G are not included.

options.text: Deciding who receives an invitation
Why most positives are not disease
The cost of running a programme
A pathway with five fixed stages
Finding what would never have appeared
How a screening test is invented
A survival gain that may be illusory
Persuading the reluctant to attend

teaching.strategy: Four of these five paragraphs exist to explain one idea each, and each one names its idea in a single sentence. Find that sentence first, in B the opening one and in C, D and E the one containing the technical term, and match the heading to it before reading anything else.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, so nothing bounds the search. All five paragraphs must be read, which is why this group is worth doing first.
teaching.watch_out: Two headings describe things the passage is about in general rather than what any one paragraph does. A heading true of the whole text is wrong for every paragraph in it.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence_quote: A programme is a pathway rather than a test, and the pathway has the same shape wherever it is run
questions.explanation: Paragraph B opens by insisting that a programme is a pathway rather than a test, and then walks through that pathway from invitation to diagnosis or return to the list. Every sentence after the first names one stage of it.
questions.trap_note: The first test is described here in detail, but as one stage among several.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: A pathway with five fixed stages
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the pathway has the same shape wherever it is run
paraphrase_link.note: 'The same shape wherever it is run' is what 'fixed' means here; the number is supplied by counting the sentences.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's controlling sentence is an explicit not-X-but-Y, and the body of the paragraph is a sequence. A heading naming the sequence is the only one matching both.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph explains why the first test was chosen, which reads like an account of how that test came about.
distractors.why_wrong: It says the test was selected for cost and tolerability. Nothing here is about inventing a test.

distractors.why_tempting: Cheapness is named in the same sentence as the first test, and cost is a natural heading for a paragraph about running a programme.
distractors.why_wrong: Cheapness is one criterion for choosing a test. The paragraph never discusses what a programme costs.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph opens by denying one description and offering another, the second is the heading.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence_quote: in this example the false positives outnumber the true ones fifty to one
questions.explanation: Paragraph C works through the arithmetic of a rare condition and reaches one conclusion: nearly every positive result belongs to somebody without the disease. It then says why, which is that prevalence matters more than test quality.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Why most positives are not disease
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the false positives outnumber the true ones fifty to one
paraphrase_link.note: A ratio in the text becomes the quantifier 'most' in the heading, and the heading adds the word 'why'.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph gives both a result and an explanation for it, so the heading must carry the explanatory word. A heading naming only the arithmetic would leave out the paragraph's last sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph discusses how accurate the test is at length, which sounds like an account of the test itself.
distractors.why_wrong: Accuracy is one of two inputs to the calculation, and the paragraph ends by saying it is the less important one.

distractors.why_tempting: Both this heading and the paragraph are about a number that misleads.
distractors.why_wrong: This heading is about survival figures, which belong to paragraph E. Nothing in C concerns how long anybody lives.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that ends with a because clause needs a heading that promises an explanation.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence_quote: the correct identification of a real abnormality that would never have caused symptoms in that person's lifetime
questions.explanation: Paragraph D defines overdiagnosis by first ruling out what it is not, a mistaken diagnosis, and then stating what it is: the correct detection of something real that would never have shown itself. The paragraph closes on why this inflates the programme's own figures.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph contains the word 'mistaken' and is not about mistakes.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Finding what would never have appeared
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: would never have caused symptoms in that person's lifetime
paraphrase_link.note: 'Caused symptoms' becomes 'appeared', which moves the claim from the disease to what the patient would have noticed.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph defines a term, and the definition turns on the abnormality being real but silent. Only one heading keeps both halves of that.

distractors.why_tempting: Both paragraphs are about findings that lead nowhere, and a reader who has not yet placed C may put this heading here.
distractors.why_wrong: In C the finding is not a disease at all; in D it is a genuine abnormality. That difference is the point of the paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: The final sentences are about a statistic that improves misleadingly, which this heading also describes.
distractors.why_wrong: Those sentences are the consequence of the definition, not its subject, and the survival illusion is paragraph E.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph defines a term, head the definition, not the consequence the definition leads to.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence_quote: Survival measured from the moment of diagnosis therefore improves without a single life being extended
questions.explanation: Paragraph E describes a survival figure that rises although nobody lives any longer, names it, and then gives the one measure that is not vulnerable to it. The word 'illusion' opens the paragraph and sets its subject.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: A survival gain that may be illusory
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: improves without a single life being extended
paraphrase_link.note: The heading names the effect; the passage describes the mechanism that produces it.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's subject is a measurement that misleads about survival specifically. A heading about counting problems in general would fit the paragraph before it just as well.

distractors.why_tempting: Both paragraphs describe a way in which a programme appears to succeed without succeeding, and they sit next to each other.
distractors.why_wrong: That heading is about the detection of harmless abnormality, which is paragraph D. Nothing here is about what is found.

distractors.why_tempting: The last sentence mentions a trial lasting a decade, which is plainly an expensive undertaking.
distractors.why_wrong: Length is not cost, and the sentence is about what a reliable measure requires rather than what it costs.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two adjacent paragraphs can describe two versions of one problem. Head each by what it is a version of.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence_quote: Who receives the letter is a decision about arithmetic rather than about fairness
questions.explanation: Paragraph F is about eligibility: why an age band and an interval are set where they are, what happens when either is widened, and why requests to widen them are misunderstood. Its first sentence states the subject exactly.
questions.trap_note: The word 'fairness' appears in the first sentence in order to be dismissed.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Who receives the letter is a decision
paraphrase_link.note: 'The letter' becomes 'an invitation', which is the word paragraph B used for the same object.

teaching.decision_rule: Every sentence in the paragraph is about the boundary of the invited group. A heading about persuading people to attend would need a paragraph about those already invited.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph's last sentence is about requests from the public, which sounds like a paragraph concerned with the public's willingness.
distractors.why_wrong: Those requests are to be included, not to be excused. Nobody here is being persuaded to attend anything.

distractors.why_tempting: Widening a band clearly makes a programme bigger, and bigger programmes cost more.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph measures the effect of widening in harm to healthy people, and never in money.

teaching.reusable_rule: A word introduced only to be rejected is not the paragraph's subject. Read the rest of the sentence.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the flow chart below with words taken from the passage.

layout.title: The screening pathway
steps: An {{19}} is sent to everyone in a defined age band
The person who accepts attends for a first {{20}}
The result is read against a {{21}} fixed in advance
Anyone above the line is recalled for a more precise {{22}}
Everyone else is invited again at the next interval

teaching.strategy: All four boxes come from paragraph B and the paragraph narrates the stages in the chart's own order, so read it once from the top with a finger on the chart. Each gap wants the name of a stage, not the result of one.
teaching.order_note: Everything is in paragraph B, in this order. Locate the paragraph once and work down it beside the chart.
teaching.watch_out: The commonest loss in a flow chart is writing what comes out of a box instead of what goes into it. Box three wants the thing the result is compared with, not the verdict that follows.

questions.prompt: An {{gap}} is sent to everyone in a defined age band
questions.evidence_quote: It opens with an invitation, sent by post or message to everyone inside a defined age band
questions.explanation: Paragraph B begins the pathway with an invitation sent to everyone inside a defined age band, and adds that the width of the band determines the size of the programme. The chart keeps the passage's own frame.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: sent to everyone in a defined age band
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: sent by post or message to everyone inside a defined age band
paraphrase_link.note: The chart drops the channel and keeps the recipients, so the box is findable by its ending rather than its opening.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'An' and 'is sent', so it must be a singular countable noun beginning with a vowel sound that names something posted.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage uses 'letter' for the same object twice, in paragraphs A and F, and it is the everyday word.
distractors.why_wrong: 'An' before the gap requires a vowel sound, and paragraph B, which the chart follows, uses a different noun.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the noun phrase nearest the gap that a scanner meets when matching the box's wording.
distractors.why_wrong: The band is who the thing is sent to. It is already printed at the end of the box.

teaching.reusable_rule: An article before a gap fixes the first sound of the answer. Reject candidates on that alone before searching.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'An' before the gap forces a singular noun beginning with a vowel sound.

questions.prompt: The person who accepts attends for a first {{gap}}
questions.evidence_quote: The person who accepts attends for a first test, selected because it is cheap, quick and tolerable
questions.explanation: The second stage in paragraph B is a first test, chosen for cost, speed and tolerability rather than for accuracy. The chart reproduces the clause and gaps the noun.
questions.trap_note: Paragraph B distinguishes this first test from the later investigation, and the distinction matters for the fourth box.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The person who accepts attends for a first
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: attends for a first test, selected because it is cheap
paraphrase_link.note: The box is a verbatim opening clause, which makes this the anchor box for locating the rest of the chart.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows the ordinal 'a first', so it takes a singular countable noun naming a procedure, and the paragraph names two such procedures in a fixed sequence.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other procedure named in the paragraph and it is the one that produces the diagnosis.
distractors.why_wrong: The investigation is the second stage, reached only after a threshold is crossed. The chart places it in a later box.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Attends for' invites a word about turning up somewhere, and appointment is the natural completion.
distractors.why_wrong: The word does not appear in the passage, and a completion answer must be copied rather than supplied.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a text names two procedures in sequence, the ordinal in the gapped line tells you which one is wanted.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'a first' before the gap wants a singular countable noun, not a plural or a verb.

questions.prompt: The result is read against a {{gap}} fixed in advance
questions.evidence_quote: The result is then read against a threshold fixed in advance, not judged case by case
questions.explanation: The third stage is a comparison. Paragraph B says the result is read against a threshold fixed in advance rather than judged case by case, which is what makes the pathway a procedure rather than a series of opinions.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The result is read against a
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The result is then read against a threshold
paraphrase_link.note: One adverb is dropped and nothing else changes, so the whole difficulty is knowing which noun the box wants.

teaching.decision_rule: The box asks what the result is compared with, so the answer is the standard rather than the outcome of applying it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the most important noun in the paragraph and it is what the whole pathway is aiming at.
distractors.why_wrong: The diagnosis is produced two stages later by the second investigation. Reading a result against a diagnosis is not what the passage describes.

distractors.why_tempting: The next sentence says anyone whose result crosses the line is recalled, so 'line' names the same idea.
distractors.why_wrong: 'The line' is a back-reference in the following sentence. The box copies the sentence that introduces the standard, and it uses a different noun.

teaching.reusable_rule: A box asking what something is compared with wants the yardstick, never the verdict.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'against a' before the gap requires a singular countable noun naming a standard.

questions.prompt: Anyone above the line is recalled for a more precise {{gap}}
questions.evidence_quote: recalled for a second and more precise investigation, and it is that investigation, rather than the first test, which produces a diagnosis
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says that anyone crossing the threshold is recalled for a second and more precise investigation, and that it is this, not the first test, which produces a diagnosis. The chart keeps 'more precise' and gaps the noun.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: recalled for a second and more precise investigation
paraphrase_link.note: Only the word 'second' is dropped, which is what makes the wrong sequence answer so easy to write.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows the adjective phrase 'more precise', which the paragraph attaches to exactly one noun, and that noun is the stage after the threshold rather than before it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the noun used for the earlier stage and it is the word most readers expect after 'more precise'.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage deliberately uses a different noun for the second stage and then contrasts the two in the same sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: The same sentence ends with the word, and a diagnosis is certainly more precise than a screening result.
distractors.why_wrong: The diagnosis is what the second stage produces, not the stage itself. The box wants the procedure.

teaching.reusable_rule: A box wants the name of a step. If your answer is what the step yields, you are one line too far ahead.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'a more precise' before the gap requires a singular countable noun naming a procedure.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Answer the questions below with words taken from the passage.

teaching.strategy: Every one of these asks what something is called, so the answer is a technical term the passage introduces and never repeats. Scan for the naming verbs, called, known as, calls, and take the words immediately after them.
teaching.order_note: In order, and the four terms are introduced in four different paragraphs. Work forward and never search behind your last answer.
teaching.watch_out: The limit is three words. Two of these terms are two words long and adding the article in front of them puts you over it in one case and not in the other, so count before you write.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what does a screening programme make out of healthy people?
questions.evidence_quote: Every screening programme therefore begins by creating patients out of the healthy
questions.explanation: Paragraph A closes by saying that every screening programme begins by creating patients out of the healthy, and that its justification is that it creates fewer than it saves. The answer is the noun the healthy are turned into.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: creating patients out of the healthy
paraphrase_link.note: 'Creating' becomes 'make' and 'the healthy' becomes 'healthy people'; the preposition is left in place as the anchor.

teaching.decision_rule: The wh-word asks what, so the answer is a noun, and the sentence supplies exactly one noun in the object position of the verb.

distractors.why_tempting: Anxiety is the harm named two sentences earlier and it is what a healthy person actually receives.
distractors.why_wrong: Anxiety is what they are put through, not what they are made into. The question asks what they become.

distractors.why_tempting: It combines both nouns in the sentence and stays inside the three-word limit.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage does not contain that phrase, and a short answer must be copied contiguously from the text.

teaching.reusable_rule: The wh-word tells you the word class of the answer before you read anything. Use it as a filter.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What does it make out of' wants a plural noun naming people.

questions.prompt: What is a positive result in a person without the condition called?
questions.evidence_quote: A positive result in somebody who does not have the condition is called a false positive
questions.explanation: Paragraph C defines the term in the middle of its worked example: a positive result in somebody without the condition is called a false positive. The paragraph then shows that in a rare condition these outnumber the true positives heavily.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: a positive result in a person without the condition
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A positive result in somebody who does not have the condition
paraphrase_link.note: A relative clause becomes a prepositional phrase, which is the cheapest way to hide a definition from a word search.

teaching.decision_rule: The question ends in 'called', so the answer is the term the passage attaches to the description, taken exactly as printed and within the limit.

distractors.why_tempting: The phrase 'the true ones' appears in the very next clause and the two terms sit together.
distractors.why_wrong: That names the opposite case, a positive result in a person who does have the condition.

distractors.why_tempting: It is what the fifty unaffected people are marked as needing, in the sentence just before the definition.
distractors.why_wrong: That is what happens to them next, not what the result is called.

teaching.reusable_rule: A question asking what a thing is named wants a label. Search for the naming verb, not the description.
teaching.grammar_cue: The question asks what something is called, so the answer is a noun phrase of two or three words.

questions.prompt: What name is given to the apparent survival gain produced by earlier diagnosis?
questions.evidence_quote: improves without a single life being extended, an artefact known as lead-time bias
questions.explanation: Paragraph E describes a survival figure that rises although nobody lives longer, and names the effect at the end of the sentence: an artefact known as lead-time bias. The paragraph then names the one measure that avoids it.
questions.trap_note: The hyphen makes this a two-word answer, not three.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: improves without a single life being extended
paraphrase_link.note: The question turns the passage's clause into a noun phrase, so the sentence cannot be found by matching a verb.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks for a name, so the answer follows the phrase 'known as' and is copied with its hyphen intact.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other named effect in the passage and it also makes a programme's figures look better than they are.
distractors.why_wrong: Overdiagnosis is about what is found; this is about when it is found. They are defined in different paragraphs.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the noun immediately before the naming phrase and it describes the effect accurately.
distractors.why_wrong: 'An artefact' is the category. The name the question asks for is the two words after 'known as'.

teaching.reusable_rule: A hyphenated compound counts as one word. Copy it whole rather than trimming it to fit a limit.
teaching.grammar_cue: The question asks for a name, so a noun phrase, and the hyphen keeps it inside the limit.

questions.prompt: What does an invitation letter now print in the same type size as the benefits?
questions.evidence_quote: The letter sets out the benefits and the harms in the same type size
questions.explanation: Paragraph G describes how invitation letters have changed. They now set out the benefits and the harms in the same type size, give the numbers per thousand people, and state that attending is a choice.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: in the same type size as the benefits
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the benefits and the harms in the same type size
paraphrase_link.note: A coordinated pair in the text becomes a comparison in the question, which moves one item out of reach of a scan.

teaching.decision_rule: The question names one half of the pair, so the answer is the other half, taken from the same clause and in the same form.

distractors.why_tempting: The next clause is about giving numbers for a thousand people, and numbers are the most concrete thing in the sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: That is a separate change listed after this one, and it is not what shares the type size with the benefits.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the striking phrase at the end of the sentence and it is what the whole paragraph is arguing for.
distractors.why_wrong: That is what the letter says about attending, not what it prints alongside the benefits.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a question quotes one item of a pair, the answer is the item beside it in the text.
teaching.grammar_cue: The question wants a plural noun matching 'the benefits' in form.

paragraphs.text: Behavioural policy begins from a small and awkward observation: the manner in which an option is presented alters how often it is selected, even when the options themselves are identical. The order of items on a menu, the wording of a form, the position of a switch, the day on which a letter arrives, all of these modify behaviour by amounts that are straightforward to measure and difficult to defend as rational. The arrangement doing the altering is usually called the choice architecture. What made the idea attractive to governments was not its novelty, since marketing departments had exploited it for decades, but its cost. Redesigning an arrangement is cheap. Redesigning an incentive is not.

The strongest instrument in the collection is the default, the outcome that occurs when nobody makes a decision. One county converted its cycle allowance from an application form into an automatic enrolment with an opt-out, and participation rose from a fifth of eligible staff to more than four fifths inside a year, with no other feature of the scheme altered. Comparable reversals have been documented for pension contributions, for the renewal of insurance policies and for donor registration. The consistency of the pattern across such different domains is what persuaded ministries that they had acquired a general instrument rather than a curiosity.

Three explanations compete, and they are not mutually exclusive. The first is effort: acting requires a decision and a form, whereas not acting requires neither. The second is endorsement, since whoever established the default is assumed to have had a reason for it, so the default reads as advice. The third is the inertia of preference, the tendency to treat the current arrangement as the reference point against which every alternative registers as a loss. Which explanation dominates matters practically, because a default operating through endorsement collapses the moment the public stops trusting the institution that set it.

The evidence has not aged as well as the enthusiasm. Trials of behavioural interventions published before roughly 2015 report average effects two to three times larger than the same interventions generate when they are repeated at scale, and the discrepancy is widest in precisely those areas where the original results were most frequently quoted. Part of this is ordinary publication bias: for most of that period, a small trial with a null result was very difficult to place in a journal. Part of it is that the early trials were conducted by the people who designed the intervention, in settings they had selected themselves. Ellwood, who has assembled the largest register of replications, argues that the effects are genuine but that the field spent a decade quoting its upper bound.

Scale imposes a second discount, and this one is arithmetical rather than methodological. An intervention that shifts behaviour by four percentage points among those who read the letter shifts the population by very much less, because most of the population never reads the letter. Reach, response and effect multiply together, and each of the three is a fraction. A programme reported as effective in a trial can therefore be entirely genuine and still deliver a change too small to appear in any national statistic. That is not a failure of the science. It is a failure of the arithmetic performed on its behalf.

The political objection is different in kind and is not answered by better measurement. Norbury's case is that a government able to reduce a problem by ten per cent with a redesigned form will be tempted to stop there, and that the redesigned form then occupies the place a tax or a regulation would have occupied. On this reading the technique is not merely modest; it is actively displacing. Whether that has in fact occurred is an empirical question, and the evidence assembled so far is thin in both directions.

The standard defence is that there is no alternative to designing something. A form has to put its questions in some order; a menu has to list its dishes in some sequence; a scheme has to specify what happens when nobody replies. Havering states it sharply: the choice is not between an architecture and no architecture, but between an architecture that has been reasoned about and one that has been inherited. That argument is sound as far as it goes, and it goes less far than it is usually taken to go, because it justifies deliberating about the default without justifying any particular default.

Two questions seem to me worth asking before any of this is adopted. Does the intervention survive being administered by somebody who does not believe in it? And is the effect substantial enough to matter once reach and response have taken their share? An intervention that passes both is a cheap and legitimate instrument of policy. One that passes neither is a press release. The real difficulty of the field is that the second question is arithmetic, which anybody can check, whereas the first is temperament, which nobody has yet found a method of measuring.

difficulty_rationale.note: The text concedes almost everything it reports and then withdraws part of it again, three times over, and the writer's own position is stated only in the last paragraph after five paragraphs of other people's.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It makes an arithmetical argument in prose, with three fractions that have to be multiplied mentally and none of them written as a figure.

skim_plan.skip: The three worked examples in G. They are one point repeated three times, and the sentence after them states it.

layout.title: Summary: the case for choice architecture (paragraphs A-C)
lines: Behavioural policy rests on the finding that presentation alters choice even when the alternatives are {{27}}.
Governments were drawn to the approach because redesigning an arrangement is {{28}}.
A default works partly because whoever set it is assumed to have had a reason, so it functions as {{29}}.
In one county, moving to automatic enrolment raised participation to over four fifths without altering the rest of the {{30}}.
Such a default collapses as soon as the public loses {{31}} in the institution behind it.

teaching.strategy: The bank words are the item writer's synonyms, not the passage's wording, so matching on vocabulary will find nothing. Read the summary first, decide the meaning and the word class each gap needs, and only then look for the sentence in paragraphs A to C that carries that meaning.
teaching.order_note: All five come from the first three paragraphs. Locate that section once, then work inside it.
teaching.watch_out: This summary is deliberately not in passage order: gap 29 comes from paragraph C and gap 30 goes back to paragraph B. Check each gap against the text rather than assuming you are moving forward.

bank_analysis.why_wrong: The paragraph names the withdrawal of trust, not the arrival of opposition. Nobody in that section objects to anything.
It is the passage's own noun, and it names the expensive half of the contrast rather than the cheap one.
A default can be declined, so it is the opposite of obligatory. The gap wants how the default is read.
Nothing in the county example concerns custom. The gap wants the thing that was otherwise left unaltered.

questions.prompt: Behavioural policy rests on the finding that presentation alters choice even when the alternatives are {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: alters how often it is selected, even when the options themselves are identical
questions.explanation: Paragraph A states the founding observation: the way an option is presented changes how often it is chosen even when the options themselves are identical. The summary keeps the concession clause and replaces the passage's adjective with a synonym.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: even when the options themselves are identical
paraphrase_link.note: 'Alternatives' replaces 'options' in the summary and the bank replaces 'identical'; two swaps in one clause.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows a plural subject and 'are', so it takes an adjective, and the clause needs one meaning that the choices do not differ from each other.

distractors.why_tempting: It is an adjective and it fits the frame grammatically, and the paragraph is about how policy shapes behaviour.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing about the options being obligatory is claimed. The clause concedes that they are indistinguishable.

distractors.why_tempting: Marketing departments having used the idea for decades reads like a claim about long practice.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a noun where the gap needs an adjective, and custom is never said to be a property of the options.

teaching.reusable_rule: Fix the word class from the frame before you consider meaning. It removes most of a nine-word bank at once.

questions.prompt: Governments were drawn to the approach because redesigning an arrangement is {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: Redesigning an arrangement is cheap. Redesigning an incentive is not.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says the appeal to governments was cost rather than novelty, and then puts the point in two short sentences: redesigning an arrangement is cheap, redesigning an incentive is not. The bank word restates 'cheap'.
questions.trap_note: Both nouns in the contrast are available in the bank, and only one of them is the subject of the cheap half.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Redesigning an arrangement is cheap
paraphrase_link.note: The clause is copied whole and only the final adjective is replaced, which makes the grammar the only discriminator.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap completes a copular clause about the arrangement, not about the incentive, so it needs the adjective attached to the cheap half of the passage's two-sentence contrast.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the passage's own word, it appears in the very next sentence, and a reader matching vocabulary lands on it at once.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a noun and the gap needs an adjective. It also names the expensive half of the contrast.

distractors.why_tempting: An adjective is required and this one is available, and the paragraph does argue that presentation is what differs.
distractors.why_wrong: It would say arrangements are the same as something. The clause needs their cost, which is what attracted governments.

teaching.reusable_rule: A bank word taken straight from the text is usually the lure. The bank is built out of synonyms.

questions.prompt: A default works partly because whoever set it is assumed to have had a reason, so it functions as {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: whoever established the default is assumed to have had a reason for it, so the default reads as advice
questions.explanation: The second of the three explanations in paragraph C is endorsement: the person who set the default is assumed to have had a reason, so the default reads as advice. The summary keeps the reasoning and replaces the final noun.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: is assumed to have had a reason
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is assumed to have had a reason for it
paraphrase_link.note: The clause is reproduced word for word, so the only work is choosing the synonym for what follows it.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'functions as' and needs an uncountable noun naming what a default is taken to be. Only one bank word means a recommendation.

distractors.why_tempting: If a default is followed by almost everybody, treating it as obligatory is a natural inference.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph's whole point is that the default is a suggestion nobody is required to accept.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a noun of similar shape and the paragraph does describe people not acting.
distractors.why_wrong: Not acting is inertia, not opposition, and this gap is about how the default is interpreted rather than resisted.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a gap follows a verb of interpretation, the bank word names how something is read, not what it is.

questions.prompt: In one county, moving to automatic enrolment raised participation to over four fifths without altering the rest of the {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: participation rose from a fifth of eligible staff to more than four fifths inside a year, with no other feature of the scheme altered
questions.explanation: Paragraph B gives the county example: participation rose from a fifth to more than four fifths within a year, with no other feature of the scheme altered. The summary substitutes a synonym for 'scheme'.
questions.trap_note: This gap comes from paragraph B although the gap before it came from paragraph C.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: without altering the rest of the
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: with no other feature of the scheme altered
paraphrase_link.note: A passive absolute becomes a prepositional phrase, and 'no other feature' becomes 'the rest'.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap needs the noun for the thing that was otherwise unchanged, which the passage identifies as the arrangement the county was running rather than any wider practice.

distractors.why_tempting: 'The rest of the tradition' reads acceptably and the paragraph is about a long-standing way of doing things.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the county example concerns custom. What was left alone was the arrangement itself.

distractors.why_tempting: A cycle allowance is a financial encouragement, so the word describes the thing being redesigned.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage's contrast puts incentives on the opposite side from arrangements, and here nothing financial was altered.

teaching.reusable_rule: Do not assume a summary walks forward through the text. Check each gap against the section, not against the last one.

questions.prompt: Such a default collapses as soon as the public loses {{gap}} in the institution behind it.
questions.evidence_quote: collapses the moment the public stops trusting the institution that set it
questions.explanation: Paragraph C ends by saying that a default working through endorsement collapses the moment the public stops trusting the institution that set it. The summary turns the verb into a noun the public can lose.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the public stops trusting
paraphrase_link.note: Stopping trusting and losing confidence are the same event, expressed once as a verb and once as a noun.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap is the object of 'loses' and is followed by 'in', so it must be an abstract noun that takes that preposition and means trust.

distractors.why_tempting: A collapse suggests opposition, and losing ground to resistance is a familiar way of describing a policy failing.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage names the withdrawal of trust, not the arrival of opposition. Nobody in paragraph C objects to anything.

distractors.why_tempting: It is an abstract noun of the right shape and it has just been used two lines above about the same default.
distractors.why_wrong: The public does not lose guidance in an institution. The preposition after the gap rules it out.

teaching.reusable_rule: The preposition after a gap narrows an abstract noun faster than the meaning does. Use it first.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the passage? Write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

teaching.strategy: Three named people are quoted in this passage and the writer appears only in the last paragraph and in a handful of verdict sentences. Before searching, mark whether the statement claims a view for the writer or for one of the three, because the passage endorses some of what it reports and declines the rest.
teaching.order_note: In order. The five answers run from paragraph C to paragraph H, one paragraph apart or more, so bracket each search between the last answer and the end.
teaching.watch_out: The writer twice states that a question has not been settled. A statement claiming the writer has settled it is contradicted, not unaddressed.

questions.prompt: The writer thinks it makes a practical difference which explanation for defaults is correct.
questions.evidence_quote: Which explanation dominates matters practically, because a default operating through endorsement collapses the moment the public stops trusting
questions.explanation: Paragraph C sets out three explanations and then says outright that which one dominates matters practically, giving the reason: a default resting on endorsement fails when trust in the institution fails. The claim and its justification are both the writer's.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: matters practically
paraphrase_link.note: An adverb in the text becomes an adjective plus noun in the statement; the proposition is untouched.

teaching.decision_rule: The sentence is unattributed and evaluative, so it is the writer's own, and the statement adds no quantity or condition that the passage does not supply.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens by saying the three explanations are not mutually exclusive, which sounds like a refusal to choose between them.
distractors.why_wrong: Not choosing between them is different from thinking the choice unimportant, and the last sentence says the opposite.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who takes 'not mutually exclusive' as the paragraph's verdict will treat any claim of a practical difference as denied.
distractors.why_wrong: That phrase concerns whether the explanations can coexist. The final sentence separately asserts that the balance between them matters.

teaching.reusable_rule: A sentence with no reporting verb and an evaluative adverb is the writer speaking. Treat it as their position.

questions.prompt: The writer accepts that the behavioural results published before 2015 were invented.
questions.evidence_quote: argues that the effects are genuine but that the field spent a decade quoting its upper bound
questions.explanation: Paragraph D explains the shrinking effects by publication bias and by trials run by their own designers, and closes with Ellwood's verdict that the effects are genuine and only the reported size was inflated. Exaggeration and invention are different charges.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial arrives as the single word 'genuine' inside a reported clause at the end of the paragraph.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the effects are genuine but that the field spent a decade
paraphrase_link.note: 'Genuine' is the direct denial of 'invented', and the writer endorses it by giving two innocent mechanisms first.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage states the opposite of the statement and supplies two explanations that require the results to have been real. That is a contradiction, so NO rather than NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: Publication bias, designer-run trials and effects two to three times too large add up to a paragraph that sounds like an accusation.
distractors.why_wrong: Every mechanism named is a distortion of reporting, not of the data. The paragraph ends by calling the effects genuine.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'invented' never appears, so a reader searching for it finds nothing to point at.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Genuine' is its denial, and it is stated in a clause the writer presents approvingly rather than as an opposing view.

teaching.reusable_rule: A single adjective can carry a whole denial. Read the concessive clause before you decide the writer agrees.

questions.prompt: The writer considers letters a more effective channel than direct personal contact.
questions.evidence_quote: because most of the population never reads the letter
questions.explanation: Paragraph E uses a letter as its worked example and says most of the population never reads it, which is a point about reach rather than about channels. No other way of contacting people is mentioned anywhere in the passage, so no comparison is available.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the paragraph is severe about what a letter achieves, and severity reads as a ranking against something better.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: considers letters a more effective channel
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: most of the population never reads the letter
paraphrase_link.note: The letter is the only element the statement and the paragraph share; the comparison has nothing to attach to.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage discusses one channel and never introduces a second, so it neither supports the ranking nor denies it. A comparison with an entity the text never mentions is NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph says the letter reaches almost nobody, which reads like a verdict that letters do not work well.
distractors.why_wrong: A statement about how many people read a letter is not a statement about whether some other method would do better.

distractors.why_tempting: The letter is the passage's standard example of an intervention, and being chosen as the example suggests approval.
distractors.why_wrong: It is an example of the arithmetic, not a recommendation, and the paragraph names no rival to prefer it to.

teaching.reusable_rule: A ranking needs two things in the text. If the second one is missing, the answer is not given however clear the first is.
teaching.nearest_text: An intervention that shifts behaviour by four percentage points among those who read the letter

questions.prompt: The writer treats it as established that these techniques have crowded out stronger measures.
questions.evidence_quote: Whether that has in fact occurred is an empirical question, and the evidence assembled so far is thin in both directions
questions.explanation: Paragraph F sets out Norbury's displacement argument in full and then, in the writer's own voice, refuses to treat it as settled: whether it has happened is an empirical question and the evidence is thin in both directions.
questions.trap_note: The displacement claim occupies three sentences and the writer's refusal occupies one, which is the whole difficulty of the item.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is an empirical question, and the evidence assembled so far is thin
paraphrase_link.note: Calling something an open empirical question is the direct denial of treating it as established.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement attributes a settled belief to the writer, and the writer's own sentence declares the matter unsettled. A stated refusal to conclude contradicts a claim to have concluded.

distractors.why_tempting: Norbury's argument is given at length and with no counter-argument beside it, so the paragraph reads as endorsing it.
distractors.why_wrong: It is introduced as Norbury's case, and the writer's next sentence declines to say whether it is true.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer never says the displacement has not happened, so there appears to be no statement of the writer's own view.
distractors.why_wrong: Saying the evidence is thin in both directions is a view, and it is incompatible with regarding the matter as established.

teaching.reusable_rule: Declaring a matter unsettled is itself a position. Do not read it as the absence of one.

questions.prompt: The writer wants an intervention tried by people who are unconvinced by it.
questions.evidence_quote: Does the intervention survive being administered by somebody who does not believe in it?
questions.explanation: The final paragraph gives the writer's two tests in the first person. The first asks whether an intervention survives being administered by somebody who does not believe in it, which is exactly the trial the statement describes.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: tried by people who are unconvinced by it
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: administered by somebody who does not believe in it
paraphrase_link.note: 'Does not believe in it' becomes 'unconvinced by it', and the singular becomes a plural without changing the claim.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph opens with an explicit first-person marker, so everything in it is the writer's. The statement reproduces the first test without adding a condition.

distractors.why_tempting: The question form of the sentence looks like a question being raised rather than a position being taken.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph introduces both questions as ones the writer thinks worth asking before adoption, which makes them requirements.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends by saying the first test cannot be measured, which sounds like the writer withdrawing it.
distractors.why_wrong: The difficulty of measuring a test is not an argument against wanting it applied, and the writer says so in the same sentence.

teaching.reusable_rule: A rhetorical question in the writer's own voice states a requirement. Convert it to a statement before judging it.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

teaching.strategy: Answer each stem from the passage before reading the four options. Two of these items offer an option that is a true statement about a different paragraph, and one offers the reported view where the stem asks for the writer's, so an option can be accurate and still be the wrong answer.
teaching.order_note: In order, running from paragraph D to paragraph H. Each search begins where the last answer was found.
teaching.watch_out: Question 39 asks how the writer assesses an argument, not whether the argument is popular. The verdict is a single clause in the middle of a long sentence.

questions.prompt: What does the passage give as one reason for the fall in reported effect sizes?

options.text: Journals rarely accepted small trials that found nothing.
Later trials were run on samples that were too small.
The interventions were altered before being repeated.
No register of replications existed until after 2015.

questions.evidence_quote: for most of that period, a small trial with a null result was very difficult to place in a journal
questions.explanation: Paragraph D gives two reasons for the gap between early and later results. The first is ordinary publication bias, spelled out as the difficulty of placing a small trial with a null result in a journal; the second is that early trials were run by the designers in settings of their own choosing.
questions.trap_note: Both reasons concern how the early trials were reported and conducted, not how the later ones were.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Journals rarely accepted small trials that found nothing
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a small trial with a null result was very difficult
paraphrase_link.note: 'Difficult to place' becomes 'rarely accepted', which turns the author's problem into the journal's decision.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a reason the passage supplies, so an option must match one of the two mechanisms named, and both of those concern the early trials rather than the repetitions.

distractors.why_tempting: Small samples are mentioned in the paragraph and are the standard explanation for results that do not replicate.
distractors.why_wrong: The small trials in the passage are the early ones. The repetitions are described as being run at scale.

distractors.why_tempting: If effects shrink on repetition, something must have differed between the two runs, and the intervention is the obvious candidate.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says the same interventions were repeated. What differed was who ran them and where.

distractors.why_tempting: Ellwood's register of replications is named in the paragraph's last sentence and the date 2015 appears in its second.
distractors.why_wrong: The register is where the comparison came from. The passage never dates it or blames its absence for anything.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph compares two sets of studies, check which set an option is actually describing.

questions.prompt: What is Norbury's objection to behavioural policy?

options.text: It measures its own effects far too generously.
It occupies the space a stronger measure would fill.
It cannot be applied to problems of any size.
It depends on defaults that the public will resent.

questions.evidence_quote: the redesigned form then occupies the place a tax or a regulation would have occupied
questions.explanation: Norbury's case is that a government able to reduce a problem by ten per cent with a redesigned form will stop there, and that the form then occupies the place a tax or a regulation would have occupied. The passage calls the technique actively displacing.
questions.trap_note: The objection is not that the technique fails but that it succeeds enough to prevent something better.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: occupies the space a stronger measure would fill
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: occupies the place a tax or a regulation would have occupied
paraphrase_link.note: 'A tax or a regulation' becomes 'a stronger measure', which names the category the passage gives two members of.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the objection this paragraph attributes to one person, and the paragraph states it twice: once as a mechanism and once as the verdict that the technique is actively displacing.

distractors.why_tempting: Over-generous measurement is the subject of the previous two paragraphs and is a genuine complaint in the passage.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph opens by saying this objection is different in kind and is not answered by better measurement.

distractors.why_tempting: The scale paragraph does argue that effects become invisible across a whole population.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the arithmetical discount, not Norbury's political objection, and it concerns size rather than applicability.

distractors.why_tempting: Public trust in the institution setting a default is discussed earlier, so resentment feels like part of the argument.
distractors.why_wrong: Trust appears in the paragraph about why defaults work. Norbury's objection is about what the technique replaces.

teaching.reusable_rule: An opening sentence that distinguishes this objection from the previous one is telling you which options to discard.

questions.prompt: How does the writer assess Havering's argument?

options.text: It is unsound, because every form must have an order.
It shows that a reasoned default is the better one.
It applies only to schemes with a fixed deadline.
It is correct, but is generally pushed too far.

questions.evidence_quote: That argument is sound as far as it goes, and it goes less far than it is usually taken to go
questions.explanation: The writer accepts Havering's point that there is no alternative to designing something, and then limits it: the argument is sound as far as it goes and is usually taken further than it will bear, because it justifies thinking about a default without justifying any particular one.
questions.trap_note: The whole verdict is one clause inside a sentence that begins by agreeing.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: It is correct, but is generally pushed too far
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is sound as far as it goes, and it goes less far
paraphrase_link.note: The option compresses a repeated 'goes' construction into 'pushed too far' and keeps the concession that precedes it.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for an assessment, and the writer supplies one built from an agreement and a limitation. An option carrying only one of the two halves misreports the verdict.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage does insist that every form must be ordered somehow, so the reason attached to this option is genuinely in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: That is Havering's premise, which the writer accepts. Accepting the premise cannot make the argument unsound.

distractors.why_tempting: A reasoned architecture against an inherited one is the contrast Havering draws, and preferring the reasoned one seems to follow.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer says the argument justifies deliberating about a default without justifying any particular default.

distractors.why_tempting: Deadlines are close in sense to the passage's clause about what happens when nobody replies.
distractors.why_wrong: That clause is one of three parallel examples of unavoidable design. No restriction to timed schemes is stated.

teaching.reusable_rule: A verdict that concedes and then limits needs an option doing both. One half is always available and always wrong.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main point in the final paragraph?

options.text: Governments should abandon behavioural policy in most areas.
The two tests are about equally easy to apply.
One test can be checked and the other cannot.
Press releases outnumber trials in this field today.

questions.evidence_quote: the second question is arithmetic, which anybody can check, whereas the first is temperament, which nobody has yet found a method of measuring
questions.explanation: The final paragraph sets two tests and then names the difficulty with them: the second is arithmetic and can be checked by anyone, while the first is temperament and has no known method of measurement. That asymmetry is the paragraph's point.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: One test can be checked and the other cannot
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: which anybody can check, whereas the first is temperament
paraphrase_link.note: 'Nobody has found a method of measuring' becomes 'cannot be checked', which is the paragraph's own contrast compressed.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the paragraph's main point, and its final sentence begins by naming the real difficulty, which makes that sentence the point rather than the two tests preceding it.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage has spent five paragraphs discounting the field's claims, so a reader tracking the direction of travel expects a rejection.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer calls an intervention that passes both tests a cheap and legitimate instrument of policy.

distractors.why_tempting: Two tests offered side by side in consecutive sentences invite the assumption that they are equivalent in practice.
distractors.why_wrong: The last sentence exists to say they are not: one is checkable arithmetic and the other is not measurable at all.

distractors.why_tempting: The phrase 'a press release' is the paragraph's most memorable expression and it clearly disparages something.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes an intervention that passes neither test. No claim is made about how many such interventions there are.

teaching.reusable_rule: The last sentence of a closing paragraph usually names the difficulty rather than restating the proposal above it.

paragraphs.text: A peat bog looks like poor ground. It grows little that anyone can sell, it will not carry a tractor, and for most of the last three centuries it was treated as land waiting to be improved. Underneath the surface, however, lies one of the largest stores of carbon on land. Peat is not soil in the ordinary sense. It is plant matter that has failed to rot, laid down layer on layer at a rate of about a millimetre a year. A bog two metres deep has therefore been building for roughly two thousand years, and the carbon in it has been out of the air for that long. Northern countries hold most of the world's peatland, because cool summers and steady rain are the conditions the process needs.

The mechanism is simple and depends entirely on water. When a plant dies in a dry field, fungi and bacteria break it down within a season or two, and the carbon it holds returns to the atmosphere. In a bog the dead plants sink into standing water instead. Below the water table there is almost no oxygen, and the organisms that do the fastest decay cannot work without it. What decay there is proceeds slowly and stops early. The result is an accumulation rather than a cycle. Sphagnum moss, the plant that dominates most northern bogs, makes the conditions still more difficult by acidifying the water around it, which slows the surviving microbes further.

Draining a bog reverses all of this in a few seasons. Ditches cut to dry the surface lower the water table, and air reaches peat that has been sealed away for centuries. The old plant matter begins to decompose at last, and the bog turns from a place that absorbs carbon into a place that releases it. The peat surface also sinks as it dries and shrinks, so the ditches have to be deepened, which lowers the water table again. Across the uplands of Britain and Ireland, millions of hectares were drained in this way between the 1940s and the 1980s, mostly for sheep grazing and for planting conifers on ground that had never carried trees.

Establishing what a particular bog is doing now is harder than it sounds. The standard instrument is the dipwell, a perforated tube sunk into the peat in which the water level can be read by hand or by a logger. Water-table depth is a good proxy for whether peat is gaining or losing carbon, and it is cheap enough to measure at many points. Direct measurement of the gases is done with sealed chambers placed on the surface, or with a tower carrying an instrument that samples the air many times a second and works out the net exchange over the field around it. Cores taken with a narrow auger give the long record, since the depth of a dated layer fixes the rate at which the peat below it accumulated.

Restoration begins by putting the water back. Contractors work along the old ditches installing dams, built from peat blocks cut on site, from plastic sheet piling or from bales of heather, until the channel is a chain of shallow pools rather than a drain. On bare peat, where the vegetation has gone entirely, the surface must also be covered, since dry peat blows away and washes off in rain. Crews spread cut heather brash over the ground and plant plugs of sphagnum through it. Conifers planted during the drainage years are felled and, increasingly, their stumps are turned over so that the furrows they left do not go on carrying water off the site.

How quickly the benefit arrives is a genuine question. The water table rises within months of the dams going in, and the loss of carbon slows accordingly. Rebuilding a functioning bog surface takes far longer: sphagnum spreads at a few centimetres a year, and a site that has been bare for decades may need twenty years of cover before it behaves like a bog again. There is also a complication that restoration schemes rarely advertise. Wet peat produces methane, a gas that traps heat far more effectively than carbon dioxide over a short period, and a newly rewetted site can emit more of it than a drained one. Most assessments conclude that the carbon dioxide saved outweighs the methane released, but the balance takes years to turn positive.

The money now follows a different logic from the one that dug the ditches. Restoration is expensive, since clearing trees, blocking ditches and revegetating bare ground on a large upland site runs to a few thousand pounds a hectare, and the landowner gains nothing directly from carbon that stays underground. Voluntary carbon codes have grown up to bridge the gap, certifying the emissions a project avoids and allowing a company to buy that reduction. The arrangement is criticised on the grounds that avoided emissions are not the same as removed ones, and that the estimates depend on a counterfactual nobody can observe. It has nevertheless paid for most of the restoration carried out in the last decade.

paragraphs.text: Concrete is the most used manufactured material in the world, and it cracks. Some cracking is unavoidable: the material shrinks as it cures, it moves with temperature, and it is deliberately designed to crack in tension so that the steel inside it can take the load. The trouble is what a crack lets in. Water carrying chloride from de-icing salt or from the sea reaches the reinforcement, the steel corrodes, and corroded steel occupies more space than sound steel, so the surrounding concrete is pushed apart from within. By the time the damage is visible from outside, the repair is structural rather than cosmetic. Across the life of a bridge or a tunnel, maintenance of this kind commonly costs more than the original construction.

Concrete already repairs itself to a small degree, and always has. A batch never fully reacts: grains of cement in the interior stay unhydrated for years because no water reaches them. When a crack opens and rain gets in, those grains hydrate at last and the products of the reaction grow into the opening. Dissolved calcium in the pore water also combines with carbon dioxide from the air and deposits calcium carbonate along the crack faces. Engineers call this autogenous healing. It is real, it costs nothing, and it is severely limited: it closes cracks of about a fifth of a millimetre and no wider, and it works only where water arrives often enough to keep the reactions going.

The best known attempt to extend that process borrows from biology. Certain bacteria survive in strongly alkaline conditions and form spores that stay viable for decades without food or water. Mixed into the wet concrete together with a calcium-rich nutrient, usually calcium lactate, the spores lie dormant in the hardened material. A crack lets in water and oxygen, the spores germinate, the bacteria consume the nutrient and deposit calcium carbonate as a by-product, and the deposit seals the opening. Laboratory work has closed openings close to a millimetre wide by this route, roughly five times the width that autogenous healing can manage. The bacteria then exhaust the nutrient and return to the spore state, ready for the next time water arrives.

The difficulty is the packaging. Spores and nutrient cannot simply be stirred into the mix, because the alkalinity and the crushing that goes on inside a mixer destroy most of them before the concrete has set. They are therefore enclosed in capsules of clay, glass or polymer. This creates a requirement that works against itself: a shell tough enough to survive the mixer is often tough enough to survive the crack as well, and a shell that breaks readily at the crack rarely reaches the crack intact. There is a second penalty. Capsules are weaker than the aggregate they displace, so the more healing agent a mix carries, the lower its strength, and beyond a few per cent by volume the remedy begins to cost more than the fault.

Three other approaches avoid the packaging problem in different ways. Superabsorbent polymers swell when they meet water and plug the crack physically, then draw water in to feed the ordinary reactions around them; they are cheap and act within hours, but they leave a soft pore behind when they dry. Vascular systems run hollow fibres through the element and pump a sealing agent along them. That is the only approach that can be refilled, and the only one that survives repeated damage in the same place, though the network must be designed into the structure and cannot be added later. Shape-memory tendons take a different route again: a strand cast into the beam is heated after cracking, contracts, and pulls the crack faces back together mechanically, which no chemical method can do.

Evidence is where the field is thinnest. Almost all published results come from small laboratory specimens cracked to a chosen width under controlled conditions and then stored in water. Recovery is reported in two quite different currencies. One is regained tightness, measured by how much water or air passes through the specimen afterwards, and it is the figure that matters for durability. The other is regained strength, measured by loading the specimen to failure a second time, and it is the figure that sounds impressive. A specimen can recover almost all of the first and very little of the second. Field trials are rare, because a structure has to be built, damaged and then watched for a decade. The Norland viaduct panels, cast in the mid-2010s with three competing systems side by side, remain one of the few long comparisons anybody has.

So the case is economic before it is technical. A self-healing mix costs somewhere between a tenth and a half more per cubic metre than an ordinary one, which is trivial against the cost of reaching a leaking tunnel lining and irrelevant against the cost of a garden wall. The technology therefore belongs where access is expensive and failure is slow: marine works, buried pipes, deep foundations, the underside of long-span decks. A second obstacle is duller and probably larger. No accepted standard yet says what a designer may assume, so an engineer who specifies a self-healing mix must still design as though it will not heal, and pays for the additive without being allowed to bank the benefit. Until a code recognises the property, the material improves and the design does not.

difficulty_rationale.note: Each paragraph states a property and its cost in the same breath, and paragraph E does it three times in three sentences with no signpost between them. The vocabulary is ordinary; the bookkeeping is not.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Three systems, each with one gain and one drawback, arrive in three long sentences and nothing marks where one ends.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It sets up the problem the whole passage is a set of answers to.
