question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the summary below using words taken from the passage.

layout.title: How concrete heals
lines: A batch of concrete never fully reacts, so grains of cement deep inside stay {{14}} for years.
When rain enters a crack, dissolved calcium combines with carbon dioxide and leaves {{15}} along the crack faces.
Engineers call this process {{16}} healing, and it closes cracks no wider than about a fifth of a millimetre.
The bacterial method uses {{17}} that stay viable for decades without food or water.
In the laboratory it has sealed openings roughly {{18}} times wider than the natural process can.

teaching.strategy: All five gaps come from the two paragraphs that describe healing itself, and they run in order through them. Decide the word class of each gap before you read: two want nouns, two want modifiers and one wants a number.
teaching.order_note: One section only, paragraphs B and C, and in order. Find them once, then never leave them.
teaching.watch_out: Two of these gaps take a word the passage uses as a modifier. Writing the related noun instead scores zero.

questions.prompt: A batch of concrete never fully reacts, so grains of cement deep inside stay {{gap}} for years.
questions.evidence_quote: grains of cement in the interior stay unhydrated for years because no water reaches them
questions.explanation: Paragraph B explains that a batch of concrete never fully reacts: cement grains in the interior stay unhydrated for years because no water reaches them. Those are the grains that hydrate later, when a crack lets rain in.
questions.trap_note: The word for the same idea one paragraph later, 'dormant', is used of spores rather than of cement.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: in the interior
paraphrase_link.note: 'in the interior' becomes 'deep inside' - the register changes and the position does not.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows the copular verb 'stay' and precedes a time phrase, so it takes the modifier the passage puts in that slot. No noun fits the frame.

distractors.why_tempting: It describes something inert inside hardened concrete and appears only one paragraph later.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Dormant' is used of the bacterial spores, not of cement grains, and it sits outside this summary's section.

distractors.why_tempting: The line's own words, 'never fully reacts', invite the reader to build the modifier out of them.
distractors.why_wrong: A completion answer is copied from the passage, and the passage's word is a different one.

teaching.reusable_rule: A completion answer is copied, never constructed. A word you built out of the question line is wrong by definition.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'stay' before the gap wants a modifier, and 'for years' after it rules out a noun.

questions.prompt: When rain enters a crack, dissolved calcium combines with carbon dioxide and leaves {{gap}} along the crack faces.
questions.evidence_quote: deposits calcium carbonate along the crack faces
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says that dissolved calcium in the pore water combines with carbon dioxide from the air and deposits calcium carbonate along the crack faces. The summary swaps one verb and keeps the rest of the clause.
questions.trap_note: The passage's other calcium compound is the bacteria's food, and it is in the next paragraph.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: deposits
paraphrase_link.note: One verb is swapped; everything on either side of the gap is the passage's own wording.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap is the object of the verb and the phrase after it is copied from the passage, so the answer is the compound noun that already stands between them.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the passage's other calcium compound and it sits one paragraph away in a sentence about the same chemistry.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the food the bacteria are given. What is left along a crack face is the carbonate.

distractors.why_tempting: A learner watching the two-word limit drops the first word to stay safely inside it.
distractors.why_wrong: The limit allows two words and the passage's phrase is two words. Cutting one changes the substance named.

teaching.reusable_rule: A limit of two words is permission, never a target. Cutting a compound noun to fit changes what it names.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'leaves' before the gap and 'along the crack faces' after it fix a noun as its object.

questions.prompt: Engineers call this process {{gap}} healing, and it closes cracks no wider than about a fifth of a millimetre.
questions.evidence_quote: Engineers call this autogenous healing.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B names the process in a sentence of its own and then gives its limit: it closes cracks of about a fifth of a millimetre and no wider. The summary inserts the word process, which moves the gap by one word.
questions.trap_note: The second half of the passage's phrase is already printed after the gap.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Engineers call this autogenous healing
paraphrase_link.note: The summary inserts a general noun where the text goes straight to the name, shifting the gap one place.

teaching.decision_rule: The noun 'healing' is already printed after the gap, so the gap takes only the modifier that the passage places in front of it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the passage's own phrase and both words sit inside the two-word limit.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Healing' is already printed after the gap. Repeating it makes the line ungrammatical and the answer wrong.

distractors.why_tempting: The line calls it a process and the paragraph contrasts it with an engineered method, so a reader supplies the obvious modifier.
distractors.why_wrong: It is not the passage's word, and completion answers come out of the text unchanged.

teaching.reusable_rule: Read what is already printed after a space. Anything repeated there cannot be part of your answer.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'healing' after the gap wants one modifier, not the phrase that contains it.

questions.prompt: The bacterial method uses {{gap}} that stay viable for decades without food or water.
questions.evidence_quote: form spores that stay viable for decades without food or water
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says that the bacteria form spores which stay viable for decades without food or water, and that those spores lie dormant in the hardened concrete until a crack admits water and oxygen.
questions.trap_note: The subject of the passage's sentence is the bacteria; the thing that survives decades is what they form.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Certain bacteria survive in strongly alkaline conditions and form spores
paraphrase_link.note: The bacteria form them in the text; a method uses them in the summary, which moves the agent.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap is the object of 'uses' and the relative clause after it is copied from the passage, so it takes the plural noun that clause already modifies.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the subject of the passage's sentence and the summary line is about the bacterial method.
distractors.why_wrong: The bacteria do not stay viable for decades without food. What does is the spore they form.

distractors.why_tempting: The singular reads naturally after 'uses' and the plural marker is easy to lose when copying at speed.
distractors.why_wrong: The relative clause takes a plural verb, and the passage writes the plural.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a relative clause is copied from the text, the answer is the exact noun that clause was attached to.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'that stay' after the gap carries a plural verb, so the noun must be plural.

questions.prompt: In the laboratory it has sealed openings roughly {{gap}} times wider than the natural process can.
questions.evidence_quote: roughly five times the width that autogenous healing can manage
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says laboratory work has closed openings close to a millimetre wide, roughly five times the width that autogenous healing can manage. The summary replaces the technical name with a plain description.
questions.trap_note: The other fraction in these two paragraphs, a fifth of a millimetre, is a width and not a multiple.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: autogenous healing
paraphrase_link.note: The technical name is replaced by its plain description, so the number is findable only through meaning.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'roughly' and 'times wider', a frame that admits a number and nothing else, and only one multiple appears anywhere in the section.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other fraction in these two paragraphs and it also describes a crack width.
distractors.why_wrong: A fifth of a millimetre is what the slower process reaches. It is not the multiple by which the bacterial route beats it.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two figures in one section usually measure different things. Match the frame around the space, never the digit.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'roughly' before the gap and 'times wider' after it admit a number only.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Which paragraph contains the following information? NB You may use any letter more than once.

options.text: Paragraph A
Paragraph B
Paragraph C
Paragraph D
Paragraph E
Paragraph F
Paragraph G

teaching.strategy: Read each stem for the kind of statement it describes rather than for its topic. Three of the four name a rhetorical move - a reason, an admission, an example - and the paragraph that makes that move is what you are hunting.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, and a letter may repeat. Do this group after the summary, when two paragraphs are already known.
teaching.watch_out: Each of these ideas is touched in at least two paragraphs. The stem asks which one contains it, not which one mentions it.

questions.prompt: a description of how a crack eventually damages what lies inside the concrete
questions.evidence_quote: the steel corrodes, and corroded steel occupies more space than sound steel, so the surrounding concrete is pushed apart from within
questions.explanation: Paragraph A traces the whole chain: water carrying chloride reaches the reinforcement, the steel corrodes, corroded steel takes up more room, and the concrete around it is forced apart from inside.
questions.trap_note: Two later paragraphs use the word crack far more often than this one does.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: reaches the reinforcement
paraphrase_link.note: The stem names the steel by position rather than function, which is how it hides from a keyword search.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a causal chain ending inside the material. Only one paragraph runs that chain from water to steel to splitting; the rest describe repair.

distractors.why_tempting: It is also about something breaking inside hardened concrete, and it uses the word crack four times.
distractors.why_wrong: What breaks there is a capsule, and deliberately. No damage to reinforcement is described anywhere in it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is about damage and how the recovery from it is measured, so a scanner hunting the word damage lands there.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes how recovery is reported, never how the damage arises in the first place.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem asking how something happens wants the paragraph that runs the chain, not the one with the matching noun.

questions.prompt: a reason why the quantity of healing agent in a mix cannot simply be increased
questions.evidence_quote: the more healing agent a mix carries, the lower its strength
questions.explanation: Paragraph D gives the second penalty of capsules. They are weaker than the aggregate they replace, so strength falls as the dose rises, and past a few per cent by volume the remedy costs more than the fault.
questions.trap_note: One earlier paragraph limits how often healing can happen, which is a different limit from how much agent a mix may hold.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the more healing agent a mix carries, the lower its strength
paraphrase_link.note: A correlative construction in the text becomes a flat prohibition in the stem.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem wants a stated obstacle to scaling up. Only one paragraph names a penalty that grows with the dose; the others say what the agent does, not what more of it costs.

distractors.why_tempting: It explains that the bacteria exhaust their food supply, which sounds like a limit on quantity.
distractors.why_wrong: Running out of food limits how often healing can happen, not how much agent a mix may carry.

distractors.why_tempting: It is about money, and a reader who converts 'cannot be increased' into 'too expensive' goes straight there.
distractors.why_wrong: The cost there is the price of the mix set against the price of access, not a penalty inside the concrete.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem about raising a quantity points at a penalty that grows with the dose, not at a price on a page.

questions.prompt: an admission that designers are not yet allowed to rely on the effect
questions.evidence_quote: an engineer who specifies a self-healing mix must still design as though it will not heal
questions.explanation: Paragraph G names the second obstacle. Because no accepted standard says what may be assumed, the engineer must design as if the concrete will not heal, so the additive is paid for and its benefit cannot be counted.
questions.trap_note: Thin evidence and an unwritten rule are different things, and they live in different paragraphs.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: not yet allowed to rely on the effect
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: must still design as though it will not heal
paraphrase_link.note: An obligation to ignore the effect is restated as a ban on relying on it - one rule, two sides.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem wants a concession about permission. Only one paragraph states what an engineer is required to assume, and it states it as a rule rather than as a difficulty.

distractors.why_tempting: It says the evidence is thin, which a reader hears as nobody trusting the material yet.
distractors.why_wrong: Thin evidence is a fact about research. It says nothing about what a designer is permitted to assume.

distractors.why_tempting: It admits a genuine design conflict and uses the vocabulary of design throughout.
distractors.why_wrong: The conflict there is inside the capsule, not inside a code of practice.

teaching.reusable_rule: An admission about permission is a rule rather than a doubt. Look for what someone is obliged to assume.

questions.prompt: an example of a repair that works mechanically rather than chemically
questions.evidence_quote: pulls the crack faces back together mechanically, which no chemical method can do
questions.explanation: Paragraph E describes shape-memory tendons. A strand cast into the beam is heated after cracking, contracts, and pulls the crack faces together, and the passage says outright that no chemical method can do this.
questions.trap_note: A repair with no machinery in it is not therefore a mechanical repair.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: mechanically, which no chemical method can do
paraphrase_link.note: A relative clause denying the alternative is restated as a straight contrast in the stem.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem wants a repair that closes a crack by force. Only one paragraph describes a strand contracting; every other method described deposits something or swells.

distractors.why_tempting: It describes a repair with no machinery of any kind, which a reader may take for the opposite of chemical.
distractors.why_wrong: Autogenous healing is chemistry throughout: hydration and carbonation and nothing else.

teaching.reusable_rule: Look for a verb of force when a stem contrasts two kinds of action; the absence of a substance name proves nothing.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

teaching.strategy: Read the stem, answer it in your own words from the paragraph, and only then look at the four options. Three of these stems name their paragraph, so the search is bounded before you begin.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, one paragraph each, running D to G. Question 25 lies below question 24.
teaching.watch_out: Every wrong option here is true of some paragraph. Truth is not the test; answering this stem is.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph D, what makes capsules difficult to design?

options.text: The materials available are too costly to use in bulk.
A shell strong enough to be mixed may not break when needed.
Clay, glass and polymer all react with the alkaline mix.
The spores inside them lose viability within a few years.

questions.evidence_quote: a shell tough enough to survive the mixer is often tough enough to survive the crack as well
questions.explanation: Paragraph D calls this a requirement that works against itself. Toughness is wanted twice over and for opposite reasons: to get through the mixer intact, and to fail at the crack. A shell that does one well tends to do the other badly.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph's other penalty, loss of strength, is a separate problem and not the design difficulty being asked about.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is often tough enough to survive the crack as well
paraphrase_link.note: Surviving the crack and failing to break are the same event described from opposite sides.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what makes the capsule hard to design, and the paragraph answers with a conflict between two requirements. An option naming one requirement alone is not a difficulty.

distractors.why_tempting: Cost is the passage's closing subject, and glass and polymer sound expensive beside gravel.
distractors.why_wrong: This paragraph's penalty is lost strength, not price. Price arrives three paragraphs later.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does say alkalinity destroys spores, and the three shell materials are listed in the very next sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the spores the alkalinity attacks. The shells are what protects them from it.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage gives a figure in decades for how long spores last, so a reader half-remembering it supplies a limit.
distractors.why_wrong: Decades is the figure, and the loss the paragraph describes happens in the mixer rather than in storage.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a stem asks what makes something difficult, look for two demands that cannot both be met.

questions.prompt: What does the writer identify as unique to vascular systems?

options.text: They start to work within hours of a crack appearing.
They can be fitted to a structure that already exists.
They can be refilled and can work more than once.
They leave no soft pore behind once they have dried.

questions.evidence_quote: That is the only approach that can be refilled, and the only one that survives repeated damage in the same place
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says of vascular systems that they are the only approach that can be refilled and the only one that survives repeated damage in the same place. Both halves of the correct option come out of that single sentence.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph describes three systems in three sentences, and two of the wrong options belong to the first of them.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: survives repeated damage in the same place
paraphrase_link.note: Surviving repeated damage is restated as working more than once - the consequence rather than the property.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what is unique, and the paragraph marks exactly one property as exclusive. An option describing something a second system also does answers a different stem.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does say something acts within hours, and speed is the most quotable claim in it.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the superabsorbent polymer, described two sentences earlier.

distractors.why_tempting: A network of tubes sounds like plumbing, and plumbing is normally put into buildings that already stand.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says the reverse: the network must be designed into the structure and cannot be added later.

distractors.why_tempting: The soft pore is the one drawback named in the paragraph, so a reader hunting an advantage takes its absence.
distractors.why_wrong: The pore belongs to the polymer method. Nothing is said about pores in a vascular system at all.

teaching.reusable_rule: A phrase marking exclusivity is the writer's own signal. An option a rival also satisfies answers a different question.

questions.prompt: What point does the writer make about laboratory results?

options.text: The two measures of recovery reported can diverge widely.
Specimens are usually stored in conditions that are too dry.
Cracks are made narrower than those in real structures.
Strength is measured less often than tightness is.

questions.evidence_quote: A specimen can recover almost all of the first and very little of the second.
questions.explanation: Paragraph F separates two currencies of recovery: regained tightness, which matters for durability, and regained strength, which sounds impressive. It then says that a specimen can score almost full marks on one and very low marks on the other.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph mentions storage and crack width, but it argues from neither.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: can recover almost all of the first and very little of the second
paraphrase_link.note: 'Almost all' set against 'very little' is restated as one word naming the gap between them.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the writer's point, and the paragraph's own emphasis falls on the two figures disagreeing. Options about storage or crack width name conditions the paragraph mentions but never argues from.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does say specimens are stored in water, and a reader who inverts that detail produces a plausible criticism.
distractors.why_wrong: Water storage is stated; dryness is not, and the paragraph does not criticise the storage at all.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Cracked to a chosen width' sounds artificial, and artificial is usually taken to mean unrealistically small.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says the width is chosen, never that it is smaller than a real one.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph clearly values one figure above the other, so a reader converts the preference into a frequency.
distractors.why_wrong: Both figures are reported. The passage compares what they mean, never how often each is quoted.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that separates two ways of counting is usually arguing that they disagree.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the writer, does the absence of a standard matter?

options.text: It stops manufacturers from selling the additive at scale.
It obliges designers to pay for a benefit they cannot count.
It leaves owners unsure how often a structure needs checking.
It makes the additive dearer than it would otherwise be.

questions.evidence_quote: must still design as though it will not heal, and pays for the additive without being allowed to bank the benefit
questions.explanation: Paragraph G says that with no accepted standard an engineer must design as if the mix will not heal. The additive is bought and its benefit cannot be entered into the calculation, which is exactly what the missing standard costs.
questions.trap_note: The price premium is real and it is a separate point, made before the standards obstacle is raised.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: pay for a benefit they cannot count
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: pays for the additive without being allowed to bank the benefit
paraphrase_link.note: 'Bank' becomes 'count' and a withheld permission becomes an inability - the same situation from the designer's side.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks why the missing standard matters, and the paragraph answers with one specific cost falling on the designer. Options about price or inspection name consequences the passage never draws.

distractors.why_tempting: A material nobody may rely on sounds like a material nobody can sell.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says engineers do specify it. What they cannot do is take credit for what it does.

distractors.why_tempting: Inspection is the natural subject of a paragraph about expensive access and slow failure.
distractors.why_wrong: Access appears as a reason the technology suits certain structures. Inspection intervals are never mentioned.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens with the price premium of the mix, so the money is already on the page.
distractors.why_wrong: That premium is the material's own cost and has nothing to do with the standard being missing.

teaching.reusable_rule: Ask what the missing thing prevents, then find who bears the loss. That person is usually named.

paragraphs.text: Everything a rocket has ever left in low orbit is still there, or was until it fell. The region between two hundred and two thousand kilometres up holds several thousand working satellites, as many dead ones, several thousand spent stages, and something over a hundred million fragments larger than a millimetre. What makes the fragments dangerous is not their size but their speed. Two objects meeting head-on close at nearly fifteen kilometres a second, and at that speed a fleck of aluminium the size of a grain of rice carries the energy of a grenade. Shielding can be built against the smallest particles. Against anything above about a centimetre nothing useful can be built, and the only defence is to move.

The debris was not mostly made by collisions. Until recently the great majority of catalogued fragments came from explosions: a spent upper stage left in orbit with residual propellant and a charged battery is a pressure vessel that eventually fails, and each failure scatters hundreds of pieces along its own orbit. Two events in the late 2000s changed the arithmetic. One was a deliberate destruction of a satellite by a missile; the other was the first accidental collision between two intact satellites. Between them they added more trackable objects than the previous four decades of spaceflight, at altitudes where the air is too thin to pull them down for centuries.

The theoretical worry is older than either event. The rate at which objects collide rises roughly with the square of how many of them there are, while the rate at which the atmosphere removes them does not, so there is a population above which the debris field feeds itself: fragments produce collisions, collisions produce fragments, and the total climbs even if every launch stops. The cascade, as it is usually called, was set out by the orbital analyst Ruth Delane, who has argued for two decades that certain shells near nine hundred kilometres passed that threshold long ago.

Not everyone reads the models the same way. The aerospace engineer Piotr Renwick accepts the mathematics and rejects the conclusion, since the projections assume nothing changes: no manoeuvring, no disposal, no replacement of a broken satellite by one that leaves when it is finished. The insurance economist Hana Norland is less interested in the physics than in the incentives, and observes that no operator has ever paid for the debris it created, so the models forecast the behaviour of people who face none of the costs. The space lawyer Tomas Verdon notes that an object in orbit remains the property of the state that launched it, whatever condition it is in, so nobody may remove another country's derelict without permission. The astronomer Iris Marlow, whose interest is the sky rather than the traffic, argues that the discussion has been framed too narrowly around collision risk and says nothing about the brightening of the night sky by reflective objects.

Knowing where anything is turns out to be the binding constraint. Ground radar and optical telescopes hold orbits for objects down to about ten centimetres, roughly forty thousand items. Below that size the population is estimated rather than tracked, and it is the untracked centimetre-scale debris that operators fear most, since it can destroy a spacecraft and cannot be avoided. Even for catalogued objects the predictions are coarse: a warning of a close approach arrives days ahead with an uncertainty measured in hundreds of metres, so most warnings are false alarms. Operators manoeuvre anyway, and they are right to, since each burn costs fuel that would have extended the mission but the alternative is losing the spacecraft altogether.

The agreed remedy is to stop adding. Guidelines drawn up in the 1990s ask operators to vent propellant and discharge batteries at end of life, and to remove a satellite from the crowded region within twenty-five years of finishing its work. Both are voluntary, and compliance with the disposal rule has run between a third and two-thirds of eligible missions, improving as regulators have begun attaching the requirement to launch licences. Passivation, the cheaper measure, has been far more widely adopted, and the explosion rate has fallen accordingly.

Removing what is already there is harder in every respect. A derelict stage tumbles, has no fitting designed to be grabbed, and may be leaking. Demonstration missions have caught targets with nets, harpoons and robotic arms, so the engineering is no longer the obstacle; the cost is. A single removal is priced in tens of millions, and the modelling consistently shows that pulling down a handful of the largest, most collision-prone objects each year does more for the long-term population than sweeping up a thousand small ones. I find that conclusion persuasive, and I notice how little it has changed a public conversation still fixed on the image of a vacuum cleaner in space.

What is missing is not technology, and not agreement about the physics. It is a mechanism that makes anybody responsible. A derelict belongs to its launching state and imposes its costs on everyone else, which is the oldest shape in economics. Deposits refunded on disposal, insurance priced against debris, a removal fund: all have been proposed and none adopted. Until one is, the guidelines will do useful work at the margin, and the population will go on being decided by how many satellites are launched rather than by how carefully they are retired.

difficulty_rationale.note: Four named positions arrive in one paragraph without a connective between them, and the writer's own two verdicts are short clauses inside longer sentences. Whose claim is whose is the whole difficulty.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Four specialists, four objections, no signposting, and two of them sound economic while only one is.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A, then the first sentence of D. A tells you the danger; D tells you there is a dispute.
skim_plan.skip: The altitudes and speeds in A and the list of proposals in H. Both are illustrative and no question turns on the figures.

hinge_words.why_here: 'nothing useful can be built' is the absolute that forces the ending in question 36.
'estimated rather than tracked' is the contrast question 39 has to reproduce.

'is not technology, and not agreement' is the negated list that makes question 35 NO.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Match each statement with the person who makes it. NB One of the options is not needed.

options.text: Piotr Renwick
Ruth Delane
Hana Norland
Tomas Verdon
Iris Marlow

teaching.strategy: Four of the five people are introduced by their field before their claim arrives. Read the four labels first - engineer, economist, lawyer, astronomer - and you can place three of these statements before reading a single argument.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, and one letter is never used. Work from the labelled fields, not from the sequence of sentences.
teaching.watch_out: Four of the five appear in one paragraph, so locating them is free. The difficulty is telling two economic-sounding claims apart.

questions.prompt: Existing law prevents one country from clearing up another's abandoned hardware.
questions.evidence_quote: an object in orbit remains the property of the state that launched it, whatever condition it is in, so nobody may remove another country's derelict without permission
questions.explanation: Verdon, introduced as a space lawyer, makes the ownership point: a launched object stays the property of its launching state whatever state it is in, so removal by anyone else requires permission.
questions.trap_note: Two of the five speakers talk about who bears a cost; only one talks about who holds a title.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: prevents one country from clearing up another's
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: nobody may remove another country's derelict without permission
paraphrase_link.note: A conditional permission becomes a flat prohibition - one rule, stated from the opposite end.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement is about what the law forbids, and only one speaker is introduced through law. The others are introduced through engineering, insurance and astronomy.

distractors.why_tempting: The economist also talks about who is left holding something, and a reader hearing 'nobody pays' and 'nobody may remove' treats them as one complaint.
distractors.why_wrong: Her subject is who bears the expense, not who holds the title. Removal never appears in what she says.

distractors.why_tempting: She is the most prominent name in the passage and the only one given a whole paragraph, so unattached statements drift towards her.
distractors.why_wrong: Her claim is about which altitudes have already passed the threshold. She says nothing about ownership.

teaching.reusable_rule: Match the speaker's field to the kind of claim. A legal point belongs to whoever was introduced as a lawyer.

questions.prompt: The forecasts describe conditions that nobody intends to allow to continue.
questions.evidence_quote: the projections assume nothing changes: no manoeuvring, no disposal, no replacement of a broken satellite by one that leaves when it is finished
questions.explanation: Renwick's objection is not to the mathematics, which he accepts, but to what it is fed. The projections hold every practice constant, and none of those practices is being held constant in reality.
questions.trap_note: Accepting the mathematics and rejecting the conclusion is one position, not two.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: nobody intends to allow to continue
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the projections assume nothing changes
paraphrase_link.note: 'Assume nothing changes' is restated from the other side: the conditions assumed are the ones nobody plans to keep.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement attacks the inputs of a model rather than its output. Only one speaker is described as accepting the mathematics and rejecting what it is used to conclude.

distractors.why_tempting: The projections are hers, so a reader who has attached the model to its author attaches the objection to her as well.
distractors.why_wrong: She defends the model's conclusion. The objection is made against her by the speaker introduced next.

distractors.why_tempting: The astronomer also complains about how the problem has been set up, so both sound like objections to a framing.
distractors.why_wrong: Her complaint is that a consequence has been left out. His is that the assumptions are frozen.

teaching.reusable_rule: A speaker who grants the method and denies the result is attacking a premise, not the arithmetic.

questions.prompt: The costs of creating debris have never fallen on those who create it.
questions.evidence_quote: no operator has ever paid for the debris it created, so the models forecast the behaviour of people who face none of the costs
questions.explanation: Norland is introduced as an insurance economist and her point is about incentives. Nobody has ever been billed for what they left behind, so a model of behaviour is modelling people who bear none of the consequences.
questions.trap_note: The lawyer also describes a rule that leaves a burden with the wrong party, but his rule is about property rather than payment.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: fallen on those who create it
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: no operator has ever paid for the debris it created
paraphrase_link.note: Paying and having a cost fall on you are one event told from opposite ends, so the words barely overlap.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement is about who bears an expense, and only one speaker is introduced through money. The lawyer's claim concerns a title, and titles are not costs.

distractors.why_tempting: Property and payment both sound like the language of liability, and his sentence also ends in a burden nobody wants.
distractors.why_wrong: He says who owns a derelict and who may touch it. He says nothing about who pays for one.

distractors.why_tempting: He is the speaker who challenges the models, and this statement also ends in a criticism of what the models represent.
distractors.why_wrong: His criticism is that the assumptions are frozen. Hers is that the people modelled have no reason to change.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a statement is about who bears an expense, look for the speaker introduced through money rather than through science.

questions.prompt: The discussion has left out a consequence that has nothing to do with collisions.
questions.evidence_quote: argues that the discussion has been framed too narrowly around collision risk and says nothing about the brightening of the night sky by reflective objects
questions.explanation: Marlow's interest is the sky rather than the traffic. Her objection is that framing the subject as a collision problem excludes an effect that has no collisions in it at all: tens of thousands of reflective objects lighting the night sky.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: framed too narrowly around collision risk
paraphrase_link.note: Framing something too narrowly and leaving something out are the same complaint stated positively and negatively.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement names an omission rather than an error, and only one speaker is described as objecting to the boundaries of the subject rather than to a claim inside it.

distractors.why_tempting: She works on shells of orbit and altitudes, which is the vocabulary of the sky, so an astronomical statement drifts to her.
distractors.why_wrong: Her subject is when a threshold was crossed. The night sky is somebody else's objection entirely.

distractors.why_tempting: He also objects to the way the question has been set up, and both objections are about what the analysis excludes.
distractors.why_wrong: He objects to what the model assumes. She objects to what the subject was defined as covering.

teaching.reusable_rule: A complaint that a topic was set up to exclude something belongs to whoever works outside it.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer?

teaching.strategy: This writer states a position twice in the first person and rules one out with a negative construction. Find those three places before you start and the group becomes five decisions rather than five searches.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, running E to H. Question 34's answer lies below question 33's.
teaching.watch_out: Two verdicts here are clauses of three or four words inside longer sentences. Do not hold out for a whole sentence of opinion.

questions.prompt: The writer thinks operators are wrong to manoeuvre so often on uncertain warnings.
questions.evidence_quote: Operators manoeuvre anyway, and they are right to
questions.explanation: Paragraph E spends three sentences establishing how coarse the warnings are and then endorses the manoeuvring in four words. The writer's judgement is that the wasted fuel is worth it because the alternative is losing the spacecraft.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the writer's verdict is a four-word clause after a comma, and the paragraph before it reads like a criticism.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Operators manoeuvre anyway, and they are right to
paraphrase_link.note: The statement is the writer's clause with its evaluative word reversed, and nothing else changed.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer's own evaluation is on the page and it is the opposite of the statement. A stated opposite is NO, and it removes NOT GIVEN from consideration.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph dwells on coarse predictions, hundreds of metres of uncertainty and mostly false alarms, which reads for three sentences as a complaint.
distractors.why_wrong: Those sentences describe the difficulty. The clause that evaluates the response comes last and approves of it.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader hunting for a whole sentence of opinion finds only description, because the verdict is four words long.
distractors.why_wrong: The verdict is explicit and first-hand. Length is not what makes an opinion count.

teaching.reusable_rule: A four-word clause can carry a writer's verdict. Do not require a whole sentence of opinion before accepting one.

questions.prompt: The writer expects the disposal rule to become legally binding within a few years.
questions.evidence_quote: improving as regulators have begun attaching the requirement to launch licences
questions.explanation: Paragraph F reports that compliance is improving as regulators attach the requirement to launch licences. It reports a change already under way and makes no prediction about it, here or later.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: a trend pointing in one direction is not a forecast, and the passage never offers one.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: regulators have begun attaching the requirement to launch licences
paraphrase_link.note: The text describes a practice starting; the statement converts it into a completed legal status with a date attached.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the direction of travel is given, but no sentence predicts an outcome or a timescale. Nothing supports the statement and nothing denies it.

distractors.why_tempting: Licence conditions are how rules become binding, so the sentence reads as the first step of exactly the process described.
distractors.why_wrong: A first step is not a forecast. The writer reports what regulators have begun and stops there.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Both are voluntary' is emphatic and sits two sentences earlier, so a reader treats it as a denial that the rule will ever bind.
distractors.why_wrong: That sentence describes the present. It says nothing about what will happen next.

teaching.reusable_rule: A direction of travel is not a forecast. A text that reports a trend has still predicted nothing.
teaching.nearest_text: improving as regulators have begun attaching the requirement to launch licences

questions.prompt: The writer accepts that removing a few large objects is worth more than removing many small ones.
questions.evidence_quote: I find that conclusion persuasive
questions.explanation: Paragraph G reports the modelling result, that a handful of large collision-prone objects a year does more than a thousand small ones, and the writer then endorses it in the first person before turning to how little difference it has made.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: I find that conclusion persuasive
paraphrase_link.note: A first-person endorsement becomes a third-person report of the same endorsement.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer endorses a stated conclusion in the first person, and the statement reproduces that conclusion without strengthening it. Everything is supported, so YES.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens by saying removal is harder in every respect, so a reader takes the whole paragraph as sceptical about removal.
distractors.why_wrong: Difficulty and priority are different claims. The writer's scepticism is about cost, and the endorsement is explicit.

distractors.why_tempting: The endorsement is a short first-person clause, and readers do not expect one in an expository passage.
distractors.why_wrong: A first-person verdict is the clearest evidence of a writer's position that a text can carry.

teaching.reusable_rule: A first-person verdict is the strongest signal of a writer's position. Search for one before answering NOT GIVEN.

questions.prompt: Public interest in the subject has fallen since the cost of removal became known.
questions.evidence_quote: I notice how little it has changed a public conversation still fixed on the image of a vacuum cleaner in space
questions.explanation: Paragraph G gives the price of a removal and, separately, says that the modelling result has changed the public conversation very little. It never says that interest has fallen, and it never connects the two facts.
questions.trap_note: Two facts, one invented link: the price and the state of the conversation are both given, and the passage never joins them.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a public conversation still fixed on the image of a vacuum cleaner
paraphrase_link.note: The text describes what the conversation is about; the statement converts that into how much of it there is.

teaching.decision_rule: Both halves of the statement touch the passage and the join between them does not. A causal claim the text never makes is unsupported and undenied.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer does complain about the public conversation, so any critical statement about the public feels like the same complaint.
distractors.why_wrong: The complaint is that the conversation has the wrong content, not that there is less of it than there was.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Still fixed' asserts continuity, which a reader converts into a denial that anything about the public has changed.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Still fixed' is about what the conversation is about. It makes no claim about the level of interest at all.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two facts side by side are not a cause. A sentence has to say that the one produced the other.
teaching.nearest_text: I notice how little it has changed a public conversation still fixed on the image of a vacuum cleaner in space

questions.prompt: In the writer's view the main obstacle is now a technical one.
questions.evidence_quote: What is missing is not technology, and not agreement about the physics.
questions.explanation: Paragraph H opens by ruling out two candidates and then names the third: what is missing is a mechanism that makes anybody responsible. The writer's answer to the statement is on the page and it is negative.
questions.trap_note: The denial is a negated list with no evaluative verb in it, so a reader hunting an opinion word passes straight over it.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the main obstacle is now a technical one
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: What is missing is not technology
paraphrase_link.note: The statement asserts precisely what the sentence rules out, with the technical term turned into an adjective.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer names what is missing and explicitly excludes technology from the list. That is a stated contradiction, so NO rather than NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous paragraph spends four sentences on how hard a tumbling derelict is to capture, so a reader arriving from it already believes the statement.
distractors.why_wrong: That paragraph says the engineering is no longer the obstacle and the cost is. The next one rules technology out by name.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence that denies the statement carries no evaluative verb, so a reader scanning for the writer's opinion skips it.
distractors.why_wrong: A negated list is a claim. Naming what is missing states a position as clearly as an adjective would.

teaching.reusable_rule: A negated list rules things out. The sentence after it names whatever is left.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete each sentence with the correct ending. There are more endings than sentences.

options.text: abandoned stages had burst under their own stored energy.
the only remaining response is to get out of its way.
their numbers are worked out rather than observed.
it continues to grow with no further launches at all.
it is the less costly of the two things asked for.
regulators had made the requirement a licence condition.
the atmosphere removes them within a decade or so.

teaching.strategy: Read the seven endings once and mark the one the passage flatly contradicts. Then take the stems in order, reading each pair aloud as a whole sentence, because these answers run down the passage from A to F.
teaching.order_note: This is the one matching type that runs in passage order. Use it: each answer sits below the last.
teaching.watch_out: Two endings are true of the passage and complete a different sentence. Truth is not what is being tested here.

questions.prompt: Because a fragment above a centimetre across cannot be shielded against,
questions.evidence_quote: Against anything above about a centimetre nothing useful can be built, and the only defence is to move.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A separates the two size ranges. Shielding works for the smallest particles; above about a centimetre nothing useful can be built, and the passage names moving as the only defence left.
questions.trap_note: The ending about the atmosphere is contradicted by the passage, which says fragments at these altitudes stay for centuries.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: nothing useful can be built
paraphrase_link.note: 'Nothing useful can be built' becomes the passive 'cannot be shielded against', with the shield named instead of the building.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem gives a cause and the ending must be its stated consequence. Only one ending names a response, and the passage marks that response as the only one available.

distractors.why_tempting: It offers a comforting resolution and the atmosphere really is described as removing objects elsewhere in the passage.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says the air at these altitudes is too thin to pull fragments down for centuries, so this ending is contradicted.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the passage's most dramatic consequence and it follows a cause grammatically without any friction.
distractors.why_wrong: Self-sustaining growth is what happens above a population threshold, and it belongs to a different sentence in this set.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a stem states a cause, its ending must be the consequence. A true statement on the topic is still a decoy.

questions.prompt: Until the late 2000s, most catalogued fragments existed because
questions.evidence_quote: a spent upper stage left in orbit with residual propellant and a charged battery is a pressure vessel that eventually fails
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the great majority of catalogued fragments came from explosions rather than collisions, and describes the mechanism: leftover propellant and a charged battery make an abandoned stage into a pressure vessel that eventually bursts.
questions.trap_note: The two events of the late 2000s changed the arithmetic afterwards; the stem asks about the period before them.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the great majority of catalogued fragments came from explosions
paraphrase_link.note: 'The great majority' becomes 'most', and a noun for the source becomes a verb in the ending.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem is fixed to the period before the late 2000s, and only one ending describes what was happening then. The endings about licences and collisions belong to later periods.

distractors.why_tempting: It is true of the passage and it is in the past perfect, which fits the stem's timeframe perfectly.
distractors.why_wrong: Licence conditions arrive in the paragraph about mitigation guidelines and have nothing to do with how fragments were made.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who has decided the passage is about a chain reaction supplies the chain reaction wherever a cause is asked for.
distractors.why_wrong: The cascade is a theoretical mechanism, and the passage explicitly says collisions were not what made most of the debris.

teaching.reusable_rule: Try each ending as a whole sentence before judging its truth. Grammar and time eliminate faster than meaning does.

questions.prompt: Once a debris population passes a certain size,
questions.evidence_quote: there is a population above which the debris field feeds itself
questions.explanation: Paragraph C explains why a threshold exists: collision rate rises with the square of the population while removal by the atmosphere does not. Above that point the total climbs even if every launch stops.
questions.trap_note: The passage says the total climbs even with no further launches, which is stronger than saying launches make it worse.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: there is a population above which the debris field feeds itself
paraphrase_link.note: A relative clause about a threshold population is compressed into a verb phrase about passing a size.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem names a threshold, so the ending must state what happens beyond it. Only one ending describes growth continuing without further input.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the natural opposite and a reader who has half-followed the argument may take the atmosphere as the limiting factor.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph's whole point is that atmospheric removal does not keep pace, and elsewhere it puts the timescale at centuries.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a true statement about a population and it fits the stem's grammar without alteration.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes how small debris is counted, which is a measurement problem rather than a consequence of a threshold.

teaching.reusable_rule: An ending naming a self-sustaining result belongs to a stem that names a threshold, not to one that names a rate.

questions.prompt: Because objects under ten centimetres across are not catalogued,
questions.evidence_quote: Below that size the population is estimated rather than tracked
questions.explanation: Paragraph E puts the tracking limit at about ten centimetres, roughly forty thousand items. Below that the population is estimated rather than tracked, which is why untracked centimetre-scale debris is what operators fear most.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph's other numbers, forty thousand items and hundreds of metres, belong to different claims.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: estimated rather than tracked
paraphrase_link.note: 'Tracked' is the passage's word for catalogued, and the ending keeps the contrast the passage draws around it.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem states the cause and the passage's own contrast supplies the effect in the same clause. Only one ending reproduces that contrast.

distractors.why_tempting: Small objects are exactly the ones a reader assumes the atmosphere clears fastest, so the ending sounds like common sense.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage never says small fragments come down quickly, and it puts the removal timescale at centuries.

distractors.why_tempting: It is true of the passage and, as an explanation of a shortfall, it feels administrative in the same way the stem does.
distractors.why_wrong: Licence conditions govern disposal of satellites, not whether a fragment can be seen from the ground.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a text sets one verb against another in a single clause, that contrast is what an ending must reproduce.

questions.prompt: Passivation has spread more widely than the disposal rule because
questions.evidence_quote: Passivation, the cheaper measure, has been far more widely adopted
questions.explanation: Paragraph F asks operators to do two things: vent propellant and discharge batteries, and remove the satellite within twenty-five years. It then names passivation as the cheaper of the two and says it has been far more widely adopted.
questions.trap_note: The licence ending is true of the passage and it explains the rise in disposal compliance, not the spread of passivation.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: has been far more widely adopted
paraphrase_link.note: An agentless passive becomes an active verb with the practice as subject, hiding the comparison's second term.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the reason behind a comparison, and the passage supplies it in apposition: the cheaper measure. Endings describing the other measure answer a different sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: It is true of the passage, it explains a rise in compliance, and it stands in the same sentence region as the answer.
distractors.why_wrong: Licence conditions are given as the reason disposal compliance improved. They are not the reason passivation spread.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who thinks passivation is about letting things come down naturally will take the atmosphere as its mechanism.
distractors.why_wrong: Passivation is venting propellant and discharging batteries. The passage contradicts the removal timescale in the ending.

teaching.reusable_rule: An ending that is true of the passage may still belong to a different sentence. Check which one it completes.

paragraphs.text: Ask which animals pollinate the crops and the wild plants of a temperate country and almost everyone answers bees. Bees are worth the attention: they are numerous, they are easy to watch, and a hive can be moved to an orchard and counted. But the count is taken during the day, because that is when observers are awake. Moths are harder to study for reasons that have nothing to do with their importance. They fly at night, most species look alike to anyone but a specialist, and they cannot be kept in a box beside an orchard. A different set of insects is at work between dusk and dawn, and until recently almost nobody was counting it.

A moth does not forage like a bee. It has no colony to provision and no store to fill, so it visits flowers for its own fuel and moves on when it has enough. It finds them mainly by smell, following a plume of scent upwind, and the flowers that depend on it advertise accordingly: pale or white petals that show up in low light, a strong sweet odour released after sunset, and a narrow tube of nectar reachable only by a long tongue. Because a moth hovers rather than lands, pollen collects on its head, its legs and the underside of its body, where a casual observer would not think to look.

Counting what happens in the dark has needed three methods, none of them new but all of them recently cheaper. The first is to catch moths at light traps, swab the pollen from their bodies and identify the grains under a microscope, which is slow and demands a specialist. The second, which has changed the field, is to sequence the pollen instead: a short section of plant DNA is enough to name the species it came from, and one machine can process hundreds of samples in a day. The third is to watch. Cameras triggered by movement and lit by infrared record what visits a flower and for how long, without the light that would itself alter the behaviour.

The results have been consistent enough to be surprising. Pollen loads on night-flying moths regularly carry grains from a wider range of plant species than loads taken from daytime visitors in the same field, and marked individuals turn up further from where they were released. Both patterns hold across the studies that have measured them. The two findings fit together, since an insect that ranges widely and visits many species moves pollen between populations that daytime insects keep apart. The night shift is not, on this evidence, a substitute for the day shift. It is a different service, and the plants that receive both do better than the plants that receive either alone.

The pressure that has attracted most attention is light. A streetlight draws moths out of the vegetation and holds them, sometimes for hours, in a column of illumination where they neither feed nor breed. Experiments comparing lit and unlit plots have measured fewer visits to flowers under the lamps and, in several trials, a measurable drop in the seed set of the plants growing there. The effect depends on the lamp. White light with a strong blue component attracts far more insects than the older orange lamps it replaced, which is an unwelcome consequence of a lighting change made for other reasons entirely.

Light is not the largest pressure, however, and the researchers who study it say so themselves. Adult moths need nectar, but a moth population is limited by what its caterpillars can eat, and caterpillars are far fussier than adults. Most species will feed on only a handful of plants, often only one. Hedgerows removed, verges mown before the plants have set seed, and grassland reseeded with a single grass have taken those food plants out of the landscape over sixty years. A garden full of nectar-rich flowers feeds adults very well and adds nothing at all to the next generation.

What follows from this is a set of measures that are cheap rather than dramatic. Lamps can be shielded so that they light the ground and not the hedge, shifted towards the warmer end of the spectrum, and switched off for part of the night, all of which have been done somewhere and none of which costs much. Verges can be cut later and in rotation. None of it will matter unless the caterpillar food comes back, and that is a question about how land is managed rather than about how it is lit. The honest summary is that we know what to stop doing rather more clearly than we know what the benefit will be.

difficulty_rationale.note: Plain vocabulary, short sentences and one qualified claim after another, with the relations between paragraphs left unmarked. Paragraph F reverses the emphasis of paragraph E without announcing that it is doing so.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Two findings are given, then joined, then set against an inference the reader has probably already drawn.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It tells you the subject is what nobody was counting, and why.
skim_plan.skip: The list of flower features in B and the list of lamp measures in G. Both are detail, and one question each needs them.

rewordings: tracking an odour on the breeze
working back along a trail of perfume

paraphrase_families.passage_form: a short section of plant DNA is enough to name the species
rewordings: sequencing settles which plant it was
naming it from its genetic material
