hinge_words.why_here: 'mainly by smell' is the scope question 11 has to keep and not widen.
'in several trials' licenses 'some experiments' in question 9 and nothing stronger.
'not the largest pressure' is the ranking that makes question 10 FALSE.
'only a handful of plants' is the narrowness question 2 turns on.

mineable.meaning: a trail of smell drifting on the air
wipe it off in order to collect it
the pollen an insect is carrying
how many seeds a plant manages to produce
produce ripe seed
a different part each time, in turn

question_groups.instructions_extra: Which paragraph contains the following information? NB You may use any letter more than once.

options.text: Paragraph A
Paragraph B
Paragraph C
Paragraph D
Paragraph E
Paragraph F
Paragraph G

teaching.strategy: Turn each stem into a question about what a paragraph is doing. Two of these five ask for an admission or a comparison, and only one paragraph in the passage performs each of those moves.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, and a letter may repeat. Leave this group until you have read for the other two.
teaching.watch_out: Three of these five ideas appear in more than one paragraph. The stem asks which contains it, not which mentions it.

questions.prompt: a change in method that has made a slow task much faster
questions.evidence_quote: The second, which has changed the field, is to sequence the pollen instead
questions.explanation: Paragraph C sets the microscope method, which is slow and needs a specialist, against sequencing, which the passage says has changed the field and lets one machine process hundreds of samples in a day.
questions.trap_note: The camera method is also new, but the passage does not describe it as replacing anything slow.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: made a slow task much faster
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: one machine can process hundreds of samples in a day
paraphrase_link.note: A throughput figure in the text becomes a comparative about speed in the stem.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem needs a before and an after in the same paragraph. Only one paragraph names an old method, calls it slow, and then names its replacement.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph about what should change, and 'change' is the stem's most prominent word.
distractors.why_wrong: The changes there are to lamps and to mowing, not to a method of counting.

distractors.why_tempting: It describes a lighting change and a consequence, which reads like a change with an effect.
distractors.why_wrong: That change made things worse for moths and had nothing to do with how they are studied.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem naming an improvement wants the paragraph that gives both states, not the one that uses the word.

questions.prompt: a reason why providing food for adult insects is not enough
questions.evidence_quote: A garden full of nectar-rich flowers feeds adults very well and adds nothing at all to the next generation.
questions.explanation: Paragraph F distinguishes what adults need from what limits a population. Adults need nectar, but caterpillars eat a handful of plants or one, so a nectar garden supports the adults and does nothing for the generation after them.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: providing food for adult insects is not enough
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: feeds adults very well and adds nothing at all to the next generation
paraphrase_link.note: Two clauses, one positive and one negative, are compressed into the single judgement 'not enough'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for an insufficiency, which needs a paragraph that grants the benefit and then withholds it. Only one paragraph does both in the same sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph about what a moth eats and where it gets its fuel, so a scanner following the word food lands there.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes how an adult feeds. It never says that feeding adults is insufficient.

distractors.why_tempting: It says none of the measures will matter unless the caterpillar food returns, which sounds like the same insufficiency.
distractors.why_wrong: That sentence is about lighting measures, not about feeding adults.

teaching.reusable_rule: An insufficiency needs one paragraph that grants a benefit and then takes it away. Find both halves before choosing.

questions.prompt: a description of the features that make a flower attractive after dark
questions.evidence_quote: pale or white petals that show up in low light, a strong sweet odour released after sunset, and a narrow tube of nectar reachable only by a long tongue
questions.explanation: Paragraph B lists three features of a moth-pollinated flower: petals pale enough to be seen in low light, a scent released after sunset, and nectar at the bottom of a tube only a long tongue can reach.
questions.trap_note: Another paragraph mentions flowers under lamps, but it describes what happens to visits, not what the flowers look like.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a strong sweet odour released after sunset
paraphrase_link.note: 'After sunset' becomes 'after dark', and three named features become the single category 'attractive'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem wants a list of properties belonging to the flower. Only one paragraph gives properties rather than events.

distractors.why_tempting: It puts flowers and light in the same sentences, which is the stem's own combination of ideas.
distractors.why_wrong: There the light is artificial and the subject is how many visits a flower receives, not what it looks like.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem asking for features wants a paragraph of properties. A paragraph of events answers a different question.

questions.prompt: an admission that the size of the gain is uncertain
questions.evidence_quote: we know what to stop doing rather more clearly than we know what the benefit will be
questions.explanation: Paragraph G ends by conceding the limit of the case it has just made: the measures to stop are clear, and how much they will achieve is not.
questions.trap_note: An earlier paragraph says the results were surprisingly consistent, which is the opposite of an admission of uncertainty.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the size of the gain is uncertain
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: we know what to stop doing rather more clearly than we know what the benefit will be
paraphrase_link.note: A comparison between two degrees of knowledge is restated as a flat statement of uncertainty about one of them.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem wants a concession made by the writer about the writer's own case. Only one paragraph closes by limiting what it has just argued.

distractors.why_tempting: It contains the passage's only other discussion of how strong the evidence is, and the word evidence appears in it.
distractors.why_wrong: It says the results were consistent enough to be surprising, which asserts confidence rather than doubt.

distractors.why_tempting: 'In several trials' is a hedge, and hedged findings feel like uncertainty about the size of an effect.
distractors.why_wrong: That hedge limits how many studies found the drop, not how uncertain the eventual benefit is.

teaching.reusable_rule: A concession is a writer limiting an argument just made. Look at the last sentence of a paragraph before the first.

questions.prompt: a comparison between two kinds of street lighting
questions.evidence_quote: White light with a strong blue component attracts far more insects than the older orange lamps it replaced
questions.explanation: Paragraph E compares the new white lamps with the orange ones they replaced and says the newer kind draws far more insects, which it calls an unwelcome consequence of a change made for other reasons.
questions.trap_note: Another paragraph recommends warmer lamps, but recommending is not comparing.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the older orange lamps it replaced
paraphrase_link.note: The stem counts two lamp types where the text names one, so the other is inferred from 'replaced'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem wants a stated comparison with both terms present. Only one paragraph puts two lamp types in one sentence and ranks them.

distractors.why_tempting: It names a spectrum shift for lamps, which a reader takes as a contrast between two kinds.
distractors.why_wrong: It recommends a direction of change without comparing what the two kinds actually do.

teaching.reusable_rule: A comparison needs both terms and a ranking word in one sentence. A recommendation supplies neither.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage?

teaching.strategy: These five run A, B, D, E, F, roughly one paragraph apart. Two of them turn on a single quantifier and one on a single negative, so mark those words in the statement before you look for the sentence.
teaching.order_note: In passage order. Once you have found question 8's sentence, question 9's is below it.
teaching.watch_out: Two statements share almost no vocabulary with the sentence that decides them. Absence of matching words is not absence of information.

questions.prompt: Bees pollinate more plants in temperate countries than any other group of insects.
questions.evidence_quote: Ask which animals pollinate the crops and the wild plants of a temperate country and almost everyone answers bees.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A reports what people say when asked, and then gives three reasons why bees are studied more. It never states how much of the pollination any group actually does, and no later paragraph ranks them either.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the paragraph is clearly about bees and clearly about pollination, and it still makes no claim about totals.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the crops and the wild plants of a temperate country
paraphrase_link.note: The topic matches exactly; what has no counterpart in the text is the ranking the statement adds to it.

teaching.decision_rule: The subject is addressed and the quantity is not. No sentence gives any group a share of the pollination, so there is nothing to confirm and nothing to deny.

distractors.why_tempting: Almost everyone answers bees, the passage says they are numerous, and most readers already believe the statement before they open the text.
distractors.why_wrong: What people answer is a fact about people. The passage never counts what bees actually pollinate.

distractors.why_tempting: The whole passage argues that moths have been overlooked, so a reader primed for a correction reads the statement as the mistake being corrected.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says the night shift is a different service, not a larger one. It denies no ranking because it offers none.

teaching.reusable_rule: A text can be entirely about a subject and still say nothing about how much. Check for the quantity, not the topic.
teaching.nearest_text: Ask which animals pollinate the crops and the wild plants of a temperate country and almost everyone answers bees.

questions.prompt: A moth carries pollen on parts of its body that an observer might not think to check.
questions.evidence_quote: pollen collects on its head, its legs and the underside of its body, where a casual observer would not think to look
questions.explanation: Paragraph B explains that a moth hovers rather than landing, so pollen gathers on the head, the legs and the underside, and it adds that a casual observer would not think to look there.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: would not think to look
paraphrase_link.note: One verb is swapped and one modal softened; nothing about the claim changes.

teaching.decision_rule: Every element of the statement appears in one clause of the passage, including the observer and the failure to look. Nothing is added, so TRUE.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is mostly about how a moth finds flowers, so a reader skimming for a claim about pollen finds the hovering and stops.
distractors.why_wrong: The clause about the observer is the last thing in the paragraph and it states the claim outright.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement's verb, 'check', appears nowhere in the passage, so a keyword search fails.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Look' and 'check' are the same act here, and the rest of the clause matches word for word.

teaching.reusable_rule: A swapped verb is the cheapest disguise there is. Read the clause for its meaning before deciding a match is missing.

questions.prompt: The evidence suggests that moths do the work daytime insects would otherwise do.
questions.evidence_quote: The night shift is not, on this evidence, a substitute for the day shift.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says explicitly that on this evidence the night shift is not a substitute for the day shift, and adds that it is a different service and that plants receiving both do better than plants receiving either alone.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial is a single negative in the middle of a sentence whose two halves both look like agreement.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: do the work daytime insects would otherwise do
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: not, on this evidence, a substitute for the day shift
paraphrase_link.note: 'Substitute' is glossed by what a substitute does, and the passage's negative has to be carried across with it.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage addresses the relation between the two groups and states the opposite of the statement in one clause. That is a contradiction, so FALSE rather than NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does say moths visit more species and travel further, which reads like doing more of the same job.
distractors.why_wrong: Doing more of something is not doing it instead. The next sentence rules the substitution out by name.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'substitute' is one the reader has to translate, and the sentence around it is short and easy to skim past.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the passage's own summary of what the findings do and do not mean, and it is unambiguous.

teaching.reusable_rule: One negative in the middle of a sentence can reverse everything around it. Read it out slowly before deciding.

questions.prompt: Some experiments have recorded fewer seeds on plants growing under street lighting.
questions.evidence_quote: in several trials, a measurable drop in the seed set of the plants growing there
questions.explanation: Paragraph E reports that experiments comparing lit and unlit plots measured fewer visits under the lamps and, in several of them, a measurable drop in the seed set of the plants growing there.
questions.trap_note: The statement keeps the passage's quantifier: 'some' matches 'several' and claims nothing about the rest.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a measurable drop in the seed set
paraphrase_link.note: 'A drop in the seed set' becomes the plain comparative 'fewer seeds', and the technical phrase is what hides it.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement's quantifier is no stronger than the passage's, and the effect it names is the one the passage measured. Everything is supported, so TRUE.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph's main finding is fewer visits, so a reader fixed on visits treats a claim about seeds as unsupported.
distractors.why_wrong: The seed measurement is in the same sentence, introduced by 'and'.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Seed set' is a technical phrase, and a reader hunting for the word 'seeds' on its own may not recognise it.
distractors.why_wrong: Seed set is how many seeds a plant produces, and the passage says it dropped.

teaching.reusable_rule: Match the quantifier first. A statement that claims no more than the text claims has nothing left to be wrong about.

questions.prompt: The scientists who study artificial light regard it as the greatest threat to moths.
questions.evidence_quote: Light is not the largest pressure, however, and the researchers who study it say so themselves.
questions.explanation: Paragraph F opens by ranking the pressures and attributes the ranking to the very people who work on light. The rest of the paragraph gives the reason: what limits a population is the food its caterpillars can eat.
questions.trap_note: The statement gets the researchers right and their view exactly backwards.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: not the largest pressure
paraphrase_link.note: The superlative survives the paraphrase and the negative in front of it is what the statement drops.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage attributes a ranking to these researchers and the statement reverses it. A stated opposite is FALSE, and the attribution is explicit rather than inferred.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous paragraph is entirely about light and it is the longest treatment of any pressure in the passage.
distractors.why_wrong: Space given is not importance claimed. The next paragraph opens by denying the ranking.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement is about what scientists think, and readers expect opinions to be reported in a quotation rather than a clause.
distractors.why_wrong: 'The researchers who study it say so themselves' attributes the view directly and unambiguously.

teaching.reusable_rule: The amount of space a topic gets is not a claim about its importance. Look for the sentence that ranks.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Answer the questions below using words from the passage.

teaching.strategy: Each question begins with a word that fixes the form of the answer: what kind of thing, what material, what must return. Decide the shape of the answer before you look, and take no more words than the question asks for.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, running B, C, G. Nothing above question 11's sentence can answer question 13.
teaching.watch_out: Three words are allowed and one or two are wanted. Padding an answer with an article throws the mark away.

questions.prompt: What do moths mainly use to find flowers?
questions.evidence_quote: It finds them mainly by smell, following a plume of scent upwind
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says a moth finds flowers mainly by smell, following a plume of scent upwind. The question keeps the passage's own quantifier, so the answer is the sense named after it.
questions.trap_note: 'Scent' is in the next clause and describes what is followed, not the sense that does the finding.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: What do moths mainly use to find flowers
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: It finds them mainly by smell
paraphrase_link.note: A pronoun and an object are made explicit in the question, which is why the sentence looks unfamiliar at first.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks for a means, and the passage supplies one in a 'by' phrase. The noun governed by that preposition is the answer and nothing longer is wanted.

distractors.why_tempting: It is three words, exactly the limit, and it sits in the same sentence as the answer.
distractors.why_wrong: That is what the moth follows once it is on a trail. What it uses is the sense named before it.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph mentions pale petals showing up in low light, so a reader adds vision to be safe.
distractors.why_wrong: The petals are described from the flower's side. The passage names one sense for the moth and qualifies it with 'mainly'.

teaching.reusable_rule: Answer with the shortest phrase that answers the question. Extra words that are true will still lose the mark.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What do they use' wants a bare noun, with no article in front of it.

questions.prompt: What kind of material is sequenced in order to name the plant a pollen grain came from?
questions.evidence_quote: a short section of plant DNA is enough to name the species it came from
questions.explanation: Paragraph C describes the second method: instead of examining grains under a microscope, the pollen is sequenced, and a short section of plant DNA identifies the species it came from.
questions.trap_note: The passage says the pollen is sequenced; what is read in the sequence is the plant's own genetic material.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: name the plant a pollen grain came from
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: name the species it came from
paraphrase_link.note: 'Species' becomes 'plant' and the pronoun is spelled out, so the sentence is recognised by shape.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks what kind of material, so the answer is a substance and not a process. Only one noun phrase in the paragraph names a substance that is read.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage literally says the pollen is sequenced, so it looks like the direct answer to the question.
distractors.why_wrong: The question asks what kind of material carries the identification, and the passage names that separately.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the phrase immediately before the answer and it sounds like a technical unit.
distractors.why_wrong: It says how much is needed, not what it is made of.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a question asks what kind of material, the answer names a substance. A verb phrase cannot be one.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What kind of material' wants a noun phrase naming a substance, not a process.

questions.prompt: According to the final paragraph, what must return before the other measures will matter?
questions.evidence_quote: None of it will matter unless the caterpillar food comes back
questions.explanation: Paragraph G lists cheap measures for lamps and verges and then makes them conditional: none of it will matter unless the caterpillar food comes back, which is a question about land management rather than lighting.
questions.trap_note: The condition arrives after 'unless', in the second half of the sentence.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: comes back
paraphrase_link.note: 'Comes back' becomes 'must return', and the question adds an obligation the passage expresses as a condition.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks for the subject of a condition, so the answer is the noun phrase governed by 'unless'. Nothing before that conjunction can supply it.

distractors.why_tempting: It appears earlier in the paragraph and it is exactly the sort of thing that could come back to a landscape.
distractors.why_wrong: The hedge appears as something a shielded lamp should not light. The condition names something else.

distractors.why_tempting: It is what most readers assume a moth needs, and it is named in the previous paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says a garden of those feeds adults and adds nothing to the next generation.

teaching.reusable_rule: A question about a condition is answered after the conjunction, never before it.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What must return' wants the noun phrase that is the subject of the verb after 'unless'.

paragraphs.text: A great deal of the energy a country uses ends as warmth that nobody wants. It leaves through cooling towers, exhaust stacks, ventilation grilles and the back of every refrigerator, and in most industrial economies the total is larger than the amount of heat used to warm buildings. The obstacle is not quantity. It is temperature. Heat is only useful at or above the temperature you need it at, and most waste heat leaves at thirty or forty degrees, which is warmer than a room and far too cool to send down a pipe to one. The arithmetic that follows from that single fact governs everything about the systems built to recover it, and explains why a country can throw away more heat than it uses and still find recovery hard.

A heat network is the machine for moving it. Insulated pipes carry hot water from a central source out to buildings and back again, and each building has a substation, a heat exchanger about the size of a wardrobe, in place of a boiler. The temperature the network runs at governs almost everything else about it. The first systems, laid in the middle of the last century, circulated water above ninety degrees, which made them simple to design and expensive to run, since every metre of pipe loses heat in proportion to how much hotter it is than the ground around it. Modern networks run cooler, and the newest designs circulate water at little more than the temperature of the soil and let each building lift it as required.

Once the network temperature falls, sources that were useless become usable. Sewers hold water that rarely drops below twelve degrees even in winter, and a heat exchanger set into a large sewer can serve several hundred flats. A data centre rejects almost all the electricity it draws as warm air, continuously and predictably, which is the profile a network likes best. Metro tunnels accumulate heat from braking trains. Supermarket refrigeration, flue gas from a bakery, the cooling water of a small foundry: none of these is a large source by itself. The point is not that any one of them is impressive but that a network can take several at once, and that a mixture is steadier than any single supply.

Most of them need a heat pump to be worth anything. A heat pump moves heat from a cooler place to a warmer one using electricity, and its efficiency is the ratio of heat delivered to electricity consumed. That ratio depends almost entirely on the lift, the gap between the temperature of the source and the temperature required. Raise water from twelve degrees to fifty and the machine may deliver four units of heat for one of electricity. Raise it to eighty and the same machine may deliver barely two. This is the argument for running a network cool: it is not the pipes that benefit most, it is the pumps.

The economics are decided in the trench. Pipework is the dominant cost of a heat network, and it is a cost per metre, so what matters is how much heat is sold along each metre of route. Planners call this the linear heat density, and it explains the geography of the technology: terraces, tower blocks, hospitals and university campuses are viable, and streets of detached houses with large gardens are not, whatever the ambitions of the people living in them. The same arithmetic explains why new districts are cheaper to serve than old ones. Laying pipe into a street that has already been built costs several times what it costs to lay it before the street exists.

The customer's position is unusual and it is not always comfortable. A household connected to a heat network cannot change supplier, because the pipe goes to one place and a second network to the same street would be absurd. It is a natural monopoly at the scale of a few streets, and it has often been built without the regulation that other monopolies attract. The complaints that follow are consistent across countries: prices that rise faster than the alternatives, long outages with no obligation to compensate, and standing charges that make a small flat expensive to heat. Regulation has arrived in several places, late, and mostly after the complaints.

The constraint that decides most schemes is duller than any of this. A network is a fifty-year asset and the source has to be there for most of that time. A data centre may be rebuilt or moved within fifteen years; a factory may close; a sewer will not. Schemes that have lasted are the ones built on a source nobody can take away, or on enough separate sources that losing one is survivable. That is a planning judgement rather than an engineering one, and it is the reason a technology with no scientific difficulty at all has spread so unevenly. The lesson drawn by the engineers who have built them is that the pipe is the easy part.

difficulty_rationale.note: Two quantities do most of the work here, the lift and the heat sold per metre, and both are defined once and then used as though familiar. The prose is plain and the bookkeeping is not.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It defines a ratio, then the quantity the ratio depends on, then illustrates both with figures running in two directions.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It gives you the one fact the rest of the passage is arithmetic about.
skim_plan.skip: The list of small sources in C and the list of complaints in F. Both are examples and no question turns on the items.

paraphrase_families.passage_form: far too cool to send down a pipe
rewordings: not warm enough to be worth moving

paraphrase_families.passage_form: the gap between the temperature of the source and the temperature required
rewordings: how far the heat must be raised
the span between input and output
the climb the machine has to make

paraphrase_families.passage_form: how much heat is sold along each metre of route
rewordings: the yield of every metre laid
revenue for each metre in the ground
is locked in to the operator

hinge_words.why_here: 'only useful at or above' is the constraint that question 14's heading is built on.
'depends almost entirely on the lift' is the near-absolute question 17 has to match.
'several times what it costs' is the quantified comparison behind question 18.
'cannot change supplier' is the impossibility question 25 copies word for word.

question_groups.instructions_extra: There are more headings than paragraphs, so you will not use them all. Paragraphs F and G are not included.

options.text: Plenty of it, at the wrong heat
The pipes, and the temperature in them
Sources that only now make sense
Why the lift decides the gain
Why the trench settles the map
A customer who is unable to leave
The source that has to stay put
Fifty years of falling demand

teaching.strategy: Two of the eight headings belong to paragraphs the group excludes, so they are decoys by design. Place A and E first: each states its whole point in a sentence of six or seven words near the top.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, so read all five paragraphs. Nothing bounds the search on this type.
teaching.watch_out: Temperature appears in four of these five paragraphs. A heading about temperature belongs to the paragraph temperature is the subject of.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.evidence_quote: The obstacle is not quantity. It is temperature.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A establishes that there is more waste heat than there is demand for heating, and then names the real problem in two short sentences: not how much of it there is, but how cool it is.
questions.trap_note: Temperature is named here, but as a problem rather than as a design variable.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: far too cool to send down a pipe
paraphrase_link.note: The text names the direction of the fault and the heading names only that there is one.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph makes a quantity claim and then withdraws it as the point. A heading has to carry both halves, the abundance and the disqualifying temperature.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends on a pipe and a temperature, which is the exact pairing the pipes heading names.
distractors.why_wrong: The pipe appears here as an illustration of why the heat is useless. The paragraph about networks comes next.

distractors.why_tempting: A paragraph about a quantity going to waste sounds like an accounting story told over time.
distractors.why_wrong: No period of time appears in the paragraph and no demand is said to be falling anywhere in the passage.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph names a false problem and then the real one, the heading has to hold both.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence_quote: The temperature the network runs at governs almost everything else about it.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes the machine and then makes one claim about it: the operating temperature decides everything else. The history of hot early systems and cool modern ones is there to demonstrate that claim.
questions.trap_note: The heading about the lift is also about temperature deciding an outcome, but the lift is a heat-pump quantity introduced later.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The temperature the network runs at
paraphrase_link.note: A relative clause becomes a prepositional phrase, and the network becomes the pipes that carry it.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's controlling sentence names one variable as decisive, and everything after it is evidence for that. A heading naming the machine alone omits the argument.

distractors.why_tempting: This paragraph is about a temperature that decides an outcome, which is exactly what that heading promises.
distractors.why_wrong: The lift is the gap a heat pump has to bridge, and it is defined two paragraphs later.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who has not yet placed the first heading may put it here, since this paragraph also contrasts hot and cool water.
distractors.why_wrong: The contrast here is between two network designs, not between supply and usefulness.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that names one variable as decisive is arguing, not describing. Take the variable into the heading.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence_quote: Once the network temperature falls, sources that were useless become usable.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C opens with the condition and the consequence in one sentence, and the rest of it is a list of the sources that the condition brings into play, ending on why a mixture of them is better than any one.
questions.trap_note: One heading names a source and its durability, which is a subject the passage takes up in its final paragraph.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: sources that were useless become usable
paraphrase_link.note: A change of state in the text becomes a point in time in the heading, carried by the word 'now'.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph exists to list what a condition makes possible, and its first sentence states that. A heading naming one property of one source describes a sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is a list of sources, and this is the only other heading with the word source in it.
distractors.why_wrong: Whether a source lasts is the subject of the final paragraph, which this group does not cover.

distractors.why_tempting: The opening clause is about network temperature, which is the pipes heading's own subject.
distractors.why_wrong: Here the temperature is a condition on the list that follows, not the paragraph's topic.

teaching.reusable_rule: A shared noun between a heading and a paragraph proves nothing. Ask what the paragraph does with the noun.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence_quote: That ratio depends almost entirely on the lift, the gap between the temperature of the source and the temperature required.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D defines the heat pump, defines the ratio that measures it, and then names the single quantity that ratio turns on. The two worked figures are there to show how much difference the lift makes.
questions.trap_note: Two figures appear here and neither is the paragraph's point; the point is what the figures depend on.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: That ratio depends almost entirely on the lift
paraphrase_link.note: Depending on something and being decided by it are the same relation read from opposite ends.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's controlling claim is a dependency, and it is stated once and then illustrated twice. A heading naming the machine or the numbers misses the dependency.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph closes by drawing a conclusion about how a network should be run, which sounds like a claim about pipes.
distractors.why_wrong: That sentence explicitly says it is the pumps rather than the pipes that benefit.

distractors.why_tempting: The whole paragraph is about heat at temperatures that need raising, which is the wrong-heat idea again.
distractors.why_wrong: The first paragraph states the problem; this one gives the machine that answers it and the quantity governing the answer.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a paragraph states a dependency once and illustrates it twice, the dependency is the heading.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence_quote: The economics are decided in the trench.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E derives the geography of the technology from one cost structure. Because the dominant cost is per metre, what matters is heat sold per metre, and that decides which kinds of street can be served at all.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph names who can and cannot be connected, which is not the same as what happens to those who are.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The economics are decided in the trench
paraphrase_link.note: 'Decided' becomes 'settles', and 'the geography of the technology' is compressed into the single word 'map'.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph runs a cost structure through to a spatial conclusion, and both ends are needed. A heading naming only the cost, or only the geography, carries half of it.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about households and which of them can be served, so a heading about the customer looks close.
distractors.why_wrong: What happens to a connected customer is the next paragraph. This one is about whether connection is affordable.

distractors.why_tempting: The closing sentences are about new and old districts, which sounds like something staying or not staying.
distractors.why_wrong: They compare the cost of laying pipe before and after a street exists, and say nothing about a source enduring.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph reasons from money to a map, the heading names the step, not either end.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the table below using words and figures from the passage.

layout.title: Figures quoted in the passage
rows: heat pump lifting water to fifty degrees
delivers about {{19}} units of heat per unit of electricity
heat pump lifting water to eighty degrees
a heat exchanger the size of a {{22}}

teaching.strategy: Two of these rows come from the paragraph about the network itself and two from the paragraph about heat pumps. Read the whole table first and assign each row to a paragraph, because the table does not present them in the order the passage does.
teaching.order_note: Two paragraphs only, and the rows run backwards through them. Locate both before filling anything in.
teaching.watch_out: This table deliberately runs against the passage: rows three and four are found earlier in the text than rows one and two.

questions.prompt: A heat pump lifting water to fifty degrees delivers about {{gap}} units of heat per unit of electricity.
questions.evidence_quote: the machine may deliver four units of heat for one of electricity
questions.explanation: Paragraph D works the example twice. Raising water from twelve degrees to fifty gives about four units of heat for one of electricity; raising it to eighty gives barely two.
questions.trap_note: Two figures for the same machine sit in consecutive sentences, and only the temperature in the row tells them apart.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: for one of electricity

paragraphs.text: More is recorded now than at any time in history, and less of it can be read than at any time since paper. The phrase usually reached for is the digital dark age, and it does real damage, because it suggests a single catastrophe that will arrive rather than a slow attrition that is already under way. Nothing is going to go dark. Material is going to become gradually more expensive to retrieve until, for most of it, nobody pays. The distinction matters because the two stories point at different work. A catastrophe calls for a rescue; attrition calls for a budget line that nobody has to defend again each year.

Three failures are routinely run together and they have nothing in common. The first is the medium: a disc oxidises, a tape stretches, a drive fails, and the bits are simply gone. The second is the format: the bits survive perfectly and no software will open them, because the program that wrote them was withdrawn and its specification was never published. The third is the hardest and the least discussed. A file arrives with no record of who made it, when, from what, or why, and it becomes unreadable in a sense no amount of engineering can repair, because what is missing is not the data but the account of what the data is.

Two strategies compete for the second problem. Migration converts a collection into a current format at intervals, which keeps it openable and loses something at every conversion, since no two formats encode the same thing in the same way. Emulation preserves the original files and rebuilds the environment that read them, which is faithful and expensive and pushes the problem back a layer, because an emulator is itself software that will need preserving. Practitioners argue about the balance and agree on the principle: whichever is chosen has to be chosen repeatedly, and an archive that has not converted or rebuilt anything for twenty years is not a stable archive but an unopened one.

The routine work is unglamorous and mostly arithmetic. Every file is checksummed when it arrives, and the checksum is recalculated on a schedule so that silent corruption announces itself before it spreads into the backups. Copies are held in several places, on different kinds of storage, under different administrators, on the principle that failures which are independent are survivable and failures which are correlated are not. Audits check that the copies still match, that the media are still readable and that somebody still knows the password. None of this is difficult. All of it has to continue. The discipline of it is the whole of it, and the failure mode is not a dramatic loss but a year in which nobody ran the check.

That last sentence is where the money is. Building an archive is a project with an end, and every institution knows how to fund a project. Keeping one is an obligation with no end, and the accounting instruments for that are poor. Endowment models exist, in which a sum is set aside whose income covers storage for ever, and they depend on assumptions about return and about the cost of storage decades ahead that no one can defend for long. Costs per terabyte have fallen for thirty years, which invites the assumption that they will keep falling and that the problem solves itself. The staff costs have not fallen at all, and in a mature archive they are most of the bill.

It follows that nothing can be kept indiscriminately, and the profession has always known it. Appraisal, the deliberate decision about what is worth the cost, is the oldest skill in archives and the one that transfers least comfortably to material arriving by the terabyte. The web is the extreme case. A crawl is a sample, taken at an interval, of pages that change between visits, and what it captures is neither the site as it was on any particular day nor the site as its readers experienced it. That is a genuine limitation and not a fault of the crawlers, and it is routinely misdescribed as one.

Opinions differ about what to do with that. The archivist Helen Ashfield argues that the discipline's habit of describing every gap as a technical shortfall has been costly, because it invites solutions that are engineering rather than editorial and postpones the selection decisions that actually determine what survives. The computer scientist Adam Sandmouth takes the opposite line: format specifications should simply be deposited by law when software is sold, which he says would dissolve the second failure entirely. The economist Nadia Brackenfield is unimpressed by both, and points out that the binding cost is neither format nor selection but the wage of the person who checks the checksums, which no legislation and no appraisal policy reduces.

Ashfield seems to me plainly right, and Brackenfield's objection does not weaken her case so much as price it. What is preserved will be what somebody chose to preserve and went on paying for, which has been the condition of every archive that has ever existed and is not made new by the technology. The digital difference is speed. A neglected paper collection deteriorates over a century and can be rescued in its eightieth year. A neglected digital collection is unreadable in fifteen and there is nothing left to rescue.

difficulty_rationale.note: The passage classifies, compares, then adjudicates between three named positions, and the writer's verdict is one clause of one sentence. Almost nothing here is concrete enough to scan for.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Three failures are distinguished in one paragraph, and the third is defined by what is absent rather than by anything that breaks.

layout.title: Three failures and two strategies
lines: When the medium itself fails, the content is {{27}} and no software can help.
A format failure leaves the bits intact but the program that read them has been {{28}}.
The third failure removes the {{29}} that explains what a file is and where it came from.
Emulation is more {{30}} than migration, but it pushes the problem back a layer.
Whichever strategy is used, the choice has to be {{31}} at intervals.

teaching.strategy: Every gap comes from the two paragraphs that classify the failures and compare the strategies. Sort the bank by word class before you read: three of the eight name things and five describe a state, which halves the work at every gap.
teaching.order_note: One section only, paragraphs B and C, and in order. Find them once, then work down inside them.
teaching.watch_out: Bank words are the examiner's synonyms, not the passage's wording. Do not expect to find any of these eight in the text.

bank_analysis.why_wrong: It borrows the word stable from the next clause, and it describes the archive rather than the choice.
It names what somebody would attempt after a loss, where the frame wants the state the content is in.
It is a noun in a frame that wants a participle, and the failure described is in the software.

questions.prompt: When the medium itself fails, the content is {{gap}} and no software can help.
questions.evidence_quote: a disc oxidises, a tape stretches, a drive fails, and the bits are simply gone
questions.explanation: Paragraph B's first failure is physical. When the disc, tape or drive goes, the bits themselves are gone, and nothing that could be done to a file afterwards is relevant because there is no file.
questions.trap_note: One bank word names the process that would be attempted after a loss rather than the state the content is in.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the bits are simply gone
paraphrase_link.note: 'The bits' becomes the category word 'content', and the bank supplies a stronger verb for 'gone'.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows a copular verb, so it wants a state and not an action. Only the words describing what has happened to the content survive that test.

distractors.why_tempting: Losing a disc is exactly the situation in which somebody would attempt one, and the word sits comfortably beside media failure.
distractors.why_wrong: It names a process, and the gap follows 'is', which wants a state. It also says nothing about what the content now is.

distractors.why_tempting: The line is about a disc, a tape and a drive, which are the obvious examples of it.
distractors.why_wrong: The hardware is what failed. The gap describes what happened to the content as a result.

teaching.reusable_rule: After a copular verb the space wants a state. A word naming an action cannot fill it however well it fits the topic.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'is' before the gap wants a participle or adjective describing a state.

questions.prompt: A format failure leaves the bits intact but the program that read them has been {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: the program that wrote them was withdrawn and its specification was never published
questions.explanation: Paragraph B's second failure leaves the data untouched and removes the means of reading it. The program was withdrawn and its specification never published, so nothing can be built to replace it.
questions.trap_note: The bits are explicitly said to survive, which rules out every bank word describing a loss of content.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the program that wrote them
paraphrase_link.note: Writing and reading are the same relation from opposite ends, and swapping them is what makes the line look unfamiliar.

teaching.decision_rule: The line concedes that the bits survive, so the gap must describe something that happened to the software rather than to the data.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the strongest word in the bank and this line is about a failure, so a reader working quickly reaches for it.
distractors.why_wrong: The line says the bits are intact. Nothing has been destroyed here except the ability to open them.

distractors.why_tempting: A program that will not run is often assumed to need a particular machine, so the equipment word feels adjacent.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a noun where the frame wants a participle, and the passage attributes the failure to the software.

teaching.reusable_rule: A line that concedes one thing survives has ruled out every option describing its loss. Use the concession.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'has been' before the gap wants a past participle.

questions.prompt: The third failure removes the {{gap}} that explains what a file is and where it came from.
questions.evidence_quote: what is missing is not the data but the account of what the data is
questions.explanation: Paragraph B's third failure is the loss of context. The file survives and the record of who made it, when, from what and why does not, so what is gone is the account of what the data is.
questions.trap_note: This is the one gap in the summary that wants a noun rather than a description of a state.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: explains what a file is and where it came from
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the account of what the data is
paraphrase_link.note: The passage's noun for the missing thing becomes a relative clause saying what that thing does.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows a definite article and precedes a relative clause, so it takes a noun. Only three bank words are nouns and only one of them can explain anything.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a noun, it fits the article, and the paragraph is about something being lost.
distractors.why_wrong: A process of getting something back cannot be the thing that explains where a file came from.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other noun in the bank and readers associate missing context with missing equipment.
distractors.why_wrong: Equipment cannot explain a file's origin, and the passage locates this failure entirely away from machinery.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a space sits between an article and a relative clause, only a noun will fit, and the clause says which noun.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'the' before the gap and 'that explains' after it force a singular noun.

questions.prompt: Emulation is more {{gap}} than migration, but it pushes the problem back a layer.
questions.evidence_quote: which is faithful and expensive and pushes the problem back a layer
questions.explanation: Paragraph C sets the two strategies against each other. Migration loses something at every conversion, while emulation keeps the original files and rebuilds the environment around them, which the passage calls faithful, expensive, and a way of moving the problem rather than removing it.
questions.trap_note: The comparison is the reader's to build: the passage praises one method and criticises the other in separate sentences.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: pushes the problem back a layer
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: pushes the problem back a layer
paraphrase_link.note: The clause is carried across unchanged, which is what marks this line as being about emulation and not about migration.

teaching.decision_rule: The comparative frame wants a quality one method has more of. The passage attaches exactly one favourable quality to emulation and it is the one it names first.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph's closing sentence uses the word stable, and a reader who half-remembers it reaches for its opposite here.
distractors.why_wrong: That word describes an archive nobody has converted, and it is negative where this frame wants a merit.

distractors.why_tempting: Repetition is the paragraph's real conclusion and it is a plausible thing for one method to require more of.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says repetition applies whichever method is chosen, so it cannot distinguish them.

teaching.reusable_rule: A comparative frame wants a quality one side has more of. An option true of both sides cannot fill it.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'more' before the gap and 'than' after it want an adjective, not a noun.

questions.prompt: Whichever strategy is used, the choice has to be {{gap}} at intervals.
questions.evidence_quote: whichever is chosen has to be chosen repeatedly
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says practitioners argue about the balance and agree on the principle: whichever strategy is chosen has to be chosen repeatedly, and an archive that has done nothing for twenty years is not stable but unopened.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: has to be chosen repeatedly
paraphrase_link.note: The text's adverb becomes a participle in the bank, which is why the word is absent from the passage.

teaching.decision_rule: The frame takes a past participle describing what happens to the choice, and only one bank word turns the passage's adverb into that form.

distractors.why_tempting: The next clause of the passage contains the word stable, and its opposite fits this frame grammatically.
distractors.why_wrong: It would describe the archive rather than the choice, and it makes the sentence say the opposite of the paragraph's principle.

teaching.reusable_rule: A bank word rarely appears in the text. Convert the passage's adverb into the form the frame demands and then look for it.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'has to be' before the gap wants a past participle.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer?

teaching.strategy: The writer states three verdicts in this stretch and each is a short clause: one about how hard the routine work is, one about whose fault a limitation is, and one about which of two specialists is right. Find those three and the group is half done.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, running D to H, one paragraph per question. Nothing above question 34's sentence answers question 35.
teaching.watch_out: Two of these statements are about what somebody achieved or adopted, and the passage only ever describes what they proposed or assumed.

questions.prompt: The writer regards the routine checking work as technically demanding.
questions.evidence_quote: None of this is difficult. All of it has to continue.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D describes checksums, replication and audits and then grades the whole set in two short sentences. It is not the technical content that is the problem; it is that the work never stops.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the verdict is a four-word sentence following a paragraph dense with technical vocabulary.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: None of this is difficult
paraphrase_link.note: The passage's negated adjective becomes an unnegated one in the statement, which is the whole of the disagreement.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer grades the work explicitly and the statement reverses that grade. A stated opposite is NO, and nothing here is left unaddressed.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is full of specialist vocabulary, and a reader meeting checksums and correlated failures for the first time infers difficulty.
distractors.why_wrong: The vocabulary belongs to the description. The sentence that grades the work says the opposite of the statement.

distractors.why_tempting: The grading sentence is four words long and carries no evaluative adverb, so a reader scanning for an opinion passes over it.
distractors.why_wrong: It is an explicit judgement on the whole paragraph, and its position immediately after the description is what makes it one.

teaching.reusable_rule: Technical vocabulary is not a claim about how hard something is. Look for the sentence that grades the work.

questions.prompt: Endowment funds have generally failed to cover the storage costs they were set up to meet.
questions.evidence_quote: they depend on assumptions about return and about the cost of storage decades ahead that no one can defend for long
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says what an endowment model is and what it rests on, and criticises the assumptions rather than the record. No sentence anywhere reports what any endowment has actually covered or failed to cover.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: doubt about the reasoning is easily read as a report of the outcome.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the storage costs they were set up to meet
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a sum is set aside whose income covers storage for ever
paraphrase_link.note: The instrument's design matches exactly; what has no counterpart is any record of how it performed.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage evaluates the reasoning behind the instrument and never its results. There is nothing to confirm the outcome and nothing that denies it.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage calls the assumptions indefensible, and a reader converts a criticism of the reasoning into a record of the result.
distractors.why_wrong: A model may rest on weak assumptions and still have covered its costs so far. The passage reports no outcome at all.

distractors.why_tempting: Endowment models are said to exist and are described without any collapse being mentioned, which reads as an absence of bad news.
distractors.why_wrong: Silence about failure is not a claim of success. No sentence contradicts the statement.

teaching.reusable_rule: Doubt over the reasoning behind a method is not a record of what it achieved. Ask whether an outcome is stated.
teaching.nearest_text: they depend on assumptions about return and about the cost of storage decades ahead that no one can defend for long

questions.prompt: The writer regards the incompleteness of web archives as a fault in the crawling software.
questions.evidence_quote: That is a genuine limitation and not a fault of the crawlers, and it is routinely misdescribed as one
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says what a crawl is and what it cannot capture, and then rules on it: the shortfall is a genuine limitation, it is not the crawlers' fault, and calling it one is a routine mistake.
questions.trap_note: The statement's own noun stands in the passage two words from a negative that reverses it.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: a fault in the crawling software
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: not a fault of the crawlers
paraphrase_link.note: One preposition and one noun change; the negative that decides the item is the part the statement drops.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer names the statement as a misdescription in the same sentence in which it is denied. That is an explicit contradiction rather than an absence.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement's key noun sits in the passage right beside the word for the software, and readers match nouns before they check negatives.
distractors.why_wrong: The noun is inside a negation, and the clause after it says the description is routinely mistaken.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence is long and its verdict sits in the middle, so a reader may locate the topic and record no ruling.
distractors.why_wrong: The ruling is unusually explicit for this writer, and it is made twice in one sentence.

teaching.reusable_rule: A noun beside the word you want may sit inside a negation. Read what governs it.

questions.prompt: Sandmouth's proposal has already been adopted in at least one country.
questions.evidence_quote: format specifications should simply be deposited by law when software is sold
questions.explanation: Paragraph G states Sandmouth's position and what he claims it would achieve. It is given entirely as a proposal, in a modal construction, and the passage never says whether anyone has legislated for it.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: a proposal expressed in the language of law reads as a law that exists somewhere.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: should simply be deposited by law
paraphrase_link.note: A recommendation becomes a completed act, which is precisely the step the passage never takes.

teaching.decision_rule: The proposal is addressed and its adoption is not. No sentence reports any jurisdiction acting on it, and none denies that any has.

distractors.why_tempting: The proposal is described as simple and is expressed in the vocabulary of legislation, which makes it sound like something already on a statute book.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Should be deposited' is a recommendation. The passage reports what he wants, not what exists.

distractors.why_tempting: The economist's reply says no legislation reduces the binding cost, which a reader takes for a statement that no legislation has been passed.
distractors.why_wrong: That clause says what legislation would not achieve, not whether any has been enacted.

teaching.reusable_rule: A proposal is a thing somebody wants. Nothing in the wanting says whether anyone has done it.
teaching.nearest_text: format specifications should simply be deposited by law when software is sold

questions.prompt: The writer thinks the economist's objection leaves the archivist's case standing.
questions.evidence_quote: Brackenfield's objection does not weaken her case so much as price it
questions.explanation: Paragraph H opens with the writer's ruling. Ashfield is called plainly right, and Brackenfield's objection is said to put a price on that position rather than to damage it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: does not weaken her case
paraphrase_link.note: 'Does not weaken' becomes 'leaves standing', with the person named by role instead of by surname.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer states in the first person which specialist is right and explicitly declines to treat the objection as damaging. Every part of the statement is supported.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Objection', and the earlier 'unimpressed by both', set the two against each other so firmly that a reader expects the writer to choose.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer does choose, and chooses the archivist. The objection is admitted and then reinterpreted as a cost.

distractors.why_tempting: The ruling arrives inside a construction that looks like a hedge rather than an endorsement.
distractors.why_wrong: The same sentence opens by calling the archivist plainly right, which settles the matter before the qualification arrives.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a writer denies one criticism and accepts a different one, that is endorsement with a qualification, never neutrality.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

teaching.strategy: Three of these four stems name a paragraph or a person, so the search is bounded before you start. Answer each stem from the text in your own words, then find the option that says the same thing rather than the option that shares words with it.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, running A, B, C and then the paragraph of named positions. Nothing here sends you backwards.
teaching.watch_out: Each of these stems has one option that is true of the passage and answers a different question.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer object to the phrase 'the digital dark age'?

options.text: It exaggerates how much material has already been lost.
It implies a single event rather than a gradual process.
It was invented by people outside the archive profession.
It confuses the problem of media with that of formats.

questions.evidence_quote: it suggests a single catastrophe that will arrive rather than a slow attrition that is already under way
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says the phrase does real damage because it points at the wrong shape of problem, and then explains why the shape matters: a catastrophe calls for a rescue and attrition calls for a permanent line in a budget.
questions.trap_note: The passage does separate media failures from format failures, but three paragraphs later and not as a complaint about this phrase.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: a single event rather than a gradual process
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a single catastrophe that will arrive rather than a slow attrition
paraphrase_link.note: Both nouns are replaced by category words and the contrast between them is carried across untouched.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the writer's stated objection, and the paragraph gives one reason in one clause. Options describing other faults of the phrase are not the reason offered.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Dark age' does sound like an exaggeration, and the writer plainly disapproves of the phrase.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage's complaint is about the shape of the story, not its scale. It never says the losses are overstated.

distractors.why_tempting: The phrase is described as one people reach for, which suggests a popular rather than a professional origin.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says nothing about who coined it or where they worked.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage does insist that different failures are run together, and that is a genuine complaint it makes.
distractors.why_wrong: That complaint is about how the three failures are discussed, and it is made in the next paragraph about a different target.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem asking why someone objects wants the reason given, not every other criticism the text supports.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say is distinctive about the third kind of failure?

options.text: No technical measure can undo it once it has happened.
It happens more often than the other two together.
It affects only files created by withdrawn software.
It is caused by administrators rather than by machines.

questions.evidence_quote: it becomes unreadable in a sense no amount of engineering can repair
questions.explanation: Paragraph B calls the third failure the hardest and the least discussed, and gives the reason: what is missing is not the data but the account of it, and no engineering can supply an account that was never written down.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph ranks the third failure for difficulty, never for frequency.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: No technical measure can undo it
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: no amount of engineering can repair
paraphrase_link.note: 'No amount of engineering' becomes 'no technical measure', which is the same denial with the quantity dropped.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what makes it distinctive, and the paragraph answers with irreparability. Options about how often it occurs or who causes it name properties the passage never assigns.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage calls it the hardest and the least discussed, and a reader converts a ranking on one axis into a ranking on another.
distractors.why_wrong: Hardest is not commonest. No frequency is given for any of the three failures.

distractors.why_tempting: Withdrawn software appears two sentences earlier and both failures leave a file that cannot be used.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the second failure. The third is about a file with no record of its origin, whatever wrote it.

distractors.why_tempting: The failure is human rather than physical, and administrators are the humans the passage mentions elsewhere.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage does not say who failed to record the context, and administrators appear in a different paragraph doing a different job.

teaching.reusable_rule: A ranking on one axis is not a ranking on another. Hardest, commonest and costliest are three separate claims.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph C, what do practitioners agree about?

options.text: Emulation is preferable to migration in most cases.
Whichever method is used must be applied again and again.
Conversion loses less than rebuilding an environment.
Twenty years is the safe interval between conversions.

questions.evidence_quote: whichever is chosen has to be chosen repeatedly
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says explicitly that practitioners argue about the balance and agree on the principle, and then states the principle: the choice has to be made repeatedly, whichever way it goes.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph names the thing they argue about immediately before the thing they agree on.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: must be applied again and again
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: has to be chosen repeatedly
paraphrase_link.note: One adverb becomes a phrase of the same meaning, and the modal is swapped for another of equal strength.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what is agreed, and the passage marks the agreement with an explicit verb. Options stating a preference are what the same sentence says is disputed.

distractors.why_tempting: Emulation is called faithful and the paragraph spends more words on it, which reads as a preference.
distractors.why_wrong: The balance between the two is exactly what the passage says practitioners argue about.

distractors.why_tempting: Migration is said to lose something at every conversion, and a reader who has fixed on that reverses it into an advantage.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage attributes losses to migration, so this option contradicts the paragraph as well as answering the wrong stem.

distractors.why_tempting: Twenty years is the only figure in the paragraph and it stands beside a warning.
distractors.why_wrong: Twenty years is the period after which an archive is described as unopened. It is the failure, not the recommended interval.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a sentence names what is disputed and what is settled, take only the second for a question about agreement.

questions.prompt: What is the economist's objection to the other two positions?

options.text: Neither of them addresses the cost that actually binds.
Both of them underestimate how fast formats disappear.
Both rely on legislation that is unlikely to be passed.
Neither has been tested on a collection of any size.

questions.evidence_quote: the binding cost is neither format nor selection but the wage of the person who checks the checksums
questions.explanation: Brackenfield's reply is that both of the other positions attack the wrong expense. What limits an archive is neither the format problem nor the selection problem but the salary of whoever performs the routine checks.
questions.trap_note: One of the two positions does rely on legislation, but the objection is aimed at both of them together.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the binding cost
paraphrase_link.note: An adjective in the text becomes a relative clause in the option, which is enough to hide a two-word phrase.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for one objection covering both positions, and the passage supplies one by naming what neither of them is about. An option true of only one position cannot be it.

distractors.why_tempting: Format obsolescence is the second position's whole subject, so speed of loss feels like the natural axis of disagreement.
distractors.why_wrong: No rate of format loss is given anywhere, and the objection is about expense rather than about speed.

distractors.why_tempting: One of the two positions is a proposal for a law, and the reply does mention legislation by name.
distractors.why_wrong: It is true of one position only, and the reply says legislation would not reduce the cost rather than that it would fail.

distractors.why_tempting: An economist is the kind of speaker who might ask for evidence, and neither position is described as having been tried.
distractors.why_wrong: Her point is about which cost binds. Testing is never mentioned in the paragraph.

teaching.reusable_rule: An objection aimed at two positions must apply to both. An option true of one of them is the standard decoy.

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists work to a rule that a settlement tells you less about itself than its rubbish does. A house is built to be looked at, and a grave is furnished by people who know that their neighbours are watching. A rubbish heap is edited by nobody. Whatever went into it went in because it had stopped being useful, and it was covered by the next day's waste without ceremony and without arrangement. The heaps have a name of their own in the discipline. A midden is any accumulated deposit of domestic waste, and middens have been dug from coastal shell mounds to the back yards of nineteenth-century terraces.

A midden grows from the bottom up, and that is the property which makes it worth excavating. Each tipping episode leaves a thin layer, and the layers pile in the order they were made, so the deepest material is normally the oldest. Excavators record these layers as separate contexts and lift them one at a time. The sequence is rarely tidy. Animals burrow, children dig, a wall falls into the heap, and a later pit may cut down through forty years of deposit in an afternoon. Reading a midden is therefore a matter of working out which disturbances happened when. Only then can an object in it be trusted to belong where it was found.

Dating a layer usually depends on the least valuable thing in it. Pottery is the standard, because kitchen wares changed shape and decoration steadily and cheap vessels were replaced often. A layer holding a type of jug that was made for only thirty years can be placed within a generation. Glass bottles and clay pipes do the same work for more recent periods. A coin, when one appears, gives a date before which the layer cannot have formed. What a coin does not give is the date the layer did form, since coins stay in circulation for decades and the worn ones circulate longest.

The material that survives is not the material that was thrown away, and the gap between the two is the oldest problem in the field. Bone, shell, pottery, glass and metal endure in most soils. Cloth, basketry, leather, wooden handles, feathers and the greater part of what a household ate do not. A midden dug from ordinary dry ground therefore records a version of daily life weighted heavily towards the hard and the fired. The bias is predictable enough to be corrected for in part, but only in part. Every correction rests on an assumption about how much of the original waste has gone.

Two conditions suspend the usual decay. Permanently waterlogged deposits shut out the oxygen that most decomposing organisms need, and very dry deposits deny them water. At Verdon, a silted ditch on the edge of the old town held water from the medieval period onwards. The excavation there recovered leather shoe soles cut down for reuse, the seeds of at least sixty plants, and large quantities of beetle remains. Of the three kinds of find, the beetles proved the most informative. Different species live in stored grain, in stable litter and in standing water. Their proportions describe the immediate surroundings of the ditch more closely than any of the objects did.

No excavation removes everything, and the choice of what to keep shapes the result more than most published reports admit. Deposits are usually sieved, and the size of the mesh decides which bones come through. A ten-millimetre mesh recovers cattle and sheep and loses almost every fish. When sites began to be sieved at two millimetres, the recorded share of fish in coastal diets rose sharply. It rose because of the mesh rather than because of anything the inhabitants had done differently. Column samples are now taken as a matter of routine for the same reason. A narrow block of deposit is lifted intact and processed in a laboratory.

What a midden cannot supply is people. It can describe a household's consumption across several decades with a precision no document of the period approaches. It can show a change of diet or of fuel inside a single generation. It cannot say who did the eating, and it is often unclear how many households contributed to one heap. Where a yard was shared, and in the crowded districts of the industrial towns most yards were, the waste of six families may lie in a single deposit. Some excavators treat a backyard midden as the record of one household unless there is a reason to think otherwise; others regard that assumption as unsupportable. The argument has not been settled, and it matters, because almost every statement about a household's standard of living begins with it.

difficulty_rationale.note: Everyday vocabulary and short declarative sentences, but each paragraph states a rule and then immediately qualifies it, and the qualification is usually attached without a connective.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It reports a change in the evidence and then says the change happened in the method, not in the past, which reverses what the figures first suggest.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It states the passage's one claim: rubbish is evidence nobody arranged.
skim_plan.skip: The lists of materials in D and of finds in E. They are inventory, and the questions that need them will send you back.

rewordings: the lower a layer, the earlier it formed

paraphrase_families.passage_form: the choice of what to keep

hinge_words.why_here: It hedges the oldest-at-the-bottom rule that question 2's heading turns on.
'most soils' is not all soils; it bounds the survival claim behind question 4.
It carries the whole contrast that makes question 9 TRUE.
'Some ... others' is the split that makes question 10 FALSE.
'it is often unclear' is the hedge question 10 tries to remove.
