question_groups.instructions_extra: There are more headings than paragraphs, so you will not use them all. Paragraph G is not included.

options.text: A record that nobody arranged
Layers, and what disturbs them
The value of a cheap object
Why the trades left no trace
What decays and what remains
Two places where decay stops
The mesh decides the diet
Counting the people of a town
One heap, how many homes?
How the coins reached the town

teaching.strategy: Four of these six paragraphs open with the sentence that states their whole job, so read first sentences across the passage before you look at the list. Place D and F first: one names a problem, the other a method.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, so nothing brackets the search. Every paragraph has to be looked at once.
teaching.watch_out: Three of the spare headings name something a paragraph genuinely contains. Containing is not the same as being about.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.evidence_quote: A rubbish heap is edited by nobody.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A contrasts two kinds of remains that were shaped for an audience, a house and a grave, with one that was not. Its point is that rubbish reached the ground unselected, which is what makes it evidence.
questions.trap_note: Heading ix names the question of how many households share a heap, which is raised only in the final paragraph.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: edited by nobody
paraphrase_link.note: The passive 'edited by nobody' becomes an active relative clause in the heading.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph sets up one opposition, arranged against unarranged, and every sentence in it serves that opposition. A heading has to name the opposition, not one of the things being opposed.

distractors.why_tempting: The last sentence names back yards and terraces, so a reader who has met the word 'household' expects a heading about homes.
distractors.why_wrong: Back yards appear as places middens are found, not as a problem about ownership; that problem is paragraph G.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Stopped being useful' sounds like the beginning of an account of decay.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes why an object was discarded, not whether it later survived. Survival is paragraph D.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph mentions terraces and neighbours, which reads like a paragraph about a population.
distractors.why_wrong: Nobody is counted anywhere in the paragraph, and no town is described.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph is built on one contrast, the heading names the contrast, never the more vivid of the two sides.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence_quote: the layers pile in the order they were made, so the deepest material is normally the oldest
questions.explanation: Paragraph B gives the sequence rule first and then spends the rest of its length on everything that breaks the sequence: burrowing animals, digging children, a collapsed wall, a later pit. Both halves belong in the heading.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: which disturbances happened when
paraphrase_link.note: The noun 'disturbances' in the text becomes the verb 'disturbs' in the heading, with the layers as its object.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's two halves are the rule and its failures, and only one heading carries both. A heading naming the rule alone would leave five of the paragraph's sentences unaccounted for.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends on whether an object can be trusted, and value is the obvious next thought about objects.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing here is about what an object is worth; that argument belongs to the dating paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Two' in a heading attracts a reader who has just counted the paragraph's two halves.
distractors.why_wrong: The heading names two places, and this paragraph names no places at all.

teaching.reusable_rule: If a heading accounts for only the first sentence, it is a topic, not a heading. Make it cover the longest part of the paragraph.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence_quote: Dating a layer usually depends on the least valuable thing in it.
questions.explanation: The paragraph opens by stating that dating depends on the least valuable object present, then justifies that with pottery, bottles and pipes, and closes by showing that the one valuable object, a coin, gives less than it seems to.
questions.trap_note: Heading x is built from the paragraph's most memorable noun, and the paragraph never discusses how coins moved.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The value of a cheap object
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: depends on the least valuable thing in it
paraphrase_link.note: 'Least valuable' becomes 'cheap', and the heading turns the whole clause into a noun phrase about worth.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's controlling claim is a paradox about worth: the cheap object dates the layer and the expensive one does not. Only a heading about value matches a paragraph organised around that reversal.

distractors.why_tempting: Coins occupy the last two sentences and are the only object in the paragraph a reader is likely to remember.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage uses the coin as a limit on dating. How coins travelled, or reached anywhere, is never mentioned.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'layer' appears four times here and is the subject of the previous paragraph's heading.
distractors.why_wrong: This paragraph dates layers; it does not describe how they form or what disturbs them.

teaching.reusable_rule: The noun you remember from a paragraph is often just a detail. Ask what the paragraph claims, then find that claim in the list.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence_quote: The material that survives is not the material that was thrown away
questions.explanation: Paragraph D is a two-column list, of what lasts and what does not, framed by the statement that these are different sets and closed by the admission that the difference can only partly be corrected for.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The material that survives is not the material that was thrown away
paraphrase_link.note: One sentence naming two unequal sets becomes a two-part heading naming the same two sets.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph divides material into two classes and does nothing else. A heading naming both classes covers it; a heading naming a cause of loss adds something the paragraph never supplies.

distractors.why_tempting: Cloth, basketry, leather and wooden handles are all products of crafts, so a heading about trades looks like a summary of the list.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph groups them by what they are made of, not by who made them. No trade is named or discussed.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about decay, and this heading contains the word.
distractors.why_wrong: Here decay is the rule. The two places where it stops are the subject of the next paragraph.

teaching.reusable_rule: A heading that shares a key word with two neighbouring paragraphs belongs to the one that does more than mention it.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence_quote: Two conditions suspend the usual decay.
questions.explanation: The paragraph names the two conditions in its first two sentences, waterlogged and very dry ground, and then spends the rest of its length on one site where the first of them applied.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Two conditions suspend the usual decay
paraphrase_link.note: 'Conditions' becomes 'places', which is narrower but is what the paragraph's own examples are.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph announces a count in its first three words and then supplies exactly that count. A heading that reproduces the count and the subject is forced; nothing else in the list mentions an exception to decay.

distractors.why_tempting: The opening sentence is about decay, and a reader placing headings in order will already have decay in mind.
distractors.why_wrong: Heading v names the general rule about what rots, which is the previous paragraph. This one is entirely about the exceptions.

distractors.why_tempting: Seeds, grain and stable litter read like evidence about what was eaten.
distractors.why_wrong: Diet and mesh sizes belong to paragraph F. Here the beetles describe the surroundings of a ditch, not a diet.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that opens by counting is telling you its own structure. Check that the heading matches the count.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence_quote: the size of the mesh decides which bones come through
questions.explanation: Paragraph F argues that what an excavation reports depends on what it kept, and its worked example is the mesh: coarse mesh loses fish, fine mesh finds them, and the recorded diet changes accordingly.
questions.trap_note: Heading viii picks up the counting in the paragraph, but what is counted is bones, never people.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the size of the mesh decides which bones come through
paraphrase_link.note: 'Which bones come through' becomes 'the diet', because the recorded diet is what the bones are used to reconstruct.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's example does the whole argumentative work: the sieve changes the finding, not the past. A heading naming the sieve's effect on the result is the only one that states that.

distractors.why_tempting: Shares, proportions and measurements fill the paragraph, so a heading about counting feels right.
distractors.why_wrong: The counting is of fish and cattle bones. No population and no town is counted here or anywhere in the passage.

distractors.why_tempting: Column samples and deposits are excavation vocabulary, which the reader last met in paragraph B.
distractors.why_wrong: Paragraph B is about how layers are disturbed. This paragraph is about how much of them is recovered.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two paragraphs can use the same technical vocabulary. Separate them by what each one does with it, not by the words themselves.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage?

teaching.strategy: These four run from paragraph C to paragraph G, so after question 7 you never look above the coin sentence again. Underline each statement's verb before you search: three turn on what a piece of evidence can and cannot do.
teaching.order_note: In passage order. Question 9's answer lies below question 8's; search that band and not the whole text.
teaching.watch_out: One statement is about the purpose of a feature the passage only describes. A purpose the writer never states cannot be contradicted either.

questions.prompt: A coin found in a layer establishes the date at which that layer was formed.
questions.evidence_quote: What a coin does not give is the date the layer did form
questions.explanation: The passage says a coin gives a date before which the layer cannot have formed, and then states directly that what it does not give is the date the layer did form. The reason follows: coins circulate for decades, so the coin can be much older than the layer.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial arrives in the sentence after the one that looks like the answer, and it begins with 'What'.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: establishes the date at which that layer was formed
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: What a coin does not give is the date the layer did form
paraphrase_link.note: 'Establishes' matches 'gives'; the whole difference is the negative the statement drops.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the passage states a claim the statement cannot be true alongside: the coin fixes only an earliest possible date. That is a quotable contradiction, so FALSE rather than NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous clause does say a coin gives a date, and a reader who stops at the comma has confirmed the statement.
distractors.why_wrong: The date it gives is a limit, not the date of formation, and the next clause says so explicitly.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement's verb, 'establishes', appears nowhere, so a search for it returns nothing and the passage feels silent.
distractors.why_wrong: The contradiction is in the paragraph's last sentence, worded as a negative rather than as a denial of the statement.

teaching.reusable_rule: A negative clause beginning 'What X does not' is a denial in disguise. Read it as a contradiction, not as an absence.

questions.prompt: The ditch at Verdon had been dug in order to receive waste.
questions.evidence_quote: At Verdon, a silted ditch on the edge of the old town held water from the medieval period onwards
questions.explanation: The passage says where the ditch was, that it had silted, that it held water from the medieval period, and what was recovered from it. It never says why it was dug. A ditch that later filled with rubbish need not have been made for rubbish, and the passage takes no position either way.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the finds are so clearly domestic waste that the ditch's purpose feels stated when only its contents are.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a silted ditch on the edge of the old town
paraphrase_link.note: The location matches exactly. It is the purpose, which has no counterpart at all, that decides the item.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the specific claim, the reason the ditch was made, is neither stated nor denied. No sentence would have to be false for the statement to be true, and none would have to be true.

distractors.why_tempting: The ditch is full of household refuse, and the obvious explanation for a ditch full of refuse is that it was a rubbish ditch.
distractors.why_wrong: That is an inference the reader supplies. The passage describes the contents and is silent on the purpose.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage calls it silted and says it held water, which sounds like a drainage feature and therefore like a different purpose.
distractors.why_wrong: Holding water is what happened to it, not what it was for. No sentence gives it any purpose to contradict.

teaching.reusable_rule: Contents are not purpose. A statement about why something was made needs a sentence about intention, not a list of what was inside.
teaching.nearest_text: a silted ditch on the edge of the old town held water from the medieval period onwards

questions.prompt: The recorded increase in fish was produced by the way sites were excavated, not by a difference in the inhabitants' behaviour.
questions.evidence_quote: It rose because of the mesh rather than because of anything the inhabitants had done differently
questions.explanation: The passage makes the causal statement itself: the recorded share of fish rose because of the mesh and not because the inhabitants had done anything differently. The statement restates both halves of that clause and adds nothing.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: produced by the way sites were excavated
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: because of the mesh rather than because of anything the inhabitants had done differently
paraphrase_link.note: The mesh is one instance of excavation method, so the statement generalises upward without changing the claim.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage draws the causal contrast itself, in one clause, using 'rather than'. Nothing has to be inferred, and both halves of the statement are covered, so the statement is fully supported.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement shares almost no vocabulary with the sentence that supports it: not 'excavated', not 'behaviour', not 'produced'.
distractors.why_wrong: The proposition is stated in full in different words. Silence is not the same as a failed keyword search.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does say the share of fish rose, which reads at speed as a claim about what people ate.
distractors.why_wrong: What rose was the recorded share, and the passage attributes that to the mesh. Nothing here denies the statement.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a sentence joins two causes and rejects one of them, it has already ranked them. Nothing further needs working out.

questions.prompt: Excavators agree that a shared backyard heap should be read as the waste of a single household.
questions.evidence_quote: others regard that assumption as unsupportable
questions.explanation: The passage sets out two positions on exactly this question and says the argument has not been settled. Some excavators do make the single-household assumption; others regard it as unsupportable. A statement that they agree is incompatible with a sentence that reports the disagreement.
questions.trap_note: Scope shift: the passage says some, the statement says all of them, and the word 'others' is the contradiction.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: others regard that assumption as unsupportable
paraphrase_link.note: One group's practice is widened into everybody's, and the sentence naming the second group rules that out.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the passage states that the field is divided. Universal agreement and a reported disagreement cannot both hold, so this is a contradiction rather than a silence.

distractors.why_tempting: The first half of the sentence describes exactly the practice the statement names, and a reader who stops at the semicolon has confirmed it.
distractors.why_wrong: That half is attributed to some excavators only. The clause after the semicolon reports the opposite position.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'agree' never appears, and a reader hunting for a statement about consensus finds none.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Some ... others ... has not been settled' is a report of disagreement, which settles the question directly.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement that everyone in a field agrees is refuted by a single sentence naming a second position. Look for 'others'.

teaching.watch_out: The limit is one word. Copying a whole phrase, or repeating a word already printed in the note, scores zero.

questions.prompt: Water stood in the silted ditch from the {{gap}} period onwards.

questions.explanation: Paragraph E dates the standing water in the Verdon ditch from the medieval period onwards. The note keeps the passage's own frame, 'from the ___ period onwards', so the answer is the adjective the passage already puts in that slot.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Water stood in the silted ditch
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a silted ditch on the edge of the old town held water
paraphrase_link.note: The text makes the ditch the subject; the note makes the water the subject.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'the' and 'period', so it takes a single adjective of time, and only one such word appears anywhere in the paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: 'The old town' sits beside the date phrase and reads like a period name to anyone scanning for capitals.
distractors.why_wrong: It names a place, not a period, and it is two words where one is allowed.

distractors.why_tempting: Copying the whole phrase from the passage feels safer than trusting a single word.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Period' is already printed after the gap, so the line would read twice over, and the answer is over the one-word limit.

teaching.reusable_rule: Read the words printed on both sides of a gap before you search. They usually fix the word class and the length.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap sits between 'the' and 'period', so it takes one adjective.

questions.prompt: Shoe soles of leather had been cut down for {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: leather shoe soles cut down for reuse
questions.explanation: Paragraph E lists leather shoe soles that had been cut down for reuse among the finds preserved by the waterlogged ditch. The note reorders the phrase but keeps the preposition, so the noun that follows it is unchanged.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: leather shoe soles
paraphrase_link.note: A modifier before the noun becomes a phrase after it, which defeats a search for the exact string.

teaching.decision_rule: 'For' before the gap takes a noun, and the paragraph offers exactly one noun in that position after the same preposition.

distractors.why_tempting: Learners convert the noun into a participle because the sentence describes something that was done to the soles.
distractors.why_wrong: 'For' takes a noun here, and the passage writes 'reuse'. Right meaning, wrong form, no mark.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest content word to the gap in the passage's own phrase.
distractors.why_wrong: It is already printed in the note before the gap, and it names the material rather than the purpose.

teaching.reusable_rule: Copy the form the text uses, not the form the meaning suggests. A verb where the frame wants a noun scores nothing.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap follows 'for', so it takes a noun rather than a verb.

questions.prompt: Of the three kinds of find, the {{gap}} were the most informative.
questions.evidence_quote: Of the three kinds of find, the beetles proved the most informative.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E names three classes of find from the ditch, leather, seeds and beetles, and then says the beetles proved the most informative because the species present describe the surroundings.
questions.trap_note: Two of the three finds are named in the sentence before, and both are plural nouns that would fit the frame.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: proved the most informative
paraphrase_link.note: Only the verb changes, and it changes to one that cannot be searched for.

teaching.decision_rule: 'The ___ were' forces a plural noun, and of the three plural nouns available only one is the subject of the sentence about usefulness.

distractors.why_tempting: Seeds are one of the three finds, they are plural, and they sit closer to the start of the list than the beetles do.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage names the beetles, not the seeds, as the most informative of the three.

distractors.why_tempting: A learner who has read 'beetle remains' copies the singular from that phrase.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Were' after the gap forces the plural, and the passage writes 'the beetles' in the sentence that decides the item.

teaching.reusable_rule: When several items of the same word class would fit a gap, the verb after it and the claim being made will separate them.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Were' after the gap forces a plural noun, not a singular.

paragraphs.text: For most of its history the market of a provincial town happened in the street. Stalls were pitched against the church wall or along the widest thoroughfare, they were struck at dusk, and what remained was mud and refuse. In the middle decades of the nineteenth century a new building appeared in town centres to put an end to that arrangement. The covered market hall was a permanent roof, usually of iron and glass, thrown over a fixed grid of stalls. Within two generations it had become as ordinary a feature of a provincial centre as the town hall or the railway station.

The halls were built with borrowed money, and this fact governed everything about them. A corporation raised a loan and repaid it from the rents of the stalls and from the tolls it charged on goods entering the building. It also had to show the ratepayers a surplus at the end of it. Architects were therefore instructed to fit in as many stalls as the roof would carry. Aisles are narrow in these buildings not because their designers misjudged the crowds but because every metre of aisle was a metre that earned nothing. The accounts were public.

Their family resemblance has a mundane explanation. Cast-iron columns, roof trusses, glazing bars and even the ornamental brackets were ordered from foundry catalogues, in standard sizes, by post. A borough surveyor in Norland could specify a roof that had already been erected at Sandmouth and would be erected again at Ashfield the following year. The parts arrived by rail ready to bolt together. Where local pride demanded difference it was bought at the front, in a stone facade in whatever style the council preferred, while behind it the shed was identical to a dozen others.

What the roof also bought was supervision. Trading in the open had been almost impossible to regulate: weights could not be checked, meat could not be inspected, and a seller who was warned in one street simply moved to another. Inside a hall with named tenancies and a superintendent at the door, all of that changed. The prospectuses of the period lean heavily on cleanliness and on the quality of what was sold, and the argument was not merely rhetorical, since the same decades saw the first serious powers to seize unfit food. Whether health or revenue mattered more to any particular council is rarely recoverable from the minutes.

Not everyone moved indoors. A stall inside carried a weekly rent, and traders who had sold from a basket or a barrow could not raise it or did not wish to be tied to one place. Several towns issued licences for street selling at the same time as they opened their halls, and the licences were fewer than the sellers. The effect was to sort the market: the settled trades took the hall, and the poorest sellers took the surrounding streets, where they were periodically moved on by the same authority that had built the roof.

The halls lost their trade slowly and then quickly. Chains of grocery shops took the packaged goods first. Domestic refrigeration removed the need to buy perishables three times a week, which had been the habit that filled the aisles. The decisive change was the car, because a hall stood on the most valuable ground in the town and had no room to park anything. By the middle of the twentieth century a market hall was often the largest under-used structure a council owned, and a good number were pulled down for shopping precincts and car parks between 1960 and 1980.

The survivors have been rediscovered as architecture. A hall that would have been cleared in 1968 for its site is now listed for its roof, and the arguments made for keeping it are almost entirely about the ironwork. Restoration is expensive, and the money is usually recovered by re-letting the stalls to food counters and independent shops at rents the fishmonger and the greengrocer could never meet. The building is preserved and the trade is not, and traders' associations have said as much at every consultation. Whether a hall without its original tenants is a market or a monument is a fair question, and it is not answered by the quality of the restoration.

It is tempting to file these buildings under public health, and the case is not empty. But the same halls were revenue instruments, and the two purposes were never separated even in the minds of the people who commissioned them. What the century really established was not a standard of hygiene, which arrived by other routes as well. It established an assumption that has outlived every one of these roofs: that trading in a town is an activity to be housed, licensed and given an address. Every shopping centre since has been built on that assumption, and it is worth noticing that it was once a novelty.

difficulty_rationale.note: Each paragraph carries a claim, an example and a qualification, and the qualification is usually the part the questions turn on. The final two paragraphs withdraw a verdict the earlier ones seemed to be building.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It rejects the obvious summary of the passage and replaces it with a claim about what the buildings made normal, which is easy to read as agreement.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and paragraph A. It tells you the passage is about one building type replacing an arrangement.
skim_plan.skip: The list of iron components in C and the street names of the trades in G. Both are illustration.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Which paragraph contains the following information? NB You may use any letter more than once.

options.text: Paragraph A
Paragraph B
Paragraph C
Paragraph D
Paragraph E
Paragraph F
Paragraph G
Paragraph H

teaching.strategy: Turn each item into the one thing it must contain: a mechanism, a group of people, a household change, a complaint, a date range. Then scan for that thing, not for the item's words, and accept that two items share a paragraph.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, and a letter may repeat. Do this group last, once you know the passage.
teaching.watch_out: Two paragraphs mention traders losing out. Only one of them records the traders themselves objecting.

questions.prompt: an explanation of why market halls in different towns look so similar
questions.evidence_quote: were ordered from foundry catalogues, in standard sizes, by post
questions.explanation: Paragraph C gives the cause of the resemblance directly: the structural components were bought as standard items from catalogues, so the same roof could be put up in three different towns.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: why market halls in different towns look so similar
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Their family resemblance has a mundane explanation
paraphrase_link.note: 'Family resemblance' is the passage's compressed name for looking similar.

teaching.decision_rule: The item asks for an explanation, not a description. Only this paragraph states a cause, and it states it in its first sentence and demonstrates it in the next three.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph A says the halls became an ordinary feature of every provincial centre, which sounds like a claim that they were alike.
distractors.why_wrong: It reports that they were common, not that they resembled one another, and offers no cause.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph B explains why the interiors were laid out as they were, which is also a design explanation.
distractors.why_wrong: That explains narrow aisles inside one hall, not the likeness between halls in different towns.

teaching.reusable_rule: An item asking why something is so needs a paragraph containing a cause. Paragraphs that only report the fact are decoys.

questions.prompt: a reference to sellers who were unable to afford the new accommodation
questions.evidence_quote: traders who had sold from a basket or a barrow could not raise it
questions.explanation: Paragraph E states that a stall carried a weekly rent and that basket and barrow traders could not raise it, and then follows those sellers into the surrounding streets.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: unable to afford the new accommodation
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: could not raise it
paraphrase_link.note: The pronoun 'it' stands for the weekly rent named in the clause before.

teaching.decision_rule: The item needs sellers plus an inability to pay. Only this paragraph puts both in one sentence, and the pronoun that carries the cost points back to the rent named beside it.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph G also names traders who cannot meet a rent, and uses the sharper phrase 'could never meet'.
distractors.why_wrong: Those are present-day tenants priced out of a restored hall, not sellers excluded when the halls opened.

distractors.why_tempting: Rents are introduced in paragraph B, so a reader scanning for the word lands there first.
distractors.why_wrong: Paragraph B treats rent as the corporation's income. Nobody in it is unable to pay.

teaching.reusable_rule: When two paragraphs describe the same kind of loss, separate them by date. The item's tense or period word usually decides.

questions.prompt: a change in the home that reduced how often people shopped
questions.evidence_quote: Domestic refrigeration removed the need to buy perishables three times a week
questions.explanation: Paragraph F names domestic refrigeration as the change that removed the need to buy perishables three times a week, and says that this habit was what had filled the aisles.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Domestic refrigeration
paraphrase_link.note: 'Domestic' is the only word carrying 'in the home', and it is an adjective rather than a phrase.

teaching.decision_rule: The item requires a domestic change with a shopping consequence. This sentence supplies both halves and is the only sentence in the passage that does.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph A describes how the market worked before the halls, which is also about shopping habits.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes where trade happened, not how often anyone bought anything.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph E is about buyers and sellers changing their behaviour when the halls opened.
distractors.why_wrong: The change there is where the poorest sellers stood, and nothing in it happens in a house.

teaching.reusable_rule: Match an item's two halves separately. A paragraph containing only one of them is a decoy however well it fits that half.

questions.prompt: an objection put on record by the people who trade in these buildings
questions.evidence_quote: traders' associations have said as much at every consultation
questions.explanation: Paragraph G says that the building is preserved and the trade is not, and adds that traders' associations have made that point at every consultation. That is the passage's only reported objection from traders.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: put on record by the people who trade
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: traders' associations have said as much at every consultation
paraphrase_link.note: 'Said as much at every consultation' is what being on record amounts to here.

teaching.decision_rule: The item requires a complaint with a named source. Elsewhere the passage reports harm to traders in its own voice; only here do the traders speak.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph E describes sellers being moved on by the authority that built the roof, which reads as a grievance.
distractors.why_wrong: The grievance is the writer's. No trader is quoted or reported as objecting.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph H weighs the halls up and mentions how they are usually filed, so it sounds like a place where views are collected.
distractors.why_wrong: The views there are the writer's own assessment of the century, not a statement by anyone in the trade.

teaching.reusable_rule: An item naming who spoke needs a sentence naming a speaker. The writer describing a hardship is not the same as someone complaining of it.

questions.prompt: the period during which many of these buildings were destroyed
questions.evidence_quote: a good number were pulled down for shopping precincts and car parks between 1960 and 1980
questions.explanation: Paragraph F gives the demolition window explicitly, between 1960 and 1980, and names what replaced the halls.
questions.trap_note: Paragraph G contains the passage's other date, and it belongs to a hall that was not demolished.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: many of these buildings were destroyed
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a good number were pulled down
paraphrase_link.note: 'A good number' is the passage's only quantity here, and it is vaguer than the item's 'many'.

teaching.decision_rule: The item asks for a period, so the paragraph must contain a span rather than a single year. Only one span appears in the passage.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph G opens with a specific year, 1968, which falls inside the window the item is really asking about.
distractors.why_wrong: That year is attached to a hall that would have been cleared and was not. It is a single date, not a period.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph A dates the arrival of the halls, and a reader scanning for dates meets it first.
distractors.why_wrong: It dates their construction, which is the opposite of what the item asks for.

teaching.reusable_rule: An item asking for a period is not satisfied by a single year. Scan for two numbers joined by a preposition.

questions.evidence_quote: they were struck at dusk, and what remained was mud and refuse
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says the stalls were struck at dusk and that what remained was mud and refuse. The sentence keeps the passage's preposition, so the answer is the time word that already follows it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: they were struck
paraphrase_link.note: 'Struck' is the trade's word for dismantling a stall, so a search for 'taken down' finds nothing.

teaching.decision_rule: 'At' before the gap admits only a time expression, and the paragraph offers exactly one, in the same prepositional slot.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the obvious word for the end of a trading day and completes the sentence perfectly well.
distractors.why_wrong: Completion answers must be the passage's own words, and this one does not appear in it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest place expression to the verb in the same sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: It answers where, not when, and it is three words against a limit of two.

teaching.reusable_rule: A preposition printed before a gap tells you the class of the answer. Match the class first, then hunt inside that class.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'At' before the gap admits a time word, not a place.

questions.prompt: A corporation repaid its loan out of stall rents and out of {{gap}} on goods entering the building.
questions.evidence_quote: from the tolls it charged on goods entering the building
questions.explanation: Paragraph B names the two sources of repayment: the rents of the stalls and the tolls charged on goods coming in. The sentence keeps the second phrase almost intact.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: from the rents of the stalls
paraphrase_link.note: A noun of a noun becomes a compound, which is enough to defeat a search for the exact phrase.

teaching.decision_rule: No article is printed before the gap, so a countable noun there has to be plural, and the passage supplies the plural form in the same prepositional frame.

distractors.why_tempting: A learner who has located the right sentence copies the headword rather than the form the text uses.
distractors.why_wrong: With no article in front of it, a singular countable noun is ungrammatical here, and the passage writes the plural.

distractors.why_tempting: Rents are the other source of repayment and appear in the same sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: Rents are already printed before the gap, and this phrase is charged on stalls rather than on goods.

teaching.reusable_rule: A gap with no article in front of it wants a plural if the noun is countable. Check the frame before you copy.
teaching.grammar_cue: No article before the gap, so a countable noun must be plural.

questions.prompt: The prospectuses of the period placed great weight on {{gap}} and on the quality of the goods.
questions.evidence_quote: lean heavily on cleanliness and on the quality of what was sold
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says the prospectuses lean heavily on cleanliness and on the quality of what was sold. The sentence replaces the verb but keeps both prepositional phrases, so only the first noun is missing.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: lean heavily on
paraphrase_link.note: An adverb plus verb becomes a noun phrase, and the shared preposition is the only visible anchor.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap is the first of two items joined by 'and on', and the second is printed. The passage's matching pair fixes the first without ambiguity.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's opening idea and its most memorable noun.
distractors.why_wrong: Supervision is what the roof bought the council; it is not what the prospectuses emphasised.

distractors.why_tempting: It appears in the same sentence, after a comma, and sounds like a hygiene claim.
distractors.why_wrong: It belongs to the clause about new legal powers, and it is two words describing what was seized.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a gap is one of two coordinated items and the second is printed, the text's matching pair identifies the first.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap follows 'on' and is paired with a second 'on' phrase, so it takes a noun.

questions.prompt: Towns issued {{gap}} for street selling, and there were not enough of them for all the sellers.
questions.evidence_quote: issued licences for street selling at the same time as they opened their halls, and the licences were fewer than the sellers
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says several towns issued licences for street selling and that the licences were fewer than the sellers. The sentence restates the shortage but keeps the noun and the verb that governs it.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: there were not enough of them for all the sellers
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the licences were fewer than the sellers
paraphrase_link.note: A comparative in the text becomes a negated sufficiency phrase in the sentence.

teaching.decision_rule: No article stands before the gap and the verb 'issued' takes a plural object here, so the countable noun the paragraph uses in the same slot is forced.

distractors.why_tempting: The singular is the dictionary form and reads naturally to anyone translating the idea rather than copying it.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Issued licence' without an article is ungrammatical, and the passage uses the plural twice.

distractors.why_tempting: Stalls are what towns provided inside the halls and are a plural noun in the same paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: Stalls were let, not issued, and they were indoors rather than for street selling.

teaching.reusable_rule: Grammar decides between a singular and a plural before meaning does. Read the words on both sides of the gap first.
teaching.grammar_cue: No article before the gap, so the countable noun is plural.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

teaching.strategy: Read the stem, answer it in your own words from the passage, and only then look at the options. Three of these stems ask what the writer says rather than what happened, so an accurate option can still be wrong.
teaching.order_note: In passage order: question 26 is answered in the last paragraph, question 23 in the fourth.
teaching.watch_out: Every set contains one option that is true of the passage but answers a different question.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the motives of the councils that built market halls?

options.text: Public health was usually a cover for raising revenue.
The records rarely show which motive counted for more.
Most councils admitted that revenue came first.
Health was the motive most often stated in the prospectuses.

questions.evidence_quote: Whether health or revenue mattered more to any particular council is rarely recoverable from the minutes.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D describes the health argument, insists it was not merely rhetorical, and then closes by saying the balance between health and revenue is rarely recoverable from the minutes. That refusal to decide is the writer's position.
questions.trap_note: Option D is true of the prospectuses and says nothing about motive, which is what the stem asks for.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The records rarely show which motive counted for more
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is rarely recoverable from the minutes
paraphrase_link.note: 'The minutes' are the records, and 'recoverable' is what an option calls being shown.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what the writer says, and the writer's only statement about motive is that it cannot be settled. Any option that settles it therefore goes beyond the text.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does pair health with revenue, and a sceptical reader expects a writer discussing Victorian councils to say the health talk was a pretext.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer says the opposite: the argument was not merely rhetorical, and new powers to seize unfit food back it.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is full of financial detail, so the revenue motive feels like the one the passage endorses.
distractors.why_wrong: No council is reported as admitting anything. The minutes are said not to reveal the balance at all.

distractors.why_tempting: It is accurate: the prospectuses do lean heavily on cleanliness, and the sentence sits two lines above the answer.
distractors.why_wrong: What a prospectus states is not what a motive was, and the stem asks about motive.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a writer declines to settle a question, the key is the refusal. Options that pick a side are all wrong together.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what made the decline of the halls decisive?

options.text: The arrival of chains of grocery shops.
The cost of maintaining large iron roofs.
The lack of space for motorists to park.
The falling quality of the goods on sale.

questions.evidence_quote: The decisive change was the car, because a hall stood on the most valuable ground in the town and had no room to park anything.
questions.explanation: Paragraph F lists three pressures in order and then names one of them as decisive: the car, because a hall occupied the best ground in the town and could not offer parking.
questions.trap_note: The grocery chains are named first in the paragraph, and first is not the same as decisive.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The lack of space for motorists to park
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: had no room to park anything
paraphrase_link.note: A negative clause in the text becomes a noun phrase of absence in the option.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks which pressure was decisive, and the paragraph applies that exact word to one of them. The others are named as earlier or slower losses.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the first cause listed, and readers under time pressure take the first item in a list as the main one.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph says the chains took the packaged goods first, and then names a different change as decisive.

distractors.why_tempting: Restoration is described as expensive two paragraphs later, so maintenance cost feels like something the passage says.
distractors.why_wrong: The expense of restoring a surviving hall is not a cause of decline, and no maintenance cost is mentioned.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage does discuss the quality of goods, and a decline in trade is easily assumed to follow a decline in what was sold.
distractors.why_wrong: Quality is discussed only as something the halls were built to guarantee, and never as falling.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph lists causes and then singles one out, look for the word that does the singling. Order in the list means nothing.

questions.prompt: What does the writer suggest about the halls that have been restored?

options.text: The restoration work is generally of poor quality.
The building survives although its original trade does not.
Listing has made the restoration cheaper to fund.
Traders welcomed the higher rents that followed.

questions.evidence_quote: The building is preserved and the trade is not
questions.explanation: Paragraph G says the arguments for keeping a hall are almost entirely about its ironwork, that restoration is paid for by re-letting stalls at rents the old traders cannot meet, and that the building is preserved while the trade is not.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The building survives although its original trade does not
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The building is preserved and the trade is not
paraphrase_link.note: The passage joins the two halves with 'and'; the option makes the contrast explicit with 'although'.

paragraphs.text: The age at which a child may lawfully stop attending school has been raised, in most systems that set one, several times over the past century and a half. Each rise followed a similar pattern. It was proposed by a minority, resisted on grounds of cost and of lost family income, and enacted after a delay usually measured in decades. It was then absorbed so completely that within a generation the previous arrangement seemed indefensible. The argument now attaches itself to eighteen in much the language it once attached to twelve. What is striking about the sequence is how little of it turned on evidence about what the additional year does.

Evidence of a usable kind became available only when economists noticed that a change in the law creates something close to an experiment. Two children born a few months apart sit on either side of the date at which a new minimum age took effect. They are alike in almost every respect except the amount of schooling the law required of them. Comparing their later earnings therefore isolates the effect of the extra year from the family circumstances that ordinarily accompany it. Halloran, working on a reform of this kind, reported that the compelled cohort earned measurably more in middle age than the cohort born just before it, and that the difference survived the obvious adjustments.

Devanney has pressed the standard objection, and it is not easily dismissed. An extra year confers a certificate as well as an education, and employers who cannot observe what a candidate learned may be reading the certificate as a signal of persistence rather than of skill. On that account the earnings gain is real for the individual and largely illusory for the economy, since it comes from moving up a queue rather than from producing more. The awkwardness for both parties is that the two explanations predict almost identical earnings data, and the dispute therefore turns on evidence the natural experiment was never designed to supply.

Okorie has approached the question from a direction the economists tend to skip: what the additional year actually contained. Curricula for a newly compulsory year have generally been assembled at short notice, by people who did not ask for it, for pupils who did not choose to stay. Her account of one such reform describes a first cohort taught a shortened version of material most of them had already covered, in buildings laid out for two-thirds of the number. It is a useful corrective, and it cuts in an unexpected direction. If the extra year lifts earnings even when it is delivered like that, the mechanism is unlikely to be the curriculum.

Compliance is the part of the story that policy documents record least well. Attendance in the added year ran well below attendance in the years before it, and prosecutions of parents rose for perhaps a decade and then fell away. The schools that adapted did so by changing what they taught rather than by enforcing what they had been teaching. Strand's study of a single authority found that the institutions which retained their pupils were those that introduced practical courses early, and that this happened without instruction from the centre and, in two cases, against it. The aggregate attendance figures recovered within a few years, which is why the resistance is so often described as imagined.

There is a less generous reading of the whole sequence, and it deserves a hearing. Raising the leaving age removes a cohort from the labour market at a stroke, which is convenient when work is short, and several of the rises were legislated in years when unemployment among the young was rising fast. Bramwell treats that timing as the operative motive and the educational language as decoration. The correlation is real and the inference is not compelled by it; governments legislate about young people most readily when young people are visible as a problem, and that visibility follows unemployment without any cynicism being required.

Where does this leave the case for extension? The earnings gain survives most attempts to explain it away, but it is smaller than the advocates of each successive rise have claimed, and it has been produced under conditions nobody would have designed. What the sequence does not support is the assumption that governs most of the debate: that an additional year is a quantity, and that more of it is better in proportion. Two reforms adding the same year have produced different results within a single decade, which is hard to reconcile with a view of schooling as a stock that accumulates. The comparison that would settle the matter, between two versions of the same added year, has almost never been made.

The useful question is therefore not whether to keep raising the age but what the last year is to consist of. A year designed as a bridge into work or into further study is a different object from a year that repeats the one before it. The evidence assembled so far cannot tell the two apart, because almost every reform examined has delivered the second while promising the first. Until that changes, a debate about a number will go on being conducted with data that was never about the number at all.

paragraphs.text: The words that last longest in a landscape are usually its names. Buildings fall, boundaries move and languages are replaced. The name of a hill or a crossing is passed from one set of speakers to the next, often by people who no longer understand what it means. A settlement may have been renamed twice and still carry an older word in the name of its river or its high ground. That word can come from a language nobody has spoken there for a thousand years. The study of these names is the closest thing there is to reading a landscape's own memory. Like all memory it is partial and easy to misread.

Most names describe the ground. A crossing point, a marsh, a stand of trees, a narrow valley, a ridge with a particular shape: the great majority of settlement names in any long-inhabited region began as directions. This is the least glamorous class and by far the most useful, because the features are still there to be checked. Where a name means the low crossing and the site is a low crossing, the reading is secure. Where the ground has been drained or built over, the name becomes the only record that the marsh existed at all. Drainage engineers have more than once been surprised by what a name warned them of. The class has a further advantage. Its elements repeat across a whole region, so one secure reading supports a hundred uncertain ones.

A smaller class records a person. These are the names built from somebody's name and a word for a farm, an enclosure or a share of land. They are the hardest class to work with, because the person is almost never recorded anywhere else. The name preserves that an individual held the place and nothing more: not the date, not the size of the holding, not whether the holder ever lived there. Attempts to build a social history out of such names have repeatedly run ahead of what the names can carry. The safest use of them is negative. A district thick with such names was settled by people who divided land into individual holdings, whoever those individuals were.

A third class names a function the place has lost. Mills, beacons, gibbets, toll bars, ferry landings and market crosses all left names behind them, and the name usually outlives the thing by centuries. This is where the evidence is at its most concrete and its most easily misdated. A street called after a toll bar tells you a toll bar stood there. It does not tell you when, and in several towns the bar was taken away before the street acquired the surface it now has. The name is a fact about the past with no date attached.

The fourth class is different in kind, because it describes nothing. Settlers carry names with them, and a name that meant a wooded hollow in the country of origin may be fixed to a treeless plain in the country of arrival. Once transplanted, the name stops recording the landscape and starts recording the migration. Norland in one hemisphere and Norland in another are the same word doing two entirely different jobs. Only the second is evidence about people rather than about ground. Transplanted names also cluster. The clustering is itself evidence, and a group of transplanted names in one district usually marks a single wave of arrivals rather than a series of separate decisions.

Whichever class a name belongs to, the method is the same, and its first rule is never to work from the modern spelling. Names are reshaped by speakers who want them to mean something, so a name whose original element has fallen out of use will drift towards a word that has not. Ashfield may look like a field of ash trees and turn out, in its earliest written form, to be nothing of the kind. The earliest recorded spelling is the evidence; everything after it is commentary. The more sense a modern name makes, the more suspicious a careful reader becomes. The rule holds even when the modern form looks ancient, since a spelling can be made to look old as easily as it can be made to look sensible.

There is a further difficulty that no amount of care removes. A name records the moment somebody coined it, and the earliest surviving spelling records the moment somebody wrote it down. Those two moments may be three centuries apart. Written records begin with administration, which in most regions arrives long after the naming. A name therefore gives a date by which the feature existed and no date at all for when it was named. Practitioners state this limit plainly in their own publications, and it is routinely dropped by the time the results reach a wider audience.

paragraphs.text: Money sent home by people working abroad is one of the largest financial flows in the world and one of the least visible. In several small economies it exceeds foreign aid and direct investment combined, and in a few it approaches a tenth of everything the country produces. Yet it is under-recorded almost everywhere, because it arrives in thousands of small sums to households rather than as one payment to a ministry, and a good deal of it never passes through a bank at all. Economists call these transfers remittances. The households that receive them call it the money, and the difference in vocabulary is a fair indication of how differently the two parties see the same flow.

How the money travels has changed twice in a generation. Informal networks, in which a trader accepts cash in one city and an associate pays it out in another, still handle a large share of the flow, and they are cheap, fast and unrecorded. Formal transfer companies charge more, and most of them charge per transaction rather than as a share of the sum, so the smallest transfers carry the heaviest charge. The last decade pulled in two directions at once. Costs fell sharply along the routes that mobile transfer reached, and rose along the routes where compliance rules tightened. A bank that finds a corridor expensive to monitor tends to withdraw from it altogether rather than price the risk.

The oldest argument about remittances concerns what they are spent on. Critics have said for decades that the money goes on consumption rather than investment: better food, a tiled roof, a wedding, a motorbike. The reply is that a roof is a capital good, that school fees buy earnings twenty years out, and that a motorbike in a district with no bus service is working equipment. The standard categories were built for national accounts, and they record a school fee as consumption, so the size of the investment made from this money is understated by construction. That does not settle the argument. It does mean that the figures cited in it are answering a narrower question than the one being asked.

One property of the flow is unusual enough to have changed how economists describe it. Private investment leaves an economy that is in trouble; remittances rise when the home economy falters, because a sender responds to need rather than to return. After a harvest failure or a currency collapse, transfers to the affected region typically climb within a quarter, while portfolio investment has already gone. The flow grows in exactly the years when other money is leaving. That is a valuable property for a household and an awkward one for a statistician, since it means the flow cannot be modelled as investment without producing the wrong sign on every shock.

The costs of the arrangement are borne where they are hardest to count. A household that receives money has also lost an adult, often for years at a time. Ibarra's survey of one rural district found that the care of the children fell almost entirely on grandmothers and elder sisters, and almost never on anyone paid to do it. The same survey found that the households which fared best were not those receiving most but those in which the absence was fixed in advance and known to be temporary. Uncertainty about the date of return, it concluded, cost the household more than any sum the transfers were worth.

Return migration carries a second set of expectations. Policy documents assume that people come back carrying skills acquired abroad, and some of them do. But a bricklayer who has spent nine years on high-rise sites returns to a district that grows fruit, where nobody has any use for the trade he has learned. The equipment he trained on does not exist within two hundred kilometres. Nor are returners a random selection of those who left. People come back because a contract ended, because a parent fell ill, or because the work did not go well. The composition of the returning group is settled by those reasons rather than by anything a scheme can adjust.

Governments have spent twenty years trying to capture the flow. Diaspora bonds, matching schemes that add a public contribution to a private transfer, tax exemptions and dedicated savings accounts have all been offered, and take-up has been modest almost everywhere they have been tried. The explanation most often given is poor design, and some of the designs have indeed been poor. A simpler explanation is available. The money is a transfer between households, sent for reasons that are specific to a family and legible only inside it. A policy that treats it as a national resource is asking a private decision to answer a public question. That is not a design fault. It is a category error, and it is repeated in every new scheme.

difficulty_rationale.note: Ordinary financial vocabulary carrying several qualified claims per paragraph, with the qualification attached by a comma rather than by a connective, and one paragraph that reverses the direction the reader expects.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It sets out a criticism, answers it, and then refuses to award the argument to either side, which readers looking for a verdict repeatedly misread.

questions.prompt: Remittances are measured less completely than other financial flows because of the form in which they arrive.
questions.evidence_quote: it is under-recorded almost everywhere, because it arrives in thousands of small sums to households rather than as one payment to a ministry
questions.explanation: Paragraph A states the fact and its cause in one sentence: the flow is under-recorded, and the reason given is that it arrives in many small household payments instead of a single official one. The passage draws the causal link itself.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: under-recorded almost everywhere
paraphrase_link.note: 'Under-recorded' becomes a comparative about completeness, and the hedge is preserved by 'less'.

teaching.decision_rule: Both halves of the statement, the shortfall and its cause, appear in one sentence joined by 'because'. Nothing is left for the reader to supply, so the key is TRUE.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement's key words, 'measured' and 'form', appear nowhere, so a keyword search returns nothing.
distractors.why_wrong: The proposition is stated in full in different words, and the causal connector is the passage's own.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens by calling the flow one of the largest in the world, which reads as a claim that it is well known.
distractors.why_wrong: Being large and being counted are different things, and the sentence with 'yet' separates them explicitly.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a statement pairs a fact with a cause, the text must supply both. Here the connector does half the work for you.

questions.prompt: The cost of sending money home has fallen on every route over the last decade.
questions.evidence_quote: and rose along the routes where compliance rules tightened
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the decade pulled in two directions at once: costs fell where mobile transfer arrived and rose where compliance rules tightened, since banks withdraw from corridors that are expensive to monitor. A universal fall is incompatible with a stated rise.
questions.trap_note: Scope shift: the passage says costs fell on some routes, and the statement extends that to all of them.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Costs fell sharply along the routes that mobile transfer reached
paraphrase_link.note: A claim about the routes technology reached is widened into a claim about all of them.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the passage names a set of routes on which the opposite happened. A universal claim is contradicted by one counter-example, and the passage supplies it explicitly.

distractors.why_tempting: The first half of the sentence does report a sharp fall, and a reader who stops at the comma has confirmed the statement.
distractors.why_wrong: The clause after the comma reports a rise on other routes, and 'every' requires both halves to fall.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage gives no figures for the change, so a reader looking for a measured fall finds nothing to check.
distractors.why_wrong: A direction is stated for both sets of routes, and one of them is upwards.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement containing a universal word is false as soon as the text names one case that goes the other way. Hunt for that case.

questions.prompt: Households receiving remittances spend more on schooling than households that receive none.
questions.evidence_quote: The reply is that a roof is a capital good, that school fees buy earnings twenty years out
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about how spending is classified, not about how much any household spends. School fees appear as an example of something the accounts call consumption. No household that receives nothing appears anywhere in the passage, so there is nothing to compare with.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: school fees are mentioned, which makes the silence feel like a denial rather than an absence.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: school fees buy earnings twenty years out
paraphrase_link.note: The subject matches exactly; the comparison in the statement has no counterpart at all.

teaching.decision_rule: For TRUE the passage would have to compare two groups of households; for FALSE it would have to rank them the other way. It does neither, because it never mentions a household that receives nothing.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph defends school fees as an investment, so a reader takes the defence as evidence that recipients really do spend on schooling.
distractors.why_wrong: Defending a category is not measuring an amount, and no non-receiving household is described.

distractors.why_tempting: The critics' list is all consumption, and a reader who takes their side reads the paragraph as denying that the money is spent well.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph reports the criticism and answers it. Neither side compares two kinds of household.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement that ranks two groups needs the text to have put them side by side. Facts about one group alone will never settle it.
teaching.nearest_text: school fees buy earnings twenty years out

questions.prompt: Transfers home tend to increase when the receiving economy is in difficulty.
questions.evidence_quote: remittances rise when the home economy falters, because a sender responds to need rather than to return
questions.explanation: Paragraph D states the pattern directly and gives its cause: the sender is acting on need, not on the prospect of a return, so transfers rise when the home economy is doing badly. The next sentence dates the rise to within a quarter of a shock.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: when the receiving economy is in difficulty
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: when the home economy falters
paraphrase_link.note: 'Home' from the sender's point of view is the receiving economy from the statement's.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage states the correlation and its direction in its own voice. The statement's hedge, 'tend to', is weaker than the passage's plain present tense, so nothing is overclaimed.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence begins with private investment leaving a troubled economy, and a fast reader carries that direction into the second clause.
distractors.why_wrong: The semicolon separates two opposed behaviours. The clause about remittances runs the other way.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Receiving economy' does not appear, and the paragraph is written from the sender's side.
distractors.why_wrong: 'The home economy' names the same place, and the pattern is stated outright.

teaching.reusable_rule: A semicolon can separate two opposite behaviours. Check which side of it your statement belongs to before deciding.

questions.prompt: In the district Ibarra studied, children of absent parents were looked after mainly by paid carers.
questions.evidence_quote: the care of the children fell almost entirely on grandmothers and elder sisters, and almost never on anyone paid to do it
questions.explanation: The survey found the opposite of the statement. Care fell almost entirely on grandmothers and elder sisters and almost never on anyone who was paid, so paid carers are named precisely in order to be excluded.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial sits in a second clause after a comma and turns on the word 'never'.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: almost never on anyone paid to do it
paraphrase_link.note: The text's near-zero becomes the statement's majority, which is the whole of the error.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the passage assigns the care to two named groups while explicitly excluding the group the statement names. That is a contradiction, not a silence.

distractors.why_tempting: The phrase 'paid carers' does not appear, and a reader searching for it finds only relatives.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Anyone paid to do it' is the same category, and the clause containing it is a denial.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about money arriving in the household, so paying for care looks like the obvious use of it.
distractors.why_wrong: The survey reports who actually did the caring, and payment is what it rules out.

teaching.reusable_rule: A negative buried in a second clause is easy to skim past. Read to the full stop before judging who did something.

questions.prompt: Migrants who return home are more likely to set up businesses than those who remain abroad.
questions.evidence_quote: Nor are returners a random selection of those who left.
questions.explanation: Paragraph F describes what returners bring back, what their trades are worth at home, and why particular people return. It says nothing about starting a business, and it never compares returners with the migrants who stay away.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the paragraph is sceptical about returners, which makes an unmeasured claim about them feel as though it has been denied.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: returners a random selection of those who left
paraphrase_link.note: The group is named in both, so the group is not what decides the item.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph addresses returners at length and never mentions business formation, so no sentence supports the claim and none rules it out. Scepticism about a group is not a denial of a specific claim about it.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph says the trade a returner has learned is often useless at home, which reads as a reason they could not start anything.
distractors.why_wrong: That is about one trade in one district, and starting a business is never discussed.

distractors.why_tempting: Policy documents are said to expect skills to come back, and setting up a business is the obvious thing skills would be used for.
distractors.why_wrong: The expectation belongs to the documents, and the passage neither confirms it nor measures it.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that doubts a group has still said nothing about a specific activity it never names. Doubt is not denial.
teaching.nearest_text: Policy documents assume that people come back carrying skills acquired abroad

questions.prompt: Policy documents assume that returning migrants bring home new {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: Policy documents assume that people come back carrying skills acquired abroad
questions.explanation: Paragraph F reports the expectation behind return-migration policy: that people come back carrying skills acquired abroad. The bank supplies a synonym for those skills rather than the passage's own noun.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: people come back carrying skills acquired abroad
paraphrase_link.note: 'Come back carrying' becomes 'bring home', and the bank word replaces the passage's noun.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows an adjective and completes the object of 'bring home', so it takes an uncountable noun naming what a person has learned, and only one bank word does that.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage says the bricklayer trained abroad, so the process word feels like the right register for the sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: The gap names what is carried home, not what happened while the migrant was away.

questions.prompt: In practice a trade learned abroad may have no {{gap}} in the district a migrant goes back to.
questions.evidence_quote: returns to a district that grows fruit, where nobody has any use for the trade he has learned
questions.explanation: Paragraph F gives the worked case: a bricklayer returns to a fruit-growing district where nobody has any use for the trade and the equipment is hundreds of kilometres away. The bank word names the absence of work in the plural.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: nobody has any use for the trade he has learned
paraphrase_link.note: 'Nobody has any use for' becomes 'has no', with the missing thing named by the bank word.

teaching.decision_rule: 'No' before the gap admits either a plural or an uncountable noun, and the meaning required is the absence of work, so the bank word naming available positions is the only fit.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the same word class, fits the frame perfectly, and sounds like a description of a place where something is missing.
distractors.why_wrong: A shortage of a trade means the district wants it. The passage says the opposite.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous gap is about what the migrant has, and repeating that idea keeps the sentences connected.
distractors.why_wrong: The migrant has the expertise; what the district lacks is somewhere to use it.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two bank words can fit the grammar and mean opposite things. Test each against the direction of the claim, not its topic.

questions.prompt: Take-up of bonds and matching schemes has been {{gap}} nearly everywhere.
questions.evidence_quote: take-up has been modest almost everywhere they have been tried
questions.explanation: Paragraph G lists the instruments governments have offered and reports that take-up has been modest almost everywhere. The bank word restates that verdict without using the passage's adjective.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: take-up has been modest almost everywhere
paraphrase_link.note: The frame is copied and only the adjective is replaced, which is what makes the bank word findable.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap is a predicate adjective describing take-up, so the bank word must describe a rate of uptake rather than a quality of the offer.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph lists exemptions and public contributions, all of which sound like a generous offer.
distractors.why_wrong: It would describe the schemes, not their take-up, and the sentence is about how few people used them.

distractors.why_tempting: It is another abstract noun in the bank and the reader may still be inside the paragraph about returners.
distractors.why_wrong: The gap needs an adjective, so a noun cannot occupy it whatever it means.

teaching.reusable_rule: Fix the word class of a bank gap before you weigh meanings. Half a bank is usually eliminated by grammar alone.

questions.prompt: The writer's explanation is that the money moves between {{gap}} and is being asked to answer a public question.
questions.evidence_quote: The money is a transfer between households, sent for reasons that are specific to a family and legible only inside it
questions.explanation: Paragraph G gives the writer's alternative account: the money is a transfer between households, sent for reasons that make sense only inside a family, so policy asking it to serve a national purpose has misunderstood what kind of thing it is.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The money is a transfer between households
paraphrase_link.note: The noun 'transfer' becomes the verb 'moves', which is why the bank word must be the plural after it.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Between' requires a plural noun naming the two parties, and the passage names them twice in the same sentence, once as households and once through the reasons that are specific to one.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence is about policy, and the people who make policy are the most visible actors in the paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: They are who is asking the question, not who the money passes between.

distractors.why_tempting: It has already been used once and readers often reach for a word they have confirmed.
distractors.why_wrong: Each bank word is used only once, and expertise is not something money moves between.

teaching.reusable_rule: A preposition that needs two parties fixes both the number and the meaning of the gap. Reject anything that names an onlooker.

questions.explanation: Paragraph B draws the consequence itself: a flat charge per transaction falls hardest on the smallest sums, so the smallest transfers are the ones that carry the heaviest proportional cost.

questions.explanation: Paragraph C says the accounting categories were built for national accounts, that they classify a school fee as consumption, and that as a result the investment made from remittance money is understated by the way the measure is built.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the size of the investment is understated
