paragraphs.text: For about half a century, beginning in the closing years of the nineteenth, the most confident position in design was that applied ornament was a fault. The claim did not begin as a matter of taste. It began as a claim about honesty and about waste, and it was argued in the language of morals long before anyone tried to argue it in the language of appearance. Reformers wrote of decoration as something a serious object could be cured of. That vocabulary is worth noticing, because a fault can be removed while a preference can only be disagreed with, and much of the campaign's authority came from treating its own preference as a diagnosis.

Three separate objections were usually run together. The first was economic: ornament consumed labour that produced nothing, and the labour was underpaid. The second was structural: a carved bracket or a moulded cornice disguised how a building or a cabinet actually stood up, and a viewer who could not read the construction could not judge it. The third was temporal: decoration is dated by the year it was made in a way that a plain surface is not, so an ornamented object becomes unfashionable while a plain one merely becomes old. Each of these is a different argument with a different kind of evidence behind it, and almost nobody separated them.

The economic objection is the easiest to test and the weakest of the three. By the time it was being made most loudly, machine production had already made the repetition of a moulding cheaper than a plain surface finished to the same tolerance. Carving one bracket by hand is expensive; running five hundred metres of the same profile is not, and the profile does not have to be perfect, because the shadow hides the joint. The labour argument was out of date on the day it was made. What survives of it is a narrower point about the conditions under which some hand ornament was produced, and that point is about employment rather than about decoration.

Lindholm has argued that the campaign was in substance about class. Ornament, on this reading, was what the newly prosperous bought when they had money and no inherited vocabulary for spending it, and the reformers who attacked it were marking a distance between themselves and those buyers. The claim is not absurd, and it explains the tone of the pamphlets, which is often contemptuous in a way a purely technical argument does not require. The evidence for it is uneven, however. It fits the pamphlets much better than it fits the buildings, and several of the plainest early works were commissioned by exactly the buyers the reading says were being kept out.

Trewin has restated the second objection in a form that survives scrutiny, and it is the version worth keeping. The target, on this account, was never decoration but pretence. A moulding that pretends to carry a load, a veneer laid to imitate solid timber, a bolted joint concealed to look pegged: these are the objects the argument was built for. A printed pattern that admits to being a printed pattern was never dishonest, because it makes no claim about structure at all. Read that way, the campaign is not against ornament, and a good deal of what was stripped out in its name was stripped out through a misreading of it.

What the campaign produced in practice was not the absence of a style but the arrival of an expensive one. A plain surface has nowhere to hide. Joints must be flush, fixings concealed, tolerances held to a fraction of what a carved surface would forgive, and the finish must be even across a whole plane. The labour did not disappear. It moved from the carver to the fitter, and in several documented cases the plain scheme took longer on site than the ornamented scheme it replaced. Plainness, once it had become a style, also dated, which the third objection had promised it would not.

The reassessment began quietly and is now general. Ornament returned first as printed and woven surface, where the honesty argument had never had any purchase, and then as pattern in materials that make no structural claim of their own. Conservation bodies that had once permitted the stripping of decorated interiors began to refuse it. The question under discussion is no longer whether decoration is permissible, but which of the two, the plain object or the ornamented one, is the more candid about how it was made. That is a question the original reformers would have recognised, even though the answer has moved a long way from the one they expected.

It is a mistake to score the campaign by counting mouldings. Its lasting achievement was not the disappearance of ornament but a change in what a designer is required to defend. Before it, an element could be present because elements of that kind were customary; after it, everything on a drawing has to survive the question of what it is doing there. That question can be answered by a pattern as readily as by a bracket, and the reformers would have denied it, which is the ordinary fate of arguments that win. The habit outlasted the doctrine, and the habit was the valuable part.

difficulty_rationale.note: The passage separates three arguments the sources conflated, tests each one, and then rescues a version of the second. Very little of that structure is signposted, so the reader has to hold three threads at once.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It rewrites the objection so that the thing it appears to attack turns out not to be its target, and readers carry the original meaning through the paragraph.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and paragraph A, then the first sentence of B, which announces that there are three arguments and not one.
skim_plan.skip: The list of dishonest details in E and the list of tolerances in F. Both illustrate a claim already stated.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in the passage?

teaching.strategy: Two of these statements attach a named person's argument to the writer, so find the sentence in which the writer grades that argument before you decide. The grading sentence is usually the last one in the paragraph, not the first.
teaching.order_note: In passage order: questions 27 to 31 run from paragraph C to the final paragraph.
teaching.watch_out: The writer accepts one named argument and declines another. Neither decision is marked by a contrastive connective.

questions.prompt: The claim that ornament wasted labour was well founded at the time it was made.
questions.evidence_quote: The labour argument was out of date on the day it was made.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C states that machine production had already made repeated mouldings cheaper than an equally finished plain surface, and then says plainly that the labour argument was out of date on the day it was made. The writer's verdict is that it was never sound, not that it later became unsound.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial is a short flat sentence between two longer explanatory ones and is easy to read past.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: was well founded at the time it was made
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: was out of date on the day it was made
paraphrase_link.note: 'Out of date on the day it was made' is the exact denial of being well founded at that time.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer states a claim that cannot hold alongside the statement, and dates the failure to the same moment the statement claims soundness. That is a contradiction rather than a silence.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends by saying something of the argument survives, so a reader who reaches that sentence first finds a defence of it.
distractors.why_wrong: What survives is a point about employment conditions, which the writer separates from the claim about decoration.

distractors.why_tempting: The words 'well founded' appear nowhere, and the paragraph is largely about costs rather than about whether anyone was right.
distractors.why_wrong: 'The weakest of the three' and 'out of date on the day it was made' are both verdicts, and both are the writer's.

teaching.reusable_rule: A short flat sentence between two long ones is usually the verdict. Slow down when the sentence length drops.

questions.prompt: The writer is persuaded by Lindholm's explanation of what the campaign was about.
questions.evidence_quote: The evidence for it is uneven, however.
questions.explanation: The writer grants that the class reading is not absurd and that it accounts for the tone of the pamphlets, then says the evidence for it is uneven and gives two reasons: it fits the writings better than the buildings, and some of the plainest early works were commissioned by the very buyers it says were being excluded.
questions.trap_note: Whose view: the reading is Lindholm's throughout, and the writer's own sentences are the ones that grade it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The evidence for it is uneven
paraphrase_link.note: Calling the evidence uneven is the writer's way of declining to be persuaded by it.

teaching.decision_rule: For YES the writer would have to accept the reading; the two sentences after the concession supply counter-evidence instead. A stated objection makes the key NO rather than NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: 'The claim is not absurd' and 'it explains the tone of the pamphlets' are both concessions, and they come before the objection.
distractors.why_wrong: Concessions are what the objection is set against; the sentence beginning 'The evidence' withdraws the agreement.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer never says the reading is wrong, only that its evidence is patchy, which can look like reserving judgement.
distractors.why_wrong: Two specific counter-examples follow, which is taking a position rather than withholding one.

teaching.reusable_rule: Concessions come first and objections come last. Read to the end of the paragraph before deciding whose side a writer is on.

questions.prompt: The writer thinks the objection to pretence is the version of the argument worth preserving.
questions.evidence_quote: in a form that survives scrutiny, and it is the version worth keeping
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says Trewin's restatement survives scrutiny and is the version worth keeping, and then shows what it does and does not cover: a moulding pretending to bear a load is the target, a pattern that admits to being a pattern is not.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the version of the argument worth preserving
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: it is the version worth keeping
paraphrase_link.note: One verb changes and nothing else, which is why the item is decided by attribution rather than by wording.

teaching.decision_rule: The endorsement is unattributed and evaluative, so it is the writer's, and it names the same version the statement names. Every part of the statement is supported.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is introduced with a name, so the whole of it gets assigned to that person and no authorial view remains.
distractors.why_wrong: The clause 'it is the version worth keeping' has no reporting verb attached and is therefore the writer speaking.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends by saying the campaign is not against ornament, which sounds like a rejection of the whole argument.
distractors.why_wrong: That sentence follows from the version being kept, and describes what it does not cover rather than dismissing it.

teaching.reusable_rule: A clause carrying an evaluation and no reporting verb belongs to the writer, however many names appear around it.

questions.prompt: Clients objected to paying for the extra precision that plain work demanded.
questions.evidence_quote: in several documented cases the plain scheme took longer on site than the ornamented scheme it replaced
questions.explanation: Paragraph F sets out what plainness required and reports that it sometimes took longer to build than the ornamented work it replaced. Nobody who paid for it appears anywhere in the paragraph, and no reaction of any kind is recorded.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the paragraph makes plainness sound costly, so a reader supplies the complaint the passage never records.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the extra precision that plain work demanded
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: tolerances held to a fraction of what a carved surface would forgive
paraphrase_link.note: The requirement is described in full; the client and the objection have no counterpart at all.

teaching.decision_rule: For YES the passage would have to record a reaction from someone paying; for NO it would have to record their acceptance. It records neither, only what the work involved.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph says plain schemes took longer, and anyone told a job will run over expects the client to complain.
distractors.why_wrong: That expectation is the reader's. No client, patron or purchaser is mentioned in the paragraph at all.

distractors.why_tempting: Plainness became the dominant style, so it looks as though whoever was paying must have accepted the cost.
distractors.why_wrong: Its adoption is stated; the reasoning from adoption to willing payment is supplied by the reader.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement about someone's reaction needs that person to appear in the text. A cost described is not a cost complained about.
teaching.nearest_text: tolerances held to a fraction of what a carved surface would forgive

questions.prompt: The campaign's most durable effect was on what a designer has to justify.
questions.evidence_quote: Its lasting achievement was not the disappearance of ornament but a change in what a designer is required to defend.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph states this directly in a not-X-but-Y sentence, and then spells out the change: an element used to be admissible because it was customary, and now has to answer for its presence.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Its lasting achievement
paraphrase_link.note: 'Lasting achievement' becomes 'most durable effect', which is broader but not stronger.

teaching.decision_rule: The claim is the Y half of an explicit not-X-but-Y sentence in the writer's own voice, and the following sentence supplies the mechanism. Nothing in the statement goes beyond it.

distractors.why_tempting: The same sentence begins by denying an effect, so a reader who matches on the negative reads the whole sentence as a refusal.
distractors.why_wrong: What is denied is the disappearance of ornament. The clause after 'but' is the claim the statement makes.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Justify' does not appear, and the paragraph closes on habit and doctrine rather than on designers.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Required to defend' is the same proposition, and it is stated as the campaign's lasting achievement.

teaching.reusable_rule: In a not-X-but-Y sentence the writer's claim is always the Y. Match your statement against that half only.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

teaching.strategy: Answer each stem from the passage before you read the options, because four of these five stems ask what the writer says rather than what was done. Question 36 asks about a whole paragraph, so leave it until the other four have fixed the argument.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, from paragraph B down to the last paragraph.
teaching.watch_out: Each set contains one option that is accurate about the passage but answers a stem other than this one.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the three objections to ornament?

options.text: They were rarely stated in public at the same time.
They rest on different kinds of evidence from one another.
They were all first advanced by the same reformers.
They apply to buildings more clearly than to furniture.

questions.evidence_quote: Each of these is a different argument with a different kind of evidence behind it, and almost nobody separated them.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B sets out an economic, a structural and a temporal objection, and closes by saying each is a different argument resting on a different kind of evidence, which almost nobody kept apart.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: They rest on different kinds of evidence from one another
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a different argument with a different kind of evidence behind it
paraphrase_link.note: 'With evidence behind it' becomes 'rest on evidence', and the distributive 'each' becomes a plural.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what the writer says about the set of three, and only the paragraph's last sentence makes a claim about the set rather than about a member of it.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage says almost nobody separated them, which a fast reader converts into a claim about how often they appeared together.
distractors.why_wrong: Not separating them means they were run together constantly, which is the opposite of rarely appearing at once.

distractors.why_tempting: The reformers are the paragraph's implied speakers and the passage treats the campaign as a single movement.
distractors.why_wrong: No origin is given for any of the three, and nobody is named until two paragraphs later.

distractors.why_tempting: Both a building and a cabinet are named in the structural objection, so a comparison between them seems available.
distractors.why_wrong: They are given as two instances of the same problem, and no comparison of clarity is made.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem asking about a set of items wants the sentence that describes the set, not the sentences describing its members.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer regard the economic objection as the weakest of the three?

options.text: Repeated ornament had already been made cheap by machinery.
Hand carvers were better paid than the reformers claimed.
Plain surfaces required almost no finishing work at all.
The objection was never actually stated in those terms.

questions.evidence_quote: machine production had already made the repetition of a moulding cheaper than a plain surface finished to the same tolerance
questions.explanation: Paragraph C answers the stem in one sentence: by the period when the objection was loudest, machine production had made repeated mouldings cheaper than an equally finished plain surface, so the claim about wasted labour no longer described the industry it attacked.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Repeated ornament had already been made cheap by machinery
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: machine production had already made the repetition of a moulding cheaper
paraphrase_link.note: 'A moulding' becomes 'ornament' and 'machine production' becomes 'machinery'; the timing word is unchanged.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a reason, so the key must be the clause the paragraph offers as its ground. Only one option restates that clause; the others make claims the paragraph does not.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does end on the pay and conditions of hand ornament, which is the objection's other half.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer says that point survives and is about employment. Nothing says the carvers were well paid.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph contrasts carved and plain surfaces, and plainness suggests less work to a reader who has not reached the later paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: The comparison depends on the plain surface being finished to the same tolerance, which is work rather than the absence of it.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer does say the argument was out of date, which sounds close to saying it was never properly made.
distractors.why_wrong: Being out of date is a statement about the facts, not about whether anyone said it. The passage says it was said loudly.

teaching.reusable_rule: A why-stem is answered by the clause the paragraph offers as its ground, not by the point it concedes afterwards.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's assessment of the reading that treats the campaign as being about class?

options.text: It is contradicted by the tone of the pamphlets.
It suits the writings better than it suits the buildings.
It has been accepted by most later commentators.
It rests on evidence nobody has yet examined.

questions.evidence_quote: It fits the pamphlets much better than it fits the buildings
questions.explanation: Paragraph D concedes that the class reading is not absurd and accounts for the contemptuous tone of the pamphlets, then says its evidence is uneven and gives the specific unevenness: the reading works for the writings and not for the buildings.
questions.trap_note: Option A takes the paragraph's concession and reverses it: the tone is what the reading explains, not what refutes it.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: It suits the writings better than it suits the buildings
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: It fits the pamphlets much better than it fits the buildings
paraphrase_link.note: 'Pamphlets' becomes 'writings' and 'fits' becomes 'suits'; the comparative structure is identical.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for an assessment, and the paragraph gives one graded verdict rather than a yes or a no. The key must therefore be the sentence that says where the reading holds and where it does not.

distractors.why_tempting: The tone of the pamphlets is discussed in the same paragraph and is the only thing in it a reader is likely to remember.
distractors.why_wrong: The tone is offered as evidence for the reading, so it supports it rather than contradicting it.

distractors.why_tempting: The reading is introduced with a name and treated seriously, which suggests it is the established view.
distractors.why_wrong: No other commentator is mentioned anywhere in the paragraph, and no reception is described.

distractors.why_tempting: 'The evidence for it is uneven' is a criticism of the evidence, and unexamined evidence is one way evidence can fail.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer has examined it, and names two findings from doing so in the next sentence.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a writer grades an argument rather than accepting or rejecting it, the key is the graded sentence and every absolute option is wrong.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what became of the labour that ornament had required?

options.text: It was eliminated by the use of standard components.
It was transferred to achieving precision in plain work.
It was reduced to about half of its former quantity.
It was moved abroad to workshops paying lower wages.

questions.evidence_quote: It moved from the carver to the fitter
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says the labour did not disappear but moved from the carver to the fitter, because plain work demands flush joints, concealed fixings and tight tolerances, and in several recorded cases took longer to build than the ornamented work it replaced.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: It was transferred to achieving precision in plain work
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: It moved from the carver to the fitter
paraphrase_link.note: The fitter's work is what the paragraph has just described as tolerances, flush joints and concealed fixings.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what became of a quantity, and the paragraph answers with an explicit negative followed by a destination. The key must name the destination.

distractors.why_tempting: Repeated machine profiles were discussed two paragraphs earlier, and standardisation is the obvious modern answer to a labour question.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph states the opposite in four words: the labour did not disappear.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does contain a proportion, and a halving is the sort of figure a reader expects beside one.
distractors.why_wrong: The only proportion given concerns tolerances, and no quantity of labour is measured anywhere.

distractors.why_tempting: The economic objection two paragraphs earlier is about underpaid workers, so cheaper labour is already in the reader's mind.
distractors.why_wrong: No location changes anywhere in the passage, and the move described is between two trades on the same site.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph denies one outcome and then names another, the key is what follows the denial.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's purpose in the final paragraph?

options.text: To propose a different measure of what the campaign achieved.
To show that ornament has now returned to general favour.
To blame the reformers for destroying decorated work.
To predict that plainness will shortly be abandoned.

questions.evidence_quote: It is a mistake to score the campaign by counting mouldings.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph opens by rejecting one way of assessing the campaign and then supplies another: what changed was not the quantity of ornament but the requirement that every element be defended. The paragraph exists to replace the measure, not to award a result.
questions.trap_note: Option B is true of the passage, but it belongs to the paragraph before this one.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: a different measure of what the campaign achieved
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a mistake to score the campaign by counting mouldings
paraphrase_link.note: Scoring by counting mouldings is the measure the paragraph rejects before offering its own.

teaching.decision_rule: A purpose stem asks what the paragraph is doing, not what it asserts. Its first sentence rejects a criterion and its second supplies a replacement, which is a single rhetorical move.

distractors.why_tempting: It is accurate about the passage and is the most recent thing the reader has been told before reaching this paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: The return of ornament is the previous paragraph's subject, and this one explicitly refuses to judge by counting.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage does say elsewhere that a great deal was stripped out through a misreading of the argument.
distractors.why_wrong: That is two paragraphs earlier, and the blame there falls on the misreading rather than on the reformers.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage notes that plainness dated once it became a style, which invites a forecast about its end.
distractors.why_wrong: No prediction is made anywhere. The paragraph is about what the campaign left behind, not about what happens next.

teaching.reusable_rule: A purpose stem is answered by what a paragraph does. Options describing what a neighbouring paragraph asserts are the standard trap.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Which paragraph contains the following information? NB You may use any letter more than once.

options.text: Paragraph A
Paragraph B
Paragraph C
Paragraph D
Paragraph E
Paragraph F
Paragraph G
Paragraph H

teaching.strategy: Do this group last, when you have already read every paragraph for the other two. Reduce each item to the one thing that must be physically present in the paragraph: a comment on wording, a distinction, a change of policy, a claim about fashion.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, and a letter may repeat. Nothing brackets the search here.
teaching.watch_out: Three paragraphs discuss whether ornament is honest. Only one of them draws a line between decoration and pretence.

questions.prompt: a comment on the kind of language the reformers chose
questions.evidence_quote: That vocabulary is worth noticing, because a fault can be removed while a preference can only be disagreed with
questions.explanation: Paragraph A notes that the reformers wrote about decoration as an illness to be cured, and then comments on that choice of words: calling something a fault gives an opinion the standing of a finding.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the kind of language the reformers chose
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: That vocabulary is worth noticing
paraphrase_link.note: 'Vocabulary' is the passage's word for the language chosen, and the demonstrative points back at it.

teaching.decision_rule: The item asks for a comment about wording rather than for a claim about ornament, and only one paragraph steps back to remark on how the campaign expressed itself.

distractors.why_tempting: That paragraph discusses the tone of the pamphlets, which is also a remark about how the reformers wrote.
distractors.why_wrong: Tone there is evidence for a claim about class. The comment on choosing the language of illness is in the opening paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: The last paragraph is where a writer normally reflects on the campaign as a whole.
distractors.why_wrong: It reflects on what the campaign changed, and no wording of the reformers' is quoted or discussed there.

teaching.reusable_rule: An item about how something was said needs a paragraph that steps back from the argument to remark on its wording.

questions.prompt: a distinction between decoration and a false appearance of structure
questions.evidence_quote: The target, on this account, was never decoration but pretence.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E separates the two explicitly: a moulding that pretends to carry a load is dishonest, while a printed pattern that admits to being a pattern makes no structural claim and therefore cannot be.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A moulding that pretends to carry a load
paraphrase_link.note: The item names the category; the paragraph gives three instances of it in one list.

teaching.decision_rule: The item requires the two ideas to be told apart rather than merely both present. Only this paragraph states that one of them was never the target.

distractors.why_tempting: The structural objection is first set out there, complete with a bracket and a cornice disguising construction.
distractors.why_wrong: That paragraph states the objection without separating pretence from decoration; the separation is what the later restatement adds.

distractors.why_tempting: It asks which of the plain and the ornamented object is more candid, which is also about honesty.
distractors.why_wrong: That is a comparison between two finished objects, not a distinction between two kinds of ornament.

teaching.reusable_rule: An item naming a distinction needs a sentence that separates two things, not two paragraphs that each mention one.

questions.prompt: a change in what official bodies allow to be done to old interiors
questions.evidence_quote: Conservation bodies that had once permitted the stripping of decorated interiors began to refuse it.
questions.explanation: Paragraph G records the institutional turn: bodies that had previously allowed decorated interiors to be stripped out started to refuse permission, which is presented as part of a general reassessment.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Conservation bodies that had once permitted
paraphrase_link.note: 'Conservation bodies' becomes the broader 'official bodies', and 'permitted' becomes 'allow'.

teaching.decision_rule: The item requires an organisation and a change of permission. Only one sentence in the passage contains a body with the power to permit anything.

distractors.why_tempting: That paragraph is the one that mentions material being stripped out, using almost the same word.
distractors.why_wrong: There the stripping is attributed to a misreading of the argument. No permission and no organisation appear.

distractors.why_tempting: The final paragraph is about what the campaign changed, and a change of rules is a change.
distractors.why_wrong: What changes there is what a designer must justify, and no body of any kind is named.

teaching.reusable_rule: An item naming an organisation is decided by the paragraph that contains one. Shared vocabulary elsewhere is the decoy.

questions.prompt: a claim that decorated objects go out of fashion faster than plain ones
questions.evidence_quote: an ornamented object becomes unfashionable while a plain one merely becomes old
questions.explanation: The third of the objections in paragraph B is exactly this: decoration is dated by the year it was made, so an ornamented object becomes unfashionable while a plain one only becomes old.
questions.trap_note: The claim is reported here and answered in the paragraph about what plainness cost, which is where the reader who searches for 'dated' will land.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: go out of fashion faster than plain ones
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: becomes unfashionable while a plain one merely becomes old
paraphrase_link.note: A contrast between two fates is restated as a comparison of speed, which is what the passage means by it.

teaching.decision_rule: The item asks where the claim is made, not where it is judged. The paragraph setting out the three objections is where it is stated as a claim.

distractors.why_tempting: That paragraph says plainness also dated once it became a style, which uses the same idea and is more memorable.
distractors.why_wrong: It refutes the claim rather than making it, so the item's word 'claim' points elsewhere.

distractors.why_tempting: It describes ornament coming back, which is a change of fashion and shares the vocabulary.
distractors.why_wrong: That is a change in what is accepted, and no comparison of how quickly two kinds of object date appears there.

teaching.reusable_rule: Distinguish where a claim is stated from where it is tested. An item naming a claim wants the first of the two.

texts.heading: Autumn short courses at Norland Community Centre

paragraphs.text: Bread and Baking. Thursdays, 18.30 to 21.00, for six weeks from 2 October. The fee is 78 pounds, or 62 pounds for anyone claiming a means-tested benefit. All ingredients are provided and you take home whatever you bake. Places are capped at twelve, so early enrolment is advised. No experience is needed, but bring a container for the finished loaves.

Conversational Spanish, Stage Two. Mondays, 19.00 to 20.30, twelve weeks from 29 September. The fee is 96 pounds and includes the course book. The class is for people who have finished Stage One here, or who can hold a short conversation about everyday matters. A free assessment is held on 22 September for anyone unsure of their level.

Upholstery Basics. Saturdays, 10.00 to 13.00, eight weeks from 4 October. The fee is 120 pounds, with no concessionary rate. Students work on one small chair of their own, which must be brought to the first session; the centre cannot store furniture. Tools are lent free of charge, and under-18s are not accepted.

Digital Photography. Wednesdays, 18.00 to 20.00, six weeks from 1 October. The fee is 54 pounds, or 45 pounds for students in full-time education. Bring any camera with manual settings, including a phone. The first two evenings are held indoors and the remaining four are outdoor sessions around the town. Waterproof clothing is essential.

Community Choir. Tuesdays, 19.30 to 21.00, running all term from 30 September. The charge is 4 pounds an evening, paid at the door, with no need to book. There is no audition and you do not need to read music. Members are asked to attend two thirds of the sessions before the December concert.

Allotment Gardening. Fridays, 14.00 to 16.00, ten weeks from 3 October. The fee is 70 pounds, or 55 pounds for members of the Ashfield Allotment Society. Sessions take place on the centre's own plot in all but the worst weather, so boots are needed. Anyone on the town's allotment waiting list is given priority when places are allocated.

texts.heading: Ashfield Central Library: using your card

paragraphs.text: Membership is free to anyone who lives, works or studies in the borough. Bring proof of address, dated within the last three months, to the enquiry desk on the ground floor, and your card will be issued the same day. Children under fourteen may join, but a parent or guardian must sign the form and remains responsible for anything borrowed on the card.

An adult card allows twelve items at a time, of which no more than four may be DVDs. Books are lent for three weeks and may be renewed twice, either online or by telephone, unless another reader has reserved the item. Renewals are not accepted at the self-service machines. Overdue books are charged at 20p a day.

The three study rooms on the first floor may be booked for up to two hours a day, free of charge, by any member. Bookings open two weeks ahead and are made online only. A room not claimed within fifteen minutes of the start time is released to anyone waiting. Hot drinks may not be taken into the study rooms, although covered water bottles are allowed.

texts.heading: Notice to residents: changes to recycling collections

paragraphs.text: From Monday 6 January the borough will collect recycling every fortnight instead of every week. For most households the collection day does not change. Households in the streets listed overleaf will move to a Thursday collection, and those residents will receive a separate letter in December. Bins should be at the kerb by 7.00 am on the day of collection.

The new blue bin, which will be delivered during November, replaces the green box and the clear sacks. Paper, card, tins, glass and rigid plastic may all be placed in it together; they no longer need to be sorted. Food waste is not collected in the blue bin and should continue to go in the small brown caddy, which is emptied weekly throughout the year.

Garden waste is a separate, chargeable service. The annual fee of 48 pounds covers one brown wheeled bin and runs from April to March. Residents who signed up before 30 November keep last year's price for one more year. The council does not collect soil, rubble or tree stumps, and these must be taken to the household waste centre at Marlow Road.

difficulty_rationale.note: The English is plain, but every sentence carries a figure, a day or a condition, and the qualifier that decides a question is regularly attached to a clause after a comma or a semicolon.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Four separate limits sit in one short paragraph, and three of them are numbers, so the wrong one is always within reach.

skim_plan.read_first: The three headings only. They tell you which document holds courses, which holds library rules and which holds bin collections.
skim_plan.skip: Every day and start-time in the course listings. No question asks when a class meets, and reading them costs a minute you need later.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Look at the six courses, A-F. Which course does each statement describe? You may use any letter more than once.

options.text: Bread and Baking
Spanish, Stage Two
Upholstery Basics
Digital Photography
Community Choir
Allotment Gardening

teaching.strategy: Reduce each question to a single field first: price, equipment, booking, preference, level. Then take one listing at a time and test it against all five questions, because each listing is short and re-reading it costs more than one careful pass.
teaching.order_note: Not in text order, and a letter may answer twice. Work listing by listing, not question by question.
teaching.watch_out: One listing answers two of these questions and two listings answer none. An unused letter is not a mistake.

questions.prompt: a course that charges the same for everyone
questions.evidence_quote: The fee is 120 pounds, with no concessionary rate.
questions.explanation: Every other listing names a second, lower figure for a particular group, or charges by the evening. Only the upholstery course states that no reduced rate exists, so one figure applies to everybody.
questions.trap_note: Listings A, D and F each open with a single fee and add the reduction in the same sentence.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: with no concessionary rate
paraphrase_link.note: A reduced rate that does not exist is another way of saying one price for all.

teaching.decision_rule: Only one listing states that no reduced price exists. Three others name a second figure for a named group and a fourth charges per evening, so none of them prices everybody alike.

distractors.why_tempting: A gives one headline figure, so a reader who stops at the first number sees a single price.
distractors.why_wrong: The same sentence offers a lower figure to anyone claiming a means-tested benefit, so two prices exist.

distractors.why_tempting: F reads as a flat fee until the society discount arrives at the end of the same sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: Members of the local society pay less, which is a second price for the same course.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a question says everyone, look for a second figure later in the same sentence rather than for the word itself.

questions.prompt: a course for which you must supply the object you will work on
questions.evidence_quote: which must be brought to the first session
questions.explanation: The upholstery listing says students work on one small chair of their own and that it must be brought to the first session, because the centre cannot store furniture. The item worked on is supplied by the student.
questions.trap_note: Two other listings tell you to bring something, but a camera and a container are equipment, not the thing the class works on.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the object you will work on
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: one small chair of their own
paraphrase_link.note: The question names the category; the listing names the instance and puts it in the passive.

teaching.decision_rule: Two listings ask you to bring something, but only one asks you to bring the thing the class is about. A camera is a tool and a container is for taking work home.

distractors.why_tempting: D also opens an instruction with 'Bring', and a camera is the thing the class uses throughout.
distractors.why_wrong: A camera is the tool of that class; what it works on is the photograph, which nobody carries in.

distractors.why_tempting: A asks you to bring a container, which reads as a required item like any other.
distractors.why_wrong: The container is for carrying the bread away afterwards, not for working on during the class.

teaching.reusable_rule: Separate the tool a class needs from the material it acts on. Both may appear as things to take along.

questions.prompt: a course that can be joined without booking in advance
questions.evidence_quote: paid at the door, with no need to book
questions.explanation: The choir charges by the evening at the door and states that no booking is needed. Every other listing runs for a fixed number of weeks and takes a single fee, which implies enrolment.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: with no need to book
paraphrase_link.note: The listing's 'no need to' becomes 'without', and the verb becomes a gerund.

teaching.decision_rule: Only one listing removes the requirement to reserve a place. The others cap numbers, hold an assessment or allocate places, all of which assume a place is arranged first.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who sees 'no experience is needed' reads the whole listing as having no entry conditions at all.
distractors.why_wrong: The places are capped at twelve and early enrolment is advised, which is the opposite of arriving unbooked.

distractors.why_tempting: B's free assessment looks like an open session that anyone may walk into.
distractors.why_wrong: The assessment settles your level; it says nothing about joining the class itself without arranging it.

teaching.reusable_rule: Find the sentence that removes a step, not the one that limits numbers. They sit in the same field and mean opposite things.

questions.prompt: a course that prefers applicants who are already waiting for something else
questions.evidence_quote: Anyone on the town's allotment waiting list is given priority when places are allocated.
questions.explanation: The gardening listing is the only one that states how places are decided between people who all qualify: those already on the town's allotment waiting list come first.
questions.trap_note: Other listings name conditions of entry, which decide who may apply rather than who is chosen.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: prefers applicants who are already waiting
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is given priority when places are allocated
paraphrase_link.note: The listing uses a passive with no named agent; the question makes the course the active subject.

teaching.decision_rule: Only one listing gives a rule for choosing between people who all qualify. The others state who may join at all, which is a different decision.

distractors.why_tempting: B restricts entry to people who have finished Stage One, which reads like a preference for insiders.
distractors.why_wrong: That is a condition of entry, not a way of ranking applicants who all meet it.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Early enrolment is advised' suggests a queue, and a queue suggests being ahead of other people.
distractors.why_wrong: Advising speed gives nobody an advantage; it only warns that the twelve places will go.

teaching.reusable_rule: A rule that ranks candidates is not a warning about scarcity. One decides who is chosen; the other only decides how fast you must act.

questions.prompt: a course that offers a way of checking you have chosen the right level
questions.evidence_quote: A free assessment is held on 22 September for anyone unsure of their level.
questions.explanation: The Spanish listing sets an entry standard and then supplies a way of testing yourself against it before the course begins. No other listing offers any measurement.
questions.trap_note: Two listings say that nothing is required, which removes a standard rather than measuring you against one.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: checking you have chosen the right level
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: unsure of their level
paraphrase_link.note: The listing names the problem, being unsure; the question names the remedy, checking.

teaching.decision_rule: Only one listing supplies a procedure that settles the question of level before enrolment. Others state a level requirement, or waive one, without offering any test.

distractors.why_tempting: A says no experience is needed, which answers exactly the worry the question describes.
distractors.why_wrong: Removing a requirement is reassurance, not a way of checking anything.

distractors.why_tempting: E states that there is no audition and no need to read music, which is the listing that talks most about ability.
distractors.why_wrong: It also cancels a test rather than offering one, so nothing here measures you.

teaching.reusable_rule: Saying that a standard is not required is not the same as offering to measure you against it.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Answer the questions below using words from the library information sheet.

teaching.strategy: Every answer is in the library sheet, in the order the questions ask for it. Fix the shape of each answer from its question word first - a document, a quantity, a period - and reject any span without that shape.
teaching.order_note: In text order. Question 9's answer lies below question 8's, so never search upwards.
teaching.watch_out: Three words means three words. Two of these spans sit beside a qualifying clause that would take a copied answer over the limit.

questions.prompt: What must you take to the enquiry desk in order to join?
questions.evidence_quote: Bring proof of address, dated within the last three months, to the enquiry desk
questions.explanation: The sheet names one document: proof of address. The clause about the last three months is a condition on that document, not part of what it is called.
questions.trap_note: Copying the date clause as well takes the answer over the three-word limit, which scores zero however right the content is.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: to the enquiry desk
paraphrase_link.note: Only the verb changes: the sheet says bring, the question says take, and the rest is copied.

teaching.decision_rule: The limit is three words and the sheet names exactly one document. The dating clause is a separate condition, so it is outside the answer.

distractors.why_tempting: The qualifying clause sits inside the same comma group and feels like part of what you must bring.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a condition on the document, and copying it pushes the answer past the word limit.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the last noun phrase in the sentence and the question names the desk directly.
distractors.why_wrong: The desk is where you take the document; the question asks what you take.

teaching.reusable_rule: Cut the qualifying clause. A word limit is usually the item writer telling you where an answer stops.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What must you take' wants a noun phrase, so no verb and no clause belong in the gap.

questions.prompt: How many DVDs may an adult borrow at one time?
questions.evidence_quote: of which no more than four may be DVDs
questions.explanation: An adult card allows twelve items in total, and the relative clause caps one category of them at four. The question names that category, so the cap is the answer.
questions.trap_note: Twelve is the total for all items and is the more prominent number in the paragraph.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: How many DVDs may an adult borrow
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: no more than four may be DVDs
paraphrase_link.note: The sheet states the ceiling inside a relative clause; the question asks for it directly.

teaching.decision_rule: One sentence carries two limits for the same card: a total and a cap on one category. The question names the category, which selects the smaller figure.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the first and largest number in the paragraph and it is attached to the same card.
distractors.why_wrong: Twelve covers everything borrowed; the DVD ceiling is the figure in the clause that follows.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the next number in the paragraph and it also describes what a borrower is allowed.
distractors.why_wrong: It is how long a book may be kept, not how many of anything you may take.

teaching.reusable_rule: When one sentence carries two quantities, take the one attached to the noun the question names.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'How many' wants a number alone; adding the noun risks the limit and adds nothing.

questions.prompt: For how long may a member use a study room each day?
questions.evidence_quote: may be booked for up to two hours a day, free of charge, by any member
questions.explanation: The sheet gives a daily ceiling of two hours for any member. 'Up to' hedges the figure and 'a day' is already in the question, so neither belongs in the answer.
questions.trap_note: Two weeks appears in the very next sentence and is also a period of time.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: may a member use a study room each day
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: booked for up to two hours a day
paraphrase_link.note: The sheet writes a passive with a hedge; the question asks the member to act and drops the hedge.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks for a daily maximum and the sheet states one. The answer is the quantity itself, not the hedge in front of it or the frequency after it.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Up to' sits immediately in front of the figure and reads like part of it.
distractors.why_wrong: It hedges the quantity and it takes the answer past the three-word limit.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the next number in the paragraph and it is also a length of time.
distractors.why_wrong: Two weeks is how far ahead a booking may be made, not how long a room may be used.

teaching.reusable_rule: Strip the hedge before writing a quantity. Words like about and nearly belong to the writer, not to the measurement.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'For how long' wants a period: a number and its unit, and nothing on either side of them.

questions.prompt: What kind of drink may be taken into a study room?
questions.evidence_quote: although covered water bottles are allowed
questions.explanation: The final sentence bans hot drinks from the study rooms and then permits one exception. The question asks for the permitted item, which is named in the concessive clause.
questions.trap_note: The sentence opens with the prohibition, so a reader who stops at the comma answers with the banned item instead.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: may be taken into a study room
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: covered water bottles are allowed
paraphrase_link.note: The permission arrives as a concession after a prohibition, so it reads as an afterthought rather than an answer.

teaching.decision_rule: One sentence bans one category and permits another. The question asks what is permitted, so the answer is the noun phrase inside the 'although' clause, with its modifier.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the subject of the sentence and the first noun phrase a scanner meets after the room is named.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the item that is forbidden; 'may not' is the whole difference between the two halves.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the shorter, more natural phrase and it fits the limit comfortably.
distractors.why_wrong: The sheet writes covered water bottles, and the modifier is the condition that makes them allowed.

teaching.reusable_rule: Read to the end of the sentence. A concession after a comma often reverses what the main clause has just said.
teaching.grammar_cue: The question wants a noun phrase copied whole, including the adjective in front of it and the plural.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the notice to residents?

teaching.strategy: Mark the quantity, the modal or the frequency in each statement before you go near the notice: separately, must, every week, may. Four of these five turn on one such word, and the fifth turns on a reason the notice never gives.
teaching.order_note: In text order across the three paragraphs, so each answer lies below the last.
teaching.watch_out: The notice states a general rule and then its exception. Answering from the general rule alone produces two wrong answers here.

questions.prompt: The council moved to fortnightly collections in order to reduce its costs.
questions.evidence_quote: the borough will collect recycling every fortnight instead of every week
questions.explanation: The notice states the change and dates it, but gives no reason for it anywhere. No sentence supports a cost motive and no sentence denies one.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: a change this obvious feels as though it must have been explained, and the silence is read as a denial of any other motive.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: collect recycling every fortnight instead of every week
paraphrase_link.note: The change itself matches word for word; the purpose clause has no counterpart anywhere in the notice.

teaching.decision_rule: The change is stated and dated, but the notice never says why it was made. There is no support and nothing to point at as a denial, which is the NOT GIVEN condition exactly.

distractors.why_tempting: Halving a service obviously costs less, so the motive feels like something the notice has already said.
distractors.why_wrong: That reasoning is the reader's. A purpose the reader supplies is not a purpose in the text.

distractors.why_tempting: Money appears twice further down, so a reader who has found charges in the notice decides it is about raising income instead.
distractors.why_wrong: Those charges are for garden waste, and nothing anywhere denies a cost motive for the change.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stated change plus an obvious motive is still two facts, one of which you supplied. Purpose has to be written down.
teaching.nearest_text: the borough will collect recycling every fortnight instead of every week

questions.prompt: Households whose collection day is changing will be told individually.
questions.evidence_quote: those residents will receive a separate letter in December
questions.explanation: The notice identifies the households moving to a Thursday collection and says in the same sentence that they will receive their own letter in December. Both halves of the statement are supported.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: will receive a separate letter
paraphrase_link.note: Receiving a letter is one way of being told; the statement uses the category and turns the sentence round.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and every element is stated: which households move, and that they are written to separately. Nothing in the statement is stronger than the notice.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous sentence says the collection day does not change, so a reader who fixes on it treats any change of day as a contradiction.
distractors.why_wrong: That sentence is limited to most households; the next one names the streets that do move.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'told' appears nowhere, so a search for it returns nothing at all.
distractors.why_wrong: A separate letter is a form of being told, and it is promised in the same sentence as the change of day.

teaching.reusable_rule: A general statement early in a notice is often qualified by the exception after it. Read both before deciding.

questions.prompt: Different materials must be kept apart inside the new blue bin.
questions.evidence_quote: they no longer need to be sorted
questions.explanation: The notice lists five materials and says they may all be placed in the bin together, adding that they no longer need to be sorted. That cancels the obligation the statement asserts.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial is in the clause after the semicolon, so a reader who stops at the list of materials sees only categories.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: no longer need to be sorted
paraphrase_link.note: An obligation in the statement meets a cancelled obligation in the notice, which is a contradiction rather than a silence.

teaching.decision_rule: The notice addresses the same materials and states the opposite requirement in the same sentence. A cancelled obligation contradicts an asserted one, so the key is FALSE and not NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph names five distinct materials, and a list of types reads like a set of categories to be kept apart.
distractors.why_wrong: The list is followed by 'may all be placed in it together', which is the point the sentence is making.

distractors.why_tempting: The phrase 'kept apart' never appears, so a reader hunting that wording finds nothing.
distractors.why_wrong: The same proposition is there, negated, in the clause after the semicolon.

teaching.reusable_rule: An obligation that the text cancels is a contradiction, not an absence. Find the word that cancels it.

questions.prompt: Food waste will be collected every week throughout the year.
questions.evidence_quote: the small brown caddy, which is emptied weekly throughout the year
questions.explanation: Food waste is excluded from the blue bin and stays in the brown caddy, which the notice says is emptied weekly throughout the year. Both the frequency and the year-round scope are stated.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph's headline change is to fortnightly collection, and readers carry that frequency across to the caddy.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: collected every week throughout the year
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: emptied weekly throughout the year
paraphrase_link.note: One verb and one adverb are swapped and the frequency is untouched, so nothing is added or strengthened.

teaching.decision_rule: One clause supports both parts of the statement: how often the caddy is emptied and that this does not change with the season. There is nothing left over to check.

distractors.why_tempting: The notice's main announcement is a move from weekly to fortnightly, and the reader applies it to everything the council collects.
distractors.why_wrong: That change is stated of the blue bin only; the caddy is given its own frequency in the same paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Throughout the year' reads as a phrase about seasons, so the sentence looks as though it never commits to a frequency.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Emptied weekly' is the commitment, and the phrase about the year extends it rather than hedging it.

teaching.reusable_rule: One notice can carry two frequencies. Attach each to its own container before judging a statement about either.

questions.prompt: Rubble may be left beside the garden waste bin for collection.
questions.evidence_quote: The council does not collect soil, rubble or tree stumps
questions.explanation: The last sentence names rubble in a short list of things the council does not collect, and then says where such material must be taken instead. Both halves deny the statement.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: left beside the garden waste bin
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: does not collect soil, rubble or tree stumps
paraphrase_link.note: The permission in the statement is precisely the service the notice says it does not provide.

teaching.decision_rule: The item is named and the notice states that it is not collected, then names the alternative destination. That is a quotable denial, so the key is FALSE.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement is about what may be left out, and the notice talks about what is collected, so the two read as different questions.
distractors.why_wrong: Refusing to collect an item is the same proposition as refusing to take it from the kerb, and the alternative site is named.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph describes a service that is paid for, and a paid service sounds as though it takes whatever is put out.
distractors.why_wrong: The fee covers one wheeled bin, and the exclusions arrive in the final sentence of the same paragraph.

teaching.reusable_rule: The last sentence of a paragraph about a service is usually its list of exclusions. Read it before answering.

texts.heading: Leave and absence: a summary for staff

paragraphs.text: Full-time employees are entitled to 25 days of annual leave in each leave year, which runs from 1 April to 31 March, in addition to public holidays. Staff who work part of the week receive the same entitlement pro rata, calculated on the hours in their contract rather than on the hours they happen to work in a particular month. Leave is earned month by month, so anyone joining in October may take only the proportion accrued by the date of the holiday. Requests go through the online system and must be approved by a line manager before any travel is booked; the department will not meet the cost of a booking made before approval.

No more than five days may be carried into the following leave year, and any days carried over must be used by 30 June or they are lost. Carry-over above five days is granted only where a manager has refused leave for operational reasons and has recorded that refusal at the time. Staff in their probationary period may take leave, but not more than the amount accrued. The standard notice applies to everyone: a request for five or more consecutive days should reach your manager at least four weeks in advance, and a request for a shorter absence at least one week in advance.

An absence through illness of up to seven calendar days is covered by self-certification. Complete the return-to-work form on your first day back and give it to your manager. From the eighth day a certificate from a doctor is required, and a further certificate must be supplied for each period the doctor states. Telephone your manager before 9.30 on the first morning of any sickness absence. A message passed on by a colleague does not count as notification, and repeated failure to notify may be treated as unauthorised absence.

Compassionate leave of up to three days on full pay is available on the death or serious illness of a close relative, and a manager may extend it by agreement. Leave to deal with a sudden problem involving a dependant, such as a school closure or a care arrangement that fails, is unpaid, and staff are advised to give as much notice as circumstances allow. Requests for unpaid leave of more than one month are considered only after two years of continuous service and must be made in writing to the head of department.

texts.heading: Staff facilities at Norland House

paragraphs.text: Car park permits. The staff car park has 60 spaces, and permits are allocated once a year by a points system that takes account of distance travelled, shift pattern and caring responsibilities. Applications close on 31 January. A permit holder who does not use the space for three consecutive months loses it. Staff without a permit may use the visitor bays after 16.00 if a ticket is displayed.

Cycle scheme. Staff who have completed six months of service may buy a bicycle through the scheme and repay the cost from their salary over twelve or eighteen months. The maximum value is 1,200 pounds. If you leave Norland House before the repayments are finished, the balance is deducted from your final salary. Two secure cycle stores are open at all hours to registered users.

Staff canteen. The canteen on the second floor serves hot food from 11.45 to 14.15 on weekdays, and drinks and sandwiches from 8.00 until 16.00. It does not open at weekends, when the vending machines in the ground-floor lobby are the only option. A hot main course costs 3.90 pounds for staff and 5.60 pounds for visitors, and payment is by card only.

Lockers and changing rooms. Every member of staff may request a half-height locker, while full-height lockers are kept for those who cycle or run to work. Lockers are emptied each August and anything left in them is given to a charity shop, so clear yours before the summer. The changing rooms include four showers, which cannot be booked.

Out-of-hours access. The building is open from 7.00 to 19.00 on weekdays. Outside those hours staff need a coded card, issued by the facilities office on the written approval of a head of department. The card goes back to the office when the reason for it ends. Anyone in the building after 19.00 must sign the register at the entrance so that the fire warden knows who is on site.

Visitor reception. Visitors report to the desk in the main lobby, where they are given a badge that must be worn at all times and returned on leaving. Staff meet their own visitors at the desk and accompany them in the parts of the building that are not open to the public. Deliveries are taken at the rear entrance only.

difficulty_rationale.note: The leave document states a rule, then the exception to it, then the condition on the exception, and it uses the vocabulary of entitlement rather than of everyday English.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Two limits, one exception and two notice periods sit in five sentences, and each is stated once only.

skim_plan.read_first: The two headings and the first sentence of each paragraph. Every paragraph announces its subject in its first six words.
skim_plan.skip: The pro rata calculation in the first paragraph. It is background, and no question turns on how the figure is worked out.

rewordings: what has been earned so far
the share built up to date
taken out of what you are owed
the first months in the job

hinge_words.why_here: It restricts the carry-over exception that question 20 asks you to name.
It marks advice rather than obligation, which is the whole of question 22's neighbour.
It separates the reporting duty in question 18 from what is merely recommended.
It marks the pro rata contrast behind the figure question 19 asks for.

mineable.meaning: have an official right to receive
in proportion to hours worked
because the work of the team required it
reporting your own illness without a doctor
time off nobody agreed to
unbroken time working for the same employer
what is still owed is taken off

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the notes below with words taken from the leave and absence summary.

layout.title: Absence: what to do
lines: Leave carried into the next year must be used by {{15}}.
Illness of up to seven days needs only {{16}}.
Hand your manager the completed {{17}} on your first day back.
A message passed on by a colleague does not count as {{18}}.

teaching.strategy: Everything here comes from the carry-over paragraph and the sickness paragraph, so find those two and stay inside them. Decide the word class of each gap from the word in front of it before you search: one wants a date, three want nouns.
teaching.order_note: All four come from two neighbouring paragraphs. Locate that band once, then work down inside it.
teaching.watch_out: Two answers are compound nouns written with hyphens. Copy the hyphens; a rewritten form is a different word and scores zero.

questions.prompt: Leave carried into the next year must be used by {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: any days carried over must be used by 30 June or they are lost
questions.explanation: The carry-over paragraph gives one deadline for using days brought forward: 30 June, after which they are lost. The note keeps the document's own frame, so the answer is the date exactly as written.
questions.trap_note: Four other dates appear in the same two paragraphs, and three of them are also deadlines.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: must be used by 30 June
paraphrase_link.note: The note keeps the verb frame and drops the consequence clause, which is what makes the gap findable by shape.

teaching.decision_rule: The note asks for the point at which carried leave expires. Only one date in the paragraph is attached to that verb; the others govern notice periods and the leave year.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the end of the leave year, so it feels like the natural expiry point for anything left over.
distractors.why_wrong: It ends the year in which the days were earned; the extension runs three months past it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest other figure and it is also a deadline expressed in time.
distractors.why_wrong: That is how much notice a long absence needs, not when carried leave expires.

teaching.reusable_rule: A document about time is full of deadlines. Match each one to the verb it governs before writing anything.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'by' before the gap wants a point in time, so a date and not a length.

questions.prompt: Illness of up to seven days needs only {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: An absence through illness of up to seven calendar days is covered by self-certification.
questions.explanation: Short illnesses are covered by self-certification; a doctor's certificate is required only from the eighth day. The note asks what the shorter absence needs, so the answer is the single hyphenated noun.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Illness of up to seven days
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: absence through illness of up to seven calendar days
paraphrase_link.note: The note drops two words from the noun phrase, which is enough to defeat a search for the exact string.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph splits absence at the seventh day and names a different requirement on each side of the split. The note names the shorter side, which selects the first requirement.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's most prominent requirement and appears twice in the following sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: That applies from the eighth day, which is the other side of the split.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the phrase nearest the answer and it is what the note's own line is measuring.
distractors.why_wrong: It states the length of the absence, not what covers it, and it runs to three words.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a rule has two halves divided by a number, check which half the question is standing in before you copy anything.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'needs only' wants a noun, and the gap ends the line, so no verb belongs in it.

questions.prompt: Hand your manager the completed {{gap}} on your first day back.
questions.evidence_quote: Complete the return-to-work form on your first day back and give it to your manager.
questions.explanation: The document names one document to be completed on the first day back and given to the manager. The note reorders the sentence but keeps every element of it.
questions.trap_note: The word 'certificate' is the paragraph's other document and sits two sentences away.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: give it to your manager
paraphrase_link.note: One verb is swapped and the object moves in front of it, which is why the sentence looks new.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'the completed' and a time phrase, so it takes a noun naming a document, and only one document in the paragraph is completed by the employee.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other paper named in the paragraph and it is also handed over.
distractors.why_wrong: A certificate comes from a doctor and applies from the eighth day; the employee completes nothing.

distractors.why_tempting: Three separate words look more natural in English than a hyphenated string.
distractors.why_wrong: The hyphens are part of the written form and also keep the answer inside the two-word limit.

teaching.reusable_rule: A hyphenated compound counts as one word. Writing it out separately can push you past the limit.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'the completed' before the gap forces a singular noun naming a document.

questions.prompt: A message passed on by a colleague does not count as {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: A message passed on by a colleague does not count as notification
questions.explanation: Sickness must be reported by telephone to the manager before 9.30. The document states directly that a message left with a colleague is not notification, and that repeated failure may be treated as unauthorised absence.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: does not count as notification
paraphrase_link.note: The line is lifted whole, so the only work is deciding where the answer stops.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'count as' and closes the sentence, so it takes an abstract noun. The clause that follows names a consequence, not the thing itself.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the very next noun phrase and it is the more striking piece of vocabulary in the sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: That is what repeated failure may be treated as; the gap names what the message is not.

distractors.why_tempting: The verb appears in the same sentence and carries the same meaning.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Count as' takes a noun, and the document supplies one four words earlier.

teaching.reusable_rule: When two nouns sit in one sentence, the gap takes the one on its own side of the comma.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'count as' is followed by a noun, and the gap ends the line.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the table below with words taken from the leave and absence summary.

layout.title: Types of leave
rows: Full-time staff receive {{19}} days in each leave year.
Granted only where a manager refused leave for {{20}}.
Up to three days on {{21}} for a close relative.
Unpaid leave of over a month
Considered only after {{22}} of continuous service.

teaching.strategy: The table's left column names the type of leave, so use it as the index: find the sentence that names that type and read only that sentence. Three of the four answers sit in the clause immediately after the type is named.
teaching.order_note: All four come from the leave summary, in the order its paragraphs run. Never search the facilities text.
teaching.watch_out: Two of these gaps sit next to a longer phrase that reads better but breaks the two-word limit. Length is checked before meaning.

questions.prompt: Annual leave: full-time staff receive {{gap}} days in each leave year.
questions.evidence_quote: Full-time employees are entitled to 25 days of annual leave in each leave year
questions.explanation: The opening sentence gives the full-time entitlement as 25 days, with public holidays counted separately. Part-time staff get the same figure pro rata, so the number itself does not change.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph carries four other numbers, two of which are dates in the same sentence.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Full-time employees are entitled to
paraphrase_link.note: The employer's word 'entitled' becomes the employee's word 'receive', and the sentence turns round.

teaching.decision_rule: The row names full-time annual leave, and the document states one figure for exactly that. The pro rata sentence changes who gets it, not how much a full-time year is worth.

distractors.why_tempting: It is inside the same sentence and it is attached to the leave year the row names.
distractors.why_wrong: It ends the year; the row asks how many days the year contains.

distractors.why_tempting: It reads as the complete answer, and copying the noun feels safer than leaving it out.
distractors.why_wrong: The word 'days' already follows the gap, so repeating it makes the line ungrammatical.

teaching.reusable_rule: Read the words on both sides of a gap before copying. Anything already printed there must not be written twice.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'days' follows the gap, so it wants a bare number and nothing else.

questions.prompt: Carry-over above five days: granted only where a manager refused leave for {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: granted only where a manager has refused leave for operational reasons
questions.explanation: Carrying more than five days forward is allowed in one circumstance: the manager refused the leave for operational reasons and recorded the refusal at the time. The table asks for that circumstance.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: granted only where a manager refused leave for
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: granted only where a manager has refused leave for
paraphrase_link.note: Only the tense changes, so the row is a near-copy and the gap is fixed by position alone.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'for' and names the ground of a refusal, so it takes a noun phrase. The document offers exactly one, and the recording requirement is a separate condition.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the number in the row's own left column and it appears twice in the paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the ordinary limit the exception overrides, not the ground for the exception.

distractors.why_tempting: Copying the whole clause guarantees the right content and feels safest under time pressure.
distractors.why_wrong: It is four words against a limit of two, and an over-length answer scores nothing.

teaching.reusable_rule: A limit is part of the question, not a guideline. Copy the shortest span that completes the line.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'for' before the gap wants a plural noun phrase naming a cause.

questions.prompt: Compassionate leave: up to three days on {{gap}} for a close relative.
questions.evidence_quote: Compassionate leave of up to three days on full pay is available
questions.explanation: Compassionate leave is paid in full for up to three days, and a manager may extend it. The next kind of leave described in the same paragraph is unpaid, which is the contrast the row is built on.
questions.trap_note: The word 'unpaid' appears twice in the paragraph and belongs to a different kind of leave.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: up to three days on full pay
paraphrase_link.note: The row copies the phrase and stops one word early, so the gap is the word that was removed.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph describes three kinds of leave and states the pay position of each. The row names the first, which is the only one paid in full.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's most repeated pay word and sits in the very next sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: It belongs to dependant leave and to long unpaid leave, not to the compassionate days.

distractors.why_tempting: It ends the same sentence and answers the question of how leave can be lengthened.
distractors.why_wrong: That is how an extension is arranged, not how the first three days are paid.

teaching.reusable_rule: When one paragraph covers several categories, fix the category first and read only its own clause.
