teaching.grammar_cue: 'on' before the gap wants a noun phrase describing how the time is paid.

questions.prompt: Unpaid leave of over a month: considered only after {{gap}} of continuous service.
questions.evidence_quote: considered only after two years of continuous service and must be made in writing
questions.explanation: Unpaid leave longer than a month has two conditions: two years of continuous service, and a written request to the head of department. The table asks for the length of service.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: considered only after two years
paraphrase_link.note: The row stops where the figure begins, so the gap is fixed without any rewording at all.

teaching.decision_rule: Two conditions govern this leave and only one of them is a length of time. The words after the gap name what the time is made of, which rules out the written request.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the number the row's own left column repeats, so it is already in the reader's head.
distractors.why_wrong: That is how long the leave is, not how long you must have been employed.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other condition in the same sentence and it follows the word 'must'.
distractors.why_wrong: The gap is followed by 'of continuous service', which only a period of time can precede.

teaching.reusable_rule: Let the words after a gap do the eliminating. They usually rule out three of the four candidates for free.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'of continuous service' after the gap forces a length of time.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Look at the facilities described, A-F. Which facility does each statement describe?

options.text: Car park permits
The cycle scheme
The staff canteen
Lockers and showers
Out-of-hours access
Visitor reception

teaching.strategy: The facilities text gives each item its own short paragraph opening with its name, so build the index first and then read the statements. Four of the six paragraphs describe something being issued, withdrawn or returned, which is where the confusion lies.
teaching.order_note: Not in text order. Six paragraphs, five statements: one facility is never the answer.
teaching.watch_out: Three paragraphs describe something handed out and later given back. Only the timing tells them apart.

questions.prompt: It is taken away from anyone who leaves it unused for a set period.
questions.evidence_quote: A permit holder who does not use the space for three consecutive months loses it.
questions.explanation: The car park paragraph is the only one that withdraws something for non-use: a permit holder who leaves the space empty for three consecutive months loses the permit.
questions.trap_note: Two other paragraphs describe something being given up, but at a fixed date or when a reason ends.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: leaves it unused for a set period
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: does not use the space for three consecutive months
paraphrase_link.note: A named number of months in the text becomes the general phrase 'a set period' in the statement.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement makes non-use the cause of the loss. Only one paragraph makes that link; elsewhere things are given back on a date or when a purpose ends.

distractors.why_tempting: Lockers are also cleared after a period, so the August emptying reads like the same rule.
distractors.why_wrong: Every locker is emptied on that date, whether it has been used or not.

distractors.why_tempting: The coded card is the other thing described as issued and later surrendered.
distractors.why_wrong: It goes back when the reason for it ends, not because it has gone unused.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two rules can end in the same outcome for different causes. Match the cause, not the outcome.

questions.prompt: Anything still owed is recovered from your last payment if you resign.
questions.evidence_quote: the balance is deducted from your final salary
questions.explanation: The cycle scheme spreads the cost over twelve or eighteen months of salary, and if an employee leaves before the repayments end, the remaining balance comes out of the final salary.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: deducted from your final salary
paraphrase_link.note: Two words are swapped and the structure is identical, which is the cheapest kind of paraphrase to miss.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement joins money owed to leaving the organisation. Only one paragraph mentions repayment at all, and it states exactly that consequence.

distractors.why_tempting: Permits are also lost, and the statement's 'if you resign' reads like another way of losing one.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing about permits involves money owed or a final payment.

distractors.why_tempting: The canteen paragraph is the other one full of prices, so a reader scanning for money lands there.
distractors.why_wrong: Its prices are paid at the till by card; nothing there is ever recovered later.

teaching.reusable_rule: Scanning for a topic word finds every paragraph that mentions money. Scan for the relation instead.

questions.prompt: It is not available on Saturdays or Sundays.
questions.evidence_quote: It does not open at weekends
questions.explanation: The canteen serves food only on weekdays and does not open at weekends, when the lobby vending machines are the alternative. No other facility is described as closed on particular days.
questions.trap_note: The access paragraph also names weekday hours, which is where a reader hunting days will land first.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: not available on Saturdays or Sundays
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: does not open at weekends
paraphrase_link.note: The statement names the two days; the paragraph names the category they belong to.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement is about days of the week, not hours. Only one paragraph closes for whole days; the other weekday reference gives opening times and a way in outside them.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other paragraph that names weekdays and a closing time, so a scan for days stops there.
distractors.why_wrong: It gives the hours the building is open and the route in outside them; it never closes for a whole day.

distractors.why_tempting: The showers 'cannot be booked', and a refusal reads like unavailability.
distractors.why_wrong: Not being bookable is a different restriction from not opening on particular days.

teaching.reusable_rule: Distinguish a facility that shuts on some days from one that shuts at some hours. Both are written as times.

questions.prompt: A senior manager must approve it in writing before it is issued.
questions.evidence_quote: issued by the facilities office on the written approval of a head of department
questions.explanation: The coded card for entering the building outside opening hours is issued by the facilities office only on the written approval of a head of department. No other facility requires anyone's signature.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: A senior manager must approve it in writing
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: on the written approval of a head of department
paraphrase_link.note: A noun phrase becomes a verb and the named post becomes the category 'senior manager'.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement requires a named person's written consent before issue. Only one paragraph makes issue conditional on anyone's approval; the rest allocate or hand out automatically.

distractors.why_tempting: Permits are allocated by a points system, which sounds like a decision somebody has to make.
distractors.why_wrong: The points system is a formula; nobody signs anything and no post is named as approving it.

distractors.why_tempting: Reception issues something as well, and issuing implies somebody authorised it.
distractors.why_wrong: A visitor badge is handed over on arrival with no approval of any kind.

teaching.reusable_rule: Allocation by a formula and permission from a person are different processes. Only one names who decides.

questions.prompt: What is handed out here has to be given back the same day.
questions.evidence_quote: a badge that must be worn at all times and returned on leaving
questions.explanation: Visitors are given a badge at the lobby desk which must be worn throughout and returned when they leave, so it goes back within the visit itself.
questions.trap_note: The coded card is also issued and also returned, but months may pass first.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: has to be given back the same day
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: returned on leaving
paraphrase_link.note: 'On leaving' fixes the moment; the statement converts that moment into a length of time.

teaching.decision_rule: Two paragraphs describe something issued and later returned. Only the timing separates them, and only one ties the return to the end of the same visit.

distractors.why_tempting: The coded card is issued, carried and eventually handed back, which matches every word of the statement except one.
distractors.why_wrong: It goes back when the reason for it ends, which may be months after it was issued.

distractors.why_tempting: Lockers are also allocated to individuals and emptied later in the year.
distractors.why_wrong: A locker is requested rather than handed out, and nothing is returned by the member of staff.

teaching.reusable_rule: When two candidates share a process, the deciding word is almost always the one that fixes when.

texts.heading: Life Between the Tides

paragraphs.text: Anyone who walks out onto a rocky shore at low water is crossing a boundary twice a day. For six hours the ground underfoot is part of the sea, and for six hours it belongs to the air, the rain and the sun. Very few habitats change so completely, so quickly and so often. The plants and animals that live there are not, for the most part, sea creatures that put up with a little dryness, nor land creatures that put up with a little salt. They are specialists in the boundary itself, and their whole design is an answer to the question of how to survive being drowned and then abandoned, twice a day, for a lifetime.

The first thing a visitor notices, once the eye adjusts, is that the shore is striped. Bands of colour run along the rock roughly parallel to the water line: a grey-black crust near the top, then a broad belt of brown seaweed, then a zone of pink and green that is uncovered only on the lowest tides. This banding is called zonation, and it is one of the clearest patterns in any habitat. The bands are not decorative. Each marks the vertical range within which a particular set of species can survive, and the boundaries between them are often sharp enough to be traced with a finger.

Life at the top of the shore is governed by what happens when the water goes. A barnacle stranded for nine hours on a July afternoon faces heat, fresh rainwater and the steady loss of its own moisture. Its answer is a set of overlapping plates that close like a trapdoor, sealing a teaspoon of sea inside until the tide returns. Periwinkles withdraw and glue themselves down with dried mucus. Limpets grind a shallow scar into the rock, return to it before every ebb, and clamp so tightly that the seal holds. None of these animals is fast, and none of them needs to be. Their problem is not escape but endurance.

Lower down the shore the problem changes. The rock there is uncovered for only an hour or two, so drying out is a minor threat, and the limiting factor becomes other organisms. Space on a lower-shore rock is scarce and permanently contested. Fast-growing weeds shade slower ones, mussels crowd out barnacles, and predators that cannot tolerate the upper shore work steadily along the lower boundary of each band. It is competition and predation, rather than heat and drought, that hold the lower edge of most species in place. The upper edge is set by physics and the lower edge by biology, and the width of a band is the space between the two.

Timing decides what a visitor sees. The tide does not follow the clock but the moon, so the water is roughly fifty minutes later each day, and the range between high and low water swells and shrinks over a fortnight. Around the new and full moon the tides are large, and the lowest of them uncover ground that is exposed for perhaps an hour a month. Halfway between, at the neaps, the shore barely moves. A visitor who arrives at the same hour on successive weekends may find the same beach transformed, or, if every visit has fallen at the neaps, may never see the lower shore at all and go home believing it is not there.

The shore is also, increasingly, a place under pressure. Rockpooling is a mild and popular pastime, but a well-visited shore shows its wear. Turning a boulder and leaving it upside down kills almost everything on both of its faces. Trampling breaks the fragile turf of weed that shelters young animals. Collecting for the aquarium trade and, in some places, for food, removes exactly the large slow-growing individuals that produce most of the eggs. None of these pressures is dramatic on any single visit, which is why they accumulate unnoticed, and why the advice given at popular shores is now specific rather than general: put the stone back as you found it, and take nothing away.

Much of what is known about how these shores are changing has been gathered by people with no scientific training. A shore survey suits volunteers: the species are visible without equipment, the same stretch of rock can be recorded year after year, and the method fits on one page. Records collected in this way over several decades have tracked the slow northward movement of several southern species and the retreat of a few northern ones. A single volunteer's afternoon is worth little on its own. Ten thousand such afternoons, recorded in the same way, are worth a great deal.

What makes the rocky shore worth the wet feet is that it is legible. In most habitats the forces that decide who lives where are invisible, or work over centuries. Here they are laid out in bands a metre wide, refreshed twice a day, and readable by anyone willing to look for an hour at the right point in the month. The shore does not have to be explained before it can be understood. It only has to be visited at the bottom of the tide.

difficulty_rationale.note: The subject is concrete, but the argument is not: the text moves from a description to a general rule about what sets an upper and a lower limit, and it never signals the move.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It reverses the previous paragraph's explanation without a single contrastive connective, so a reader carries the wrong cause forward.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of the first paragraph. It sets up the twice-daily change that every later paragraph is about.
skim_plan.skip: The list of colours in the second paragraph and the list of damage in the sixth. Both are illustration, and you can return to them.

rewordings: the height a species can occupy
the strip it is confined to
the belt it is able to hold
how far up and down it can live
harm piles up without being seen

hinge_words.why_here: It hedges the fifty-minute figure that option D of question 33 quotes exactly.
'Uncovered for only an hour or two' is the premise question 39 turns on.
It carries the reversal in paragraph D that decides question 30.
'Most species' and 'most habitats' bound two claims, including question 35's.

mineable.meaning: the thing that stops something spreading further
always fought over
before each falling tide
build up without anyone seeing
the withdrawal of something from an area
able to be read and understood
animals that take a long time to reach size

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct heading for each of paragraphs B-F from the list below. There are more headings than paragraphs, so you will not use them all.

options.text: Bands that mark the limits of survival
Surviving the hours without water
Where neighbours matter more than weather
Why the same shore looks different
Small harms that add up over time
The work of untrained recorders
A habitat that changes twice a day
Why some species are moving north

teaching.strategy: Say each paragraph's job in six words before you look at the list. Start with D and F, whose opening sentences state their whole point, and leave B until last, because three headings mention bands or shores and only one names what the bands do.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, and the group covers only five of the eight paragraphs. Read the excluded three anyway.
teaching.watch_out: Three headings describe something the article genuinely contains, but in a paragraph this group does not ask about.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence_quote: Each marks the vertical range within which a particular set of species can survive
questions.explanation: The paragraph describes the stripes and then says what they are for: each band is the height range in which a set of species can live. The colours are the illustration; the limits are the point.
questions.trap_note: Heading vii is true of the article and belongs to paragraph A, which this group does not ask about.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: within which a particular set of species can survive
paraphrase_link.note: A whole relative clause in the text becomes a two-word noun phrase in the heading.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's last sentence tells you what the bands mean, and a heading has to name that meaning rather than the appearance described in the first three sentences.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about the shore and a reader who has not yet placed this heading will take the first paragraph that mentions tides.
distractors.why_wrong: The twice-daily change is set out in paragraph A; this paragraph never mentions how often anything happens.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about the shore looking a particular way, so a heading about how it looks fits the surface.
distractors.why_wrong: It is about how the shore looks to everyone, always. The heading about difference belongs to the paragraph on tides.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph describes something and then explains it, the heading names the explanation.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence_quote: Life at the top of the shore is governed by what happens when the water goes.
questions.explanation: Every example in the paragraph is a way of holding on to moisture while the tide is out, and the closing sentence names endurance as the whole problem. The heading states that.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: governed by what happens when the water goes
paraphrase_link.note: The heading turns the paragraph's controlling clause into the activity the animals are performing.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph opens by naming its subject and closes by naming it again as endurance. Three examples sit between them and none of them introduces a second subject.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is full of animals living side by side, which reads as a paragraph about neighbours.
distractors.why_wrong: They are listed as separate solutions to one physical problem; none of them interacts with any other.

distractors.why_tempting: The tide going out and coming back is mentioned three times here, so the twice-daily heading feels supported.
distractors.why_wrong: That heading names the article's opening frame, not the survival problem this paragraph sets out.

teaching.reusable_rule: A list of different solutions to one problem is a paragraph about the problem, not about the variety.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence_quote: It is competition and predation, rather than heat and drought, that hold the lower edge of most species in place.
questions.explanation: The paragraph reverses the previous one. Low on the shore, drying out hardly matters and the limit is set by other organisms competing for space and eating each other.
questions.trap_note: Heat and drought are named here, but only as the thing that is not the cause.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: competition and predation, rather than heat and drought
paraphrase_link.note: Two technical causes become 'neighbours' and two physical ones become 'weather'.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph names two candidate causes and rejects one of them in a cleft sentence. A heading must take the side the cleft puts first, not the side after 'rather than'.

distractors.why_tempting: Heat and drought are named in the key sentence, so a reader matching words finds the survival heading confirmed here.
distractors.why_wrong: They appear inside the clause that says they are not the cause on this part of the shore.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends on the upper and lower edges of a band, which is exactly what the bands heading is about.
distractors.why_wrong: That sentence generalises the earlier paragraph's point; this paragraph's own subject is what sets the lower edge.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a writer names two causes and dismisses one, take the cause that stands before the dismissal.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence_quote: may find the same beach transformed
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains the fortnightly swing between big and small tides and closes on two visitors who see completely different shores at the same place and hour. That variation is its whole subject.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: find the same beach transformed
paraphrase_link.note: 'Beach transformed' becomes 'shore looks different', and the visitor disappears from the phrase.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's first sentence promises to explain what a visitor sees, and its last delivers two different outcomes. A heading has to name the difference, not the mechanism that produces it.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about how much of the shore is uncovered, which sounds like the limits of the bands.
distractors.why_wrong: It is about what is visible on a given day, not about where a species can live.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who has met 'moving north' expects a heading about movement, and the tide moves here more than anywhere.
distractors.why_wrong: Species moving north belong to the volunteer records two paragraphs later; nothing here is about distribution.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that opens with a promise and closes with an outcome is headed by the outcome.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence_quote: which is why they accumulate unnoticed
questions.explanation: The paragraph lists four mild-looking pressures and then states the point: individually none of them is dramatic, which is precisely why the total goes unnoticed. The heading names that accumulation.
questions.trap_note: Heading vi belongs to the following paragraph and is the one an unplaced reader reaches for here.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: harms that add up over time
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: they accumulate unnoticed
paraphrase_link.note: One verb carries the whole heading: accumulating is adding up, and the paragraph says so directly.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph's own explanation is that each pressure is small and the total is not. A heading naming a single serious harm would contradict the sentence that organises it.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends on advice given at popular shores, which sounds like the work of people who look after them.
distractors.why_wrong: Recording by volunteers is the next paragraph's subject; nobody here is gathering anything.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about species being lost, and a heading about species moving is the nearest available.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing here is about where species are found; the losses described are local and immediate.

teaching.reusable_rule: If a paragraph insists each item is minor, the heading belongs to the sum, not to any item.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

teaching.strategy: Read the stem, decide what the answer has to do, and only then read the options. All three stems ask for a reason or a claim, so an option that is merely true of the article is not enough.
teaching.order_note: In article order: question 35's answer lies below question 34's, which lies below question 33's.
teaching.watch_out: One option in each set restates a nearby fact accurately and answers a different question from the one asked.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the writer, might a visitor conclude that the lower shore does not exist?

options.text: Because the lowest tides of the month happen after dark.
Because they went only when the tidal range was smallest.
Because thick weed hides the rock at the bottom of the shore.
Because the tide arrives about fifty minutes later each day.

questions.evidence_quote: if every visit has fallen at the neaps, may never see the lower shore at all
questions.explanation: At the neaps the shore barely moves, so the lowest ground stays covered. The writer says that a visitor whose every trip falls at a neap tide never sees the lower shore and goes home assuming it is not there.
questions.trap_note: Option D quotes the article accurately and explains why tides shift through the day, not why a whole zone stays hidden.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: at the neaps, the shore barely moves
paraphrase_link.note: The technical word 'neaps' is defined two sentences earlier as the point where the range is least.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a cause the writer states. Only one option names the condition the article attaches to never seeing the lower shore, and the article attaches it explicitly.

distractors.why_tempting: Big tides at odd hours is common knowledge, and darkness is the obvious reason for not seeing something.
distractors.why_wrong: The article never mentions the time of day at which any tide occurs.

distractors.why_tempting: Weed is described covering the rock in an earlier paragraph, so the words are all in the article somewhere.
distractors.why_wrong: That belt of weed is in the description of the bands and is never said to hide anything.

distractors.why_tempting: It is quoted almost word for word from the same paragraph and it is entirely true.
distractors.why_wrong: It explains why the tide shifts through the day, not why a visitor never sees the bottom of the shore.

teaching.reusable_rule: A quotation lifted from the right paragraph can still answer the wrong question. Check the stem before the wording.

questions.prompt: What does the writer give as the reason that damage to a popular shore goes unnoticed?

options.text: Each separate visit does only a very small amount of harm.
Most visitors put the boulders back exactly as they found them.
The animals that suffer are too small for a visitor to see.
The shore repairs itself between one low tide and the next.

questions.evidence_quote: None of these pressures is dramatic on any single visit
questions.explanation: The writer states the mechanism directly: no single visit does anything dramatic, so the harm builds without being seen. The four pressures listed before that sentence are the examples, not the reason.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: does only a very small amount of harm
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: None of these pressures is dramatic
paraphrase_link.note: A negative about pressures becomes a positive about visits, with the quantity unchanged.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the writer's stated reason, and the article supplies it in a because-clause. Any option describing behaviour, biology or recovery is answering a question the article never asks.

distractors.why_tempting: Replacing the stone is the article's own instruction, so the words are in the paragraph and sound approving.
distractors.why_wrong: It is advice about what visitors should do, not a claim about what they in fact do.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does mention young animals and a fragile turf, so smallness is in the reader's mind.
distractors.why_wrong: The article never says anything about whether the animals can be seen.

distractors.why_tempting: Everything on this shore is refreshed twice a day, so recovery between tides sounds like the article's own logic.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph says the opposite: the effects build up rather than clearing.

teaching.reusable_rule: Instructions about what people should do are not evidence about what they do. Keep advice out of a factual answer.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's main point about surveys carried out by volunteers?

options.text: They produce results that trained scientists could not obtain.
Their value lies in being repeated the same way many times.
They are worth supporting mainly because they are inexpensive.
They show that northern species are spreading further south.

questions.evidence_quote: Ten thousand such afternoons, recorded in the same way, are worth a great deal.
questions.explanation: The paragraph sets one afternoon against ten thousand and makes the sameness of method the thing that converts one into the other. That contrast is the writer's point.
questions.trap_note: Option D reverses the direction the article actually reports.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: being repeated the same way many times
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: recorded in the same way
paraphrase_link.note: The article's contrast between one afternoon and ten thousand becomes a single claim about repetition.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the main point, and the paragraph's last two sentences are built as a contrast whose whole weight falls on the method being identical. Nothing else in it is argued.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens by stressing that the recorders have no training, which reads as a claim about beating the professionals.
distractors.why_wrong: It says the work suits volunteers, not that trained scientists could not do it.

distractors.why_tempting: Needing no equipment and a one-page method both point at cheapness, and cheapness is a familiar argument for volunteering.
distractors.why_wrong: Those facts explain why the task suits volunteers; cost is never given as the reason the surveys matter.

distractors.why_tempting: Both directions appear in the same sentence, and under time pressure the two halves swap.
distractors.why_wrong: The article reports southern species moving north and northern ones retreating, which is the opposite claim.

teaching.reusable_rule: When one sentence names two directions, write down which belongs to which before you look at the options.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete each sentence below with words taken from the article.

teaching.strategy: These five run from the first paragraph to the last, so each answer lies below the one before it. Decide the word class of every gap before searching: three want a noun, one an adjective, and one a two-word noun phrase.
teaching.order_note: In article order. After question 38 you never need to look above paragraph D again.
teaching.watch_out: Four of these answers are single words the article uses once. Copy the spelling exactly; the technical ones are the easiest to mis-key.

questions.prompt: Rather than sea creatures or land creatures, the organisms of the shore are specialists in the {{gap}} between the two.
questions.evidence_quote: They are specialists in the boundary itself
questions.explanation: The first paragraph rejects both categories in turn and then names what the organisms actually are: specialists in the boundary itself. The sentence keeps the article's own noun.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the organisms of the shore are specialists
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: They are specialists in the boundary itself
paraphrase_link.note: Only the pronoun is expanded into its referent, which is why this gap is the cheapest in the group.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'the' and precedes 'between the two', so it takes a singular noun naming something with two sides. The paragraph offers exactly one.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's subject and appears in the sentence frame already.
distractors.why_wrong: The shore is where this happens; the noun the gap wants is what the animals are specialists in.

distractors.why_tempting: Copying two words from the article feels safer than copying one.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Itself' points back to the noun and cannot stand before 'between the two'.

teaching.reusable_rule: Read the words on the far side of a gap. They usually rule out every candidate but one.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'the' before the gap and 'between the two' after it force a singular noun.

questions.prompt: The pattern of coloured bands running along the rock is known as {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: This banding is called zonation
questions.explanation: The article names the striping directly. The sentence swaps 'is called' for 'is known as' and keeps the term itself in the gap.
questions.trap_note: The word is used once and never repeated, so a reader skimming for it a second time will not find it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is called zonation
paraphrase_link.note: A naming verb is swapped for its exact equivalent, which leaves the term as the only thing missing.

teaching.decision_rule: The frame 'is known as' introduces a technical term, so the gap takes the one word the paragraph explicitly supplies as a name.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the subject of the very sentence that gives the answer, and it describes the same thing.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the ordinary description; the term the sentence introduces comes after the verb.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the fuller phrase from two sentences earlier and reads more naturally.
distractors.why_wrong: The frame asks for the name, not for another description, and three words break the limit.

teaching.reusable_rule: A naming verb points forward. The term always sits after it, never before.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'is known as' ends the sentence, so the gap takes a single noun.

questions.prompt: A barnacle survives being uncovered by shutting its plates and trapping a {{gap}} of sea water inside.
questions.evidence_quote: sealing a teaspoon of sea inside until the tide returns
questions.explanation: The article describes the plates closing like a trapdoor and sealing a teaspoon of sea inside. The sentence keeps the quantity word and expands 'sea' to 'sea water'.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: plates that close like a trapdoor
paraphrase_link.note: The simile is dropped and the verb is swapped, so the sentence shares almost no wording with the article.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'a' and 'of sea water', so it takes a singular noun naming a quantity. Only one word in the paragraph does that.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the striking image in the same clause and it is a singular noun.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes how the plates move, and nothing is measured in trapdoors.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph's subject is holding on to water, and moisture appears two sentences earlier.
distractors.why_wrong: It names the substance rather than the amount, and the article attaches it to what is lost, not kept.

teaching.reusable_rule: A gap between an article and 'of' wants a measure word. Reject anything that names the substance instead.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'a' before the gap and 'of' after it call for a singular quantity noun.

questions.prompt: Because the rock low on the shore is uncovered only briefly, the limiting factor there becomes {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: so drying out is a minor threat, and the limiting factor becomes other organisms
questions.explanation: Because the lower rock is exposed for an hour or two at most, drying out hardly matters and the constraint shifts to the other living things competing for the same space.
questions.trap_note: 'Competition and predation' names the same idea later in the paragraph but is three words, so it breaks the limit.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: uncovered for only an hour or two
paraphrase_link.note: A measured span becomes an adverb, which is the whole reason a search for the figure fails.

teaching.decision_rule: The sentence copies the article's own clause up to the verb, so the gap is whatever the article puts after 'becomes'. The later restatement is a different, longer phrase.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's own summary of the same idea and reads as the fuller, better answer.
distractors.why_wrong: It is three words against a limit of two, so it scores nothing however right the content is.

distractors.why_tempting: It sits immediately before the gap's clause and is a two-word phrase of the right shape.
distractors.why_wrong: The article names it as the threat that has stopped mattering here.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a text says the same thing twice, take the version that fits the limit, not the one that sounds fuller.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'becomes' before the gap wants a noun phrase, and two words is the ceiling.

questions.prompt: The writer values the rocky shore above other habitats because it is {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: What makes the rocky shore worth the wet feet is that it is legible.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph contrasts the shore with habitats whose forces are invisible or too slow to watch, and gives one word for the difference. The gap takes that adjective.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: values the rocky shore above other habitats
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: What makes the rocky shore worth the wet feet
paraphrase_link.note: A cleft sentence about being worth the trouble becomes a plain statement about the writer's preference.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'it is' and closes the sentence, so it takes an adjective. The paragraph offers one adjective as the answer to its own opening question.

distractors.why_tempting: It appears later in the same paragraph and means very nearly the same thing.
distractors.why_wrong: The article applies it to the bands, not to the shore, and a completion answer is copied rather than chosen.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's most prominent adjective and sits in the sentence immediately after.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes the forces in other habitats, which is the side of the contrast the shore is not on.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two near-synonyms in one paragraph are attached to different subjects. Copy the one attached to yours.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'it is' before the gap and a full stop after it force a single adjective.

texts.heading: Places to stay near Sandmouth

paragraphs.text: Cliff End Campsite. Sixty pitches on grass above the harbour, open from 1 April to 31 October. A tent pitch for two people costs 22 pounds a night and a caravan pitch 28 pounds. There is a shower block, a small shop and a laundry. Dogs are welcome on a lead. The site is a twenty-minute walk from the town, and the last part of it is steep.

Harbour View Guest House. Eight rooms above the fish market, all with a private bathroom. From 68 pounds a night including breakfast, with a reduction of 10 pounds a night for stays of four nights or more. The house has no lift and every room is on the first or second floor. Evening meals are served on Fridays and Saturdays only.

The Old Signal Station. A converted building on the headland, let as a whole to one party of up to six people. The weekly rate is 640 pounds in summer and 410 pounds at other times, with a changeover day of Saturday. There is no mobile signal on the headland, and the nearest shop is three miles away.

Sandmouth Youth Hostel. Dormitory beds from 19 pounds and four family rooms from 55 pounds. Members of the association pay three pounds less a night. The kitchen is open to guests until 22.00 and there is a drying room for wet clothing. Reception closes at 23.00, after which the door is opened by code only.

Marlow Farm Bed and Breakfast. Two rooms on a working farm two miles inland, reached by a lane with no pavement. Rooms are 74 pounds a night and breakfast uses the farm's own eggs and bread. Children of any age are welcome and a cot is provided at no charge. Cash and cheques only; there is no card machine.

The Anchor Guest Rooms. Six rooms above a public house in the town centre, from 58 pounds. The bar below is open until midnight and music is played on Thursdays, so the rooms at the front can be noisy. Breakfast is not provided but is served next door from 8.00. Guests may park free of charge in the yard behind.

texts.heading: The Sandmouth Coast Travelcard

paragraphs.text: The Coast Travelcard gives unlimited travel on the 14, 15 and 22 bus routes and on the harbour ferry between Sandmouth and Wray Point. It is not valid on the summer open-top service, which takes cash fares only. Cards are sold at the bus station, at the tourist office on Pier Street and by the driver, though drivers cannot give change for notes.

Prices are as follows. One day, 9 pounds adult and 4.50 pounds child; three days, 21 pounds adult and 10 pounds child; seven days, 34 pounds adult and 16 pounds child. A family card, covering two adults and up to three children, costs 58 pounds for seven days. Children under five travel free at all times and do not need a card.

A card is valid from the first journey made on it rather than from the date of purchase, so it may be bought in advance. It must be shown to the driver each time it is used, and a card that has been folded or written on is not accepted. Lost cards are not replaced. Holders may take one bicycle on the ferry without charge, though not at weekends between 10.00 and 16.00.

texts.heading: Sandmouth Maritime Museum: visitor information

paragraphs.text: The museum is open from 10.00 to 17.00 from Tuesday to Sunday, and on Mondays in August only. Last admission is forty-five minutes before closing. Entry costs 8 pounds for adults and is free for anyone under sixteen. The ticket is valid for a year, so you may return as often as you like, provided you sign it on your first visit.

The lifeboat gallery on the upper floor is reached by stairs, and a lift is available on request at the desk. Photography without flash is permitted everywhere except in the chart room, where the early maps are sensitive to light. Bags larger than a small rucksack must be left in the lockers by the entrance, which take a returnable pound coin.

Guided tours of the harbour leave from the museum door at 11.30 and 14.30 and last about an hour. They are free but must be booked at the desk on the day, and each tour takes no more than fifteen people. In poor weather the tour is replaced by a talk in the lecture room. The museum cafe closes half an hour before the museum itself.

difficulty_rationale.note: Nothing here is hard to read, but the deciding detail is almost always a qualifier at the end of a sentence, and three of the texts describe overlapping prices for overlapping groups.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Five separate conditions on one card, two of them expressed as exceptions to something stated in the previous sentence.

skim_plan.read_first: The three headings and the first line of each listing. The name of a place tells you what kind of accommodation it is.
skim_plan.skip: Every price in the accommodation listings on the first pass. Only two questions need one, and both name the condition rather than the figure.

paraphrase_families.passage_form: a reduction of 10 pounds a night
rewordings: a discount for a longer booking
a lower nightly rate over time

paraphrase_families.passage_form: must be booked at the desk
rewordings: a place has to be arranged
you need to sign up beforehand
operating only in the warmer months
unavailable for part of the year

hinge_words.why_here: It carries the photography exception that question 12 asks you to name.
It adds the weekend limit on bicycles in the paragraph question 8 draws on.
'Cash and cheques only' is the whole of question 4.
It separates first journey from date of purchase, which decides question 8.
It caps the tour party and supplies the figure for question 14.

mineable.meaning: an amount taken off the usual price
the day one booking ends and the next begins
given back to you afterwards
the latest time you may go in
as many journeys as you want
damaged by being lit or photographed
held on a rope or strap

question_groups.instructions_extra: Look at the six places to stay, A-F. Which place does each statement describe? You may use any letter more than once.

options.text: Cliff End Campsite
Harbour View Guest House
The Old Signal Station
Sandmouth Youth Hostel
Marlow Farm B and B
The Anchor Guest Rooms

teaching.strategy: Turn each question into a single field before you read anything: season, length of stay, stairs, payment, noise. Then read one listing at a time against all five, because every listing is short and the deciding detail is usually its last sentence.
teaching.order_note: Not in text order, and one listing answers two questions. Two listings answer none.
teaching.watch_out: Four listings mention money and three mention a reduction. Only one reduction depends on how long you stay.

questions.prompt: a place that is not available during part of the year
questions.evidence_quote: open from 1 April to 31 October
questions.explanation: The campsite gives an opening season of seven months, which means it is shut for the rest of the year. No other listing limits itself to particular months.
questions.trap_note: Two other listings restrict particular services to particular days, which is a restriction on a service and not on the place.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: not available during part of the year
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: open from 1 April to 31 October
paraphrase_link.note: A pair of dates in the listing becomes a statement about the months that are missing from it.

teaching.decision_rule: Only one listing states a season. The others give hours or days for particular services, which limits what happens there rather than whether it is open at all.

distractors.why_tempting: Evening meals are served on two days only, so the listing does contain a restriction expressed in time.
distractors.why_wrong: It limits one service; the rooms themselves are available every night of the year.

distractors.why_tempting: It quotes a summer rate and another for the rest of the year, which reads like two seasons.
distractors.why_wrong: Two prices means it is let all year; a closed season would have no second rate.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two prices for two seasons proves a place opens in both. A closed period has no price at all.

questions.prompt: a place that costs less per night if you stay for several nights
questions.evidence_quote: with a reduction of 10 pounds a night for stays of four nights or more
questions.explanation: The guest house takes ten pounds a night off once a booking reaches four nights. It is the only listing whose price depends on the length of the stay.
questions.trap_note: One listing reduces the price for members and another quotes a weekly rate, and neither depends on how long you stay.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a reduction of 10 pounds a night
paraphrase_link.note: A named figure becomes the general claim that the nightly price falls.

teaching.decision_rule: The question makes the length of the stay the cause of the lower price. Only one listing does that; the other reductions turn on who you are or on a fixed period.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other listing that names a specific amount taken off a nightly price.
distractors.why_wrong: That reduction depends on belonging to the association, not on the number of nights.

distractors.why_tempting: A weekly rate is obviously cheaper per night than paying nightly, so the arithmetic feels right.
distractors.why_wrong: No nightly price is given there at all, so nothing in the listing falls.

teaching.reusable_rule: A discount has a condition attached. Match the condition, not the fact that money comes off.

questions.prompt: a place that would not suit a guest unable to use stairs
questions.evidence_quote: The house has no lift and every room is on the first or second floor.
questions.explanation: The guest house has no lift and no ground-floor room, so every guest has to climb. The listing joins the two facts in one sentence for exactly this reason.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: every room is on the first or second floor
paraphrase_link.note: The listing never writes the word stairs; it states the two facts that make them unavoidable.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement needs a place where climbing cannot be avoided. One listing rules out the alternative and puts every room above the ground floor in the same sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: Rooms above a public house are obviously upstairs, and the listing says nothing about a lift either.
distractors.why_wrong: Saying nothing is not the same as ruling it out, and no floor is named.

distractors.why_tempting: The listing warns that the last part of the walk is steep, which reads as a difficulty of the same kind.
distractors.why_wrong: A steep path to the town is not a stair inside the accommodation.

teaching.reusable_rule: A listing that names no obstacle has not promised there is none. Only an explicit statement counts.

questions.prompt: a place where you cannot pay by card
questions.evidence_quote: Cash and cheques only; there is no card machine.
questions.explanation: The farm states the position twice in one sentence: two accepted methods, and no equipment for a third. No other listing mentions how payment is taken.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: there is no card machine
paraphrase_link.note: The listing denies the equipment; the question denies the action it would make possible.

teaching.decision_rule: Only one listing says anything at all about methods of payment, and it excludes cards explicitly rather than leaving them unmentioned.

distractors.why_tempting: A hostel with a coded door and a fixed reception hour sounds like somewhere with limited facilities.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in that listing is about payment, so there is no basis for the claim either way.

distractors.why_tempting: The free parking and the breakfast served next door suggest an informal arrangement.
distractors.why_wrong: Informality is an impression; the listing never mentions how the bill is paid.

teaching.reusable_rule: In a matching set, only one text usually mentions the field at all. Find the field, not the impression.

questions.prompt: a place that warns guests about noise
questions.evidence_quote: so the rooms at the front can be noisy
questions.explanation: The listing names the cause, a bar open until midnight with music one night a week, and then states the effect on the rooms overlooking it. It is the only warning of its kind.
questions.trap_note: Two other listings sit above working premises, but neither says anything about sound.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the rooms at the front can be noisy
paraphrase_link.note: The listing states the consequence for particular rooms; the question turns it into the act of warning.

teaching.decision_rule: The question needs an explicit warning, not a situation a reader could deduce. One listing supplies the cause and the consequence in the same sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: Rooms above a fish market sound noisy in the early morning, and markets are proverbially loud.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the reader's knowledge of markets; the listing mentions only the location.

distractors.why_tempting: A campsite of sixty pitches beside a harbour suggests a crowded and busy place.
distractors.why_wrong: Size is not sound, and the listing warns only about the walk into town.

teaching.reusable_rule: Deduction is not information. If the text has not said it, no amount of plausibility puts it there.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the table below with words and numbers taken from the travelcard leaflet.

layout.title: The Coast Travelcard
rows: Not valid on the open-top service.
Must be shown to the {{7}} each time.
Valid from the {{8}} made on it.
Two adults and up to {{9}} children.

teaching.strategy: Everything is in the price paragraph and the conditions paragraph, so read only those two. Fill the prices row by row, then go back for the conditions, because the conditions are written as general rules rather than against particular cards.
teaching.order_note: Two paragraphs hold all four, but not in table order: question 9 sends you back above question 8.
teaching.watch_out: Two rows want a number written as digits and one wants it written as a word. Copy the leaflet's form, not the one you prefer.

questions.prompt: One-day card, adult price: {{gap}} pounds.
questions.evidence_quote: One day, 9 pounds adult and 4.50 pounds child
questions.explanation: The price paragraph lists three durations, each with an adult and a child figure. The one-day adult price is the first number in that list.
questions.trap_note: The child price sits in the same clause and is the number closest to the word that follows it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: One day, 9 pounds adult
paraphrase_link.note: The table turns a price list into rows, so the work is picking the right figure.

teaching.decision_rule: Each duration in the leaflet carries two figures in a fixed order, adult then child. The column heading names which of the pair the row wants.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the second figure in the same clause and a reader taking the nearest number to the row label finds it first.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the child fare; the column is headed adult price.

distractors.why_tempting: Copying the unit with the figure feels more complete and more like the leaflet.
distractors.why_wrong: The word pounds is already printed after the gap, so writing it again breaks the line.

teaching.reusable_rule: A table column heading is part of the question. It decides which of two adjacent figures the gap wants.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'pounds' follows the gap, so it takes the bare figure.

questions.prompt: Three-day card: must be shown to the {{gap}} each time.
questions.evidence_quote: It must be shown to the driver each time it is used
questions.explanation: The conditions paragraph states one rule about showing the card, and it applies to every card rather than to one duration. The person it must be shown to is the driver.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: must be shown to the driver
paraphrase_link.note: The row copies the leaflet's clause and stops one word short, so the gap is the word removed.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'to the' and names a person, and the conditions paragraph names exactly one person a card is shown to.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other place named in the leaflet and it does handle cards.
distractors.why_wrong: That is where a card may be bought, not where it is shown on each journey.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the first sales point listed and the most obvious place to produce a ticket.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a place, and the frame 'shown to the' calls for someone who can look at it.

teaching.reusable_rule: A gap after a verb of presenting wants a person. A place cannot fill it however plausible.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'to the' before the gap wants a singular noun naming a person.

questions.prompt: Seven-day card: valid from the {{gap}} made on it.
questions.evidence_quote: valid from the first journey made on it rather than from the date of purchase
questions.explanation: A card starts running when it is first used, not when it is bought, which is why the leaflet says it may be bought in advance. The table copies the first half of that contrast.
questions.trap_note: The rejected alternative, the date of purchase, sits in the same sentence and is the more familiar rule.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: valid from the first journey made on it
paraphrase_link.note: The row lifts the clause and drops the contrast, so everything depends on stopping at the right word.

teaching.decision_rule: The leaflet states the rule and then names the alternative it is not. The gap sits before 'made on it', which only the journey can precede.

distractors.why_tempting: It is how most tickets work, and it appears in the same sentence in the same grammatical slot.
distractors.why_wrong: It follows 'rather than', which marks it as the reading the leaflet rejects.

distractors.why_tempting: Copying one word further along feels safer than stopping early.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Made' is already printed after the gap, so the line reads with it twice.

teaching.reusable_rule: The version a writer refuses stands after the contrast marker. Take what comes before it.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'made on it' after the gap forces a noun phrase naming an event.

questions.prompt: Family card: two adults and up to {{gap}} children.
questions.evidence_quote: covering two adults and up to three children
questions.explanation: The family card covers two adults and a maximum of three children for seven days. The leaflet writes the figure as a word, and the answer is copied in that form.
questions.trap_note: Under-fives travel free in the next sentence and are not counted against this limit.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: two adults and up to three children
paraphrase_link.note: The row copies the leaflet phrase with the figure removed, so the item is pure location.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'up to' and a plural noun, so it takes a quantity. Only one quantity in the paragraph is attached to children on a family card.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the next number about children in the paragraph and sits in the following sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: It is an age, not a count, and it belongs to the rule about travelling free.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the number already in the row and the eye carries it across the conjunction.
distractors.why_wrong: It counts the adults; the leaflet gives the children a different figure.

teaching.reusable_rule: A number is meaningless without its noun. Check what each figure counts before you write one down.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'up to' before the gap and a plural noun after it call for a quantity.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Answer the questions below using words from the museum visitor information.

teaching.strategy: All five answers are in the museum information and run down it in order. Read each question word first and fix the shape of the answer: a period, an action, a place, an object, a number.
teaching.order_note: In text order. Once you have answered question 12 you never need the first paragraph again.
teaching.watch_out: Three of these answers sit inside a longer phrase that reads better but breaks the three-word limit.

questions.prompt: How long before closing time is the last admission?
questions.evidence_quote: Last admission is forty-five minutes before closing.
questions.explanation: The information gives one figure for the gap between the last admission and closing time. The question copies the frame, so the answer is the period itself.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: before closing time is the last admission
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Last admission is forty-five minutes before closing
paraphrase_link.note: The question moves the period out of the sentence and asks for it back, changing nothing else.

teaching.decision_rule: 'How long' asks for a duration, and the paragraph carries exactly one duration measured against closing time.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the closing time itself and sits in the sentence immediately before.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a point in the day; the question asks for the length of the gap in front of it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other short period in the text and is also measured against closing.
distractors.why_wrong: It applies to the cafe, which shuts before the building does.

teaching.reusable_rule: A clock time and a length of time look alike on the page. The question word tells you which is wanted.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'How long' wants a number and its unit, with nothing before or after them.

questions.prompt: What must a visitor do to a ticket in order to use it again?
questions.evidence_quote: provided you sign it on your first visit
questions.explanation: A ticket lasts a year and allows unlimited returns, but only on one condition, which the information attaches with 'provided'. The condition is signing the ticket on the first visit.
questions.trap_note: The condition arrives after the promise, so a reader who stops at 'as often as you like' misses it entirely.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: in order to use it again
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: you may return as often as you like
paraphrase_link.note: Returning to the museum and using the ticket again are the same act described from two sides.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Provided' introduces the one condition on the year-long ticket, so the answer is the action inside that clause and not the entitlement in front of it.

distractors.why_tempting: Keeping a ticket is the obvious requirement for reusing one and needs no reading at all.
distractors.why_wrong: The information never says it, and inventing a plausible condition is not reading.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the phrase that makes returning possible and sits in the same sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: It states how long the ticket lasts, not what the visitor has to do.

teaching.reusable_rule: The word that introduces a condition is where the answer starts. Read past the promise to reach it.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What must a visitor do' wants a verb and its object, not a noun phrase.

questions.prompt: In which part of the museum is photography forbidden?
questions.evidence_quote: permitted everywhere except in the chart room
questions.explanation: Photography without flash is allowed throughout the building apart from one room, where the early maps would be damaged by light. That room is the exception the question asks for.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: permitted everywhere except in the chart room
paraphrase_link.note: The information writes a permission with an exception; the question writes the exception as a prohibition.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Except' marks the single place the general permission does not reach, so the answer is the noun phrase inside that clause.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the only other room named in the paragraph and it has its own access rule.
distractors.why_wrong: Its rule is about stairs and a lift, and photography there is permitted like everywhere else.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the word attached to the verb the question uses, so a keyword search lands on it.
distractors.why_wrong: It names where photography is allowed, which is the opposite of what is asked.

teaching.reusable_rule: A permission with an exception answers two opposite questions. Decide which one you were asked.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'In which part' wants the name of a place, without a preposition in front of it.

questions.prompt: What is required in order to use one of the lockers?
questions.evidence_quote: the lockers by the entrance, which take a returnable pound coin
questions.explanation: Large bags must be left in the lockers, which are operated by a pound coin that is given back afterwards. The question asks what the locker needs, so the answer is the coin.
questions.trap_note: 'Returnable' describes what happens to the coin later and is not part of what the locker requires.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: required in order to use one of the lockers
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: which take a returnable pound coin
paraphrase_link.note: The information says what the locker takes; the question asks what the visitor must supply.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks what is needed, so the answer is the object itself. The adjective describes what becomes of it and is outside the requirement.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the complete noun phrase and copying it whole feels safer than trimming it.
distractors.why_wrong: It runs to four words against a limit of three, and the article is a word too.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other object in the sentence and defines who has to use a locker at all.
distractors.why_wrong: It sets the size at which a bag must be left, not what operates the locker.

teaching.reusable_rule: Adjectives that describe what happens later are rarely part of the answer. Cut them before counting.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What is required' wants a bare noun phrase, so no article and no adjective clause.

questions.prompt: What is the largest number of people allowed on one guided tour?
questions.evidence_quote: each tour takes no more than fifteen people
questions.explanation: Tours are free but have to be booked on the day, and each one is capped. The cap is stated as a maximum, which is what the question asks for.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the largest number of people allowed
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: takes no more than fifteen people
paraphrase_link.note: 'No more than' is a maximum written as a negative, which is why a search for 'maximum' finds nothing.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks for a ceiling, and the paragraph gives one figure expressed as a limit. The other numbers there are clock times.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's first number and sits beside the word tours.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a departure time, and the question asks how many people, not when.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other quantity attached to the tour and follows the same verb pattern.
distractors.why_wrong: It is how long the tour lasts rather than how many may join it.

teaching.reusable_rule: A maximum is often written as a negative. Search for the limit, not for the word that names one.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'the largest number of people' wants a bare figure, with no noun after it.

texts.heading: Your first month: a guide for new staff

paragraphs.text: Your first day begins at 9.00 in the training room on the ground floor of Verdon House, not in your own department. Bring photographic identification and your bank details; without them the payroll office cannot enter you on the system in time for the first pay date. You will be given a temporary badge on the morning of your first day and a permanent one within ten working days, once your photograph has been taken. The temporary badge does not open the clinical areas. Parking on the Verdon House site is not available to staff in their first year, and the nearest public car park is on Ashfield Road.

In your first week your manager will arrange a meeting to agree your objectives for the probationary period, which lasts six months. Three pieces of training must be completed before the end of the first month: fire safety, manual handling and information governance. Fire safety is a classroom session held every Tuesday afternoon; the other two are online and take about ninety minutes each. Staff who have completed the same training with another trust in the past twelve months may apply for an exemption, which the training office decides.

Your probationary review takes place at three months and again at six. The first is informal and its purpose is to identify any support you need; the second decides whether the appointment is confirmed. A probationary period may be extended once, by up to three months, and only where the manager has recorded specific concerns in writing at the three-month meeting. During probation the notice period on either side is one week. Anyone whose appointment is not confirmed is entitled to a written statement of the reasons within ten working days.

Everyone new to the trust is offered a workplace buddy, a member of staff from another team who agrees to answer the questions people are reluctant to put to a manager. The scheme is voluntary on both sides and no record is kept of what is discussed. It is not a substitute for supervision, and a buddy has no part in the probationary decision. Staff are advised to meet their buddy at least once a fortnight during the first three months. A buddy may be changed at any time by telling the induction coordinator, and no reason has to be given.

texts.heading: Pay, allowances and pension

paragraphs.text: Salaries are paid on the 25th of each month, or on the last working day before it when the 25th falls at a weekend. A payslip is available online three days beforehand and is not sent on paper unless you ask the payroll office in writing. Staff who join after the 12th of a month are paid for that month with the following month's salary, which means the first payment is larger than the ones that follow. Expenses claims must reach the payroll office by the 10th to be paid in the same month.

Every post sits on a grade with several increments. You move up one increment each year on the anniversary of your appointment until you reach the top of the grade, provided your last review was satisfactory. Moving to a higher grade is not automatic and requires an application to a vacant post. Acting up into a more senior post for more than four weeks attracts an allowance, paid from the first day of the period rather than from the fifth week. Each grade and its increments are listed on the pay scale published every April.

Overtime is paid at time and a half on weekdays and at double time on Sundays and public holidays. It must be authorised in advance by a manager; work done without authorisation is not paid, however necessary it turns out to have been. A claim for overtime must be submitted within two months of the work being done. Staff above Grade 7 do not receive overtime and take time off in lieu instead, at plain time, to be used within three months. Sunday working is not compulsory for staff appointed before the current contract was introduced.

The trust's pension scheme is open to all staff and you are entered automatically unless you choose to leave it. Your contribution depends on your salary band and rises in steps from five to twelve per cent, and the trust adds a fixed sum on top for everyone. Contributions are taken before tax, so the cost to you is smaller than the percentage suggests. If you leave within two years you may take a refund of your own contributions, less tax, but the trust's share is not returned.

difficulty_rationale.note: Two institutional documents in which almost every sentence carries a threshold, a deadline or an exception, and in which advice and obligation are worded almost identically.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Four different rules about overtime, each with its own limit, and one of them applies to a group defined by grade.

skim_plan.read_first: The two headings and the opening sentence of each paragraph. Each one announces whether it is about time, money or a decision.
skim_plan.skip: The list of three training courses. Only one question needs any of them, and it names the course itself.

rewordings: you are signed up unless you object

paraphrase_families.passage_form: Acting up into a more senior post
rewordings: filling a superior position for a time
taking on a bigger job temporarily
can seek to be let off
may ask not to repeat it

hinge_words.why_here: It carries the pension opt-out that decides question 23.
It marks advice rather than obligation and is the whole of question 20.
'May be extended once' is the limit question 19 asks you to test.
It rejects the fifth week as the start of the allowance in question 22.

mineable.meaning: the first months, before a job is made permanent
ask to be excused from a requirement
how much warning either side must give
a fixed yearly step up within a pay grade
doing a more senior job for a time
instead of, in place of something else
agreed by a manager before the work is done

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the notes below with words taken from the guide for new staff.

layout.title: Before you start and in week one
lines: Day one: report to the {{15}} on the ground floor, not to your department.
Take photographic identification and your {{16}} for the payroll office.
The probationary period lasts {{17}}.
Fire safety is taught in a classroom every {{18}}.

teaching.strategy: Everything is in the first two paragraphs of the induction guide, so read those and close the rest. Two gaps want a place or an object and two want a period or a day, as the word in front of each shows.
teaching.order_note: All four come from the first two paragraphs, in the order they appear. Work straight down.
teaching.watch_out: Three of these answers are two-word noun phrases. Dropping the second word loses the mark even though the first one is right.

questions.prompt: Day one: report to the {{gap}} on the ground floor, not to your department.
questions.evidence_quote: begins at 9.00 in the training room on the ground floor of Verdon House
questions.explanation: The guide sends new staff to the training room rather than to their own department on the first morning. The note keeps the contrast, so the answer is the place named before it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: on the ground floor of Verdon House
paraphrase_link.note: The note drops the building's name and keeps the floor, which is enough to locate the sentence.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'the' and a prepositional phrase naming a floor, so it takes a noun naming a room. The paragraph names one.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other office named in the paragraph and it is the reason for bringing the documents.
distractors.why_wrong: Nobody reports there on the first day; it is named as what cannot act without your details.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest proper noun and it follows the phrase about the ground floor.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the building; the gap is the room inside it, and the building name is already implied.

teaching.reusable_rule: Match the level of detail the frame asks for. A wider name is wrong even when it contains the right place.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'the' before the gap and a floor after it force a singular noun naming a room.

questions.prompt: Take photographic identification and your {{gap}} for the payroll office.
questions.evidence_quote: Bring photographic identification and your bank details
questions.explanation: Two things must be brought on the first day, and the guide names them in one clause. Without them the payroll office cannot register a new employee in time for the first pay date.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Bring photographic identification and your
paraphrase_link.note: One verb is swapped and nothing else changes, so the gap is fixed by position alone.

teaching.decision_rule: The note reproduces the clause and removes its second item, so the answer is whatever the guide lists after 'and your'.

distractors.why_tempting: It appears two sentences later and is also something the trust needs from a new employee.
distractors.why_wrong: That is taken for the permanent badge, and it is not among the things brought on day one.

distractors.why_tempting: One word is inside the limit and looks like the content word of the pair.
distractors.why_wrong: The guide writes two words, and half a noun phrase is not the phrase.

teaching.reusable_rule: A limit of two words is permission, not an instruction to shorten. Copy the whole phrase if it fits.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'your' before the gap wants a plural noun phrase naming something you own.

questions.prompt: The probationary period lasts {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: your objectives for the probationary period, which lasts six months
questions.explanation: The guide gives the length of probation in a relative clause attached to its first mention. Later paragraphs give the review points and the possible extension, which are different figures.
questions.trap_note: Three months, three months again and ten working days all appear nearby and all describe probation.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the probationary period, which lasts six months
paraphrase_link.note: A relative clause becomes a main clause, which is why the sentence looks different from the guide's.

teaching.decision_rule: The note asks for the whole length, not a review point or an extension. Only one figure in the guide is attached to the verb 'lasts'.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the first review point and the length of a possible extension, so it appears twice.
distractors.why_wrong: It measures a stage inside probation, not the period itself.

distractors.why_tempting: Adding the extension to the standard period gives a plausible maximum.
distractors.why_wrong: The figure is calculated by the reader and appears nowhere in the guide.

teaching.reusable_rule: Find the verb the gap depends on, then take the figure attached to that verb and no other.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'lasts' before the gap wants a length of time, not a point in one.

questions.prompt: Fire safety is taught in a classroom every {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: Fire safety is a classroom session held every Tuesday afternoon
questions.explanation: Of the three compulsory courses, one is taught face to face on a fixed afternoon each week and the other two are online. The note asks when the classroom session runs.
questions.trap_note: Ninety minutes belongs to the online courses in the same sentence.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: is taught in a classroom every
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is a classroom session held every
paraphrase_link.note: A noun phrase becomes a passive verb, and the frequency word survives untouched on both sides.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'every' and names a recurring slot, so it takes a day and, if the guide gives one, the part of the day with it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other time expression in the sentence and follows the same semicolon.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the length of the two online courses, not when the classroom one meets.

distractors.why_tempting: The day alone answers the question 'when' and comfortably fits the limit.
distractors.why_wrong: The guide writes 'Tuesday afternoon', and both words fit inside two.

teaching.reusable_rule: Stopping short of the full phrase is as costly as running past it. Copy exactly what the limit allows.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'every' before the gap wants a recurring day, with any part of the day attached.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the two documents?

teaching.strategy: Underline the modal and the quantity in each statement before you search: must, once, no pay, only, without applying. Three of these five turn on the difference between what the documents require and what they merely recommend or permit.
teaching.order_note: In document order, running from the probation paragraph through to the pension paragraph.
teaching.watch_out: One statement is about a motive the documents never give. Being unable to find a reason is not the same as the reason being denied.

questions.prompt: A probationary period can be extended more than once.
questions.evidence_quote: A probationary period may be extended once, by up to three months
questions.explanation: The guide permits one extension of up to three months, and only where the manager recorded concerns in writing at the three-month meeting. A second extension is ruled out by the word 'once'.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the whole denial is carried by one unstressed word in the middle of a long sentence.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: may be extended once
paraphrase_link.note: The statement widens a stated maximum, and a widened maximum is contradicted by the maximum itself.

teaching.decision_rule: The document permits exactly one extension, so a statement allowing more is denied by the sentence that grants it. That is a contradiction, not an absence.
