distractors.why_tempting: The sentence does grant an extension, and a reader checking only whether extensions exist finds that they do.
distractors.why_wrong: Existence is not the claim. The statement adds a number the document has already fixed at one.

distractors.why_tempting: The phrase 'more than once' appears nowhere, so a search for it returns nothing and the topic looks unaddressed.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Once' in the same sentence settles it; a stated maximum denies every number above it.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stated maximum is a denial of everything above it. Look for the number, not for the comparison.

questions.prompt: New staff are required to meet their buddy at least every two weeks for the first three months.
questions.evidence_quote: Staff are advised to meet their buddy at least once a fortnight during the first three months
questions.explanation: The frequency and the period in the statement are both correct. What is wrong is the modality: the guide advises the meetings, and it describes the whole scheme as voluntary on both sides.
questions.trap_note: Everything checkable checks out except the one word that decides the item.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: are required to meet their buddy
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: are advised to meet their buddy
paraphrase_link.note: Advice becomes obligation. Nothing else in the sentence moves, which is why the swap is so easy to miss.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the frequency matches, but the document states advice where the statement states a requirement. Advice plus an explicit 'voluntary' contradicts a duty.

distractors.why_tempting: The fortnight and the three months are both exactly right, so three of the statement's four elements confirm on sight.
distractors.why_wrong: A statement is TRUE only if all of it holds. The verb is the element that fails.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'required' appears nowhere in the paragraph, so a reader hunting the obligation finds none.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph says the scheme is voluntary and that staff are advised, which denies the requirement rather than passing over it.

teaching.reusable_rule: Check the verb before the numbers. Advice, permission and obligation look alike and are worth one mark each.

questions.prompt: Someone who starts work on the 20th of a month receives no salary until the following month.
questions.evidence_quote: Staff who join after the 12th of a month are paid for that month with the following month's salary
questions.explanation: The 20th falls after the 12th, so the rule applies: the first month's pay is carried over and arrives with the next salary. The document adds that the first payment is therefore larger than the rest.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: receives no salary until the following month
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: with the following month's salary
paraphrase_link.note: Being paid later is restated as not being paid yet, with the same timing on both sides.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement's date falls inside the range the rule covers, and the consequence it names is the one the document states. No step of reasoning beyond reading the date is needed.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens by saying salaries are paid on the 25th, which is after the 20th and looks like the answer.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the general pay date; the following sentence gives the exception for new joiners.

distractors.why_tempting: The 20th is never mentioned, so a reader searching for the date itself finds nothing.
distractors.why_wrong: The rule is written as a threshold, and any date above the threshold is covered by it.

teaching.reusable_rule: A threshold covers every value beyond it. You are not adding information by reading a date against one.

questions.prompt: Acting up in a senior post improves an employee's chance of being appointed to that grade.
questions.evidence_quote: Acting up into a more senior post for more than four weeks attracts an allowance
questions.explanation: The document explains what acting up pays and when the allowance starts, and separately that moving up a grade needs an application to a vacant post. It never connects the two.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: two facts sit in neighbouring sentences and the link between them is supplied by the reader.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Acting up in a senior post
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Acting up into a more senior post
paraphrase_link.note: The activity is named identically; the consequence the statement attaches to it is what has no counterpart.

teaching.decision_rule: Both halves of the statement appear in the paragraph as separate facts, and nothing joins them. There is no support for the link and no sentence denying it.

distractors.why_tempting: Doing a job before applying for it obviously helps, and the two sentences sit side by side.
distractors.why_wrong: The link is common sense, not text. A promotion advantage is never stated anywhere.

distractors.why_tempting: The document says moving up a grade is not automatic, which reads as a refusal of any advantage.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Not automatic' denies a guarantee, not an improved chance, so it contradicts nothing here.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two facts in neighbouring sentences are still two facts. A causal link has to be written down to count.
teaching.nearest_text: Moving to a higher grade is not automatic and requires an application to a vacant post.

questions.prompt: Employees join the pension scheme without having to apply for it.
questions.evidence_quote: you are entered automatically unless you choose to leave it
questions.explanation: The scheme is open to all staff and entry happens by default; the only action available is leaving. That is exactly what joining without applying means.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: without having to apply for it
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: you are entered automatically
paraphrase_link.note: The document states the mechanism; the statement states what the mechanism saves you doing.

teaching.decision_rule: Entering automatically and joining without applying are the same proposition. The exception clause allows leaving, which does not affect how you got in.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'unless' signals a condition, and a reader who sees a condition assumes some action is required.
distractors.why_wrong: The condition governs leaving, not joining, so it cannot make entry conditional.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'apply' appears in the other document about exemptions, not here, so a keyword search misleads.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Entered automatically' states the proposition in full, in different words.

teaching.reusable_rule: Check which verb an exception clause attaches to. It often qualifies the opposite action from the one asked about.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete each sentence below with words taken from the pay, allowances and pension document.

teaching.strategy: All four answers are in the pay document and run down it in order. Two gaps want a bare figure and two want a short noun phrase, and in each case the words on both sides of the gap fix the choice before you search.
teaching.order_note: In document order. After question 26 the pension paragraph is the only place left to look.
teaching.watch_out: One correct phrase has a three-word version that reads better. Length is checked before content, so the fuller answer scores nothing.

questions.prompt: A payslip appears online {{gap}} days before the salary is paid.
questions.evidence_quote: A payslip is available online three days beforehand
questions.explanation: Payslips go online three days ahead of the pay date and are only issued on paper if you ask in writing. The sentence copies the frame and removes the figure.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph carries four other numbers, three of which are dates in the month.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: available online three days beforehand
paraphrase_link.note: 'Beforehand' is unpacked into the clause it refers to, which is why the wording looks new.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits before 'days', so it takes a quantity rather than a date. Only one number in the paragraph counts days rather than naming one.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's first and most prominent number and it is about when salary arrives.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the pay date itself, and the gap counts days in front of that date.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other deadline in the paragraph and also sits before the pay date each month.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the cut-off for expenses claims, which the sentence is not about.

teaching.reusable_rule: A date and a count look identical on the page. The noun after the gap tells you which is wanted.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'days' follows the gap, so it takes a bare number and no ordinal ending.

questions.prompt: Provided the last review was satisfactory, one increment is added each year on the {{gap}} of the appointment.
questions.evidence_quote: You move up one increment each year on the anniversary of your appointment
questions.explanation: Increments are annual and are tied to the date of appointment rather than to a common date for all staff. Moving to a higher grade is a separate process that requires an application.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: one increment is added each year
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: You move up one increment each year
paraphrase_link.note: The employee disappears into a passive, which is the only change between the two sentences.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'on the' and precedes 'of the appointment', so it takes a singular noun naming a recurring date. The paragraph supplies one.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's only named month and it is attached to the pay scale.
distractors.why_wrong: That is when the scale is published, and increments are tied to each person's own date.

distractors.why_tempting: It fits the frame grammatically and is the obvious general word for what is wanted.
distractors.why_wrong: The document uses a more specific noun, and a completion answer is copied rather than chosen.

teaching.reusable_rule: A word that would fit the frame is not the answer. The answer is the word the writer actually used.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'on the' before the gap and 'of the appointment' after it force a singular noun.

questions.prompt: Instead of overtime pay, staff above Grade 7 are given {{gap}} at plain time.
questions.evidence_quote: Staff above Grade 7 do not receive overtime and take time off in lieu instead
questions.explanation: Above Grade 7 the arrangement changes: no overtime payment, and time off instead, calculated at plain time and to be used within three months.
questions.trap_note: 'Time off in lieu' is the document's full phrase and runs to three words plus a preposition.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: take time off in lieu instead
paraphrase_link.note: A negative plus 'instead' becomes the single preposition 'instead of' at the front of the sentence.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'are given' and precedes 'at plain time', so it names what is received. The Latin tag after it is a modifier, not part of the thing.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the document's own phrase and the version anyone who works in an office would write.
distractors.why_wrong: It is four words against a limit of two, so it scores nothing however exact it is.

distractors.why_tempting: It sits at the end of the same clause and is a two-word phrase of the right shape.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the rate at which the time is calculated, and it already appears after the gap.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a phrase has a short core and a formal tail, the limit tells you to write the core.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'are given' before the gap wants a noun phrase naming what is received.

questions.prompt: An employee who leaves within two years may reclaim their own contributions, {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: you may take a refund of your own contributions, less tax, but the trust's share is not returned
questions.explanation: A refund is available for the employee's own contributions in the first two years, reduced by tax, and the trust's contribution is kept. The gap takes the qualifier on the refund.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: may take a refund of your own contributions
paraphrase_link.note: A noun phrase becomes a verb and the second person becomes the third, which defeats a word search.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap closes the sentence after a comma, so it takes the qualifier the document attaches in the same position. The clause after 'but' concerns a different sum.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph uses that phrase two sentences earlier and it is the more familiar formula.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes how contributions are taken from pay, not how a refund is reduced.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the noun phrase nearest the end of the sentence and is clearly relevant to a refund.
distractors.why_wrong: It names what is not returned, so writing it reverses the meaning of the line.

teaching.reusable_rule: A short phrase between commas qualifies the noun before it. Prefer it to the clause after a conjunction.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap ends the sentence after a comma, so it takes a short qualifying phrase.

title: The Craft of the Drystone Wall

passage_json.title: The Craft of the Drystone Wall

texts.heading: The Craft of the Drystone Wall

paragraphs.text: A drystone wall is built without mortar of any kind. Every stone is held in place by its own weight and by the stones around it, and the whole structure depends on nothing but friction and the care with which each piece was chosen. Walls of this sort divide fields across a large part of upland Britain and Ireland, and comparable structures are found wherever there is more stone than timber and more sheep than money. From a distance they look like a single object. They are in fact several thousand separate decisions, each made once and never revisited. The oldest surviving examples are hard to date, because a wall rebuilt in the same place from the same stone is indistinguishable from the original.

The method has changed very little. A trench is opened and the largest stones are laid as a foundation, wide side down. Above them the wall rises in two leaning faces, each course set back a little from the one below, so that the wall tapers as it climbs. The gap between the faces is packed with small stone called hearting, which is not rubble and is placed by hand. At intervals a long throughstone is laid across the full width to tie the faces together, and a line of coping stones is set upright along the top to weigh the whole thing down.

The wall stands because it is trying to fall inwards. The taper means that each face leans against the other, and the hearting stops them settling into the space between. A mortared wall resists movement; a dry wall accommodates it. When frost lifts the ground beneath it, or a tree root pushes at the foundation, the stones shift a few millimetres and lock again in a slightly different arrangement. This is why a well-built dry wall on unstable ground will outlast a mortared one, and why the commonest cause of collapse is not weather but a wall that was hearted carelessly.

What the wall looks like is decided by the stone, not by the builder's taste. Where the rock splits into flat slabs the courses are level and the wall looks almost brick-built. Where it comes out of the ground in rounded lumps the courses wander and the faces are irregular, and a builder from the slab country would call the result untidy. Coping varies in the same way: upright and even in some districts, laid flat in others, and in a few places finished with a row of stones set at an angle so that the top resembles a saw. A walker can often tell which valley they are in from the top of a wall.

The economics have always been awkward. A wall is far more expensive to build than a fence and far cheaper to keep, and it lasts a century or more if it is looked after. That combination suited a landowner with cheap labour and a long view, and it suited nobody at all after the middle of the twentieth century, when wages rose and wire became cheap. Farms that had maintained their walls for generations began to repair the gaps with posts and wire, which works, costs almost nothing and takes an afternoon. A gap repaired that way is also, in practice, permanent, because the stone beside it is soon taken for something else.

The decline was steep and largely unrecorded. Nobody counted the walls, so nobody could say what was being lost, and a survey of one upland county in the 1990s found that a substantial proportion of its field walls were derelict or gapped. Neglect is slow at first. A single displaced coping stone admits rain and stock, the gap widens over a winter or two, and a wall that would have taken a day to repair becomes a week's work. By the time a wall looks ruined, most of its stone is still there, lying where it fell.

The revival began with training rather than with money. A certification scheme, in which a candidate rebuilds a set length under observation and is assessed against a published standard, gave the craft a ladder that could be climbed and made it possible to advertise a skill rather than an acquaintance. Grants followed, usually paid by the metre and usually conditional on the work meeting that standard. The effect has been to turn an activity that was learned from a relative into an occupation that can be entered from outside it, and the people entering are markedly more varied than the previous generation.

A wall is also a habitat, and this is now part of the argument for keeping it. The cavities that make the structure work shelter voles, lizards, wrens and a great many invertebrates; the outer faces carry lichens that take decades to establish and are removed by a single repointing. None of this was in anyone's mind when the walls were built. It is nevertheless the reason a good many of them are now repaired with public money, which is a fair description of how most old landscapes survive: they are kept for reasons their makers would not recognise.

difficulty_rationale.note: The subject is physical, but the piece argues about value: it explains a technique, shows why it stopped paying, and ends on a reason for keeping it unrelated to either.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It explains stability by saying the wall is trying to fall, which reads as a contradiction until the second half of the paragraph.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of the first paragraph. It defines the object and warns that the walls are older and more numerous than they look.
skim_plan.skip: The description of coping styles in the fourth paragraph. It is illustration of a point the first sentence has already made.

Paragraph B

teaching.strategy: Do this group after the multiple choice, when you have already read six of the eight paragraphs for something else. Reduce each statement to one noun before searching: joining, measuring, movement, entry. Each names a process rather than a topic.
teaching.order_note: Not in article order, so nothing bounds the search. Every paragraph has to stay in play.
teaching.watch_out: Two paragraphs describe rebuilding and two describe standards. In each pair only one is about the thing the statement names.

questions.prompt: a reason why a wall without mortar survives ground movement better than one with it
questions.evidence_quote: the stones shift a few millimetres and lock again in a slightly different arrangement
questions.explanation: The paragraph contrasts resisting movement with accommodating it, then describes what happens when frost or a root disturbs the foundation, and concludes that a dry wall on unstable ground outlasts a mortared one.
questions.trap_note: Another paragraph explains how a small displacement grows into a gap, which is movement of a different kind.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: on unstable ground will outlast a mortared one
paraphrase_link.note: 'Outlast' becomes 'survives better', and 'unstable ground' becomes 'ground movement'.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement asks for a cause, not a description. Only one paragraph explains the mechanism and states the comparison in the same place.

distractors.why_tempting: It also describes stones being displaced and a wall failing, so the vocabulary matches closely.
distractors.why_wrong: There the movement is neglect turning into a gap, and no comparison with mortar is made.

distractors.why_tempting: It explains the taper and the hearting, which are the features the mechanism depends on.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes how a wall is put together and never says what happens when the ground moves.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement asking why needs a paragraph that argues, not one that describes. Find the comparison.

questions.prompt: an explanation of why the scale of the loss could not be established
questions.evidence_quote: Nobody counted the walls, so nobody could say what was being lost
questions.explanation: The paragraph states the reason directly: because there was never a count, there was no baseline against which loss could be measured. A single county survey is offered as the exception that proves it.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the scale of the loss could not be established
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: nobody could say what was being lost
paraphrase_link.note: A clause with an agent becomes an agentless passive, so the sentence shares almost no words with the statement.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement asks why something could not be measured. One paragraph names the absence of a count as the cause and draws the consequence in the same sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph about why walls were abandoned, and abandonment is the loss being counted.
distractors.why_wrong: It gives the economic reason for the decline, not the reason its size is unknown.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other paragraph full of measurement and standards.
distractors.why_wrong: Those measure the quality of new work, not the quantity of what was lost.

teaching.reusable_rule: A cause of something and a cause of not knowing about it are different claims. Match the one asked for.

questions.prompt: a description of how the two sides of a wall are fastened to each other
questions.evidence_quote: a long throughstone is laid across the full width to tie the faces together
questions.explanation: The building paragraph names the component whose whole purpose is to bind the two faces: a stone long enough to cross the full width, laid at intervals up the wall.
questions.trap_note: Another paragraph explains why the faces lean on each other, which is support rather than fastening.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: to tie the faces together
paraphrase_link.note: One verb is swapped for a near equivalent, which is enough to defeat a search for the word itself.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement asks how the faces are joined, so it needs the component that crosses between them. Only one paragraph names a part with that job.

distractors.why_tempting: It says each face leans against the other, which sounds like the two sides being held together.
distractors.why_wrong: Leaning is mutual support from geometry; nothing there passes between the faces.

distractors.why_tempting: It states that every stone is held by the stones around it, which reads as a general answer to the question.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the principle of the whole wall, not a description of how the two faces are joined.

teaching.reusable_rule: A general principle is not a description of a part. When a statement names a component, look for a component.

questions.prompt: a change in who is now able to take up the craft
questions.evidence_quote: into an occupation that can be entered from outside it
questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that certification turned a trade passed down inside families into one that an outsider can enter, and notes that the people now entering are more varied than before.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: who is now able to take up the craft
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: an occupation that can be entered from outside it
paraphrase_link.note: The article describes the occupation; the statement describes the people, which is the same fact from the other end.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement is about the range of possible entrants. Only one paragraph contrasts how the craft used to be learned with how it can be joined now.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other paragraph about who did the work and why they stopped doing it.
distractors.why_wrong: It is about landowners and the cost of labour, not about who may learn the trade.

distractors.why_tempting: It also describes a change in why walls are looked after, and change is the word in the statement.
distractors.why_wrong: That change is in the reasons for repair, not in the people doing it.

teaching.reusable_rule: The same fact can be told about an activity or about the people in it. Match the subject the statement chooses.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

teaching.strategy: Answer the stem in your own words before reading the options, because in each of these sets two options are drawn from the right paragraph and only one answers the question asked. Question 34 needs the writer's view rather than a fact.
teaching.order_note: In article order. Question 34 comes from the last paragraph, so it can be done from a single reading.
teaching.watch_out: One option in each set inverts the direction of an argument the article makes. Read the whole option before choosing it.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what decides the appearance of a drystone wall?

options.text: The preferences of the person who built it.
The kind of stone that is available locally.
The purpose the wall was originally built for.
The district in which the wall happens to stand.

questions.evidence_quote: What the wall looks like is decided by the stone, not by the builder's taste.
questions.explanation: The paragraph opens by naming the cause and ruling out the obvious alternative, then illustrates it twice: flat slabs give level courses, rounded lumps give wandering ones.
questions.trap_note: Option D reverses the article's final sentence, which says a walker can infer the place from the wall, not the wall from the place.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The kind of stone that is available locally
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is decided by the stone
paraphrase_link.note: The option adds 'available locally', which the paragraph supplies through its two examples rather than in words.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what decides appearance, and the paragraph's first sentence states one cause and denies another. Anything after 'not by' is excluded by the writer.

distractors.why_tempting: Craft is normally a matter of skill and choice, so the builder is the obvious agent.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the reading the opening sentence explicitly rejects.

distractors.why_tempting: Walls do have a purpose, dividing fields, and purpose usually shapes a structure.
distractors.why_wrong: The article never links the wall's purpose to how it looks; the purpose is the same everywhere.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends with a walker identifying a valley from a wall, which sounds like the district deciding the style.
distractors.why_wrong: The district is where the stone comes from, and the article treats the wall as the evidence, not the effect.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a sentence names a cause and denies another, both are in the option list. Take the one before the denial.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer say walls stopped being maintained after the mid-twentieth century?

options.text: Farmers no longer believed that walls could contain stock.
The stone needed for repairs had become hard to obtain.
Labour grew expensive at the same time as wire grew cheap.
Public money was withdrawn from farms that kept walls up.

questions.evidence_quote: when wages rose and wire became cheap
questions.explanation: The paragraph makes the economics turn on two prices moving in opposite directions. The arrangement had suited an owner with cheap labour, and it suited nobody once labour stopped being cheap and wire did not.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: when wages rose and wire became cheap
paraphrase_link.note: Wages become labour and the two verbs are swapped, with the simultaneity kept by 'when'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the writer's stated cause, and the paragraph supplies a two-part one inside a single time clause. An option naming only one price movement would be incomplete.

distractors.why_tempting: Walls exist to hold stock, so a change of mind about that would explain abandoning them.
distractors.why_wrong: The article never questions whether walls work; it says a wire repair also works.

distractors.why_tempting: The article does say stone beside a gap gets taken for something else, so scarcity is in the paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: That happens after a gap is wired, as a consequence, and is never given as a cause.

distractors.why_tempting: Grants appear later in the article, so money from outside is part of the story.
distractors.why_wrong: Grants arrive with the revival, decades afterwards, and nothing is described as being withdrawn.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a cause has two halves joined by 'and', an option giving one half is not the answer.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's view of the reason old walls are now repaired at public expense?

options.text: It has nothing to do with the purpose they were built for.
It reflects a wider public interest in traditional rural crafts.
It is cheaper than allowing an old wall to collapse entirely.
It follows from a legal duty placed on the owners of walls.

questions.evidence_quote: they are kept for reasons their makers would not recognise
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states that the wildlife value was in nobody's mind when the walls were built, and then generalises: old landscapes survive for reasons their makers would not recognise. That is the writer's view.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the purpose they were built for
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: in anyone's mind when the walls were built
paraphrase_link.note: 'Not in anyone's mind at the time' becomes 'nothing to do with the original purpose'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a view, not a fact, and the paragraph ends on an explicit judgement about the mismatch between why walls were built and why they are kept.

distractors.why_tempting: The article's whole second half is about a revival, which reads as public interest in the craft.
distractors.why_wrong: That revival is explained by training and grants; nothing attributes it to public sentiment.

distractors.why_tempting: Cost drives the argument in an earlier paragraph, and repairing early is cheaper there.
distractors.why_wrong: That comparison is between an early repair and a late one, not between repairing and doing nothing.

distractors.why_tempting: Grants are described as conditional, and conditions sound like an obligation of some kind.
distractors.why_wrong: The condition is on the standard of the work, and no legal duty is mentioned anywhere.

teaching.reusable_rule: A question about a view is answered by the writer's own judgement, not by the facts that led up to it.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete each sentence below with words taken from the article.

teaching.strategy: All three answers are in the first three paragraphs and run in order. Two of them are technical words the article defines as it introduces them, so read the clause after each term rather than hunting for a definition elsewhere.
teaching.order_note: In article order, and all three sit above the paragraph on regional styles.
teaching.watch_out: Two answers share a root with another word in the same paragraph. The frame decides which form the gap wants.

questions.prompt: No mortar is used: the stones are held by their own weight and by {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: the whole structure depends on nothing but friction and the care with which each piece was chosen
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph names two things the wall depends on: friction between the stones and the care taken in choosing them. The sentence keeps the first.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: held in place by its own weight
paraphrase_link.note: The article's singular stone becomes plural and 'in place' is dropped, but the frame is otherwise identical.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'by' and names a physical force acting between stones. Only one word in the paragraph does that; the other item in the pair names a human action.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the second half of the article's own pair and sits in the same clause.
distractors.why_wrong: The frame is about what physically holds the stones, and care is exercised before the wall exists.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the first noun in the sentence frame and the most prominent word in the paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: The sentence has already said none is used, so writing it contradicts the line.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a text pairs a physical cause with a human one, the frame tells you which kind the gap wants.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'by' before the gap and a full stop after it want a single uncountable noun.

questions.prompt: The small stone packed by hand between the two faces is known as {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: packed with small stone called hearting, which is not rubble and is placed by hand
questions.explanation: The article names the material that fills the gap between the faces and insists in the same clause that it is placed deliberately rather than tipped in.
questions.trap_note: 'Rubble' appears in the same clause as the thing hearting is not.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: small stone called hearting
paraphrase_link.note: A naming verb is swapped for its equivalent, so the term itself is the only element missing.

teaching.decision_rule: The frame 'is known as' introduces a technical term, so the gap takes the word the article supplies as a name rather than any description of the same material.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest noun to the term and describes broken stone of exactly this size.
distractors.why_wrong: The article names it only to deny that hearting is rubble.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the description immediately in front of the term and fits the two-word limit.
distractors.why_wrong: The frame asks for the name, and the name comes after the naming verb.

teaching.reusable_rule: A naming verb points forward. Whatever stands in front of it is a description, not the term.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'is known as' closes the sentence, so the gap takes a single noun.

questions.prompt: Where a mortared wall resists movement, a dry wall {{gap}} it.
questions.evidence_quote: A mortared wall resists movement; a dry wall accommodates it.
questions.explanation: The article puts the two behaviours in one sentence divided by a semicolon. The gap takes the verb on the dry side of that contrast.

teaching.decision_rule: The frame reproduces one side of a two-part contrast, so the gap takes the verb the article uses on the other side, in the same tense and person.

distractors.why_tempting: It is already in the sentence and a hurried reader completes the parallel with the same verb.
distractors.why_wrong: The article uses it of the mortared wall, and the two halves are opposites.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Answer the questions below using words from the article.

teaching.strategy: These three run from the paragraph on regional styles to the one on the revival, so start below the wall-building description. Each question word fixes the shape of the answer, and all three answers are short noun phrases lifted whole.

questions.explanation: The paragraph lists three coping styles and gives the third a comparison of its own: stones set at an angle produce a toothed line along the top.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a row of stones set at an angle

teaching.decision_rule: 'Resemble' is the article's own verb, so the answer is the noun that follows it. The other coping styles are described without any comparison.

distractors.why_wrong: It applies to the whole wall in slab country, not to a row of stones along the top.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the term for the row of stones itself and opens the sentence.

questions.prompt: What did farmers use instead of stone when they repaired gaps?
questions.evidence_quote: began to repair the gaps with posts and wire
questions.explanation: The paragraph says farms that had kept their walls for generations turned to a repair that works, costs almost nothing and takes an afternoon. The materials are named in that sentence.
questions.trap_note: 'Wire' alone appears in the previous sentence and is only half of what the article names.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: began to repair the gaps with posts and wire
paraphrase_link.note: The question drops the aspect verb and the article, leaving the material as the only thing missing.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks what was used, so the answer is the full noun phrase after 'with'. The article names two materials joined by 'and', and both are inside the limit.

distractors.why_tempting: It is named on its own in the previous sentence, as the thing that became cheap.
distractors.why_wrong: The repair itself uses two materials, and the article names them together.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens by comparing a wall with a fence, which is what posts and wire amount to.
distractors.why_wrong: That comparison is about cost; the sentence about repairs names the materials instead.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a text names two materials with 'and', a limit of three words is telling you to write both.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'use instead of stone' wants a noun phrase, and a pair joined by and counts as one.

questions.prompt: How are grants for walling work usually calculated?
questions.evidence_quote: Grants followed, usually paid by the metre and usually conditional on the work meeting that standard
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives two facts about the grants in one sentence: how they are measured and what they depend on. The question asks for the measure.
questions.trap_note: The second half of the same sentence gives the condition, which answers a different question.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: usually paid by the metre
paraphrase_link.note: 'Paid by' becomes 'calculated', which is why searching for the question's own verb returns nothing.

teaching.decision_rule: 'How calculated' asks for the unit of measurement. One half of the sentence gives a unit and the other gives a condition, and only a unit answers this.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other half of the same sentence and is genuinely how the grant is decided.
distractors.why_wrong: It says whether a grant is paid at all, not how the amount is worked out.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other measurement in the paragraph and also concerns how much wall is built.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the length rebuilt in the assessment, which is part of the certificate rather than the grant.

teaching.reusable_rule: One sentence often answers two questions. Decide which half you were asked for before you copy.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'How calculated' wants a prepositional phrase naming a unit.

texts.heading: Rooms and flats to rent in Norland

paragraphs.text: Willow Court. A studio flat on the top floor of a converted mill, twelve minutes on foot from Norland station. Rent is £560 a month and covers water and heating; electricity is billed separately. The flat is furnished and has a small balcony. A deposit of one month's rent and two written references are required. Pets are not allowed and the minimum let is six months. Viewings take place on Saturday mornings only.

Beckside House. Three single rooms in a shared house near the market, let to students and to people in work alike. Rent is £330 a month for each room and includes gas, electricity, water and broadband. The kitchen and the two bathrooms are shared. Tenants under twenty-five must supply a guarantor, who signs an undertaking to pay the rent if the tenant does not. Rooms are let for a minimum of three months.

Cross Street. A one-bedroom flat above a working bakery, unfurnished except for a cooker and a fridge. Rent is £495 a month and every bill is paid by the tenant. There is a parking space at the rear, and its use is included in the rent. The bakery opens at four in the morning, so the flat suits a tenant who is out at night or who sleeps heavily.

Harbour View. A two-bedroom flat with a sea view, available from the first of September to the end of May only, because the owner returns for the summer. Rent is £620 a month including council tax. The flat is fully furnished and has a washing machine. No deposit is charged, but the last month's rent is payable in advance. Well-behaved dogs are welcome.

Chapel Corner. A ground-floor room in a family home, with breakfast provided every day and an evening meal on weekdays. Rent is £400 a month and every bill is included. The room is furnished and has its own washbasin. Guests may not stay overnight. The landlady prefers a tenant who is out during the day, and the let can begin at a week's notice.

Kiln Gardens. Two newly built flats on the edge of town, each with two bedrooms and a garden. Rent is £700 a month, excluding all bills. A deposit of six weeks' rent is required and is held under the Norland Deposit Protection Scheme. The flats are unfurnished. A bus runs into the centre every twenty minutes until half past ten in the evening.

texts.heading: The Norland Deposit Protection Scheme

paragraphs.text: Most landlords in Norland ask for a deposit before you move in. Since April 2022 every deposit taken on a private tenancy of six months or more must be paid into the Norland Deposit Protection Scheme within thirty days of the tenancy starting. The scheme holds the money until the tenancy ends. Landlords who let rooms in their own home are outside the scheme, and so are lets of less than six months, although a landlord may join voluntarily in either case.

Your landlord must give you written confirmation that the deposit has been protected, together with the scheme's reference number. If you have not received this within thirty days, write to the landlord first: the scheme cannot act until the landlord has been asked directly. The written confirmation is not the same as a receipt for the money, and tenants are advised to keep both.

At the end of the tenancy the landlord may propose a deduction for damage, unpaid rent or cleaning. Fair wear and tear is never a valid deduction. If you accept the proposal, the balance is returned within ten working days. If you do not, either side may ask the scheme for a free adjudication, and the deposit stays with the scheme until the adjudicator has decided.

texts.heading: Registering with a doctor in Norland

paragraphs.text: Anyone who is living in Norland for three months or more may register with a medical practice. Take proof of address, and a letter from your previous doctor if you have one, to the reception desk of the practice you have chosen. A practice may refuse a registration only if its list is full or if you live outside the area it covers.

Registration takes about a week. Until it is complete you can still be seen as a temporary patient at any practice. The out-of-hours service, which operates from six in the evening until eight the next morning, is reached on 0800 555 118 and is separate from your own practice.

difficulty_rationale.note: The prose is easy but the facts are packed: six adverts each carry a price, a condition and an exclusion, and the deposit notice states three rules and then removes two classes of landlord from them.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It states a duty, then a deadline, then two exemptions and an option, all in four sentences with no signposting between them.

skim_plan.read_first: The three headings, then the first line of each advert. That tells you which text holds money, which holds rules and which holds an address.
skim_plan.skip: Every description of furniture, views and balconies. Nothing in this section is asked about how a room looks.
fields: monthly price and what it covers
what is excluded from the rent
who is eligible and who is exempt
what you must bring or send

rewordings: name a person who will cover the debt
give the name of somebody responsible
arrange for another person to stand behind the payments
put forward a claim against the money
seek to retain some of it

hinge_words.why_here: 'to the end of May only' is the whole of question 2.
It rules out every condition the reader might add in question 10.
It introduces the half-answer that makes question 8 NOT GIVEN.
The duty it creates is removed two sentences later, which decides question 7.
'either side may ask' is even-handed about access and silent about outcomes in question 11.

has to be paid before the period it covers
not covered by the arrangement
