question_groups.instructions_extra: Look at the six properties, A–F. Which property is described by each statement below? NB You may use any letter more than once.

options.text: Willow Court
Beckside House
Cross Street
Harbour View
Chapel Corner
Kiln Gardens

teaching.strategy: Read the five statements first and turn each into a field: meals, dates, a promise about money, parking, a deposit. Then read the six adverts once, marking those fields in the margin. Two adverts mention money in almost the same words, so decide what kind of money each statement wants before you scan.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, and a letter may be used twice. Work statement by statement, never advert by advert.
teaching.watch_out: Four adverts use the word 'includes' or 'included'. The word is not the answer; what follows it is.

questions.prompt: a let that includes meals
questions.evidence_quote: with breakfast provided every day and an evening meal on weekdays
questions.explanation: Chapel Corner is the only property where food is supplied: breakfast every day and an evening meal from Monday to Friday. Every other advert lists utilities.
questions.trap_note: Three adverts say that something is 'included'. In A, B and D what is included is a bill, not a meal.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: breakfast provided every day and an evening meal
paraphrase_link.note: Two named meals in the advert become the single category word in the statement.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement asks for food, not for cost. Only one advert names anything eaten; the others name gas, water, broadband or tax.

distractors.why_tempting: B carries the longest 'includes' list of any advert, so a reader scanning for that verb stops there first.
distractors.why_wrong: Everything in B's list is a utility supply. Nothing in B is eaten.

distractors.why_tempting: A says the rent 'covers' things, which reads as the same inclusive promise.
distractors.why_wrong: What A covers is water and heating, and it excludes electricity.

teaching.reusable_rule: Turn the statement into a category before you scan, then reject every match whose category is different.

questions.prompt: a tenancy that is not available all year round
questions.evidence_quote: available from the first of September to the end of May only, because the owner returns for the summer
questions.explanation: Harbour View can be rented for nine months of the year and no more, because the owner takes the flat back each summer. No other advert restricts the calendar.
questions.trap_note: A and B set a minimum length of let. A minimum length is not the same as a closed season.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: from the first of September to the end of May only
paraphrase_link.note: Two dates in the advert become a negative statement about the rest of the calendar.

teaching.decision_rule: Only a rule that closes part of the year satisfies the statement. A rule about how long you must stay leaves every month of the year open.

distractors.why_tempting: A's 'minimum let is six months' looks like a limit on time, and the statement is about time.
distractors.why_wrong: Six months is a floor on the length of the let, not a period when the flat cannot be had.

distractors.why_tempting: B also fixes a minimum, at three months, and a reader comparing the two numbers treats the shorter one as the exception.
distractors.why_wrong: Neither number closes a season; B is available in every month.

teaching.reusable_rule: A rule about how long you must stay is a different fact from a rule about when you may stay.

questions.prompt: a requirement for someone else to promise to pay the rent
questions.evidence_quote: must supply a guarantor, who signs an undertaking to pay the rent if the tenant does not
questions.explanation: Beckside House asks younger tenants for a guarantor, and the advert defines a guarantor as a person who signs an undertaking to pay if the tenant does not.
questions.trap_note: A asks for two written references. A reference is somebody's opinion, not somebody's promise to pay.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: someone else to promise to pay the rent
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a guarantor, who signs an undertaking to pay the rent
paraphrase_link.note: The advert supplies its own definition of the term, and the statement uses the definition instead.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement describes a third party taking on a debt. Only one advert names a third party at all in connection with money.

distractors.why_tempting: A demands 'two written references', which is the other advert that brings a third person into the let.
distractors.why_wrong: A referee vouches for the tenant's character; nobody in A agrees to pay anything.

distractors.why_tempting: D mentions rent 'payable in advance', so a reader hunting for an unusual payment rule lands there.
distractors.why_wrong: The person paying in advance is the tenant, not somebody else.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a text defines a term in its own sentence, the definition is what the question will be written from.

questions.prompt: somewhere to leave a vehicle at no extra cost
questions.evidence_quote: There is a parking space at the rear, and its use is included in the rent
questions.explanation: Cross Street offers a parking space behind the building and states that using it costs nothing beyond the rent.
questions.trap_note: F mentions a bus every twenty minutes. That is transport, not parking, and the statement is about leaving a vehicle.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: leave a vehicle at no extra cost
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a parking space at the rear, and its use is included in the rent
paraphrase_link.note: 'Included in the rent' becomes 'at no extra cost' — the same fact stated as an absence of charge.

teaching.decision_rule: Two conditions must both hold: a place for a car, and no separate charge for it. Only one advert satisfies both.

distractors.why_tempting: F is the only other advert that discusses getting about, and 'every twenty minutes' reads like a convenience the rent buys.
distractors.why_wrong: F describes a bus service; it says nothing about where a car may be left, and its bills are excluded.

distractors.why_tempting: D includes council tax, so a reader looking for the advert with the fewest extra charges chooses it.
distractors.why_wrong: The statement is not about which rent is most inclusive; it is about parking, which D never mentions.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement with two conditions needs both of them in one text. Half a match is not a match.

questions.prompt: a deposit that will be held by an outside body
questions.evidence_quote: A deposit of six weeks' rent is required and is held under the Norland Deposit Protection Scheme
questions.explanation: Kiln Gardens is the only advert that names the protection scheme, so it is the only one where the money leaves the landlord's hands.
questions.trap_note: A also asks for a deposit, but says nothing about where the money goes.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: held under the Norland Deposit Protection Scheme
paraphrase_link.note: A named scheme in the advert becomes the general category in the statement.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement turns on custody, not on the existence of a deposit. Two adverts ask for a deposit; only one says who ends up holding it.

distractors.why_tempting: A opens its money sentence with 'A deposit of one month's rent', which is the phrase the statement seems to be looking for.
distractors.why_wrong: A never says what happens to the money after it is paid.

distractors.why_tempting: D talks about a deposit in the same breath as an advance payment, and 'in advance' suggests money being held.
distractors.why_wrong: D charges no deposit at all, and the advance rent is held by the landlord.

teaching.reusable_rule: When two texts share a noun, the question is usually about what happens to it, not about whether it exists.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the deposit scheme notice?

teaching.strategy: This notice is built out of exceptions. Before you read a statement, underline every 'unless', 'outside', 'never' and 'only' in the three paragraphs; four of these six items are decided by one of those words rather than by the main clause it hangs off.
teaching.order_note: In passage order. Question 9's answer is below question 8's, so search the band between them and nothing else.
teaching.watch_out: Two statements name somebody the notice never names — who pays a fee, and who usually wins. A rule that applies to everybody says nothing about any one of them.

questions.prompt: A landlord has thirty days from the start of the tenancy to pay a deposit into the scheme.
questions.evidence_quote: must be paid into the Norland Deposit Protection Scheme within thirty days of the tenancy starting
questions.explanation: The notice sets a deadline of thirty days measured from the day the tenancy starts, which is exactly the window the statement describes.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: thirty days from the start of the tenancy
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: within thirty days of the tenancy starting
paraphrase_link.note: The verb 'starting' becomes the noun 'the start', and the deadline itself is unchanged.

teaching.decision_rule: Every element of the statement — the actor, the period and the event it counts from — is stated in one clause. Nothing is added and nothing is contradicted, so TRUE.

distractors.why_tempting: The same sentence carries the words 'six months or more', and a reader who mixes the two numbers decides one of them must be wrong.
distractors.why_wrong: Six months describes which tenancies the rule covers; thirty days is the deadline. They are different facts in the same sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: The notice never uses the word 'deadline', so a reader hunting for it finds nothing and calls the point unaddressed.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Within thirty days' is a deadline written out in full.

teaching.reusable_rule: One sentence can carry two numbers doing two different jobs. Name the job before you compare the figures.

questions.prompt: A landlord who rents out a room in the house where they live must use the scheme.
questions.evidence_quote: Landlords who let rooms in their own home are outside the scheme
questions.explanation: The notice places resident landlords outside the scheme. Being outside the scheme is incompatible with being required to use it, so the statement is contradicted.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the exception arrives in the last sentence of the paragraph, after three sentences that all say 'must'.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: rents out a room in the house where they live
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: let rooms in their own home
paraphrase_link.note: 'Their own home' is compressed from the statement's relative clause; the people described are the same people.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the notice states the opposite obligation: the class of landlord in the statement is expressly excluded. A contradiction on the page makes it FALSE, not NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens with 'every deposit ... must be paid into' the scheme, and a reader who stops at the rule never reaches the exception.
distractors.why_wrong: The final sentence removes this landlord from the rule. TRUE requires the whole statement to survive the paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: The phrase 'in the house where they live' appears nowhere, so a keyword search returns nothing.
distractors.why_wrong: The same class of landlord is described in different words in the last sentence, and it is described as being outside the scheme.

teaching.reusable_rule: Read to the end of the paragraph before accepting a rule. Exceptions are placed last because that is where they are missed.

questions.prompt: A landlord who is not obliged to use the scheme must pay a fee in order to join it.
questions.evidence_quote: and so are lets of less than six months, although a landlord may join voluntarily in either case
questions.explanation: The notice confirms that an exempt landlord may join if they wish, and stops there. Whether joining costs anything is never mentioned, in this paragraph or anywhere else.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the sentence answers half the statement, so the silence on the other half feels like a refusal.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: not obliged to use the scheme
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a landlord may join voluntarily
paraphrase_link.note: 'Voluntarily' and 'not obliged' are the same idea; the fee is the part with no partner in the text.

teaching.decision_rule: The exemption is stated and the option to join is stated. The cost of joining is neither stated nor denied, so neither TRUE nor FALSE can be argued from the page.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement reads like the natural next line of the paragraph, and a scheme that holds money plausibly charges for it.
distractors.why_wrong: That is a guess about how schemes usually work. The notice mentions no fee of any kind.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'voluntarily' suggests something freely available, and free is easily read as free of charge.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Voluntarily' describes the choice, not the price. No sentence denies that a fee exists.

teaching.reusable_rule: A sentence that answers half a statement is not evidence about the other half. Ask which words are still unpartnered.
teaching.nearest_text: a landlord may join voluntarily in either case

questions.prompt: A tenant who has had no confirmation after thirty days should contact the landlord before contacting the scheme.
questions.evidence_quote: write to the landlord first: the scheme cannot act until the landlord has been asked directly
questions.explanation: The notice gives the order of steps explicitly and then gives the reason for it: the scheme has no power to act until the landlord has been approached.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: contact the landlord before contacting the scheme
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: write to the landlord first
paraphrase_link.note: 'First' encodes the order that the statement spells out with 'before'.

teaching.decision_rule: The sequence in the statement matches the sequence in the notice, and the following clause explains why no other sequence is possible. Nothing is left over.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about the landlord's duty to send confirmation, so a reader expects the remedy to be aimed at the scheme.
distractors.why_wrong: The remedy sentence names the landlord as the first point of contact, which is what the statement says.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement uses 'contact' twice and the notice uses 'write' and 'asked', so nothing matches on the surface.
distractors.why_wrong: Writing to somebody is contacting them, and the order is stated in the same clause.

teaching.reusable_rule: Sequence markers carry whole marks. Read them as content rather than as glue between clauses.

questions.prompt: Wear caused by ordinary use may be deducted from the deposit if the landlord provides evidence.
questions.evidence_quote: Fair wear and tear is never a valid deduction.
questions.explanation: The notice rules out this deduction absolutely. 'Never' admits no exception, so no amount of evidence from the landlord can make it valid.
questions.trap_note: The sentence before it lists three deductions the landlord may propose, and a reader who stops there has three reasons to answer TRUE.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Fair wear and tear
paraphrase_link.note: The statement replaces the fixed legal phrase with its everyday meaning.

teaching.decision_rule: The notice states the topic and denies it without qualification. A statement that adds a condition under which it would be allowed is contradicted by a sentence containing 'never'.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous sentence expressly allows deductions for damage, and ordinary wear looks like mild damage.
distractors.why_wrong: The notice separates the two and forbids one of them by name in the very next sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement's condition — 'if the landlord provides evidence' — is nowhere in the notice, so the whole statement feels unaddressed.
distractors.why_wrong: An absolute prohibition disposes of every condition attached to it. The denial is on the page.

teaching.reusable_rule: An absolute word in the text defeats any condition added by the statement. Find the absolute before you weigh the condition.

questions.prompt: Most disputes referred to the scheme are decided in the tenant's favour.
questions.evidence_quote: either side may ask the scheme for a free adjudication
questions.explanation: The notice explains who may ask for an adjudication and what happens to the money meanwhile. It gives no outcomes at all, so no proportion can be checked.
questions.trap_note: Invented comparison: 'either side' tells you both parties can apply and tells you nothing about which of them wins.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph describes a procedure, not a set of results. A statement about how often one party succeeds needs figures the notice does not contain, so it can be neither confirmed nor denied.

distractors.why_tempting: The whole notice is written to protect tenants, so its tone suggests tenants usually do well out of it.
distractors.why_wrong: Tone is not evidence. No sentence reports the result of any adjudication.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Either side may ask' sounds even-handed, and even-handed reads as a denial that one side wins more often.
distractors.why_wrong: Who may apply and who tends to succeed are different facts. The second is absent, not denied.

teaching.reusable_rule: A description of a procedure is not a report of its results. If no outcome is on the page, no proportion can be judged.
teaching.nearest_text: until the adjudicator has decided

question_groups.instructions_extra: Answer the questions below using words taken from the information sheet on registering with a doctor.

teaching.strategy: The sheet is two short paragraphs, so location is not the difficulty here; form is. Decide from the question word what shape the answer must be — a document, a length of time, a set of digits — and copy it out of the sentence without adding an article or a unit of your own.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, and the three answers sit in three consecutive sentences. Once you have found the first, read on rather than back.
teaching.watch_out: Three words is the ceiling, not the target. Adding 'the' or writing 'one week' instead of the sheet's own phrase costs the mark outright.

questions.prompt: What must you take to the practice as evidence of where you live?
questions.evidence_quote: Take proof of address
questions.explanation: The sheet names two things to bring, one of them optional. The item that shows where you live is proof of address; the letter from a previous doctor is not about your home.
questions.trap_note: The same sentence offers 'a letter from your previous doctor', which is the wrong span and is also conditional.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: proof of address
paraphrase_link.note: 'Address' is compressed from the question's whole clause, and 'proof' answers 'evidence'.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks which document does one specific job. Two documents are listed; only one of them is about a place of residence.

distractors.why_tempting: It sits in the same sentence and is the only other thing the sheet tells you to bring.
distractors.why_wrong: It comes from a doctor and is required only if you have one; it says nothing about where you live.

distractors.why_tempting: Adding the article makes the answer read like a sentence rather than a label.
distractors.why_wrong: Articles count towards the limit and are not in the text at that point.

teaching.reusable_rule: Copy the span, not a sentence built round it. An article you supply yourself is an extra word.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What must you take' wants a noun phrase naming an object, with no verb and no article.

questions.prompt: How long does registration normally take?
questions.evidence_quote: Registration takes about a week.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph opens with the answer. The hedge 'about' belongs to the phrase and should be copied with it, since the question asks what normally happens.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Registration takes about a week
paraphrase_link.note: The statement is turned into a question and 'normally' picks up the hedge the sentence already carries.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks for a duration, so the answer must contain a unit of time. Only one phrase in either paragraph does.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other length of time on the sheet and it appears first.
distractors.why_wrong: Three months is how long you must have lived in the area, not how long registering takes.

distractors.why_tempting: It means the same thing and feels tidier than copying a hedge.
distractors.why_wrong: It is not what the sheet says, and a completion answer is copied rather than rewritten.

teaching.reusable_rule: A hedge inside the span is part of the span. Rewriting it into something neater is still rewriting.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'How long' wants a period of time, so the answer must carry its own unit.

questions.prompt: Which number should you ring for medical help at two in the morning?
questions.evidence_quote: is reached on 0800 555 118
questions.explanation: Two in the morning falls inside the stated window of six in the evening to eight the next morning, so the out-of-hours line is the one to ring.
questions.trap_note: The sheet says the service is separate from your own practice, so the answer is not a number you would already have.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: medical help at two in the morning
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: from six in the evening until eight the next morning
paraphrase_link.note: The question gives one time and the sheet gives a window; you have to place the one inside the other.

teaching.decision_rule: The question fixes a time of day, and only one service on the sheet is described as covering it. The number attached to that service is the answer.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other piece of advice about being seen before registration is complete.
distractors.why_wrong: It names a status, not a number, and the question asks for a number.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader in a hurry copies the first group of digits and treats the rest as a suffix.
distractors.why_wrong: The whole string is the number as printed, and a partial copy will not match.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a question gives a time and the text gives a window, the work is placing one inside the other before you copy anything.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Which number' wants the digits exactly as printed, with nothing added before or after.

texts.heading: Reporting an accident or a near miss

paragraphs.text: Every injury that happens at work must be reported, however slight it appears at the time. A near miss — an event that could have caused an injury but did not — must be reported in the same way. The purpose of the system is not to allocate blame. The site record is used to find patterns, and a pattern only becomes visible once the small events are on it. Staff who report a near miss are never penalised for doing so, and supervisors are reminded of this at every team briefing. Contractors working on site follow the same procedure as employees.

If someone is hurt, the first step is to call a first-aider. A list of the trained first-aiders on each shift is displayed beside every fire point and is also kept on the intranet. Do not move an injured person unless leaving them where they are would put them in further danger. Once the first-aider has taken over, the person who found the casualty should tell the duty supervisor what happened, in their own words and as soon as they reasonably can. A short spoken account is enough at this stage; there is no form to complete.

The supervisor then enters the event in the accident book within twenty-four hours. An entry must be made even where the injured person has already gone home, and it is written by the supervisor rather than by the injured person, so that the record does not depend on the memory of somebody who may be unwell. A copy of every entry is sent to the safety officer in the same week, and the book itself is kept in the gatehouse for three years.

An injury that keeps an employee away from work for more than seven days is reportable to the external authority, and it is the safety officer who makes that report. Any serious injury is examined by a review panel of three people, which must include one member who does not work in the department concerned. The panel's findings go to the site manager, who decides what changes are made and by when. Employees may ask to see the findings, and the request is not refused. The site manager reports to the board once a year on what has changed as a result.

texts.heading: Your annual performance review

paragraphs.text: Every member of staff who has been employed for more than six months takes part in an annual review. The review is held between the employee and their line manager, and the date is set by the manager at least three weeks in advance so that both sides have time to prepare. Staff on a fixed-term contract of less than a year are reviewed once, at the midpoint of the contract, instead of annually. The review is not a disciplinary meeting, and no record of it is placed on a personal file without the employee's knowledge. A review missed because of long-term absence is held within a month of the employee's return. Managers are given a half-day of training before their first review.

Preparation is shared. The employee completes a self-assessment form, which is returned to the manager five working days before the meeting; the manager meanwhile collects comments from two colleagues the employee has worked with during the year. The employee chooses one of those colleagues and the manager chooses the other. Comments are summarised rather than quoted, and the names of the people who gave them are not disclosed at the meeting. An employee who would rather no comments were sought may say so, and the manager will proceed without them.

The meeting itself has three parts: a look back at the objectives agreed last year, a discussion of any training that would help in the year ahead, and the setting of new objectives. Objectives are written down during the meeting and both parties keep a copy. There is no rating scale and no score. The company removed the scale in 2019 after staff reported that the number was remembered and the conversation was not, and no request to bring it back has since been made.

A summary is written by the manager within ten working days and sent to the employee, who may add a written comment of any length before the summary is filed. Where the employee disagrees with the summary and the disagreement cannot be settled between them, either party may ask the head of department to attend a second and shorter meeting. Pay is decided separately, in the spring, and is not discussed at the review at all. Copies of every summary are destroyed after six years.

difficulty_rationale.note: Two institutional documents in which almost every sentence carries a deadline, an exception or a named role. The vocabulary is bureaucratic rather than technical, and the same roles recur doing different jobs.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Four different actors appear in five clauses, and two of them choose the same kind of thing for different reasons.

skim_plan.read_first: The two headings and the first sentence of each paragraph. That tells you which document is a chain of steps and which is a set of entitlements.
skim_plan.skip: The reasons given for each rule. Sentences beginning 'so that' explain policy and are rarely the answer to a completion gap.
fields: who does what at each step
deadlines counted in days or weeks
must, may and is advised to

rewordings: is to be notified without delay
will not be held against them
steps in to manage the situation
is not brought to a close

hinge_words.why_here: It reverses the instruction that decides question 21.
'must include one member' is the obligation behind question 23.
It fixes who writes the entry that question 17 asks you to name.
It sets the notice period on the line that carries question 24.
It separates two preparation tasks whose deadlines question 25 keeps apart.

mineable.meaning: an event that almost caused harm
the manager in charge on that shift
must formally be notified to
no later than three weeks beforehand
a form on which you judge your own work
are not made known to others
agreed by the two people involved

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the flow chart below using words taken from the accident reporting procedure.

layout.title: After an injury on site
steps: Somebody is hurt at work.
A {{15}} is called; the names are displayed beside every fire point.
The person who found the casualty tells the {{16}} what happened.
The event is entered in the {{17}} within twenty-four hours.
A copy of the entry goes to the {{18}} in the same week.

teaching.strategy: Every box comes from two paragraphs, so find the sentence that starts 'If someone is hurt' and work downwards from there. Read the whole chain before you fill anything in: the four gaps are four different people or objects, and the procedure names each of them exactly once.
teaching.order_note: All four answers sit in one stretch of the text. Locate that stretch once, then work inside it rather than searching the whole document.
teaching.watch_out: A box wants the thing that goes in at that step, not the result of it. The supervisor appears in three sentences; only one of them is the moment the chart is describing.

questions.prompt: A {{gap}} is called; the names are displayed beside every fire point.
questions.evidence_quote: the first step is to call a first-aider
questions.explanation: The procedure makes calling a first-aider the first action after somebody is hurt, and the next sentence explains where the list of names is kept.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the first step is to call
paraphrase_link.note: The active instruction becomes a passive in the chart, and the person doing the calling disappears.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits before 'is called' and after the article 'A', so it needs a singular countable noun naming a person. Only one such noun is attached to the first step.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest noun phrase in the chart's own line and it appears in the same passage sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: A fire point is a place where the list hangs, and a place cannot be called.

distractors.why_tempting: The supervisor is the most prominent role in the whole procedure.
distractors.why_wrong: The supervisor is told later, at the next step; the chart is asking what happens first.

teaching.reusable_rule: In a numbered chain, fix which stage a box belongs to before you choose the noun that fills it.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'A' before the gap and 'is called' after it force a singular noun naming a person.

questions.prompt: The person who found the casualty tells the {{gap}} what happened.
questions.evidence_quote: should tell the duty supervisor what happened
questions.explanation: Once the first-aider has taken charge, the finder reports verbally to the duty supervisor. The procedure names that role in full.
questions.trap_note: The role is named twice in the document, once as 'the duty supervisor' and once simply as 'The supervisor'. The chart wants the form used at this step.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The person who found the casualty tells
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the person who found the casualty should tell
paraphrase_link.note: The chart drops the modal and states the step as a fact, which is normal in a flow chart.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows a definite article and precedes an object clause, so it names the person who receives the report. The procedure gives that person a two-word title at this point.

distractors.why_tempting: The first-aider is in the same sentence and has just taken over the casualty.
distractors.why_wrong: The first-aider is treating the injury; the account of what happened goes to the supervisor.

distractors.why_tempting: The safety officer receives paperwork later, and readers who scan for 'sent to' land there.
distractors.why_wrong: That is two steps further down the chart, and it is a copy of the written entry rather than a spoken account.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where several people appear in one chain, fix who receives the information at this step before you choose a title.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'The' before the gap wants the title exactly as the text gives it, both words included.

questions.prompt: The event is entered in the {{gap}} within twenty-four hours.
questions.evidence_quote: enters the event in the accident book within twenty-four hours
questions.explanation: The written record is made in the accident book, by the supervisor, inside a day. The chart reuses the procedure's own frame around the gap.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: enters the event in the
paraphrase_link.note: The chart turns the verb into a passive so that the supervisor need not be named again.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'in the' and precedes a time limit, so it names the place a written record is kept. The procedure names one such object.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other place named in the same paragraph and it is where the record physically lives.
distractors.why_wrong: The gatehouse is where the book is stored afterwards; the entry is made in the book itself.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other place information is kept and it appears earlier in the procedure.
distractors.why_wrong: The intranet holds the list of first-aiders, not the record of the event.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a thing is made and where it is later stored are two facts. The frame round the gap tells you which one is wanted.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'In the' before the gap wants a noun naming a thing, not a place or a person.

questions.prompt: A copy of the entry goes to the {{gap}} in the same week.
questions.evidence_quote: A copy of every entry is sent to the safety officer in the same week
questions.explanation: The last step in the chain sends a copy of the written entry to the safety officer within the same week.
questions.trap_note: The safety officer appears again in the next paragraph doing something else entirely, which is where a scanner tends to stop.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: A copy of the entry goes to
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A copy of every entry is sent to
paraphrase_link.note: 'Is sent to' becomes 'goes to', which removes the sender and shortens the box.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'goes to the' and precedes a time phrase, so it names the recipient of a document. Only one role is described as receiving a copy.

distractors.why_tempting: The site manager is the most senior person named and receives findings later in the document.
distractors.why_wrong: What the site manager receives is a panel's findings after a serious injury, not a copy of every entry.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other body outside the immediate chain, and reports do go to it.
distractors.why_wrong: That report is made only for absences of more than seven days, and it is a different document.

teaching.reusable_rule: A role that appears three times is doing three jobs. Match the job in the box, not the title.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'To the' before the gap wants the title of a person or office, in the singular.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete each sentence with words taken from the accident reporting procedure.

title: The last of the drove roads

passage_json.title: The last of the drove roads

texts.heading: The last of the drove roads

paragraphs.text: Above the village of Kilnbrae a green track leaves the road and climbs the hillside at an angle no modern engineer would choose. It is wide — in places forty paces across — and it is grassed over, though nothing grows on it that grows in the fields on either side. Walkers who follow it usually take it for an old farm lane. It is in fact a drove road, one of a network of routes along which cattle were walked from the northern glens to the markets of the lowland towns. For roughly two hundred years these tracks carried more traffic than any other route in the district, and then, within a single generation, they carried none at all. No herd has walked along it for well over a hundred years.

The trade existed because the cattle could not be brought to market any other way. A beast raised in the hills was worth two or three times as much in a lowland market as it was at home, but the distance was too great for a cart and the animal had to walk there on its own legs. Droving turned that necessity into a profession. A drover took charge of a herd he did not own, agreed a price for delivering it, and was answerable for every animal on the way. He was, in effect, a carrier whose vehicle walked. A drover who lost a beast made good the loss himself.

The routes themselves were chosen by the animals as much as by the men. Cattle travel best on soft ground, and a herd driven on stone loses condition within a day, so the drove roads avoided the hard turnpikes wherever they could and kept to grass, gravel and heather. Width mattered too. A herd of two hundred beasts moving at its own pace spreads out, and a track that narrowed forced the animals into single file and slowed everything behind them. Where a drove road crossed enclosed farmland the landowners were often paid for the right of passage, and the width was written into the agreement.

The working day was short by the standards of the time. A herd covered between ten and twelve miles between dawn and mid-afternoon, and then stopped, because cattle that walk into the evening arrive thin and sell badly. The stopping places were as much a part of the system as the road itself. A stance was a field of rough grazing beside the track, rented by the night, with water and a wall to hold the herd. Stances were spaced a day apart, and their positions, more than any map, determined where the route ran.

Around the stances a small economy grew up. Inns at the larger stances sold meal and ale to the drovers and stabled the ponies of the dealers who rode out from the towns to buy before a herd reached the market. Blacksmiths did steady work, because cattle on a long journey were shod, each hoof taking two small iron plates, and a shoe thrown on the hill had to be replaced before the animal went lame. Some smiths worked only in the droving season and farmed for the rest of the year. A few of the inns survive; almost none of the smithies do.

The end came quickly and it came from the railway. The first line to reach the northern markets opened in the 1860s, and within fifteen years the number of cattle walked south had fallen by more than four-fifths. A beast carried by train arrived in two days rather than three weeks, arrived heavier, and could be sold in a market the drover had never been able to reach. The drovers themselves did not object as often as might be expected; many took work loading the wagons, and a few became dealers on their own account. What disappeared was not the trade but the walking.

For most of the following century the roads were simply forgotten. They were not maintained, because nobody was responsible for them, and they were not built on, because they ran across ground nobody wanted. That neglect preserved them. A drove road is now one of the few places in the district where the surface has not been disturbed since the last herd passed, and botanists value the strips of grassland along them for plants that have vanished from the improved fields around. The turf, cropped for two centuries by passing cattle and then left alone, is unlike anything on either side of it.

Their second life began in the 1970s, when walkers' groups set out to map and signpost them. The legal position was awkward: a right of way for cattle is not automatically a right of way for people, and several sections had to be negotiated field by field. The work is not finished. Roughly a third of the network in the Verdon hills is now waymarked, another third is walkable but unmarked, and the remainder is under crops or lost beneath a modern road. The signposts carry a small black-and-white symbol of a cow, which is the only thing on the hill that says what the track was for.

difficulty_rationale.note: A descriptive history in which cause and effect are placed side by side without connectives. Four paragraphs state a fact, then a consequence, then a qualification, and none of them signals the shift.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It reports a collapse and then withdraws the reaction a reader expects, so the last two sentences reverse the mood of the first three.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and the whole of paragraph A. It tells you the passage is about a route that stopped being used, not about cattle.
skim_plan.skip: The list of surfaces in paragraph C and the list of businesses in paragraph E. Both are detail the questions will send you back to.

It shares the credit for the route between animals and men, which decides question 29.
It carries the comparison of journey times that question 34 turns on.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct heading for each of paragraphs B–F from the list of headings below. There are more headings than paragraphs, so you will not use them all.

options.text: Ground chosen to suit the animals
A short day and its halting places
A necessity that became a trade
Trades that grew beside the road
Rules that varied between counties
How the walking trade ended
Neglect that turned into protection
The cost of feeding a herd

teaching.strategy: Four of these five paragraphs state their whole point in the first sentence, so read those five openings first and write the job of each paragraph in six words before you look at the list. Place B and F first: both open with an explicit claim, and each one you place removes a heading from the field.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, so nothing bounds the search. Every one of the five paragraphs has to be read, but only their first and last sentences at this stage.
teaching.watch_out: Three of the headings name something that genuinely appears in one of these paragraphs but is not what the paragraph is doing. Mentioning is not the same as being about.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence_quote: The trade existed because the cattle could not be brought to market any other way
questions.explanation: Paragraph B answers one question: why was there a trade at all? Its answer is that there was no alternative to walking, and that this necessity was turned into a paid occupation with its own responsibilities.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph carries figures about value, but they explain why the journey was worth making, not what the journey cost.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: A necessity that became a trade
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: could not be brought to market any other way
paraphrase_link.note: 'No other way' becomes the noun 'necessity', and the second half of the paragraph supplies 'trade'.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph moves from an impossibility to an occupation in five sentences. A heading has to carry both halves; every other candidate carries neither or only a detail.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is full of money: what a beast was worth at home and what it fetched at market.
distractors.why_wrong: Those figures are the value of the animal, not the expense of keeping it fed on the road.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends on the animal having to walk, and walking suggests the surface it walked on.
distractors.why_wrong: What the herds walked on is the subject of the following paragraph and is not raised here at all.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph explains why something had to exist, the heading names the reason, not the figures inside it.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence_quote: Cattle travel best on soft ground, and a herd driven on stone loses condition within a day
questions.explanation: Every sentence in paragraph C explains a feature of the route by reference to the animals: soft going because stone costs condition, width because a herd spreads out. The opening sentence says so directly.
questions.trap_note: The final sentence brings in landowners and agreements, which is the only place regulation appears, and it is one clause of five sentences.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Ground chosen to suit the animals
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: chosen by the animals as much as by the men
paraphrase_link.note: The passage's shared credit becomes a heading that names only the animals, because they are what decides the surface.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph gives two features of the route and one cause for each, and both causes are the cattle. A heading naming any other agent contradicts the structure.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph closes on payments to landowners and terms written into an agreement, which read like local regulation.
distractors.why_wrong: Those are private arrangements about width, and no county or rule-making body appears anywhere in the passage.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about how herds moved, and a reader who has not yet read the next one takes the first movement heading available.
distractors.why_wrong: The length of the working day and the places herds stopped are the next paragraph's subject; this one is about the surface and the width.

teaching.reusable_rule: If every sentence explains a feature by the same cause, the heading names that cause.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence_quote: A herd covered between ten and twelve miles between dawn and mid-afternoon, and then stopped
questions.explanation: Paragraph D describes a working day that ended early and then defines the stance, the nightly halt that made such a day possible and that fixed where the route went.
questions.trap_note: A stance is rented and offers grazing, which sounds commercial, but the paragraph gives no price and describes no business.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: A short day and its halting places
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: between dawn and mid-afternoon, and then stopped
paraphrase_link.note: A clause about hours becomes the adjective 'short', and the stances become 'halting places'.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph pairs one fact about time with one about place, and its last sentence says the places determined the route. A heading naming only one half leaves the other unexplained.

distractors.why_tempting: The stance is rented from somebody, so a business appears to be starting here.
distractors.why_wrong: The trades that grew round the stances are the subject of the following paragraph; here the stance is only defined.

distractors.why_tempting: A stance is a field of grazing rented by the night, which reads as paying to feed the herd.
distractors.why_wrong: The rent is for the ground, and no figure for feeding anything appears in the passage.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that pairs a fact about time with a fact about place needs a heading holding both.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence_quote: Around the stances a small economy grew up.
questions.explanation: The paragraph opens by naming what it will describe and then gives three examples of it: innkeepers, dealers who rode out to buy early, and blacksmiths who worked the droving season.
questions.trap_note: Meal and ale are sold here, but to the drovers rather than to the herd, and no price is attached to either.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Trades that grew beside the road
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a small economy grew up
paraphrase_link.note: The heading names the instances the paragraph gives; the passage names the category they belong to.

teaching.decision_rule: Every sentence after the first names an occupation and what it earned from the herds. Only a heading about occupations survives that test.

distractors.why_tempting: The first business named sells 'meal and ale', and meal reads as feed.
distractors.why_wrong: It is sold to the men, and the paragraph gives no cost for provisioning a herd.

distractors.why_tempting: The stances are named again in the opening line, so a reader still holding that heading will place it where the word recurs.
distractors.why_wrong: The stances here are a location for other people's businesses; the day and the halts belong to the paragraph before.

teaching.reusable_rule: When the same noun opens two paragraphs, the heading belongs to the one where it is the subject rather than the setting.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence_quote: The end came quickly and it came from the railway.
questions.explanation: Paragraph F states the cause of the collapse in its first sentence, dates it, measures it, and closes by distinguishing what ended from what did not: the walking stopped, the trade did not.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph is about disappearance, but the disappearance it describes is of a method, and its consequences are described in the paragraph after.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The end came quickly and it came from the railway
paraphrase_link.note: The heading turns the paragraph's opening claim into a question the paragraph then answers.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph names a cause, gives the speed and scale of the effect, and rules out one obvious reaction. A heading naming what happened afterwards would describe the next paragraph instead.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about something vanishing, and vanishing and neglect feel like one story.
distractors.why_wrong: What was neglected, and what that neglect preserved, is the subject of the paragraph that follows this one.

distractors.why_tempting: It mentions a market the drover had never been able to reach, which suggests boundaries and permissions.
distractors.why_wrong: The barrier was distance, and no rule of any kind is named in the paragraph.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph about a cause and a paragraph about its aftermath need different headings, however alike their mood.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete each sentence with the correct ending, A–F. There are more endings than sentences.

options.text: animals that keep walking into the evening fetch a lower price.
they arrived in better condition than those that had walked.
nobody had any reason to build on them or repair them.
the landowners were paid for allowing the herds to pass.
the smiths who shod the cattle worked only part of the year.

teaching.strategy: Read the three beginnings first and decide what each one demands: two want a reason and one wants a consequence. Then read the endings for that, not for truth. Four of these six endings are accurate statements about the passage, so accuracy will not separate them.
teaching.order_note: This is the one matching type whose answers run in passage order, which most candidates do not know. Question 35's evidence is below question 34's.
teaching.watch_out: Three endings are true of the passage and complete none of these three beginnings. Test the join, not the fact.

questions.prompt: Herds were halted in the early afternoon because
questions.evidence_quote: cattle that walk into the evening arrive thin and sell badly
questions.explanation: The passage gives the reason for the early stop in the same sentence as the stop itself: animals that keep going into the evening lose weight and fetch less at the market.
questions.trap_note: The stances are the mechanism that made an early stop possible; they are not the reason for it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: arrive thin and sell badly
paraphrase_link.note: 'Sell badly' is restated as the price obtained, which is the form a question is usually written in.

teaching.decision_rule: The beginning ends in 'because', so only a cause can complete it, and the passage supplies exactly one cause for stopping early.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a true statement about drove roads and follows 'because' perfectly well grammatically.
distractors.why_wrong: Payments to landowners explain the width of a track, not the hour at which a herd stopped.

distractors.why_tempting: It is also true and also concerns the daily working life of the trade.
distractors.why_wrong: The smiths' seasonal work has no bearing on when herds were halted, and it completes a different idea altogether.

teaching.reusable_rule: After 'because' only a cause fits. Test whether the ending explains the beginning, not whether it is true.

questions.prompt: Cattle carried by train took two days rather than three weeks, and as a result
questions.evidence_quote: arrived in two days rather than three weeks, arrived heavier
questions.explanation: The passage places the shorter journey and the heavier animal in the same sentence, so the weight is presented as the consequence of the speed rather than as a separate fact.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: in better condition than those that had walked
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: arrived heavier
paraphrase_link.note: One comparative adjective becomes a full comparison, with the walked animals supplied as the standard.

teaching.decision_rule: The beginning ends in 'as a result', so the ending must be an effect of the shorter journey. Only one ending describes a change in the animals themselves.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a true statement and it follows 'as a result' smoothly, because negotiation does sound like a consequence of something.
distractors.why_wrong: The negotiations belong to the revival of the paths a century later and have nothing to do with rail transport.

distractors.why_tempting: The seasonal work of the smiths did end with the trade, so it reads as a consequence.
distractors.why_wrong: It describes how the smiths worked while droving continued, and it is not what the shorter journey produced.

teaching.reusable_rule: An ending can be true, grammatical and still wrong. Check that the event it names happened at the time the beginning describes.

questions.prompt: The drove roads came through the twentieth century intact largely because
questions.evidence_quote: They were not maintained, because nobody was responsible for them, and they were not built on, because they ran across ground nobody wanted.
questions.explanation: The passage gives two reasons for the roads' survival, and both are absences: nobody was responsible for repairing them, and nobody wanted the land they crossed.
questions.trap_note: The waymarking of the 1970s is what made them usable again; it is not what kept them intact through the years before.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: nobody had any reason to build on them
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: they ran across ground nobody wanted
paraphrase_link.note: The passage explains no building by no demand; the ending calls it a missing motive.

teaching.decision_rule: The beginning ends in 'because' and asks about survival through a century of neglect. Only an ending describing an absence of interest matches the two reasons the passage supplies.

distractors.why_tempting: It names the one organised effort the passage describes, and effort feels like the obvious cause of survival.
distractors.why_wrong: The negotiations came after the century of neglect and were about access for people, not about the tracks lasting.

distractors.why_tempting: Payments to landowners suggest a legal status that might have protected the routes.
distractors.why_wrong: Those payments belong to the droving period and secured a right of passage, not protection from development.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a text explains survival by two absences, an ending naming an activity cannot be the completion.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Answer the questions below using words taken from the passage.

teaching.strategy: These five run from the first paragraph to the last, one answer roughly every second paragraph, so treat them as a sweep rather than five separate searches. Each question word fixes the shape of the answer before you look: a period, a measurement, a figure, a group of people, an animal.
teaching.order_note: In passage order. Question 39's answer is below question 38's, which brackets the search into two paragraphs at a time.
teaching.watch_out: Two of these answers are two words in the passage and one word in most people's heads. Copy what is printed rather than what you would say.

questions.prompt: For approximately how long did the drove roads carry more traffic than any other local route?
questions.evidence_quote: For roughly two hundred years these tracks carried more traffic than any other route in the district
questions.explanation: The first paragraph closes by giving the period of the roads' dominance and then the speed of its end. The period is stated as roughly two centuries.
questions.trap_note: The same paragraph gives a width in paces and the last paragraph gives a decade. Neither answers a question about duration.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: carry more traffic than any other local route
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: carried more traffic than any other route in the district
paraphrase_link.note: 'In the district' becomes the adjective 'local', which is the only change made.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks for a duration, so the answer must contain a unit of time. One phrase in the paragraph does, and the question's 'approximately' matches the hedge attached to it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's other measurement and stands out because it is unusual.
distractors.why_wrong: Paces measure the width of the track, not the length of a period.

distractors.why_tempting: It sits in the same sentence and is also a period of time.
distractors.why_wrong: That is how long the collapse took, not how long the roads were busy.

teaching.reusable_rule: When one sentence holds two periods, decide which event each belongs to before you copy either.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'How long' wants a period, so the answer must carry its own unit of time.

questions.prompt: What detail of a drove road was recorded in agreements with landowners?
questions.evidence_quote: the width was written into the agreement
questions.explanation: Where a route crossed enclosed land, the landowner was paid and the dimension that mattered to the herd was fixed in writing. The passage names that dimension as the width.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph spends three sentences on the surface, so a reader scanning for what was agreed often stops at 'grass, gravel and heather'.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: written into the agreement
paraphrase_link.note: 'Written into' becomes 'recorded in', and the landowner moves from subject to modifier.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks what appeared in a document, so the answer is the noun that is the subject of the passive verb about writing.

distractors.why_tempting: It is what the payment bought and sits in the same sentence just before the answer.
distractors.why_wrong: That is what the landowner sold; the question asks what detail was set down, and the passage attaches the writing to a dimension.

distractors.why_tempting: The surface is the paragraph's dominant theme and appears three times.
distractors.why_wrong: No agreement is mentioned in connection with the surface.

teaching.reusable_rule: Find the verb the question is really about, then take the noun that verb governs.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What detail' wants a noun phrase, and the passage gives it with its article.

questions.prompt: How many iron plates were fitted to each hoof?
questions.evidence_quote: each hoof taking two small iron plates
questions.explanation: Cattle on a long journey were shod, and the passage gives the number of plates per hoof rather than per animal.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: iron plates were fitted to each hoof
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: each hoof taking two small iron plates
paraphrase_link.note: The participle clause becomes a passive, and the number moves to the front of the question.

teaching.decision_rule: 'How many' wants a figure, and only one figure in the paragraph is counted per hoof rather than per animal or per year.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the passage's most prominent number and is also attached to animals.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the size of a herd, in a different paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: Copying the whole phrase feels safer than copying one word.
distractors.why_wrong: The question already supplies 'iron plates', and the answer is over the limit once the adjective is included.

teaching.reusable_rule: When the question already contains the noun, the answer is only what the question is missing.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'How many' wants a bare number, with no noun after it.

questions.prompt: Which specialists place a value on the grassland along the old routes?
questions.evidence_quote: botanists value the strips of grassland along them for plants that have vanished
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains that an undisturbed surface has preserved plants lost from the farmland around, and names botanists as the people who value the strips for that reason.
questions.trap_note: Walkers' groups appear in the following paragraph and also take an interest in the routes, but for access rather than for plants.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: place a value on the grassland
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: value the strips of grassland
paraphrase_link.note: The verb becomes a noun phrase in the question, so a search for the verb alone will miss the sentence.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks who holds a view, so the answer is the subject of the verb of valuing. The paragraph supplies exactly one such subject.

distractors.why_tempting: They are the only other named group with an interest in the routes and they appear soon afterwards.
distractors.why_wrong: Their interest is in mapping and access, and it belongs to the last paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest plural noun to the phrase about grassland.
distractors.why_wrong: Plants are the reason for the valuing, not the people doing it.

teaching.reusable_rule: A question asking who values something wants the subject of that verb, not the reason attached to it.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Which specialists' wants a plural noun naming a profession.

questions.prompt: What animal appears on the modern signposts?
questions.evidence_quote: a small black-and-white symbol of a cow
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the passage describes the waymarking symbol, and the passage ends by noting that it is the only sign on the hill of what the route was for.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The signposts carry a small black-and-white symbol
paraphrase_link.note: 'Carry' becomes 'appears on', which reverses subject and object between text and question.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks for an animal, and only one animal is named anywhere in the final paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the word the passage uses everywhere else for the same animals.
distractors.why_wrong: The symbol is described in the singular and with its own article; the answer is copied from that phrase.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the fullest description of the thing on the sign.
distractors.why_wrong: The question asks which animal, so the colours are not part of the answer.

teaching.reusable_rule: Copy the phrase the text uses at that point, not the word the text uses elsewhere for the same thing.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What animal' wants a singular noun, and the text gives it with its article.

texts.heading: Local services in the Sandmouth directory

paragraphs.text: Kestrel Plumbing. Emergency call-outs across Sandmouth and the villages within eight miles. £45 for the first hour, then £30 an hour after that. There is no call-out charge between nine and five on weekdays. All work is guaranteed for twelve months. Bookings are taken by telephone only; the answering service records messages overnight and a plumber calls back before eight in the morning.

Sandmouth Locks. Locksmith, established 1994. Doors opened, locks changed, keys cut while you wait. £60 for an emergency door opening at any hour, including Sundays. Proof that you live at the address is required before any lock is opened. The workshop on Fore Street is open six days a week; there is nobody there on Wednesdays.

Green Ends Garden. Lawns, hedges and general tidying, March to October. £22 an hour with a two-hour minimum, or £180 for a full day. Green waste is taken away at no extra charge. We do not undertake tree surgery. New customers are visited once before any work is quoted, and that first visit is free.

Ivy Hill Tutoring. Mathematics and physics for students aged eleven to eighteen. £28 an hour in your own home, £24 at our room above the library. Lessons are booked in blocks of six and paid for in advance. A block may be transferred to another student in the same family. Lessons cancelled with less than a day's notice are charged in full.

Wagtail Dog Walks. One-hour group walks on the dunes, weekday mornings only. £12 a walk, or £50 for five. Dogs are collected from the door and returned to it. Our insurance covers four dogs at a time, so places are limited and a waiting list operates in the summer. A first walk is arranged with the owner present.

Bright Screens. Computer and telephone repairs at the unit behind the market. Diagnosis is free and takes two working days. Repairs are quoted before they begin and nothing is done without your agreement. Data recovery is charged separately. We open at eight on Saturdays and close at noon; the unit is shut all day on Mondays.

texts.heading: Sandmouth Cycle Store: your warranty

paragraphs.text: Every new bicycle sold at the store carries a two-year warranty on the frame and a one-year warranty on all other parts. The warranty begins on the day of purchase and cannot be passed on if the bicycle is sold on. Brake pads, tyres, inner tubes and cables are treated as items that wear out and are not covered at any point. Keep your receipt: without it we can trace the sale only if the bicycle was registered on the day you bought it.

A free safety check is offered six weeks after purchase and should be booked before the eighth week; after that a charge of £25 applies. Bicycles used for delivery work or hired out to others fall outside the warranty altogether, and staff will ask what the machine is used for when a claim is made. Repairs carried out by another shop do not cancel the warranty, but any part fitted elsewhere is your own responsibility.

texts.heading: The Sandmouth community bus

paragraphs.text: The community bus runs three services. Route 1, Sandmouth to Kestrel Bay, leaves the square at 09.15 and 13.45, Monday to Friday. Route 2, Sandmouth to the hospital at Verdon, leaves at 08.30 on Tuesdays and Thursdays only. Route 3, the market circuit, runs on Saturdays and leaves at 10.00, returning at 14.30. There is no service on Sundays or public holidays, and Route 2 does not run during the last week of December.

A single fare is £2.40 and a return is £4.00 on all routes. Holders of a Sandmouth travel pass ride free on Routes 1 and 3, but pay half fare on Route 2, which crosses the district boundary. Seats cannot be booked in advance except on Route 2, where the hospital service is often full; ring the office before four in the afternoon on the day before you travel. The bus is driven by volunteers and does not run if no driver is available, in which case a notice is posted in the square by eight in the morning.

difficulty_rationale.note: Three short documents in which almost every sentence carries a price, an hour or a condition, and in which the same words — free, included, only, at any hour — do different work in each entry.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: One sentence gives a rule, an exception to it and the reason for the exception, all joined by 'but' and a relative clause.

skim_plan.read_first: The three headings, then the first line of each directory entry. That tells you what each business does before you meet its prices.
skim_plan.skip: The descriptions of what each business will do for you. The questions turn on conditions, not on services.
fields: what is free and for whom

rewordings: for part of the year only

paraphrase_families.passage_form: Proof that you live at the address
rewordings: something showing it is your home
a document tying you to the property
are billed at the complete rate
must still be paid for entirely
have no claim under the agreement

hinge_words.why_here: 'Tuesdays and Thursdays only' fixes the days beside question 12.
'no call-out charge' is the whole of question 5.
'less than a day's notice' is the condition question 3 turns on.
It removes one route from the free-travel rule, which decides question 13.

you pay for at least two hours
