the edge of the local authority area

question_groups.instructions_extra: Look at the six directory entries, A–F. Which entry contains each piece of information below? NB You may use any letter more than once.

options.text: Kestrel Plumbing
Sandmouth Locks
Green Ends Garden
Ivy Hill Tutoring
Wagtail Dog Walks
Bright Screens

teaching.strategy: Every entry is built the same way — what we do, what it costs, when we work, one restriction — so read the restriction sentence of all six first. Four of these five statements are about a restriction, and the restrictions are the only lines that differ in kind between the entries.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, and a letter may be used more than once. Take the statements one at a time and check all six entries against each.
teaching.watch_out: Five of the six entries limit their hours in some way. A statement about time is not answered by the first set of hours you find.

questions.prompt: a service that is not offered in winter
questions.evidence_quote: Lawns, hedges and general tidying, March to October
questions.explanation: The gardening entry gives a season rather than opening hours, and the months named leave November to February uncovered.
questions.trap_note: Three other entries restrict the days or the hours they work. None of them closes for part of the year.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: March to October
paraphrase_link.note: Two months in the entry become a statement about the months they leave out.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement is about a season, so the answer must restrict a run of months. Restrictions on days of the week leave every season open.

distractors.why_tempting: E mentions the summer, which is a season, and also limits itself to weekday mornings.
distractors.why_wrong: The summer is mentioned as when the waiting list gets longer, not as a period when walks stop.

distractors.why_tempting: F closes at noon on Saturdays and all day on Mondays, so it looks like the most restricted entry.
distractors.why_wrong: Those are days and hours; the entry works in every month of the year.

teaching.reusable_rule: Restrictions come in kinds: hours, days, seasons, people. Fix the kind before you scan.

questions.prompt: a limit on numbers set by an insurance policy
questions.evidence_quote: Our insurance covers four dogs at a time, so places are limited
questions.explanation: The dog-walking entry gives a cause and an effect in one clause: the insurance covers four at once, so the group cannot be larger.
questions.trap_note: Two other entries have minimums and block sizes, but neither attributes the figure to anything outside the business.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: limit on numbers set by an insurance policy
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: insurance covers four dogs at a time, so places are limited
paraphrase_link.note: A cause-and-effect clause becomes a noun phrase with the cause folded in after 'by'.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement names both a limit and its source. Several entries give numbers; only one says what imposes the number.

distractors.why_tempting: D fixes lessons in blocks of six, which is a limit expressed as a number of places.
distractors.why_wrong: A block of six is a way of selling lessons, and no outside body is said to require it.

distractors.why_tempting: C sets a two-hour minimum, and a minimum is a limit of a kind.
distractors.why_wrong: It limits time rather than numbers, and it comes from the business itself.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a statement names both a rule and its source, check the source before the rule. Numbers are everywhere; causes are rare.

questions.prompt: a charge that applies when notice is too short
questions.evidence_quote: Lessons cancelled with less than a day's notice are charged in full
questions.explanation: The tutoring entry keeps the whole fee where a lesson is cancelled at under twenty-four hours' notice.
questions.trap_note: A also mentions a charge that is sometimes not made, but that one depends on the hour of day, not on how late the customer is.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: with less than a day's notice
paraphrase_link.note: A measured period becomes a judgement about it, which is why the figure will not be found by matching words.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement needs a penalty attached to lateness. Other entries attach money to hours worked or to the time of day, which is a different condition.

distractors.why_tempting: A is the only other entry with a charge that comes and goes, and its rule is also about time.
distractors.why_wrong: A's charge depends on when the plumber is called out, not on how much warning the customer gave.

distractors.why_tempting: F charges for data recovery separately, so an extra charge is clearly signalled.
distractors.why_wrong: That extra depends on the kind of work, not on notice of any kind.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two texts can both attach money to time and still answer different questions. Name what the time is measuring.

questions.prompt: a check on where the customer lives before work begins
questions.evidence_quote: Proof that you live at the address is required before any lock is opened
questions.explanation: The locksmith will not open a door until the customer has shown that the address is theirs, which is a check made before the work rather than after it.
questions.trap_note: C also visits before doing anything, but that visit is to price the job.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: you live at the address
paraphrase_link.note: Second person in the entry becomes third person in the statement, which defeats a search for 'you'.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement requires a check about residence carried out first. One entry conditions the work itself on that check; the others condition it on money or on a visit.

distractors.why_tempting: C visits new customers before quoting, so something does happen before work starts.
distractors.why_wrong: That visit is to see the garden and price the job; nothing about the customer is verified.

distractors.why_tempting: E arranges a first walk with the owner present, which reads as an identity check.
distractors.why_wrong: The owner is there to settle the dog, and nothing is proved about an address.

teaching.reusable_rule: Something happening first is not the same as something being verified. Ask what the step establishes.

questions.prompt: a period during which no call-out fee is charged
questions.evidence_quote: There is no call-out charge between nine and five on weekdays
questions.explanation: The plumbing entry charges for coming out at some times and not at others, and it names the hours during which the charge disappears.
questions.trap_note: B charges the same amount at every hour of the day, including Sundays, which is the opposite arrangement.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: no call-out charge
paraphrase_link.note: 'Fee' for 'charge' is the only change, and the statement adds the passive verb the entry leaves out.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement needs a stated window in which one particular fee vanishes. Only one entry names such a window.

distractors.why_tempting: B names a call-out price and mentions unusual hours in the same sentence, so both halves of the statement seem present.
distractors.why_wrong: B's price is the same at any hour; there is no period when it disappears.

distractors.why_tempting: C offers something free and says so in the last line of the entry.
distractors.why_wrong: What is free there is a first visit to quote, not a call-out charge.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement about when a fee stops needs a text where the fee sometimes applies. Never payable is a different fact.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete each sentence with words taken from the cycle store warranty.

teaching.strategy: The warranty is two paragraphs and the five answers run straight through them, three then two. Read each gapped sentence to the end before searching: two of these gaps sit inside a condition, so the words on either side tell you whether the answer is a period, a state or an activity.
teaching.order_note: In passage order. Once you have answered question 8 you never need the first paragraph again.
teaching.watch_out: Two words is the ceiling here. A hyphenated compound counts as one word, but adding an article or the noun the sentence already supplies takes you over.

questions.prompt: The store gives a {{gap}} warranty on the frame.
questions.evidence_quote: a two-year warranty on the frame
questions.explanation: The frame and the other parts are covered for different lengths of time, and the store states the frame's cover as a two-year warranty.
questions.trap_note: The same sentence gives a one-year figure for everything else, so both numbers are in view at once.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: warranty on the frame
paraphrase_link.note: The frame of the sentence is identical, which is why the gap is decided by which figure attaches to it.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between an article and a noun, so it is an adjective. Two compound adjectives are available and only one is attached to the frame.

distractors.why_tempting: It is in the same sentence, only six words away, and is the figure that covers most of the bicycle.
distractors.why_wrong: It covers all the other parts. The frame is the exception, and it is the exception the sentence asks about.

distractors.why_tempting: It means the same and is the natural way to say it aloud.
distractors.why_wrong: In this slot the store writes a hyphenated adjective, and a completion answer is copied rather than reworded.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where one sentence carries two periods, attach each to its own noun before you copy either.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap sits between 'a' and a noun, so it takes an adjective, not a plural.

questions.prompt: The warranty cannot be transferred if the bicycle is {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: cannot be passed on if the bicycle is sold on
questions.explanation: Cover belongs to the first buyer. The store expresses that by saying the warranty cannot be passed on where the bicycle changes hands.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: cannot be passed on
paraphrase_link.note: One phrasal verb is swapped for a single verb, and the condition that follows is untouched.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap completes a passive after 'is', so it takes a past participle. One participle in the paragraph describes a change of owner.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other past participle in the paragraph and also sits inside a condition.
distractors.why_wrong: Registering the bicycle is how a sale is traced without a receipt, and it has nothing to do with transfer.

distractors.why_tempting: The particle looks like part of the following clause rather than part of the verb.
distractors.why_wrong: The store writes the phrasal verb in full, and dropping the particle changes the form of the answer.

teaching.reusable_rule: A phrasal verb is one item. Dropping its particle is the same error as dropping a plural ending.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Is' before the gap forces a past participle, and here it carries a particle.

questions.prompt: Without a receipt the sale can be traced only if the bicycle was {{gap}} on the day of purchase.
questions.evidence_quote: we can trace the sale only if the bicycle was registered on the day you bought it
questions.explanation: The store keeps its own record of a sale only where the bicycle was registered on the day it was bought; otherwise the receipt is the only evidence.
questions.trap_note: 'On the day you bought it' in the text becomes 'on the day of purchase' in the sentence, so the phrase after the gap will not be found by matching.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the sale can be traced only if
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: we can trace the sale only if
paraphrase_link.note: The store disappears into a passive, so a search for 'we' misses the sentence entirely.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'was' and precedes a time phrase, so it is a past participle describing what was done to the bicycle. One such verb is attached to the day of sale.

distractors.why_tempting: It appears at the very end of the source sentence and is about the same day.
distractors.why_wrong: The sentence already says the purchase happened; the condition is about a further step taken that day.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other participle in the paragraph and also sits after 'is' or 'was'.
distractors.why_wrong: That describes what makes cover end, not what makes a sale traceable.

teaching.reusable_rule: When the text is active and the gapped line is passive, look for the verb rather than for the actor.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Was' before the gap wants a past participle in a single word.

questions.prompt: The free safety check must be booked before the {{gap}} week.
questions.evidence_quote: should be booked before the eighth week
questions.explanation: The check is offered at six weeks, but the booking deadline is stated separately as the eighth week, after which a charge applies.
questions.trap_note: The two figures in this sentence measure different things: one is when the check happens, the other is when booking closes.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: should be booked before the
paraphrase_link.note: The sentence strengthens 'should' to 'must', which is legitimate here because a charge follows.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap precedes the noun 'week' and follows the definite article, so it takes an ordinal. Only one ordinal appears in the paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the first figure in the sentence and is the one most readers remember.
distractors.why_wrong: Six weeks is when the check is offered, not the deadline for booking it, and the form is wrong for the slot.

distractors.why_tempting: The cardinal is the number a reader hears when they read the ordinal quickly.
distractors.why_wrong: 'The eight week' is not what the text says, and the ordinal is what the frame requires.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two figures in one sentence usually measure two different things. Say what each one counts before you choose.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'The' before the gap and 'week' after it force an ordinal number.

questions.prompt: Bicycles used for {{gap}} are not covered by the warranty at all.
questions.evidence_quote: Bicycles used for delivery work or hired out to others fall outside the warranty altogether
questions.explanation: Two uses take a bicycle outside the warranty entirely, and the first of them, delivery work, fits the frame of the gapped sentence.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: are not covered by the warranty at all
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: fall outside the warranty altogether
paraphrase_link.note: 'Fall outside' becomes 'not covered', and 'altogether' becomes 'at all' in the same position.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'used for', so it names an activity rather than a person or a period. The paragraph gives one activity in that exact frame.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the second excluded use and sits in the same list.
distractors.why_wrong: The text writes it as 'hired out to others', which is a different frame from 'used for'.

distractors.why_tempting: It appears in the last sentence, close to the words about the warranty.
distractors.why_wrong: Repairs by another shop expressly do not cancel cover, so it is the reverse of what the sentence needs.

teaching.reusable_rule: Copy the span that fits the frame around the gap, not the nearest item in the same list.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Used for' before the gap wants an activity, expressed as a noun phrase.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the table below using words and numbers taken from the community bus information.

teaching.strategy: Everything is in the last two paragraphs, and the first of them is written as one line per route. Find the line for the route named in the row you are filling, then read across it. The travel-pass column is the only one that needs the second paragraph.
teaching.order_note: All four answers come from one short section, and three of them from a single sentence each. Locate the route first, then read within its line.
teaching.watch_out: Times are printed with a full stop and two digits before it. Copy the form on the page; a time rewritten with a colon or without its leading zero is a rewrite, not a copy.

questions.prompt: Route 2 runs from Sandmouth to the {{gap}} at Verdon.
questions.evidence_quote: Route 2, Sandmouth to the hospital at Verdon
questions.explanation: Each route is introduced by its number and its destination. Route 2's destination is given as the hospital at Verdon.

questions.evidence_quote: leaves at 08.30 on Tuesdays and Thursdays only
questions.explanation: Route 2 has one departure, at half past eight in the morning, and it runs on two days of the week.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: leaves at

questions.prompt: On Route 2 a travel pass holder pays {{gap}}.

questions.explanation: The pass gives free travel on two of the three routes, and a reduced fare on the third because it goes outside the district.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Holders of a Sandmouth travel pass
paraphrase_link.note: A noun phrase with 'of' becomes a compound noun, and the verb moves to the pass holder.

teaching.decision_rule: The sentence turns on a contrast marked by 'but'. Everything before it applies to the other two routes, so only what follows can fill this row.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the single fare and is the only price in the paragraph expressed as a figure.

teaching.reusable_rule: A 'but' in the source sentence usually separates the general rule from the case you were asked about.

questions.prompt: Route 3 runs on {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: Route 3, the market circuit, runs on Saturdays
questions.explanation: The market circuit is a weekend service, running on Saturdays and returning the same afternoon.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph ends by naming days on which there is no service at all, which is the sentence a reader scanning for day names tends to stop at.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: runs on
paraphrase_link.note: The frame is identical, so the only work is matching the route number to its own line.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'runs on' and names days of operation. Only one set of days is attached to Route 3.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest day name to the end of the paragraph and sits in a sentence about services.
distractors.why_wrong: That sentence says there is no service then, so it is the reverse of what the column wants.

distractors.why_tempting: One row of a timetable feels like it should describe a single day.
distractors.why_wrong: The notice writes the plural, and a completion answer is copied in the form printed.

teaching.grammar_cue: 'Runs on' before the gap wants the days as the text prints them, in the plural.

texts.heading: Applying for study support

paragraphs.text: Brackenfield contributes to the cost of courses that develop skills the company needs. Any employee who has completed twelve months' service may apply, including part-time staff, whose funding is calculated pro rata. Agency workers are not eligible. The scheme covers course fees, examination entry and one set of prescribed books; it does not cover travel, accommodation or equipment. The maximum contribution in any financial year is £1,200 for a single employee. Applications are considered throughout the year and there is no closing date.

An application begins with a conversation rather than a form. Discuss the course with your line manager first and agree how the study will fit around your hours. The manager then signs the request form, which goes to the learning and development team, who check the course against the current skills plan. If the course is not on that plan the request is not refused automatically, but it goes to the head of department for a second opinion. A request that is turned down may be resubmitted once in the same year, with new supporting reasons.

A decision is normally given within three weeks. Successful applicants sign a study agreement before the course begins. The agreement sets out how much study leave has been granted — a maximum of five days a year, which may be taken in half-days if you prefer — and the terms on which the money is repaid. An employee who leaves within twelve months of finishing the course repays half of the contribution; an employee who leaves within six months repays all of it. Study leave that is not used cannot be carried into the following year.

Payment is made directly to the college or the examining body wherever possible. Where an employee has already paid, a receipt is submitted with an expenses claim and the money is refunded in the following month's salary. A failed examination may be re-entered once at the company's expense, provided the employee attended at least three quarters of the classes. Results are reported to the learning and development team by the employee rather than by the college, and certificates are copied to the personnel file. Nothing is paid out until the results have been confirmed.

texts.heading: Working flexibly at Brackenfield

paragraphs.text: All employees with twenty-six weeks' continuous service may ask to change their working pattern. The change may be to the hours worked, to the days worked, or to the place of work. A request is a formal one and must be made in writing; a conversation with a manager, however encouraging, does not start the process. Employees may make one formal request in any twelve-month period, although a manager may agree to consider a second where circumstances have clearly changed. There is no special form, and a letter or an email is equally acceptable.

The written request must state the change wanted, the date it should start, and the effect the employee thinks it will have on the work of the team. An employee is not required to give a personal reason for the request, and managers are asked not to press for one. The company must respond within two months of receiving the request, including any appeal. Where more time is needed, the employee's written agreement is required, and the revised date is confirmed in the same letter.

A request may be refused only on one of the recognised business grounds: the cost, the effect on customer service, an inability to reorganise the work among existing staff, an inability to recruit, a likely fall in quality or performance, or a planned change to the structure of the department. A refusal must name the ground relied on. Managers are advised to discuss alternatives before refusing, and in most departments a trial period of three months is offered instead of an outright refusal. The company publishes the number of requests received and the number refused each year, but not the grounds given.

An accepted change is permanent unless the employee and the manager agree in writing that it is temporary. It becomes a change to the contract of employment, and the employee cannot insist on returning to the previous pattern later. For that reason staff are encouraged to ask for a trial period first. A manager who accepts a change must confirm it in writing within fourteen days, and the employee should keep that letter. Requests to work from home are treated in the same way as any other request; there is no separate procedure and no automatic right. The policy itself is reviewed by the company every two years.

difficulty_rationale.note: Two policy documents in which the rule and its exception share a sentence. The vocabulary is bureaucratic — pro rata, continuous service, the ground relied on — and each term is used exactly once.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: A six-item list runs for three lines, and the duty that most questions turn on is the short sentence immediately after it.

skim_plan.read_first: The two headings and the opening sentence of each paragraph. Those eight lines tell you which document is about money and which is about hours.
skim_plan.skip: The list of business grounds in the flexible working policy. It is there to be returned to, not to be read now.

'refused only on one of the recognised grounds' is the limit question 26 tests.

It hedges the decision period that question 18 records.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the flow chart below using words and numbers taken from the study support scheme.

layout.title: How a study support request is handled
steps: Discuss the course with your {{15}} and agree how it will fit around your hours.
The manager signs the request form.
The learning and development team check the course against the current {{16}}.
A course that is not on it goes to the {{17}} for a second opinion.
A decision is normally given within {{18}} weeks.

teaching.strategy: The whole chain is in one paragraph and its first sentence, so find the sentence beginning 'An application begins' and read down from there. Three of the four gaps name a person or a document; decide which of the two each box wants before you look, because the paragraph names four of each.
teaching.order_note: All four answers come from one stretch of text. Locate that stretch once and stay in it.
teaching.watch_out: The chart follows the request, not the applicant. A box asking who receives the form wants the recipient, not the person who sent it on.

questions.prompt: Discuss the course with your {{gap}} and agree how it will fit around your hours.
questions.evidence_quote: Discuss the course with your line manager first
questions.explanation: The scheme opens with a conversation rather than paperwork, and the person that conversation is held with is the applicant's line manager.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Discuss the course with your line manager
paraphrase_link.note: The chart drops the word ordering the step, because the chart itself supplies the order.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows a possessive and precedes a conjunction, so it names one person defined by their relation to the applicant. The paragraph gives that person a two-word title.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other manager named in the paragraph and sounds like the person who would authorise spending.
distractors.why_wrong: That role only appears when a course is not on the skills plan, two steps further down.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph uses the bare word in the next sentence, so it looks like the scheme's own term.
distractors.why_wrong: The full title is what appears at this step, and the shortened form is a rewrite.

teaching.reusable_rule: A role named in full once and shortened afterwards is asked about in its full form.
teaching.grammar_cue: A possessive before the gap wants a noun phrase naming a person.

questions.prompt: The learning and development team check the course against the current {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: check the course against the current skills plan
questions.explanation: The team's job is to see whether the course matches what the company has decided it needs, and the document recording that is the skills plan.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: check the course against the current
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: check the course against the current
paraphrase_link.note: The frame is identical, so the only work is reading to the end of the clause.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows an adjective inside a prepositional phrase, so it names a document. Only one document is described as current.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the document named immediately before and is the thing physically travelling through the process.
distractors.why_wrong: The form is what the team receives; the plan is what they measure the course against.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other named document in the scheme and also concerns what has been approved.
distractors.why_wrong: That is signed after the decision, not consulted before it.

teaching.reusable_rule: In a process, what is examined and what it is measured by fill different slots. Read the preposition.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'The current' before the gap wants a singular noun naming a document.

questions.prompt: A course that is not on it goes to the {{gap}} for a second opinion.
questions.evidence_quote: it goes to the head of department for a second opinion
questions.explanation: A course outside the skills plan is not rejected at once; it is passed upward for a further view, and the scheme names who gives it.
questions.trap_note: The sentence begins with a negative condition, so a reader scanning for 'refused' finds the word and stops before the answer.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: it goes to the head of department
paraphrase_link.note: The chart replaces the pronoun with the thing it stands for, which is the course itself.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'goes to the' and precedes a purpose phrase, so it names the recipient of a referral. One role is attached to that referral.

distractors.why_tempting: The team is the previous recipient and is named twice in the paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: The team is what refers the course onward; the gap wants who it is referred to.

distractors.why_tempting: The manager is the first person in the chain and signs the form.
distractors.why_wrong: The manager acts before the course is checked, and gives no second opinion.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a chain passes something along, the box asks who receives it next, never who let it go.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'To the' before the gap wants a title, and here it runs to three words.

questions.prompt: A decision is normally given within {{gap}} weeks.
questions.evidence_quote: A decision is normally given within three weeks
questions.explanation: The scheme puts a usual, though not guaranteed, limit of three weeks on the decision itself, before any agreement is signed.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph carries four other periods, all of them about repayment or leave rather than about the decision.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: A decision is normally given within
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A decision is normally given within
paraphrase_link.note: The sentence is lifted whole, so the only risk is choosing the wrong number from the paragraph.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap precedes a counted unit, so it holds a number. One number in the paragraph is measured in weeks.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the most prominent figure in the paragraph and is also a period.
distractors.why_wrong: That period governs repayment after leaving, and it is counted in months.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest figure to the sentence and is expressed in days.
distractors.why_wrong: Five is the annual limit on study leave, not the time taken to decide.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph full of periods needs each one tied to its own event before you copy a figure.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Within' before the gap and 'weeks' after it want a bare number.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the notes below using words and numbers taken from the study support scheme.

layout.title: Study support: the rules
lines: Study leave: five days a year at most, and it may be taken in {{19}}.
Open to employees with {{20}} months' service; part-time funding is worked out pro rata.
Covers fees, examination entry and one set of {{21}}; travel and equipment are not covered.
One re-sit is paid for, provided you attended at least {{22}} of the classes.

teaching.strategy: The notes compress four separate rules out of one document, and they do not follow the order of the paragraphs. Read all four lines first, decide which rule each one is about, and then go looking; the eligibility rule and the leave rule are three paragraphs apart.
teaching.order_note: This set is deliberately out of order: the first line comes from the middle of the document and the second from its opening. Locate each rule by what it governs, not by where the last one was.
teaching.watch_out: Notes drop the verbs, so a line can look like a benefit when it is really a condition. Check what each line is claiming before you fill the gap.

questions.prompt: Study leave: five days a year at most, and it may be taken in {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: which may be taken in half-days if you prefer
questions.explanation: The five days may be split, and the scheme names the unit the split is allowed in. The choice belongs to the employee.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: may be taken in
paraphrase_link.note: The relative clause becomes a main clause, and the pronoun replaces the leave it refers to.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'taken in' and names a unit smaller than the day already given. One such unit appears in the paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the figure the line already gives and the most memorable thing in the sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: The line has already stated the annual maximum; the gap is about how it may be divided.

distractors.why_tempting: Writing it as two words looks more natural than copying the hyphen.
distractors.why_wrong: The scheme writes a hyphenated compound, and that is the form the answer is checked against.

teaching.reusable_rule: Copy hyphens as they are printed. A compound split into two words is a different answer.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Taken in' before the gap wants a plural noun naming a unit of time.

questions.prompt: Open to employees with {{gap}} months' service; part-time funding is worked out pro rata.
questions.evidence_quote: Any employee who has completed twelve months' service may apply
questions.explanation: Eligibility rests on a year of service, and part-time staff qualify on the same rule with their funding scaled to their hours.
questions.trap_note: Twelve months appears twice in the document: once as the qualifying period and once as the repayment window after leaving.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Any employee who has completed
paraphrase_link.note: A relative clause becomes a preposition, so the verb the note dropped is the one you must supply mentally.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap precedes a counted unit, so it holds a number, and the note is about who may apply. Only one figure is attached to eligibility.

distractors.why_tempting: Six months appears in the same document attached to an employee leaving, which also sounds like a qualifying period.
distractors.why_wrong: That figure governs full repayment of the money, not the right to apply in the first place.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the qualifying period in the other document in this section and is roughly the same length.
distractors.why_wrong: It belongs to flexible working, and it is not measured in months.

teaching.reusable_rule: The same figure can govern two different rights in one document. Match it to the right the line is about.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap precedes a counted unit, so it takes a number and nothing else.

questions.prompt: Covers fees, examination entry and one set of {{gap}}; travel and equipment are not covered.
questions.evidence_quote: one set of prescribed books
questions.explanation: Three things are covered and three are not. The third of the covered items is a single set of the books the course requires.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: one set of prescribed books
paraphrase_link.note: The note keeps the counter and drops nothing else, so the gap is the noun phrase that completes it.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap completes a phrase after 'one set of', so it takes a plural noun. Only one plural in the sentence is inside the covered list.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the head noun and reads as the whole idea.
distractors.why_wrong: The scheme qualifies it, and the adjective is what limits which books are paid for.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the item immediately before and is also part of the covered list.
distractors.why_wrong: The line already names it, so repeating it leaves the last item missing.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where an adjective narrows what is being paid for, it belongs inside the answer.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'One set of' before the gap wants a plural noun with the adjective that limits it.

questions.prompt: One re-sit is paid for, provided you attended at least {{gap}} of the classes.
questions.evidence_quote: provided the employee attended at least three quarters of the classes
questions.explanation: A second attempt at an examination is funded once, and the condition attached to it is a level of attendance stated as a proportion.
questions.trap_note: The condition sits in a subordinate clause at the end of a long sentence, which is where a reader satisfied by the first half stops.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: provided the employee attended at least
paraphrase_link.note: Third person becomes second person, which is the only change the note makes to the condition.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'at least' and precedes 'of the classes', so it names a proportion. One proportion is attached to the funded re-sit.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other quantity in the sentence and sits closer to the verb about paying.
distractors.why_wrong: It counts how many re-sits are funded, not how much of the course was attended.

distractors.why_tempting: A half is the proportion most readers expect an attendance rule to use, and the word appears elsewhere in the document.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Half' governs repayment after leaving, in a different paragraph and about money.

teaching.reusable_rule: A clause beginning with 'provided' carries the condition, and the condition is usually what the gap wants.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'At least' before the gap and 'of the classes' after it want a proportion.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the flexible working policy?

teaching.strategy: This policy states a rule and then qualifies it, usually with 'although', 'only' or 'unless'. Read each statement for the modal it uses — may, must, does not have to — and then find the sentence carrying the matching modal, not the sentence carrying the matching topic.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, and the five answers fall one to a paragraph across four paragraphs. Question 26's answer is below question 25's.
teaching.watch_out: One statement is about how often something succeeds. The policy sets out the procedure in detail and reports no outcomes at all.

questions.prompt: Staff may submit more than one formal request in a year without their manager's agreement.
questions.evidence_quote: Employees may make one formal request in any twelve-month period
questions.explanation: The entitlement is to a single request in twelve months. A second is possible only where a manager agrees to consider it, so an unconditional right to more than one is contradicted.
questions.trap_note: The sentence grants the entitlement and takes it away in the same breath; the qualification arrives after a comma and the word 'although'.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: more than one formal request in a year
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: one formal request in any twelve-month period
paraphrase_link.note: The statement enlarges the number the policy fixes, and a twelve-month period is restated as a year.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the policy names the limit. The statement claims a right that exists in the policy only with the manager's agreement, so it is contradicted rather than unmentioned.

distractors.why_tempting: The same sentence does say a second request can be considered, so the possibility of more than one is genuinely on the page.
distractors.why_wrong: That possibility depends on the manager agreeing, and the statement says the agreement is not needed.

distractors.why_tempting: The phrase 'without their manager's agreement' appears nowhere, so a search for it returns nothing.
distractors.why_wrong: The policy states the limit and states the only exception to it, which together deny the statement.

teaching.reusable_rule: A right granted with a condition attached is not the same right claimed without one. Compare the conditions, not the nouns.

questions.prompt: An employee does not have to give a personal reason for wanting the change.
questions.evidence_quote: An employee is not required to give a personal reason for the request
questions.explanation: The policy states this directly and reinforces it by telling managers not to ask, so both halves of the statement are supported.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: does not have to give a personal reason
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is not required to give a personal reason
paraphrase_link.note: One modal expression is swapped for another of the same strength and everything else is unchanged.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement and the policy carry the same negative obligation, and the following clause confirms rather than qualifies it. Nothing is left unsupported.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous sentence lists three things the request must state, so the paragraph opens by demanding information.
distractors.why_wrong: Those three are about the change and its effect on the team, not about the employee's own reasons.

distractors.why_tempting: The words 'have to' never appear, so a reader matching modals by their surface finds nothing.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Is not required to' is the same obligation, written in the policy's own register.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two different ways of writing the same modal are the same fact. Match the strength, not the wording.

questions.prompt: The two-month deadline can be extended if the employee agrees in writing.
questions.evidence_quote: Where more time is needed, the employee's written agreement is required
questions.explanation: The policy sets the deadline and then provides for extending it, on one condition: the employee must agree, and the agreement must be written.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: can be extended if the employee agrees in writing
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Where more time is needed, the employee's written agreement is required
paraphrase_link.note: 'Where more time is needed' is the extension, and the written agreement is its only condition.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement's condition is the policy's condition, and the extension the statement assumes is what 'more time' means here. Every element has a partner in the text.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence before says the company 'must respond within two months', which reads as an absolute limit.
distractors.why_wrong: The next sentence provides expressly for more time, so the limit is not absolute.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'extended' never appears, and a reader hunting for it finds only 'more time is needed'.
distractors.why_wrong: Needing more time than the deadline allows is an extension, and the condition attached to it is stated.

teaching.reusable_rule: A rule and the sentence that qualifies it usually sit next to each other. Read one more sentence before calling a limit absolute.

questions.prompt: A manager may refuse a request without stating a reason.
questions.evidence_quote: A refusal must name the ground relied on.
questions.explanation: Refusals are limited to a closed list of grounds and the policy requires the one used to be named, so a refusal with no stated reason is not permitted.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the requirement is one short sentence sitting after a very long list, and readers who have worked through the list skim past it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: must name the ground relied on
paraphrase_link.note: 'Ground relied on' is the policy's term for the reason, and 'must name' is the duty the statement denies.

teaching.decision_rule: The policy imposes a duty and the statement asserts freedom from it. That is a direct contradiction, so FALSE rather than NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: Managers clearly have the power to refuse, and the long list of grounds reads as latitude rather than restriction.
distractors.why_wrong: The list is closed and the next sentence requires the chosen ground to be named. Power to refuse is not power to refuse silently.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement is about what a manager need not do, and policies more often say what people must do.
distractors.why_wrong: The duty is stated in its own sentence, and a duty to name a ground denies a freedom not to.

teaching.reusable_rule: A short sentence after a long list is the one most often skipped, and it is often where the duty lives.

questions.prompt: Most requests to work from home are approved.
questions.evidence_quote: Requests to work from home are treated in the same way as any other request
questions.explanation: The policy says only that home working goes through the same procedure as anything else, and adds that there is no automatic right. It reports no decisions and no proportions.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: 'no automatic right' is about entitlement, and a reader who takes it for a statement about outcomes answers FALSE.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is raised and the procedure is described, but no sentence in the policy reports how many requests of any kind succeed. Neither support nor contradiction is available, so the key is NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The policy is permissive in tone, offers trial periods and limits the grounds for refusal, so approval feels like the normal outcome.
distractors.why_wrong: Tone is not evidence. The document never reports what happens to any request.

distractors.why_tempting: 'No automatic right' sounds like a denial that requests usually succeed.
distractors.why_wrong: It denies an entitlement, not a rate of success. Those are different claims.

teaching.reusable_rule: A statement about how often something happens needs a figure or a frequency word in the text. A rule about entitlement is neither.
teaching.nearest_text: there is no separate procedure and no automatic right

title: The van that is a library

passage_json.title: The van that is a library

texts.heading: The van that is a library

paragraphs.text: On the third Tuesday of every month a green van stops for fifty minutes outside the village hall at Hollowbeck. It carries about two thousand books, a small counter and one librarian who is also the driver. Nobody in Hollowbeck calls it the mobile library. It is simply the van, and for roughly a hundred households in the surrounding valley it is the only public library there is. Nothing about the vehicle suggests a library except the lettering along one side. Its route card, printed on the county website each January, lists ninety-one stops. The county has run a service of this kind, in one form or another, for eighty-one years.

The first vehicle was a converted delivery lorry with shelves bolted to its sides, sent out in 1945 to serve villages that had lost their bus service. It was not a popular decision inside the county library. Branch librarians argued that a van could carry only a fraction of a branch's stock and would take money from buildings that were already short of it. The service survived that first year largely because the council had bought the lorry before anybody objected. The argument has never entirely gone away, and it returns whenever the service is reviewed.

What settled it in the early years was not principle but arithmetic. A branch library in a village of four hundred people cost more to keep open for two days a week than a van cost to run for a month across twelve villages. Nothing in that calculation was about reading; it was about miles, hours and rent. The van also reached people who could not travel: farms without a car, older residents, and, from the 1960s, the growing number of households where the one vehicle went to work with somebody at eight in the morning.

The service now operates three kinds of route, and they are not the same thing at all. A village route calls at ten or twelve settlements in a day, for forty to sixty minutes each, once a month. A school route visits four primary schools in a morning, for about ninety minutes each, once a fortnight, and carries a stock chosen for children. A housebound route makes individual calls at private addresses, ten or twelve in a day, for about ten minutes each, once every three weeks. Every route was redrawn in 2016 and none has changed since. The third is the most expensive per borrower and the one the county has never proposed to cut.

Stock is the hardest part of the work. A van holds roughly two thousand volumes against a branch's twenty thousand, which is also close to the most the floor of a vehicle will safely carry, so the librarian is not managing a collection but making a bet about what a hundred households will want in a month. Requests soften the problem: anything in the county catalogue can be brought on the next visit, and about a third of all issues on village routes are now requests placed at the previous stop. The rest depends on the librarian knowing the route, which takes a year or more to learn and is lost entirely when a driver moves on. New drivers spend three months alongside an experienced one, which everybody concerned agrees is not long enough.

The vans themselves have changed less than might be expected. The current vehicles have a lift for wheelchair users, a heater that works, and a satellite connection so that a loan is recorded against the county system as it happens rather than at the end of the day. What they do not have is more space; the width of a lane in the Verdon hills has not increased, and every proposal for a larger vehicle has been defeated by the same handful of corners. Two of the three vans are now more than fifteen years old, and no replacement has been budgeted.

Use has fallen, as it has in every kind of library, but not evenly. Adult fiction issues on village routes are about half what they were twenty years ago. Issues to children on school routes have held up, and the housebound service is busier than it has ever been, which is a consequence of an older population rather than of anything the service has done. Counting issues alone therefore makes the van look like a service in decline, and counting visits makes it look like one in demand. The county measures both and publishes neither figure on its own.

Whether it survives is a question about what a library is for. If it is a building with a collection, the van is a poor substitute for one. If it is a way of putting a book into the hands of somebody who would otherwise not have one, the van is the only part of the county service that does that at all in half the district. The county's own review last year recommended keeping all three kinds of route and said, in a sentence widely quoted locally, that the service should be judged by where it goes rather than by how much it lends.

difficulty_rationale.note: A profile that keeps turning into an argument. Three paragraphs give a figure and then say what the figure does not show, and the last one makes the whole service depend on a definition.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It reports a fall, two exceptions to the fall and a warning about how the fall is measured, in four sentences with one connective between them.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It establishes that the subject is a service, not a vehicle, and that some households have no other library.
skim_plan.skip: The list of what the current vans contain in paragraph F. It is detail, and the question that needs it will send you back.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

teaching.strategy: Read the stem and answer it in your own words before you look at the four options; on this passage three of the five stems ask for a reason, and the passage gives its reasons in the sentence after the claim rather than before it. Then eliminate on the ground the stem names, not on whether the option sounds true.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, and the five run from the second paragraph to the seventh. After question 30 you never need the first half of the passage again.
teaching.watch_out: Several options are accurate statements about the passage that answer a different question. Truth is not the test; answering this stem is.

questions.prompt: What did branch librarians object to when the service began?

options.text: The lorry was too slow to reach the outlying villages
The villages chosen did not want a library service
The van would take money from branches already short of it
A van would be unreliable on the winter roads

questions.evidence_quote: would take money from buildings that were already short of it
questions.explanation: The objection recorded in the passage is financial: a van would draw funds away from branch buildings that were underfunded already. The librarians' other complaint, about the small stock a van could carry, is not among the options.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph gives two objections. Only one of them appears in the options, so the reader who remembers the other finds nothing and starts guessing.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: take money from branches already short of it
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: take money from buildings that were already short of it
paraphrase_link.note: 'Buildings' becomes 'branches', which is the word the same paragraph uses for the people running them.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what was objected to, so the answer must be one of the two complaints the passage attributes to the librarians. Only one option matches either.

distractors.why_tempting: The vehicle was a converted lorry sent to remote villages, so slowness is an easy inference from the description.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the passage comments on how fast it travelled or whether it arrived late.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage says the decision was unpopular, and a reader who does not check with whom assumes the villages were meant.
distractors.why_wrong: It was unpopular inside the county library. The villages had lost their bus service and are not reported as objecting.

distractors.why_tempting: Rural roads and an elderly lorry make mechanical trouble the obvious worry.
distractors.why_wrong: Reliability is never raised anywhere in the passage, in 1945 or since.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a text attributes a complaint, check who is complaining before you check what about.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, what settled the argument in the early years?

options.text: A comparison of what the two kinds of service cost
A promise that no branch library would be closed
A change in the way county services were funded
A survey of what people in the villages wanted

questions.evidence_quote: cost more to keep open for two days a week than a van cost to run for a month across twelve villages
questions.explanation: The paragraph says the matter was decided by arithmetic and then gives the sum: keeping one small branch open for two days a week was dearer than running a van across twelve villages for a month.
questions.trap_note: The passage insists the calculation was not about reading. An option about what readers wanted is therefore the reverse of the argument being made.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: what settled the argument in the early years
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: What settled it in the early years was not principle but arithmetic
paraphrase_link.note: The passage answers the stem in its opening clause and then supplies the sum that justifies it.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks what decided the matter, and the passage names the deciding factor explicitly in a not-X-but-Y sentence. The option must match Y.

distractors.why_tempting: The dispute was about branches losing money, so a guarantee to keep them open reads like the natural settlement of it.
distractors.why_wrong: No such promise appears, and the argument is said never to have gone away.

distractors.why_tempting: A funding change is the usual way such disputes end, and the paragraph is entirely about money.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage describes a comparison of existing costs, not any change in how the money arrived.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph goes on to describe the people the van reached, which sounds like evidence of demand.
distractors.why_wrong: That is offered as a further benefit, and the sentence before it rules reading out of the calculation altogether.

teaching.reusable_rule: A not-X-but-Y sentence names the answer twice: once by rejecting a candidate and once by supplying one.

questions.prompt: Which group is named as a further reason for the van's usefulness from the 1960s?

options.text: people who had recently moved into the villages
children unable to reach a school library
farmers who had given up their own vehicles
households whose only car was taken to work

questions.evidence_quote: the growing number of households where the one vehicle went to work with somebody at eight in the morning
questions.explanation: Three groups are listed as unable to travel. The one attached to the 1960s is the household with a single car that left with a commuter each morning.
questions.trap_note: The date applies to the third item on the list only. The first two are given without any period at all.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: households whose only car was taken to work
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: households where the one vehicle went to work
paraphrase_link.note: 'The one vehicle' becomes 'their only car', and the active verb becomes a passive with the driver removed.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem fixes a period, so the answer must be the item the passage dates. Two of the three listed groups carry no date and cannot satisfy the stem.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Farms without a car' is on the same list and is the closest thing in the passage to a rural household with no transport.
distractors.why_wrong: That item is undated, and the passage does not say those farms had given anything up.

distractors.why_tempting: New arrivals are a plausible reason for demand growing at a particular date.
distractors.why_wrong: Nobody moving into the villages is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

distractors.why_tempting: Children are a real user group and have a route of their own later in the passage.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the school route, described in a different paragraph and not offered as a reason from the 1960s.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a stem names a date, the answer is the list item the date is attached to, not the one that sounds oldest.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say is the main difficulty of stocking a van?

options.text: Books are often damaged by travelling on rough roads
The librarian must guess demand from a small selection
Requested books take several weeks to reach a borrower
The county catalogue cannot be searched from the van

questions.evidence_quote: the librarian is not managing a collection but making a bet about what a hundred households will want in a month
questions.explanation: With one tenth of a branch's stock, the librarian cannot cover the range of likely demand and has to predict it instead. The passage puts that as a bet rather than as management.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph names two things that soften the difficulty — requests and route knowledge — and both are easily mistaken for the difficulty itself.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The librarian must guess demand from a small selection
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: making a bet about what a hundred households will want
paraphrase_link.note: 'Making a bet about what people will want' is glossed as guessing demand, and the small stock supplies the rest.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the difficulty, so the answer must be the problem rather than either remedy. The passage states the problem in a not-X-but-Y clause.

distractors.why_tempting: Requests are discussed at length, and waiting for a book is the obvious inconvenience of a small stock.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says a requested item comes on the next visit, which is a solution and not a delay of weeks.

distractors.why_tempting: The catalogue is mentioned, and a reader who knows the vans once had no data link supplies the rest.
distractors.why_wrong: The next paragraph says the vehicles have a satellite connection, so the catalogue is reachable.

distractors.why_tempting: A vehicle on rural lanes carrying two thousand books makes damage a natural guess.
distractors.why_wrong: Damage to stock is never mentioned in the passage.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where a paragraph states a problem and then its remedies, the stem asking for the problem excludes everything after the colon.

questions.prompt: Why, according to the passage, has the housebound service become busier?

options.text: The county has advertised the service more widely
The vans now have a lift for wheelchair users
Village routes have become less frequent
There are more older people in the district

questions.evidence_quote: which is a consequence of an older population rather than of anything the service has done
questions.explanation: The passage attributes the rise to demography and expressly denies that the service itself produced it, which is unusual enough to be worth an item.
questions.trap_note: The clause naming the cause also names what is not the cause, so half the sentence exists to rule out an answer.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: There are more older people in the district
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a consequence of an older population
paraphrase_link.note: 'An older population' is spelled out as more older people, which is the same claim in plainer words.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a cause, and the passage supplies one and rejects another in the same clause. Any option describing something the service did is excluded by that clause.

distractors.why_tempting: The lift is a genuine improvement for exactly the users this route serves, so it looks like the reason.
distractors.why_wrong: It is true of the vans and belongs to another paragraph; the passage rules out anything the service has done.

distractors.why_tempting: Advertising is the usual explanation for a service growing, and the passage never denies it directly.
distractors.why_wrong: No promotion of any kind is mentioned, and the sentence attributes the rise elsewhere.

distractors.why_tempting: If one route ran less often, its users would plausibly move to another, and the paragraph is about routes.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the passage says the frequency of village routes has changed.

teaching.reusable_rule: A clause that names a cause and rejects another has already eliminated a whole class of options for you.
