layout.title: The vehicles today, and how they are judged
lines: Today's vans carry a lift, a working heater and a satellite link, so a loan is registered at the {{33}} it is made rather than later in the day.
The one thing they still lack is {{34}}, since the lanes have not grown any wider and every plan for a bigger vehicle has been {{35}} by the same corners.
The county's review chose to keep all three kinds of route and suggested judging the service by the places it {{36}} rather than by its lending figures.

teaching.strategy: The summary covers two paragraphs only, so find the one about the vehicles and read to the end of the passage. Decide the word class of each gap from the list before you search: two of these gaps want nouns, one wants a past participle and one wants a present-tense verb, which cuts the bank in half at once.
teaching.order_note: Everything is in the last two paragraphs of the passage. Locate them once, then work inside them.
teaching.watch_out: The bank is the item writer's wording, not the passage's, so no gap can be filled by matching a word you have already read. Match the meaning and then the grammar.

bank_analysis.why_wrong: It fits the frame and names time, but an hour is a span where the sentence needs a point.
A plan can be delayed, yet the passage says these proposals were beaten rather than postponed.
It reads well after 'the places it', but counting is the measure the review rejected.
The width in the passage belongs to the lanes, not to what the vehicles are short of.

questions.prompt: A loan is registered at the {{gap}} it is made rather than later in the day.
questions.evidence_quote: a satellite connection so that a loan is recorded against the county system as it happens
questions.explanation: The satellite link removes the delay: borrowing goes onto the county system while it is happening instead of being entered afterwards. 'Moment' is the bank's word for that immediacy.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: rather than later in the day
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: rather than at the end of the day
paraphrase_link.note: The contrast is preserved exactly, which is what identifies the sentence the gap comes from.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'at the' and precedes a reduced relative clause, so it takes a singular noun naming a point in time. Only one bank word means a point rather than a span.

distractors.why_tempting: It fits the frame perfectly and is the other bank word naming time.
distractors.why_wrong: An hour is a length of time, and the sentence is contrasting immediacy with delay.

distractors.why_tempting: Recording and counting are close in meaning, and the passage is about a system that tallies loans.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a verb and the slot needs a noun.

teaching.reusable_rule: In a word bank, sort by word class first. It usually leaves two candidates instead of eight.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'At the' before the gap wants a singular noun naming a point in time.

questions.prompt: The one thing they still lack is {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: What they do not have is more space
questions.explanation: The passage names one shortcoming of the modern vans and gives the reason for it: the lanes are the same size as they always were.
questions.trap_note: The next clause mentions the width of a lane, which belongs to the road rather than to the vehicle.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The one thing they still lack
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: What they do not have
paraphrase_link.note: A cleft clause becomes a noun phrase, so the summary cannot be found by searching for its own wording.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap completes 'is', so it needs an uncountable noun naming what is missing from the vans themselves. Only one bank word describes interior capacity.

distractors.why_tempting: The very next clause uses that word, so it is the nearest noun in the source sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the width of a lane, not of the vehicle, and it is why the vans cannot grow rather than what they lack.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a noun and fits the slot grammatically.
distractors.why_wrong: The sentence is about physical capacity, and nothing in the paragraph says the vans are short of time.

teaching.reusable_rule: A word standing next to the answer in the text is the most attractive wrong option there is. Check what it belongs to.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap follows 'is' and completes the sentence, so it wants an uncountable noun.

questions.prompt: Every plan for a bigger vehicle has been {{gap}} by the same corners.
questions.evidence_quote: every proposal for a larger vehicle has been defeated by the same handful of corners
questions.explanation: The corners stop the larger vehicles altogether rather than holding them up, so the bank word has to carry finality.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: Every plan for a bigger vehicle
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: every proposal for a larger vehicle
paraphrase_link.note: Two words are swapped for near equivalents and the structure is untouched.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits inside a passive after 'has been', so it takes a past participle. Between the two available, only one means stopped rather than postponed.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a past participle, fits the passive exactly, and a plan that meets an obstacle is very often merely delayed.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says the proposals were defeated, which ends them; a delay implies they are still coming.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a verb and the slot holds a verb form.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a present-tense form and cannot follow 'has been'.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two bank words of the same class can differ in strength. Take the one that matches how final the text is.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Has been' before the gap forces a past participle.

questions.prompt: The service should be judged by the places it {{gap}} rather than by its lending figures.
questions.evidence_quote: the service should be judged by where it goes rather than by how much it lends
questions.explanation: The review proposed a measure of coverage rather than of volume, and the bank word has to name the act of arriving somewhere.
questions.trap_note: The contrast in the sentence is between going somewhere and lending something, so a word about measurement sits on the wrong side of it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: judged by where it goes
paraphrase_link.note: An adverbial clause becomes a noun phrase with a relative clause, which changes what word class the gap needs.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows a noun phrase and takes a third-person present verb with 'places' as its object. Only one bank word can govern a place.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other third-person verb in the bank and the sentence is about how the service is measured.
distractors.why_wrong: Counting is the thing the review argued against, and places are not what is counted.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a verb form and the passage does use it of physical obstacles.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a participle, and the frame here needs a present-tense verb with an object.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a sentence sets two measures against each other, the gap belongs to one side of the contrast. Decide which side first.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap follows 'the places it', so it takes a third-person present verb.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the table below using words and numbers taken from the passage.

teaching.strategy: Every answer is in the paragraph that names the three kinds of route, and that paragraph gives one sentence to each. Find the sentence whose first words match the row you are filling, then read across it; each sentence supplies places, minutes and frequency in that order.
teaching.order_note: All four answers are in a single paragraph. Locate it once, then move between its three sentences rather than through the passage.
teaching.watch_out: The three sentences use the same figures for different things — ten or twelve appears twice, and about ten and about ninety are minutes on different routes. Match the row before you copy a number.

questions.prompt: A village route visits each settlement once a {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: for forty to sixty minutes each, once a month
questions.explanation: The village route is the least frequent of the three: ten or twelve stops in a day, and each of them served once a month.
questions.trap_note: The passage's other two frequencies are a fortnight and three weeks, both of them shorter, so a reader who mixes the rows makes the village route more frequent than it is.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: calls at ten or twelve settlements in a day, for forty to sixty minutes each, once a
paraphrase_link.note: 'Calls at' becomes 'visits' and the row keeps the passage's own frequency phrase.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'once a', so it names a period. One period in the paragraph is attached to the village route.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the frequency in the very next sentence and is the other single-word period in the paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: That belongs to the school route, which is the row below.

distractors.why_tempting: 'In a day' appears in the same sentence and is the nearest period to the gap.
distractors.why_wrong: That counts how many settlements are reached in one day's driving, not how often each is served.

teaching.reusable_rule: Where one sentence carries two periods, one usually measures the working day and the other the cycle. Read which is which.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Once a' before the gap wants a singular period of time.

questions.prompt: A school route visits four {{gap}} in a morning.
questions.evidence_quote: A school route visits four primary schools in a morning
questions.explanation: The school route is the only one that serves institutions rather than places or addresses, and the passage specifies which kind of school.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: visits four primary schools
paraphrase_link.note: The row keeps the verb and the number, so the gap is exactly what the row leaves out.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows a number and precedes a time phrase, so it takes a plural noun. The adjective in the passage narrows which institutions are meant and belongs with it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the head noun and the row's own label already says 'School'.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage qualifies it, and the qualifier is what distinguishes these from every other school in the county.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the plural noun in the sentence before and follows a very similar number.
distractors.why_wrong: It belongs to the village route, which is the row above.

teaching.reusable_rule: An adjective that narrows which things are meant is part of the answer, not decoration in front of it.
teaching.grammar_cue: A number before the gap wants a plural noun, with the adjective that limits it.

questions.prompt: A housebound call lasts about {{gap}} minutes.
questions.evidence_quote: ten or twelve in a day, for about ten minutes each
questions.explanation: The housebound route makes many short calls: ten or twelve of them in a day, each lasting around ten minutes.
questions.trap_note: 'Ten or twelve' appears twice in this sentence, once as a number of calls and once inside the duration, so the figure has to be taken from the right half.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: for about ten minutes each
paraphrase_link.note: A prepositional phrase becomes a verb, and the hedge stays in the row rather than in the gap.

teaching.decision_rule: The row already carries the hedge and the unit, so the gap holds only a figure. One figure in the sentence is measured in minutes.

distractors.why_tempting: It sits in the same sentence, four words from the answer, and is also a plausible length for a short call.
distractors.why_wrong: It counts calls made in a day, not the minutes spent at each.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's other duration and is also given with 'about'.
distractors.why_wrong: Ninety minutes is the time spent at each school, which is the row above.

teaching.reusable_rule: When the frame already supplies the hedge and the unit, the gap wants the figure alone.
teaching.grammar_cue: The row supplies 'about' and 'minutes', so the gap takes a bare number.

questions.prompt: A housebound address is visited once every {{gap}} weeks.
questions.evidence_quote: for about ten minutes each, once every three weeks
questions.explanation: Each private address on a housebound route is called at once in three weeks, which is more often than a village is served and less often than a school.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: once every three weeks
paraphrase_link.note: The row keeps the frequency frame whole, so the only work is choosing the right sentence.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'every' and a counted unit, so it takes a number. Only one figure in the paragraph is counted in weeks.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the neighbouring frequency and means roughly the same length of time.
distractors.why_wrong: It belongs to the school route, and it is not expressed in weeks.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the only other bare number in the paragraph and sits close to the end of it.
distractors.why_wrong: That is when the routes were redrawn, not how often anywhere is visited.

teaching.reusable_rule: A frequency and a date are both numbers. The unit after the gap tells you which one the row wants.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Every' before the gap and 'weeks' after it want a bare number.

paragraphs.text: On some dry coasts it almost never rains, yet the air is wet for most of the year. A cold current runs offshore, the sea chills the air above it, a low bank of cloud forms, and the wind pushes it inland. Where the cloud meets a hillside it becomes fog. Villages on those hillsides have lived for centuries in sight of water they could not use. Their few wells are shallow and taste of salt. The drinking water came up the hill by road, in tankers, at a price that rose with the distance. The idea behind fog collection is a simple one. If the water is already drifting through the village, it may cost less to comb it out of the air than to drive it up the hill.

Fog is made of droplets a few thousandths of a millimetre across. They are too light to fall: air resistance holds them up, and a droplet that does begin to sink usually evaporates before it reaches the ground. What they will do is travel. A steady wind carries them sideways, and anything standing in the wind's path collects some of them. A fog collector is little more than a net held upright between two posts. Droplets strike the fibres and stay there. As more arrive they merge, and once a drop is heavy enough it runs down the fibre into a gutter along the bottom edge. From there a pipe carries it to a tank. Nothing is pumped and nothing is powered. The whole system runs on wind and gravity.

The net looks like the least interesting part of the design and is the hardest to get right. A tightly woven mesh offers more surface for droplets to strike. It also blocks the wind, and blocked air does not force its way through a barrier. It flows around it instead, carrying its droplets past the net. A very open mesh lets the wind through and catches almost nothing. The meshes used on most sites are a compromise, shading rather less than half of the frame. They are often hung in two layers, so that a droplet missed by the first has a second chance. Fibre thickness matters as well: thin fibres catch a higher proportion of the droplets that reach them, though they tear more easily in the wind that the site was chosen for.

Choosing the site takes a year. Fog does not lie evenly along a coast. It gathers on ridges at a particular height, and it arrives on a wind that blows from the same quarter for most of the year. Surveyors put up a single test panel of one square metre and weigh what it yields, day by day, through every season. The figures are rarely steady: a site may give three quarters of its annual water in four months and almost nothing in the rest. That settles the size of the tank rather than the size of the net. The full-size panels are then set at right angles to the prevailing wind, high enough on the slope to sit inside the cloud rather than below it.

A good site yields between three and ten litres of water a day for every square metre of mesh. That sounds small until it is multiplied: one large collector of forty square metres returns about two hundred litres a day on such a site. That is the drinking and cooking water of roughly thirty people. Twenty collectors on one ridge will supply a small village. Where the fog is thinner, the same forty square metres may return a third of that, which is why the survey matters more than the mesh. The water is cleaner than anything the wells give, since it has never touched the ground. It picks up dust on the way down, though, and is normally filtered before it is drunk.

The physics is dependable and the projects are not. A review of installations built in the 1990s found that many had stopped producing within five years, and in almost every case the cause was maintenance rather than design. Mesh tears at a corner and the tear spreads. Gutters block with dust and dead insects. A pipe works loose and the water runs into the ground beneath the frame, where nobody sees it. None of these faults is expensive to repair, and all of them are invisible from the village below. The installations that kept working were the ones with a named person paid to walk the line of nets once a week. Engineers who have worked on both kinds of scheme argue that who owns the nets matters more than what they are made of.

Nobody who works on these schemes presents them as a whole water supply. What the nets offer is a second source, one that depends on no road, no lorry and no fuel price. It is at its best in the cool months, when the wells are lowest. Not all of the water is drunk. On several ridges it has been used to raise tree seedlings, which need help only until their roots go deep. The mature trees then comb the fog themselves, on their leaves, and the drip beneath them wets the soil for nothing. That is the oldest version of the technology, and it was working long before anyone hung a net between two posts.

difficulty_rationale.note: Plain vocabulary and short sentences, but each paragraph states a fact, then its cost, then a verdict, and the joins between the three are left to the reader.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It argues that more of a good thing gives less, and the sentence carrying the reversal has no signpost in front of it.

questions.prompt: Tanker deliveries became more expensive as the villages grew larger.
questions.evidence_quote: at a price that rose with the distance
questions.explanation: Paragraph A gives one figure for the price of tankered water and one thing it varied with: the distance it had to be carried. The size of a village, and any change in it, is never mentioned anywhere in the passage.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic, the price of tankered water, is raised. The reason offered is distance. Growth is neither given as a cause nor ruled out as one, which is the NOT GIVEN condition exactly.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage supplies one reason for the price, so a reader who has found it treats any other reason as one the text refused.

distractors.why_wrong: That chain of reasoning is the reader's, not the passage's. Nothing here mentions growth at all.

teaching.reusable_rule: One stated cause does not exclude another. An unmentioned cause is unverifiable, and unverifiable is not the same as denied.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'vanishes' is nowhere in the passage, and a reader scanning for it comes back with nothing.

title: The Ward That Keeps You Lying Down

passage_json.title: The Ward That Keeps You Lying Down

paragraphs.text: A woman of eighty is admitted with a chest infection. The antibiotics work, and after three weeks she is well enough to go home. She is also no longer able to climb the stairs to her own bedroom, and within a month she has moved into residential care. Nothing went wrong. The treatment succeeded and the patient declined, and the two facts sit side by side in a discharge summary that records only the first. Clinicians have a name for what happened to her legs: deconditioning, the loss of strength, balance and confidence that follows a long spell of lying still.

The loss is quicker than most people expect and much slower to reverse. Healthy volunteers in their seventies who agree to stay in bed for ten days lose a measurable part of the muscle in their legs, and the strength goes faster than the bulk. In an ill patient the process is quicker still, because appetite falls at the same time and the body draws on muscle to meet the cost of the illness. What the studies agree on is the asymmetry. Strength that disappears in a fortnight of lying down commonly takes several months of ordinary activity to come back, and some of it never comes back at all.

Much of what keeps a patient in bed has nothing to do with the illness. A hospital gown is not made to be walked about in. A drip stand, a catheter bag and a monitor lead all tether the body to a small radius. Bed rails, fitted to stop people falling out at night, are not easy to climb over in the morning. The lavatory may be twenty metres away along a corridor with nothing to hold on to. Above all there is time: on a busy ward it is quicker for a nurse to fetch a bedpan than to walk a patient there and back. The routine of the ward settles around a bed rather than around a person who might leave it.

Wards respond to what is measured, and only one side of this problem is measured. A fall is an incident: it is recorded, counted, investigated and reported upward, and a ward whose falls are rising will be asked to explain itself. A patient who arrives able to walk to the shops and leaves unable to climb a flight of stairs generates no report at all. Rennick, a physiotherapist who has written about the problem in a nursing journal, argues that the asymmetry explains the behaviour of staff who are careful in every other respect. Nobody is ever praised for the patient who walked, and nobody is ever criticised for the patient who stayed safely in bed.

The remedies are unglamorous and mostly cheap. Some wards ask families to bring in day clothes and shoes, on the argument that a person in trousers behaves like a person who is going somewhere. Others post a mobility level above each bed, in the way a diet or an allergy is posted, so that a healthcare assistant does not have to guess whether the patient may walk. A few have recruited trained volunteers, who are not clinical staff, to walk with patients twice daily and to sit with those who are unsteady. The schemes are popular with patients, and their survival depends on how many staff a ward has. Where a ward was already short-handed, more than one programme has quietly lapsed within a year of its launch.

Whether any of this works is harder to establish than it looks. Trials of ward mobility programmes have been run in several countries, and they do not agree. Some report a shorter stay and fewer discharges to residential care; others find no measurable difference; one or two report a small rise in falls alongside a gain in strength. Part of the difficulty is that what counts as usual care differs so much from ward to ward that the comparison group in one trial would be the treatment group in another. Part of it is the choice of outcome. A programme judged on length of stay and a programme judged on whether the patient is still living at home a year later are not measuring the same thing. Aveley, who has reviewed the field, warns that the second question is both the more useful and the harder to fund.

One suggestion costs nothing. On the day of admission somebody asks what the person could do the week before, how far they walked, whether they managed stairs, whether they dressed themselves, and writes it down. That single line is a baseline, and without it decline is invisible. A patient who cannot cross the ward on the tenth day looks, to a nurse who never saw them on the first, like someone who was always like that. Recording is not preventing, and no baseline has ever got anybody out of bed. What it does is make a second question askable at discharge: not only whether the infection has gone, but whether the person going home is the person who came in.

difficulty_rationale.note: Everyday vocabulary carrying several qualified claims a paragraph, and an argument that travels from a body to a ward to a budget without ever announcing the move.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It reports three different findings and then explains why they cannot be added together, so a reader looking for a verdict takes the first one.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It gives you the case and the word the rest of the passage explains.
skim_plan.skip: The list of equipment in C and the three trial results in F. Both are detail the questions will send you back to.

paraphrase_families.passage_form: quietly lapsed within a year of its launch
rewordings: came to a halt without announcement
stopped running after its first year
the results point in opposite directions
conclusions vary from one study to the next

hinge_words.why_here: It gives one recovery time for everybody, which is what makes question 6 NOT GIVEN.
'Some ... others' splits the trials, and that split is what makes question 10 FALSE.
The remedies are mostly cheap, not entirely, which caps the heading chosen in question 4.
'whether the patient may walk' closes the purpose clause that question 12 turns on.

mineable.meaning: loss of strength and confidence after lying still
uses muscle as a source of energy
tie something so it cannot move far
produces no official written record
in all ways except this one
without enough staff to do the work
stopped without any formal decision
a first measurement later ones are compared with

question_groups.instructions_extra: There are more headings than paragraphs, so you will not use them all. Paragraphs A and G are not included.

options.text: A cost that lands on another budget
Muscle lost quickly, regained slowly
Why the trials reach different verdicts
A daily routine built around the bed
Why cautious staff choose the bed
Schemes that stand or fall on staffing
The rising price of a hospital bed
Recording what a patient could do before
Equipment that few wards can afford

teaching.strategy: Say what each paragraph does in six words before you read the list. Take C and E first: each opens with a sentence that states its whole point, and each heading you place removes one from play for the rest.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, so nothing narrows the search. Every paragraph in the group has to be read.
teaching.watch_out: Two of the unused headings name something a paragraph really contains. What a paragraph mentions is not what it is for.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence_quote: The loss is quicker than most people expect and much slower to reverse.
questions.explanation: Paragraph B is about a rate. It measures how fast strength goes in bed and how long it takes to return, and every sentence after the first supplies part of that comparison. Heading ii names both halves of it.
questions.trap_note: Heading vii is about money; the only cost paragraph B names is the metabolic cost of an illness.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: commonly takes several months of ordinary activity to come back
paraphrase_link.note: A whole clause about months of activity is compressed into one adverb.

teaching.decision_rule: The controlling idea is a rate of loss set against a rate of recovery. A heading naming only one of the two, or naming a cause instead, leaves half the paragraph unaccounted for.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph uses the language of cost, and a reader with money in mind reads 'the cost of the illness' as a price.
distractors.why_wrong: That cost is metabolic, and no price or budget appears in the paragraph at all.

distractors.why_tempting: 'What the studies agree on' puts research on the page, and a reader placing headings quickly attaches the research heading to the first research word they meet.
distractors.why_wrong: This paragraph reports what the studies agree on; the disagreement between them is paragraph F.

teaching.reusable_rule: A heading has to cover the whole paragraph. If half its sentences are unexplained by your choice, it is the wrong choice.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence_quote: Much of what keeps a patient in bed has nothing to do with the illness.
questions.explanation: The paragraph opens by ruling out the illness and then lists what does keep a patient still: clothing, equipment, distance and the time a nurse has. It ends by naming the arrangement all of that adds up to.
questions.trap_note: Three pieces of equipment appear in one sentence, but the paragraph never says what any of them costs.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: routine of the ward settles around a bed
paraphrase_link.note: A verb with its own subject in the text becomes a participle phrase in the heading.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph rules out one cause in its first sentence and spends the rest on the other, so the heading has to name the arrangement of the ward, not the illness or the equipment.

distractors.why_tempting: A drip stand, a catheter bag and a monitor lead sit in one sentence, and a reader matching nouns finds them immediately.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph never mentions the price of anything; the equipment is there because it restricts movement.

distractors.why_tempting: Bed rails are fitted to prevent falls, which is caution, and the paragraph does end on what a nurse finds quicker.
distractors.why_wrong: Caution as a motive is explained in paragraph D. Here the obstacles are physical and the nurse's choice is about time.

teaching.reusable_rule: A paragraph that opens by ruling out one cause is announcing that its subject is the other one.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence_quote: argues that the asymmetry explains the behaviour of staff who are careful in every other respect
questions.explanation: The paragraph states two facts about measurement, one recorded event and one that is not, and then uses the pair to explain why sensible staff leave a patient where they are. The explanation is what the paragraph is for.
questions.trap_note: Recording is the paragraph's own vocabulary, which makes the recording heading feel like a match even though what is recorded here is a fall.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: staff who are careful in every other respect
paraphrase_link.note: A qualified relative clause in the text is compressed to a single adjective in the heading.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph gives facts and then an inference drawn from them. A heading naming the facts covers two sentences; only one naming the inference covers the paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: Falls here are recorded, counted and investigated, so a reader hunting for the recording heading finds its vocabulary in this paragraph and nowhere else in the group.
distractors.why_wrong: What is recorded here is an event that has happened, not what the patient could do before admission.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph closes on a patient who stayed safely in bed, which sounds like the ward routine described earlier.
distractors.why_wrong: Paragraph C explains what makes movement difficult; this paragraph explains why nobody insists on it.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a paragraph gives facts and then an inference drawn from them, the heading belongs to the inference.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence_quote: their survival depends on how many staff a ward has
questions.explanation: Three remedies are described, all of them cheap, and the paragraph then states the one condition that decides whether they last. The final sentence gives the case where that condition failed.
questions.trap_note: The remedies are called cheap in the first sentence, so a heading about affording them contradicts the paragraph rather than summarising it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: their survival depends on how many staff a ward has
paraphrase_link.note: A noun of survival becomes a pair of verbs, and a count of people becomes one noun.

teaching.decision_rule: A list followed by a single condition is organised around the condition. The heading has to name what decides whether the remedies continue, not what they are.

distractors.why_tempting: Day clothes, shoes and a posted mobility level are all things a ward has to supply, so cost feels like the issue.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph calls the remedies mostly cheap; what they run short of is people, not money.

distractors.why_tempting: A mobility level posted above the bed is a written record, which matches the heading's first word.
distractors.why_wrong: It records what the patient may do now, not what they could do before they were admitted.

teaching.reusable_rule: A list followed by a condition is a paragraph about the condition. The list is the setting, not the point.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence_quote: Trials of ward mobility programmes have been run in several countries, and they do not agree.
questions.explanation: Every sentence after the first supplies a reason the results cannot be lined up: three different findings, a comparison group that means something different in each trial, and two different outcomes to judge on.
questions.trap_note: Funding appears in the last clause, but as the question that is harder to pay for, not as a cost moved to anybody else.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: they do not agree
paraphrase_link.note: A negated verb becomes a positive noun phrase: not agreeing is reaching different verdicts.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph asks a question in its first sentence and answers it with causes. A heading beginning 'Why' matches that shape; a heading naming one of the causes does not.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends on what is harder to fund and mentions discharges to residential care, so a budget heading has two hooks in it.
distractors.why_wrong: No cost is moved anywhere. Funding appears once, as a property of a research question.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who has not yet placed the staffing heading sees another paragraph about programmes and puts it here.
distractors.why_wrong: Staffing is not mentioned in this paragraph; what varies here is what the trials measured.

teaching.reusable_rule: If every sentence after the first answers the question 'why?', the heading is the question, not one of the answers.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage?

teaching.strategy: Underline the quantifier or the attribution in each statement before you look for it. Three of these five turn on a word like 'both' or 'consistently', and one turns on a comparison the passage never makes.
teaching.order_note: In passage order: question 9's answer sits below question 8's, so search that band and not the whole text.
teaching.watch_out: One statement is contradicted by the sentence after the one you locate. Read on before you decide.

questions.prompt: Patients who were physically active before their admission recover their strength more quickly.
questions.evidence_quote: Strength that disappears in a fortnight of lying down commonly takes several months of ordinary activity to come back
questions.explanation: Paragraph B gives one recovery time and gives it for everybody: several months of ordinary activity, with some strength never returning. It separates patients by age and by illness, never by what they did before they were admitted, and it compares no two rates of recovery.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the passage is silent about earlier fitness, and silence about something this plausible feels like a denial.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: takes several months of ordinary activity to come back
paraphrase_link.note: The link is real: coming back is recovering. The comparison attached to it is not in the text.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic, how fast strength returns, is addressed, and the claim about earlier activity is neither supported nor denied. No sentence has to be true or false for the statement to stand, which is the NOT GIVEN condition.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph says recovery takes ordinary activity, and a reader who already believes that fitter people recover faster reads the sentence as agreeing with them.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage attaches no recovery rate to anything the patient did before admission.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Some of it never comes back at all' sounds like a refusal of any quick recovery, for anyone.
distractors.why_wrong: That clause limits how much returns, not who returns it fastest, so it denies nothing in the statement.

teaching.reusable_rule: A rate given for everybody is not a comparison between two groups. If the text sorts nobody, a ranking cannot be checked.
teaching.nearest_text: Strength that disappears in a fortnight of lying down commonly takes several months of ordinary activity to come back

questions.prompt: Equipment intended to protect patients can also make it harder for them to move.
questions.evidence_quote: Bed rails, fitted to stop people falling out at night, are not easy to climb over in the morning.
questions.explanation: One sentence gives both halves of the statement about the same object: what bed rails are for, which is stopping people falling out at night, and what they cost the patient in the morning, when they are not easy to climb over.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: fitted to stop people falling out at night
paraphrase_link.note: A specific purpose in the text is restated as the general category of protection.

teaching.decision_rule: Both parts of the statement are asserted of the same object in one sentence, and neither part is stronger than the text. Nothing is left over for the passage to contradict or to leave open.

distractors.why_tempting: The rails are there for the patient's safety, so a reader who has decided the paragraph blames the ward expects the passage to deny that they help.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage states the protective purpose itself and then adds a second effect; adding is not denying.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement contains no word from the paragraph, not rails, not gown, not stand, so a keyword search returns nothing.
distractors.why_wrong: The proposition is stated in full about bed rails, which are the equipment the statement means.

teaching.reusable_rule: Look for the general noun that covers a specific one in the text. A category word is the commonest place a statement hides.

questions.prompt: Wards are required to account for both a rise in falls and a loss of strength among their patients.
questions.evidence_quote: A patient who arrives able to walk to the shops and leaves unable to climb a flight of stairs generates no report at all.
questions.explanation: The paragraph creates the obligation for one of the two events and removes it for the other. A ward whose falls are rising will be asked to explain itself; a patient who leaves weaker than they arrived generates no report, so there is nothing to account for.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: half the statement is confirmed in one sentence and the other half is refused in the next.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: a loss of strength among their patients
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: leaves unable to climb a flight of stairs
paraphrase_link.note: A concrete inability becomes an abstract noun, and 'both' extends an obligation the text gives to one case only.

teaching.decision_rule: TRUE needs every clause supported. The passage supports the falls half and states the opposite of the strength half, and an explicit denial makes the statement FALSE rather than unverifiable.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence before names exactly the obligation the statement describes, so the first half checks out on sight.
distractors.why_wrong: Confirming one half of a two-part statement leaves the half that decides it unchecked.

distractors.why_tempting: The word strength does not appear in the paragraph, so a reader hunting for it finds no sentence to judge.
distractors.why_wrong: The loss is described in plain terms, as a patient who can no longer manage stairs, and the passage says it generates no report.

teaching.reusable_rule: The word 'both' turns two claims into one statement. Check the half that is easy to skip, not the half that is easy to find.

questions.prompt: On some wards, patients are walked by helpers who are not members of the clinical staff.
questions.evidence_quote: A few have recruited trained volunteers, who are not clinical staff, to walk with patients twice daily
questions.explanation: The passage says a few wards have recruited trained volunteers, states in the same sentence that they are not clinical staff, and gives what they do: walking with patients twice a day. Every element of the statement is on the page.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: helpers who are not members of the clinical staff
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: trained volunteers, who are not clinical staff
paraphrase_link.note: Volunteers become the wider category of helpers, and the qualifying clause is kept almost word for word.

teaching.decision_rule: Each part of the statement matches a part of one sentence, and the statement's quantifier is no stronger than the passage's 'a few'. Nothing unsupported is left in it.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Trained' looks like the opposite of the statement's claim, so a reader treats the sentence as a contradiction of it.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage says trained and not clinical in the same breath; being trained is not the same as being on the clinical staff.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement's word 'helpers' appears nowhere, and a reader scanning for it moves past the sentence that answers it.
distractors.why_wrong: Volunteers who walk with patients are helpers, and the sentence states the whole proposition.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two facts inside one relative clause are still two facts. A qualifier beside a noun is part of what the text asserts.

questions.prompt: Trials of ward mobility programmes have consistently failed to show any benefit.
questions.evidence_quote: Some report a shorter stay and fewer discharges to residential care
questions.explanation: The passage divides the trials three ways: some found a shorter stay and fewer discharges to residential care, others found no measurable difference, and one or two found a rise in falls with a gain in strength. A benefit was reported, so a claim about every trial is denied by the first group.
questions.trap_note: The word 'consistently' is doing all the work, and the passage's own sentence lists the exception to it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: a shorter stay and fewer discharges to residential care
paraphrase_link.note: 'Benefit' is the category the two findings belong to; 'consistently' then extends one group's result to all of them.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement claims a uniform result. The passage states a divided one and names a benefit that was found, so there is a sentence to point at, which makes it FALSE rather than merely unverified.

distractors.why_tempting: The middle of the list does say that some trials found no measurable difference, and that is the half a reader remembers.
distractors.why_wrong: It is one of three findings, and the first of the three is a benefit.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Consistently' appears nowhere in the passage, so a reader hunting for the word finds nothing to judge.
distractors.why_wrong: Consistency is judged from the list itself, and the list contains a result that breaks it.

teaching.reusable_rule: An adverb like 'consistently' makes a claim about every case. One counter-example in the text settles it.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Answer the questions below with words taken from the passage.

teaching.strategy: Read the question word first, because it fixes the form of the answer before you search. Three of these four want a noun the passage supplies after a colon or a comma, so copy what is there and stop.
teaching.order_note: In order: each answer lies further down the passage than the one before it.
teaching.watch_out: The limit is two words. An article or an adjective you did not need turns a right answer into a zero.

questions.prompt: What name do clinicians give to the decline that follows a long period in bed?
questions.evidence_quote: Clinicians have a name for what happened to her legs: deconditioning, the loss of strength, balance and confidence that follows a long spell of lying still.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph A names the condition and then defines it. The word after the colon is the name; everything after the comma answers a different question, which is what the name means.
questions.trap_note: The definition runs to three nouns and the limit is two words, so copying the definition instead of the term scores nothing.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the decline that follows a long period in bed
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the loss of strength, balance and confidence that follows a long spell of lying still
paraphrase_link.note: Three nouns in the text are compressed into one abstract noun in the question.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks for a name and the passage supplies exactly one, introduced by a colon. The words after the comma answer what it is, and they are over the limit in any case.

distractors.why_tempting: It sits immediately after the answer and it describes what happened to the patient, which is what the reader has in mind.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the definition rather than the name, and it is three words against a limit of two.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the most concrete outcome in the paragraph and it is exactly two words long.
distractors.why_wrong: It is where the patient went, not what the decline is called.

teaching.reusable_rule: A colon often introduces a term and a comma its definition. Take whichever of the two the question word asks for.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What name' asks for a single noun, not the phrase that explains it.

questions.prompt: What is displayed above the bed on some wards so that staff need not guess?
questions.evidence_quote: Others post a mobility level above each bed, in the way a diet or an allergy is posted, so that a healthcare assistant does not have to guess whether the patient may walk.
questions.explanation: The sentence names what is posted above each bed and says why: so that a healthcare assistant does not have to guess whether the patient may walk. The two words in front of 'above each bed' are the answer.
questions.trap_note: A diet and an allergy are posted too, but they arrive as a comparison; they are not what this ward is posting.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: so that staff need not guess
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: so that a healthcare assistant does not have to guess
paraphrase_link.note: One job title becomes the general word staff, and 'does not have to' becomes 'need not'.

teaching.decision_rule: The question fixes the answer by position, as the thing displayed above the bed, and only one noun phrase in the paragraph fills that slot. The comparison items are introduced by 'in the way'.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the phrase as the passage writes it, article included, and copying the passage exactly feels like the safe move.
distractors.why_wrong: The article takes the answer to three words and past the limit.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's other visible thing, and it is supplied for the same purpose.
distractors.why_wrong: Day clothes are brought in by families, not displayed above the bed.

teaching.reusable_rule: Let the question's own preposition point at the slot. The answer is the phrase that fills it, without its article.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What is displayed' wants a noun phrase, and the article is not part of it.

questions.prompt: What differs so widely between wards that trial results are hard to compare?
questions.evidence_quote: what counts as usual care differs so much from ward to ward that the comparison group in one trial would be the treatment group in another
questions.explanation: The passage gives two reasons the trials cannot be lined up. The first is that usual care itself varies, and it varies so far that one trial's comparison group would be another trial's treatment group.
questions.trap_note: 'Comparison group' is in the same clause and is two words long, but it is the consequence of the variation, not the thing that varies.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: differs so much from ward to ward
paraphrase_link.note: Only the degree adverb and the preposition change, and the verb is the passage's own.

teaching.decision_rule: The question asks what varies, so the answer is the subject of the verb 'differs'. Everything else in the sentence is a consequence of that variation.

distractors.why_tempting: It is two words, it sits in the same clause, and it is what the sentence is visibly about.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the effect of the variation. What varies is what counts as usual care.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's second reason, and it does vary from trial to trial.
distractors.why_wrong: It differs between trials rather than between wards, and it is four words long.

teaching.reusable_rule: Find the verb the question borrowed and take its subject. A question about what varies is a question about a grammatical slot.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What differs' wants the subject of that verb, so a noun phrase and not a clause.

questions.prompt: According to the last paragraph, what cannot be seen when nobody has noted what a patient could do beforehand?
questions.evidence_quote: That single line is a baseline, and without it decline is invisible.
questions.explanation: Paragraph G says the note taken on admission is a baseline and that without it decline is invisible. The question replaces 'invisible' with 'cannot be seen', so the answer is the noun that the passage calls invisible.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: decline is invisible
paraphrase_link.note: An adjective becomes a negated verb phrase, which is why scanning for 'seen' finds nothing.

teaching.decision_rule: The question's frame, what cannot be seen, matches one predicate in the paragraph, and the answer is that predicate's subject, a single noun well inside the limit.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the sentence's other noun and the paragraph's central idea.
distractors.why_wrong: The baseline is what is missing, not what cannot be seen because it is missing.

distractors.why_tempting: The rest of the passage is about a patient who cannot cross the ward, so the eye lands there next.
distractors.why_wrong: The patient is perfectly visible; what is not is the change in them.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a question negates an adjective, look for the positive one in the text and take the noun it is attached to.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'What cannot be seen' wants the subject of the passage's own 'is invisible'.

paragraphs.text: Radio spectrum is the least visible public asset in the modern economy and one of the most valuable. Every mobile call, every contactless payment and every remote door lock occupies a slice of it. Two strong signals sent on the same frequency in the same place will spoil each other, so somebody has to decide who may transmit where. Governments have made that decision for a century, and the machinery they built for it still shapes the industry. What is less often noticed is that the bands now carrying the greatest volume of everyday traffic are not the ones that were fought over. They are the leftovers: stretches of frequency set aside for industrial machinery because they were thought too dirty to be worth licensing.

For most of the twentieth century a regulator simply assigned frequencies. It weighed the claims of broadcasters, the military, shipping and the emergency services in private, and issued a licence to whichever applicant it preferred. The method was slow, and it rewarded incumbency. A company granted a band in 1950 was hard to dislodge in 1985, even when its equipment used it badly. From the 1990s most industrialised countries turned to auctions instead. Bidders paid for exclusive national use of a band for a fixed term, sums running into billions arrived in national treasuries. One proposition became the standard defence of the whole apparatus: the price a bidder will pay reveals the value it can create.

Meanwhile a handful of narrow bands had been reserved for a quite different purpose. Industrial, scientific and medical equipment radiates energy as a by-product: welders, dryers and the domestic microwave oven all leak it. Rather than police that leakage, the authorities set aside frequencies where it would be tolerated. Nothing in those bands was protected: any device operating there had to accept whatever interference it met. In the 1980s regulators went further and permitted low-power communication in the same stretches, on condition that transmitters kept their output small and spread their signal thinly. No licence was required and no payment was made. Within twenty years the unlicensed bands were carrying more data each day than the licensed mobile networks above them.

The engineer Halden Rees has argued for years that this outcome should surprise nobody, because interference was never a property of the air. It is a property of equipment. A receiver that cannot separate a weak wanted signal from a strong unwanted one beside it is a badly designed receiver. The cost of protecting it is paid by everybody else, in the form of empty guard bands. On the central point Rees is plainly right. Transmitters that hop between frequencies many times a second, listen before they speak and retreat when they hear another user have made a given slice of spectrum carry perhaps thirty times what it carried in 1990. The capacity of a band is then fixed not by physics but by the state of the art in the boxes at either end.

Against this stands a case put most forcefully by the economist Priya Nandalal, who maintains that only exclusive licences, sold at auction, will place a band in the hands of the operator able to use it best. Her reasoning is that nobody will lay out the cost of a national network on a frequency a competitor may swamp next year. There is something in it. Long-lived, capital-hungry investments do sit in licensed bands, while the shared bands house cheap equipment with short lives. But the claim proves less than it appears to. It explains why exclusivity suits one kind of investment. It does not show that exclusivity is the efficient default for a band, still less that an auction measures anything beyond what a bidder can raise.

The strongest objection to sharing is congestion, and it is not imaginary. In a dense block of flats a single unlicensed channel may be contested by forty households, and the throughput each of them sees falls accordingly. In the end a shared band offers no guarantee whatever, which is why no hospital runs its patient monitoring on one. Yet the picture is uneven. Surveys of how much licensed spectrum is actually in use keep returning the same awkward finding: one study of a mid-sized city recorded average occupancy below fifteen per cent outside the broadcasting and mobile allocations. Exclusive assignment manufactures scarcity in the bands that are shared and an abundance nobody may touch in the bands that are not.

A third arrangement has been emerging that fits neither template. Instead of granting a band to one holder or opening it to all comers, the regulator ranks users in tiers and lets a database decide, minute by minute, who may transmit and at what power. An incumbent keeps absolute priority, a second tier buys short local rights, and anyone else may use what is left. The scheme was introduced for coastal radar bands and has since been extended to others. It is administratively heavy, and it rests on a database that nobody has yet had to defend against a determined attacker. Even so, it shows that the choice was never really between an owner and a free-for-all. The question a regulator should have to answer is no longer why a band ought to be shared, but why it ought not to be.

difficulty_rationale.note: Two named positions, one endorsed and one only partly granted, with the writer's own verdict withheld until the final sentence. The reader must track whose claim is on the page at every point.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It concedes half of an argument it is about to refuse, and the concession is longer than the refusal.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It tells you the passage is about bands nobody wanted.
skim_plan.skip: The list of leaky equipment in C and the tier descriptions in G. They are detail the questions will send you back for.

paraphrase_families.passage_form: too dirty to be worth licensing
had to accept whatever interference it met
rewordings: was obliged to live with disruption
had no right to a clear channel

paraphrase_families.passage_form: proves less than it appears to
rewordings: does not carry the weight placed on it
establishes only half of the case
the share of time a band is busy
how full it turns out to be

hinge_words.why_here: 'only exclusive licences' is the strong claim question 9 is built on.
'no guarantee whatever' is what makes question 6 a NO.
It marks the motive that decides question 7.
'may be contested by forty households' hedges the claim behind question 11.

as an unintended side effect of something else
unused frequencies left as a buffer
