question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer of the passage?

teaching.strategy: Ask of every statement whose claim it is: the writer's, Rees's, or Nandalal's. Two of these six turn on that alone. Then mark the comparative or the guarantee word before you go looking, because that is what each one is really testing.
teaching.order_note: In passage order. Question 4's evidence lies below question 3's, so bracket the search and never read upwards.
teaching.watch_out: Two statements borrow a named figure's opinion and hand it to the writer. Whose view it is decides the answer.

questions.prompt: The frequencies that now carry most everyday traffic were once considered unattractive.
questions.evidence_quote: stretches of frequency set aside for industrial machinery because they were thought too dirty to be worth licensing
questions.explanation: Paragraph A ends by saying that the bands now carrying the greatest volume of everyday traffic are the leftovers, set aside for industrial machinery because they were thought too dirty to be worth licensing. Both halves of the statement are the writer's own assertion.
questions.trap_note: The proposition is stated in words the statement does not share, so a keyword search returns nothing.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: thought too dirty to be worth licensing
paraphrase_link.note: A vivid judgement in the text flattens into one evaluative adjective in the statement.

teaching.decision_rule: YES needs the writer to assert the whole statement. The final sentence supplies both halves: these are the bands now carrying most traffic, and they were dismissed as not worth a licence.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph opens by calling spectrum one of the most valuable assets there is, which reads as the opposite of unattractive.
distractors.why_wrong: That value belongs to spectrum as a whole. The leftover bands are separately described as not worth a licence.

distractors.why_tempting: Neither 'attractive' nor 'considered' appears anywhere, so a reader hunting for the statement's words finds none of them.
distractors.why_wrong: The judgement is stated in the last clause of the paragraph, in the writer's own voice.

teaching.reusable_rule: A judgement expressed as scorn is still a judgement. Match the meaning, not the register.

questions.prompt: Auctions raised more money for governments than the licensing system they replaced.
questions.evidence_quote: Bidders paid for exclusive national use of a band for a fixed term, sums running into billions arrived in national treasuries
questions.explanation: Paragraph B gives what auctions brought in but says nothing at all about the revenue of the earlier system of administrative assignment. One side of the comparison is on the page and the other is missing, so the ranking cannot be checked.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the passage is silent about the older system's revenue, and silence beside a large figure feels like a denial.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: sums running into billions arrived in national treasuries
paraphrase_link.note: The link is genuine and the comparison the statement adds on top of it is not.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and one side of the comparison is given. Nothing states or denies what the earlier system raised, so neither YES nor NO can be defended.

distractors.why_tempting: Billions in the treasury sounds decisive, and the paragraph has just called the older method slow and captured by whoever held the band.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage gives no figure, and no description, of what the assignment system earned. There is nothing to compare it with.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who cannot find the older revenue anywhere may take that absence as a denial that it amounted to anything.
distractors.why_wrong: No sentence here says auctions raised less, or the same. Absence of a figure is not a contradiction.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two amounts must both be on the page before a comparison can be checked. One figure and a gap is not a ranking.
teaching.nearest_text: sums running into billions arrived in national treasuries

questions.prompt: Devices operating in the bands reserved for industrial equipment were guaranteed protection from interference.
questions.evidence_quote: Nothing in those bands was protected: any device operating there had to accept whatever interference it met.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C states the opposite twice in one sentence: nothing in those bands was protected, and any device there had to accept whatever interference it met. An obligation to accept interference is the denial of a guarantee against it.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial arrives after a colon, in a clause a reader who has found the topic may not finish.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: had to accept whatever interference it met
paraphrase_link.note: 'Had to accept' is the negation of 'protected from', carried by an obligation rather than by a not.

teaching.decision_rule: NO requires a quotable denial. The colon splits the sentence into a claim and its consequence, and the consequence, accepting whatever arrives, cannot stand beside a guarantee.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Reserved', 'set aside' and 'tolerated' all suggest a protected status, and the paragraph is about frequencies allotted on purpose.
distractors.why_wrong: What was set aside was the tolerance of interference, not freedom from it. The next clause says so directly.

distractors.why_tempting: The word 'guaranteed' never appears, so a reader hunting for a promise or a refusal of one finds neither.
distractors.why_wrong: The contradiction is in the same sentence as the topic, worded as 'Nothing in those bands was protected'.

teaching.reusable_rule: A duty to put up with something is the denial of a right to be free of it. Read obligations as claims.

questions.prompt: In the writer's view, how much traffic a band can carry depends on the equipment using it.
questions.evidence_quote: The capacity of a band is then fixed not by physics but by the state of the art in the boxes at either end.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D endorses Rees on the central point and then draws the consequence in the writer's own voice: capacity is fixed by the state of the art in the equipment at each end rather than by physics. That is the statement exactly.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: depends on the equipment using it
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: fixed not by physics but by the state of the art in the boxes at either end
paraphrase_link.note: 'The boxes at either end' is the passage's plain gloss for the transmitter and the receiver.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer marks his agreement first, so what follows is his claim rather than a reported one. The not-X-but-Y sentence states the whole statement and hedges none of it.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Interference was never a property of the air' sounds like a denial that anything physical is involved, which overshoots the statement.
distractors.why_wrong: The statement makes the weaker claim that equipment sets the limit, and the paragraph asserts precisely that.

distractors.why_tempting: The claim is introduced through a named engineer, so a cautious reader treats the whole paragraph as somebody else's opinion.
distractors.why_wrong: 'On the central point Rees is plainly right' is the writer taking the view over. After that sentence it is his.

teaching.reusable_rule: Once a writer says a cited figure is right, everything that follows is the writer's claim too. Find that sentence before deciding.

questions.prompt: Nandalal has revised her position since the shared bands began to carry more traffic.
questions.evidence_quote: Against this stands a case put most forcefully by the economist Priya Nandalal
questions.explanation: Paragraph E reports what Nandalal maintains and then gives the writer's objection to it. Nothing anywhere says what she thought earlier or thinks now, so a change of mind can be neither confirmed nor denied.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: a present-tense report of somebody's position says nothing about its history, and that silence reads as a denial.

teaching.decision_rule: The paragraph supplies her position and the writer's objection to it. A change of mind is a separate proposition, and the text neither supports it nor rules it out.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer spends the rest of the paragraph dismantling her case, and a reader may take the rebuttal as evidence that she has since conceded.
distractors.why_wrong: The rebuttal belongs to the writer. Nothing at all is said about what Nandalal now thinks.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Maintains' is a present tense of continuing insistence, which feels like an explicit statement that she has not moved.
distractors.why_wrong: It reports her position, not its history. No earlier or later view is mentioned.

teaching.reusable_rule: A verb reporting what somebody currently holds says nothing about what they held before. Do not read a history into a present tense.
teaching.nearest_text: who maintains that only exclusive licences, sold at auction, will place a band in the hands of the operator able to use it best

questions.prompt: The writer considers shared bands suitable for services that cannot tolerate interruption.
questions.evidence_quote: a shared band offers no guarantee whatever, which is why no hospital runs its patient monitoring on one
questions.explanation: Paragraph F concedes that congestion is real and gives the consequence: a shared band offers no guarantee whatever, which is why patient monitoring is not run on one. The writer names the one service that cannot tolerate interruption and rules a shared band out for it.
questions.trap_note: Accurate but irrelevant: the paragraph's later defence of sharing is about how much room exists, not about reliability.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: no hospital runs its patient monitoring on one
paraphrase_link.note: Patient monitoring is the passage's single instance of the category the statement names.

teaching.decision_rule: NO needs a sentence the statement cannot stand beside. 'No guarantee whatever', with the hospital clause attached as its consequence, denies exactly the suitability asserted.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph goes on to say the picture is uneven and that licensed bands sit largely empty, which reads as a defence of sharing.
distractors.why_wrong: That defence concerns how much room exists, not whether a shared band can be relied on from one minute to the next.

distractors.why_tempting: Neither 'suitable' nor 'interruption' appears, and the deciding clause is subordinate, tucked in after a semicolon.
distractors.why_wrong: The clause states the writer's reason outright: no guarantee, therefore not used where reliability is required.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a writer concedes ground and then limits the concession, the position is in the limit, not in the concession.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

teaching.strategy: Read the stem alone and decide what kind of thing answers it: a motive, a cause, an objection, a verdict. Three of these four stems ask for the writer's own move, so an option that merely reports a fact in the paragraph cannot be it.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, and it starts again at paragraph C. Question 10 is in the last paragraph.
teaching.watch_out: Every wrong option here is true of something in the passage. Truth is not the test; answering this stem is.

questions.prompt: Why were the bands used by industrial, scientific and medical equipment originally set aside?
questions.evidence_quote: the authorities set aside frequencies where it would be tolerated
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says that equipment of this kind radiates energy as a by-product and that, rather than police the leakage, the authorities set aside frequencies where it would be tolerated. The motive was somewhere to put stray emissions.
questions.trap_note: Option A describes a permission granted in the 1980s, decades after the bands were reserved.

options.text: To reserve capacity for communication equipment of low power.
To provide somewhere that stray emissions could be permitted.
To keep the domestic microwave oven away from broadcasting.
To relieve the pressure on bands already sold at auction.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: somewhere that stray emissions could be permitted
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: frequencies where it would be tolerated
paraphrase_link.note: 'Tolerated' becomes 'permitted', and the pronoun 'it' is spelled out as the emissions themselves.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for the original purpose. Only the clause introduced by 'rather than' supplies a motive, and it names tolerance of leakage rather than any communications aim.

distractors.why_tempting: Low-power communication is indeed permitted in these bands, and the paragraph says so two sentences later.
distractors.why_wrong: That permission arrived in the 1980s, long after the bands were reserved. The stem asks about the original purpose.

distractors.why_tempting: The microwave oven is the one household object named, so it feels like the reason the bands exist at all.
distractors.why_wrong: It is offered as an example of equipment that leaks, not as the motive for the reservation.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous paragraph ends on auctions and crowded demand, and relieving pressure is a plausible regulatory motive.
distractors.why_wrong: The reservation came long before the auctions, and the passage never links the two.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem asking why something began is answered by the motive stated at the beginning, not by a later use.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say has changed the amount of traffic a band can carry?
questions.evidence_quote: Transmitters that hop between frequencies many times a second, listen before they speak and retreat when they hear another user have made a given slice of spectrum carry perhaps thirty times what it carried in 1990.
questions.explanation: Paragraph D makes the transmitters themselves the grammatical subject of the change: those that hop, listen before transmitting and back away from a busy channel have multiplied what a given slice of spectrum carries.
questions.trap_note: Option B borrows 'guard bands' from two sentences earlier, where they are named as a cost rather than as something removed.

options.text: A reduction in the power that transmitters are allowed to use.
The removal of guard bands between neighbouring allocations.
A physical limit that had been wrongly calculated in the past.
Behaviour built into transmitters that lets them avoid each other.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: listen before they speak and retreat when they hear another user
paraphrase_link.note: Three described behaviours are compressed into one category: getting out of one another's way.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a cause the writer states. The only causal subject in the paragraph is the transmitters' own conduct, which the sentence makes the subject of 'have made'.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage does require transmitters to keep their output small, and lower power genuinely does reduce interference.
distractors.why_wrong: That condition sits in the previous paragraph and is a rule of entry to the band, not the source of the increase.

distractors.why_tempting: Empty guard bands are named two sentences earlier as a cost, so removing them looks like the obvious remedy.
distractors.why_wrong: They are given as what a poor receiver costs everyone else. The passage never says any were removed.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph ends by denying that physics fixes capacity, which sounds like the correction of an old miscalculation.
distractors.why_wrong: It says the limit moves with the equipment, not that anybody had once worked it out wrongly.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a stem asks what produced a change, take the option describing what the things themselves now do.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's objection to Nandalal's case?
questions.evidence_quote: It explains why exclusivity suits one kind of investment. It does not show that exclusivity is the efficient default for a band
questions.explanation: Paragraph E grants her reasoning and then limits what it establishes: it explains why exclusivity suits one kind of investment, but not that exclusivity should be the default arrangement for a band. The objection is about how far the conclusion reaches.
questions.trap_note: Option D reverses the passage: short-lived shared-band equipment is offered in support of her case, not against it.

options.text: It supports a narrower conclusion than the one she draws.
It relies on evidence that other researchers have questioned.
It confuses the price of a licence with the length of its term.
It ignores the short working lives of most shared-band devices.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: a narrower conclusion than the one she draws
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: explains why exclusivity suits one kind of investment
paraphrase_link.note: 'One kind of investment' against her 'only exclusive licences': the text names the smaller claim and the option labels it.

teaching.decision_rule: The writer grants the premises and refuses the conclusion's reach: one case explained, the general default not. Only an option about scope matches that move.

distractors.why_tempting: Disagreement between experts is the usual shape of an academic objection, and the passage does set two named figures against each other.
distractors.why_wrong: No evidence of hers is challenged, and no third party is mentioned in the paragraph at all.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph contains both a price and a fixed term, and the final clause is about what an auction measures.
distractors.why_wrong: That clause says an auction measures what a bidder can raise. The length of a licence is never part of the objection.

distractors.why_tempting: Cheap equipment with short lives appears in the sentence right after the writer's concession, so it reads as a complaint.
distractors.why_wrong: He offers it in support of her point, immediately after conceding that there is something in it.

teaching.reusable_rule: An objection of the form 'this proves less than claimed' attacks the size of a conclusion, not the truth of the premises.

questions.prompt: What does the writer conclude about the tiered arrangement described in the final paragraph?
questions.evidence_quote: it shows that the choice was never really between an owner and a free-for-all
questions.explanation: Paragraph G lists the scheme's costs and its untested weakness and then draws one conclusion from it: the familiar pair of options, exclusive ownership or open access, was not the whole set. The closing question follows from that reframing.
questions.trap_note: Option D turns a question the writer puts to regulators into a prediction he never makes.

options.text: It has proved secure enough to be extended to further bands.
It costs less to run than either of the older approaches.
It shows that the familiar pair of choices was incomplete.
It will replace exclusive licensing within a single decade.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the familiar pair of choices was incomplete
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the choice was never really between an owner and a free-for-all
paraphrase_link.note: A denial about the case becomes a statement about the list of options, which is the same claim turned round.

teaching.decision_rule: The verdict sentence is about how the argument has been framed, not about cost, security or timing. Only the option describing the framing survives.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does say the scheme has been extended to others, and extension normally follows a good record.
distractors.why_wrong: The extension is reported; security is the one thing the writer says has not yet been tested.

distractors.why_tempting: A third way that settles a long argument sounds like the cheaper option, and cost is the usual ground of these debates.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer calls it administratively heavy, which is the opposite claim.

distractors.why_tempting: The last sentence shifts the burden of proof onto exclusivity, which reads like a forecast of its end.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer proposes a question a regulator should have to answer. No timetable and no replacement is offered.

teaching.reusable_rule: A closing sentence that reframes a debate is not a forecast. Separate what a writer asks from what a writer predicts.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete the summary below using words from the passage.

layout.title: Sharing in practice
lines: The strongest argument against sharing a band is {{11}}.
One survey of a mid-sized city found average {{12}} in the licensed bands below fifteen per cent.
Under a third approach the regulator sorts users into {{13}}, and a database decides who may transmit.
The arrangement was first used for {{14}} bands and later extended.

teaching.strategy: Everything here comes from the last two paragraphs, so locate that stretch once and stay inside it. Fix the word class of each gap first: two want a singular noun, one a plural, one a two-word modifier standing in front of 'bands'.
teaching.order_note: All four sit in paragraphs F and G, in that order. Find the stretch once, then work down it.
teaching.watch_out: Two words maximum, copied exactly. A dropped modifier and a singular for a plural both score zero here.

questions.prompt: The strongest argument against sharing a band is {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: The strongest objection to sharing is congestion
questions.explanation: Paragraph F opens by naming the strongest objection to sharing as congestion, and immediately concedes that it is not imaginary. The summary keeps the frame and asks for the noun the passage puts in it.
questions.trap_note: The summary writes 'argument against' where the passage writes 'objection to', so the sentence will not be found by matching the noun.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The strongest objection to sharing
paraphrase_link.note: One noun is swapped and its preposition follows it: 'objection to' becomes 'argument against'.

teaching.decision_rule: The summary reproduces the passage's own frame, 'the strongest X against sharing is ___', so the answer is the noun already filling that slot in the text.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the passage's subject in every other respect and the word a learner expects a spectrum text to supply here.
distractors.why_wrong: It does not appear in this paragraph, and a summary gap is filled from the passage's own wording.

distractors.why_tempting: It sits immediately after the noun and reads as the paragraph's verdict on the objection.
distractors.why_wrong: It completes 'it is', not 'the strongest argument against sharing is'. The frame wants the name of the objection.

teaching.reusable_rule: Swap the summary's noun for a synonym before you scan. The text rarely uses the word the summary chose.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap completes 'is', so it takes a singular uncountable noun.

questions.prompt: One survey of a mid-sized city found average {{gap}} in the licensed bands below fifteen per cent.
questions.evidence_quote: one study of a mid-sized city recorded average occupancy below fifteen per cent
questions.explanation: Paragraph F reports a study of a mid-sized city that recorded average occupancy below fifteen per cent outside the broadcasting and mobile allocations. The summary changes 'study' to 'survey' and 'recorded' to 'found' and leaves the measured quantity in the gap.
questions.trap_note: The number the sentence exists to deliver is already printed in the summary line, so it cannot be the answer.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: One survey of a mid-sized city found
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: one study of a mid-sized city recorded average occupancy
paraphrase_link.note: A noun and a verb are swapped for near-equivalents; the figures on either side are what keep the sentence findable.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between 'average' and a prepositional phrase, so it takes the name of the quantity measured. The passage offers exactly one noun in that position.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence before speaks of how much of the licensed spectrum is actually in use, and the meaning is right.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Average use' is not what the passage writes here, and a completion answer is copied from the sentence being summarised.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the figure the sentence exists to deliver, and numbers feel like the answer in a completion task.
distractors.why_wrong: It already stands after the gap in the summary line, and at three words it breaks the limit as well.

teaching.reusable_rule: A figure already printed in the gapped line is not the missing word. Fill what the line has left out.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'average' before the gap wants a singular uncountable noun, not a verb.

questions.prompt: Under a third approach the regulator sorts users into {{gap}}, and a database decides who may transmit.
questions.evidence_quote: the regulator ranks users in tiers and lets a database decide, minute by minute, who may transmit and at what power
questions.explanation: Paragraph G describes a third arrangement in which the regulator ranks users in tiers and a database decides minute by minute who may transmit. The summary substitutes 'sorts into' for 'ranks in' and leaves the plural noun in the gap.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the regulator ranks users in tiers
paraphrase_link.note: Only the verb and its preposition move: 'ranks ... in' becomes 'sorts ... into'.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap follows 'into', which requires a plural count noun, and only one noun in the matching clause meets that frame.

distractors.why_tempting: The next sentence writes 'a second tier', so the singular is on the page and looks like the passage's own form.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Into' takes the plural here, and the sentence being summarised writes 'tiers'.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the most concrete noun in the sentence and the thing that does the deciding.
distractors.why_wrong: It is already named later in the same summary line. The gap wants what the users are sorted into.

teaching.reusable_rule: A plural frame will not accept the singular you saw in a neighbouring sentence. Copy from the sentence you are summarising.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'into' before the gap wants a plural noun, not a singular one.

questions.prompt: The arrangement was first used for {{gap}} bands and later extended.
questions.evidence_quote: The scheme was introduced for coastal radar bands and has since been extended to others
questions.explanation: Paragraph G says the scheme was introduced for coastal radar bands and has since been extended to others. The summary keeps the passive frame and swaps two words, so the answer is the two-word modifier the passage puts in front of 'bands'.
questions.trap_note: One word fits the frame comfortably, which is exactly why the modifier gets dropped.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The arrangement was first used for
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The scheme was introduced for
paraphrase_link.note: Two words swapped inside an identical passive frame, which is why the sentence is still findable by shape.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap precedes 'bands', and the passage names one kind of band the scheme began with. The modifier is two words, which the limit allows.

distractors.why_tempting: One word is the safer guess under a two-word limit, and 'radar bands' reads perfectly well on its own.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage writes 'coastal radar bands', and the modifier it supplies is part of the answer.

distractors.why_tempting: The incumbent is the first tier named in the paragraph, and 'first' in the summary line pulls a reader towards it.
distractors.why_wrong: 'First' here dates the scheme's introduction. It does not rank the users.

teaching.reusable_rule: A two-word limit is a permission, not a target, but a modifier the text supplies is part of the answer.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap modifies 'bands', so it wants the two-word phrase used as an adjective.

paragraphs.text: A woodland is asked two questions about its carbon, and they are not the same question. The first is how much it holds: the mass locked up in trunks, branches, roots, dead wood and soil at a single moment. The second is whether that mass is rising or falling, and how fast. Foresters call the first a stock and the second a flux, and confusing the two is the commonest error in the field. A wood can hold an enormous stock and be adding nothing to it, much as a full reservoir is not a river. The instruments that answer the two questions are different, and they cost very different amounts. They also disagree with one another often enough that the disagreement has become a research topic in its own right.

The oldest technique is also the easiest to describe. A plot is marked out, every tree in it is measured round the trunk at chest height, and the site is surveyed again some years later. Girth is converted to mass by an equation built from a small number of trees that were felled, dried and weighed. The plots at Tarnbeck were laid out in the 1970s and have been remeasured at ten-year intervals ever since. Naysmith, who has run the network there for two decades, argues that the tape is not where the uncertainty sits. Crews measure girth to within a few millimetres. The conversion is another matter, because an equation calibrated on thirty felled trees of one species is then applied to a hundred thousand standing trees on soils it never saw.

A flux tower asks the second question directly. A mast is raised above the canopy and carries instruments that record the concentration of carbon dioxide and the movement of the air many times a second. From these data the exchange between the wood and the atmosphere is computed. Aldrich, whose tower stands on Carrow Ridge, has published figures from it for eleven years. The striking feature of the record is its instability. In most years the wood took up carbon; in the drought summer of the ninth year it released more than it absorbed and finished the year as a source rather than a sink. A single annual figure from such a record describes the weather as much as the wood.

Roughly half of the carbon in a temperate woodland is out of sight, in roots, in dead wood and above all in the soil. It is also the half that is hardest to weigh. Quintrell, who samples soil at both Tarnbeck and Carrow Ridge, maintains that the difficulty is not one of chemistry but of arithmetic. A soil core can be analysed accurately. The obstacle is one of proportion: the annual change is minute beside the stock it is part of, so a decade of sampling may not be able to distinguish a gain from no change at all. Her cores are therefore reliable for saying how much is there and close to useless for saying which way it is moving.

Neither plots nor towers can be put everywhere, which is the appeal of surveying from the air. An aircraft carrying a laser scanner sweeps a valley in an afternoon and returns a map of canopy height, from which mass is estimated by yet another equation. Bellamy, who flew the surveys over the Elsdale plantations, found that the maps agreed closely with the ground plots on young and middling stands. On the oldest stands they did not. Above a certain height the canopy closes and the signal stops separating a tall wood from a taller one, so the method understates exactly the stands that hold the most. Bellamy's remedy was to retain a subset of ground plots in the oldest blocks and calibrate the maps against them.

Ferriby's contribution has been to argue that much of the disagreement is not empirical at all. Two studies of an identical wood will differ if one counts the soil to a depth of thirty centimetres and the other to a metre. They will differ again if one counts the dead wood lying on the floor and the other does not, or if one treats timber cut and carried away as a loss on the day it leaves. None of those choices is wrong; they are boundaries, and a figure without its boundary cannot be compared with anything. Ferriby's proposal, that every published estimate should state its boundary in its first line, has been adopted by some journals and ignored by others.

What a landowner requires in the end is a number that can be repeated. Truscott compared the four approaches on cost per hectare and concluded that the cheapest method, repeated on a fixed schedule, will detect a trend sooner than the most accurate one performed once. That conclusion is uncomfortable for a discipline that has spent forty years improving accuracy, and it points at what the arguments over instruments tend to obscure. A forest changes slowly, and a measurement that is not repeated tells you where you are without telling you where you are going.

difficulty_rationale.note: Six named positions in seven paragraphs, each stated once and never restated, resting on an abstract contrast between an amount and a rate that the passage draws only in its first paragraph.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It argues that an accurate measurement can still be useless, which needs the difference between a total and its yearly change held in mind.

skim_plan.read_first: The title and all of paragraph A. It gives the one distinction, amount held against rate of change, that the rest depends on.
skim_plan.skip: The list of boundaries in F and the description of the instruments in C. They are detail, and the questions will send you back.

teaching.strategy: Six names, six paragraphs, one name each. Find the names first and write one word beside each: conversion, tower, soil, laser, boundaries, cost. Then match the statements to those words instead of rereading the paragraphs.
teaching.order_note: Not in order. Each name is used once, so every name you place removes an option from the list.
teaching.watch_out: Four of the six researchers complain that a figure cannot be trusted. Separate them by what each one distrusts.

questions.prompt: The measurements this researcher takes are accurate in themselves but too coarse to show the direction of change.
questions.evidence_quote: a decade of sampling may not be able to distinguish a gain from no change at all
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says a soil core can be analysed accurately, and then that the yearly change is tiny beside the stock it belongs to, so ten years of sampling may still not separate a gain from nothing. Accurate, and not sensitive enough.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: may not be able to distinguish a gain from no change at all

teaching.decision_rule: Only one named position in the passage separates the accuracy of a measurement from its power to detect movement. The statement asserts both halves, so it belongs to that position alone.

distractors.why_tempting: This researcher also splits an accurate measurement from an untrustworthy step, so the shape of the claim looks identical.

distractors.why_tempting: The unused name belongs to the passage's other voice on what a method can and cannot reveal over time.
distractors.why_wrong: That comparison is about cost and repetition across all four approaches, and never touches soil sampling.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Girth is converted to mass by an equation

distractors.why_tempting: This is the passage's specialist in why published figures cannot be trusted, so any statement about error attracts the name.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: cannot be set against one another
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: cannot be compared with anything
paraphrase_link.note: One idiom replaces another and nothing else changes, so the item turns on whose paragraph it sits in.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement is about the relation between two studies rather than about any instrument. Only one named position in the passage is about relations between studies.

distractors.why_tempting: This is the passage's other critic of how a number is produced, and the statement criticises numbers.
distractors.why_wrong: That criticism is aimed at a conversion step inside one method, not at comparing two studies that counted different things.

distractors.why_tempting: Soil depth is one of the choices this paragraph lists, and one researcher in the passage works entirely on soil.
distractors.why_wrong: The depth appears here as an example of a boundary. The soil researcher's own claim is about detecting movement.

teaching.reusable_rule: An example inside an argument belongs to the arguer, not to whoever studies the thing the example is about.

questions.prompt: This researcher's record contains a year in which the woodland gave out more carbon than it took in.

questions.explanation: Paragraph C reports eleven years of tower measurements and singles out the drought summer of the ninth year, when the wood released more carbon than it took up and ended the year as a source instead of a sink.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: gave out more carbon than it took in
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: released more than it absorbed
paraphrase_link.note: Two everyday verbs replace two formal ones. The comparison between them is untouched.

teaching.decision_rule: Only one method in the passage produces a yearly figure for exchange at all, so only one record can contain a year of net loss.

distractors.why_tempting: That paragraph also reports a result that held in some conditions and broke down in others.
distractors.why_wrong: The exception there is a kind of stand, not a year, and that method measures mass rather than yearly exchange.

distractors.why_tempting: This researcher studies gains and losses of carbon too, and samples at the same site as the tower.
distractors.why_wrong: Those cores measure how much is present, and the passage says outright that they cannot show which way it is moving.

teaching.reusable_rule: Before matching a statement to a person, ask which method could physically produce the number the statement mentions.

questions.prompt: This researcher's method loses accuracy on precisely the stands that hold the most carbon.

questions.explanation: Paragraph E explains that above a certain height the canopy closes and the airborne signal stops telling a tall wood from a taller one, so the maps come out low for the biggest stands. The remedy was to keep ground plots in the oldest blocks.
questions.trap_note: Another researcher's method also fails in one particular condition, but that condition is a season rather than a stand.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: loses accuracy on precisely the stands
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: understates exactly the stands
paraphrase_link.note: Understating is glossed as a loss of accuracy, and exactly becomes precisely.

teaching.decision_rule: The statement names a systematic error that grows with the size of what is measured. Only the airborne method in this passage has an error of that shape.

distractors.why_tempting: That record also fails under one particular condition, and a reader who has not yet placed the name will spend it here.
distractors.why_wrong: The failure there is a drought year. This statement is about a method that misreads the largest stands.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement names a systematic problem, and one researcher in the passage is the authority on systematic problems.
distractors.why_wrong: That problem is definitional and lies between studies. This one is an instrument limit inside a single method.

teaching.reusable_rule: Distinguish an error that occurs in one season from an error that grows with the size of what is measured.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete each sentence with words taken from the passage.

teaching.strategy: Every answer here is one word standing in the passage's own sentence, so fix the word class from the frame before you search. Two of the gaps sit inside a term whose other words are already printed for you.

questions.prompt: Foresters use the word {{gap}} for the amount of carbon a wood contains at one moment.

questions.explanation: Paragraph A poses two questions in order and then names them: the first, how much carbon is held at a single moment, is the stock; the second, whether that amount is rising or falling, is the flux.
questions.trap_note: Both terms are named in one clause, so the answer depends on which of the two questions the sentence describes.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: the amount of carbon a wood contains at one moment
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the mass locked up in trunks, branches, roots, dead wood and soil at a single moment
paraphrase_link.note: A list of five places is compressed into one abstract noun, and a single moment becomes one moment.

teaching.decision_rule: The frame asks for the term matching a quantity held at an instant, not a rate. The passage attaches its two terms to the two questions in the order it asked them.

distractors.why_tempting: It sits in the same clause, it is also a word foresters use of carbon, and it fits the frame.
distractors.why_wrong: A flux is the rate at which the amount changes. The sentence describes the amount held at one moment.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence that defines the quantity uses this noun, so a reader supplies it instead of the term.
distractors.why_wrong: It names what is measured, not the word foresters use for it, which is the one the frame asks for.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a text names two terms in one sentence, match each to the question it was introduced to answer.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'the word' before the gap wants a single noun quoted from the passage.

questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes how the conversion equation is produced: a small number of trees are cut down, dried and put on a scale, and the relationship between their girth and their mass is what the equation records.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: The equation that converts girth to mass
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Girth is converted to mass by an equation
paraphrase_link.note: The passive is turned round into a relative clause, which moves the equation from the end to the front.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap closes a three-item list whose first two items are already printed, so only the passage's third participle can fill it.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest word to the gap and it belongs to the same list.
distractors.why_wrong: It is already printed in front of the gap. A list does not repeat its own second item.

distractors.why_tempting: The three participles arrive as a unit and a reader copies the unit whole.
distractors.why_wrong: Two of the three are printed already and the answer would break the two-word limit.

teaching.reusable_rule: Read what is printed on both sides of a gap before you copy. A list never repeats the items already given.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap ends a list after 'have been', so it takes a past participle.

questions.explanation: Paragraph C says the instruments on the mast record two things very frequently, the concentration of carbon dioxide and the movement of the air, and that the exchange between wood and atmosphere is worked out from the pair.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: An aircraft carrying a laser scanner
paraphrase_link.note: Five words become two, and the aircraft disappears into the noun survey.

teaching.decision_rule: 'canopy' is printed before the gap, so the gap takes the single noun that completes the term the passage uses for what the map shows.

distractors.why_tempting: The term arrives as a pair in the passage and a reader copies both of its words.
distractors.why_wrong: The first word is printed before the gap, so only the second is missing.

distractors.why_tempting: Mass is what the whole survey exists to produce and it appears in the same sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: Mass is estimated from the map afterwards. The map itself shows something else.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the cheapest method, repeated on a fixed schedule

distractors.why_tempting: It is the obvious general noun for what a repeated measurement finds, and it fits the frame.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage's own word is different, and a completion answer has to be copied rather than invented.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage?

questions.prompt: The Tarnbeck plots were established by a government forestry department.

questions.explanation: The passage dates the plots and describes the ten-year cycle, but the sentence is a passive with no 'by' phrase and no other sentence supplies one. The only person named in connection with the network has run it for two decades, which is not the same as founding it.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the passage is silent about who laid the plots out, and silence about a plausible agent reads like a denial.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: established by a government forestry department
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The plots at Tarnbeck were laid out in the 1970s
paraphrase_link.note: The action matches exactly. The agent does not, because the passive here names nobody at all.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the date is confirmed, but the specific claim about who did it is neither stated nor denied anywhere. That is the NOT GIVEN condition, not FALSE.

distractors.why_tempting: The date and the ten-year cycle both check out, and a long public measurement network sounds like state work.
distractors.why_wrong: Confirming when something happened does not confirm who did it, and the passage never says.

distractors.why_tempting: One person is named as running the network, so a reader who reads that as ownership treats any other founder as a contradiction.
distractors.why_wrong: Running a network two decades later is not founding it, and no sentence here denies the statement.

teaching.reusable_rule: A passive with no 'by' phrase names nobody. Any statement supplying an actor cannot be checked, so it is NOT GIVEN.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: The striking feature of the record is its instability
paraphrase_link.note: An abstract noun becomes a verb phrase, which is why searching for vary finds nothing.

questions.evidence_quote: On the oldest stands they did not.
questions.explanation: The passage limits the agreement to young and middling stands and then withdraws the rest in a four-word sentence of its own. The paragraph goes on to explain why: above a certain height the signal stops separating a tall wood from a taller one.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: on young and middling stands
paraphrase_link.note: Young and middling is not all ages. The statement widens a scope the passage deliberately limits.

questions.explanation: The passage says the proposal that every estimate should state its boundary in its first line has been adopted by some journals and ignored by others. If some ignore it, adoption is plainly not universal.
questions.trap_note: The statement is a negative and the passage is positive, but they assert the same fact.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: has not been taken up by every journal
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: adopted by some journals and ignored by others
paraphrase_link.note: Some and others becomes a negative universal. The fact asserted is identical.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage states both halves of a split reception, and one half entails the statement's negative. Nothing further is needed, so TRUE rather than NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The word adopted is the one a reader is hunting for, and finding it suggests the proposal succeeded.
distractors.why_wrong: It was adopted by some and ignored by others, which is what the statement says in the negative.

distractors.why_tempting: No number of journals is given, so a reader who wants a count decides the passage never says.

paragraphs.text: A litre of milk costs what it costs. That is the assumption behind most budgeting advice, and it is wrong often enough to matter. In almost every market that supplies a basic necessity, the household with the least income pays the most for it - not in total, since it buys less, but per unit of whatever it is buying. Economists call this the poverty premium, and the phrase is not a metaphor. It is a sum of money, payable in cash, and in some markets it can be itemised to the penny. What it is not is a single charge levied by a single seller. It is the accumulated result of several dozen small transactions, each of which looks defensible on its own.

The mechanisms are unglamorous. Electricity and gas bought through a prepayment meter have historically cost more per unit than the same supply paid for by monthly transfer from a bank account. Food bought in the smallest available pack is dearer per hundred grams than the same food in a large one, and a household with no freezer and no car cannot easily buy the large one. Insurance paid in monthly instalments carries a surcharge that is almost never identified as what it is. Credit taken in small amounts over short periods is the dearest credit there is. A survey of two thousand households in the Ashfield district put the average annual premium at about 490 pounds for the lowest-earning tenth, against 60 pounds for the highest.

Not all of this is extraction. The most careful defence of the premium comes from the economist Dorian Rennard, who argues that a great deal of it is simply cost showing through. Arranging a loan of a hundred pounds takes nearly as much administrative work as arranging a loan of ten thousand, so the cost per pound lent is many times higher at the bottom. A prepayment meter has to be installed, visited and occasionally repaired. A small pack costs more to fill, label and ship per unit of contents than a large one. Rennard's arithmetic is sound, and any remedy that ignores it will fail. Where the defence stops being sufficient is the point at which a price stops tracking a cost.

That point arrives sooner than the defence allows. A household that has never switched supplier is not selecting an expensive tariff; it is being assigned one, and the assignment is profitable precisely because it is not a choice. Insurance premiums set by postcode charge one household for the claims history of its neighbours. The monthly instalment surcharge is levied at a rate that would have to be disclosed if it were called interest, and is not, because it is called a fee. Priya Iyer, who has monitored the pricing of essential services in Norland, describes charges of this kind as transfers rather than costs: nothing is produced by them, and nobody is compensated for a risk. On this Iyer is plainly right, and the line between a premium that reflects a cost and one that does not is the only line worth drawing.

A third account has become popular and deserves more scepticism than it usually receives. Marek Cowdrey argues that the premium is not a charge for being poor at all, but a charge for having no slack. What he means is storage space for a bulk purchase, a buffer in an account to absorb a direct debit, an hour on a weekday to compare tariffs. Slack, on this reading, is the commodity being priced, and it happens to be scarce at the bottom. The account is elegant, and it explains the food and energy figures well. It explains the postcode and the default tariff not at all, since neither has anything to do with a customer's storage or time.

Remedies divide along the same seam. Where a premium reflects a cost, the only honest fix is to move that cost somewhere else: a social tariff funded from general taxation, or a credit union lending at a rate that covers only its administration. Where a premium reflects a transfer, it can simply be abolished. The two most effective measures of the past decade have been of that kind - the automatic movement of long-standing customers onto the cheapest tariff, and a requirement that instalment surcharges be quoted as annual rates. Price caps are more popular than either and less reliable. A cap compresses the gap immediately, but a supplier who cannot price for risk may decline the customer instead, and the households refused are the ones the cap was written for.

The premium survives partly because it is so hard to see. No single bill records it. It is distributed across energy, food, credit and insurance in fragments too small to notice one at a time. The conventional measures of the cost of living are built on an average basket bought in average quantities at average prices - precisely the basket that nobody at the bottom buys. A household can pay several hundred pounds a year for its own lack of money without a single national statistic recording it. Until the premium is measured where it is actually paid, the argument about whether it is a cost or a transfer will be settled by whoever sounds most certain.

difficulty_rationale.note: The text concedes, limits and refuses three positions in turn without a single signposting adverb, and the writer's own verdict is always the sentence after the view being judged.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It praises an account and withdraws half of it in consecutive sentences, so a reader looking for a verdict finds the wrong one.

skim_plan.read_first: The title, then all of paragraph A. It tells you the premium is many small charges, not one big one.
skim_plan.skip: The list of remedies in F on the first pass. It is detail, and the questions that need it will send you back.

teaching.strategy: This is the one matching type that runs in passage order, so the five stems walk down the text from A to F. Predict each ending in your own words before you look at the list; every ending here is grammatically possible.
teaching.order_note: In order: question 4's ending comes from below question 3's evidence. Never search above your last answer.
teaching.watch_out: Two endings are true of the passage and complete no stem here. Truth is not the test; completing this stem is.

questions.prompt: Because the premium is spread across many separate purchases,
questions.evidence_quote: It is the accumulated result of several dozen small transactions, each of which looks defensible on its own.
questions.explanation: Paragraph A denies that the premium is one charge from one seller and says instead that it accumulates out of several dozen small transactions, each of which looks defensible on its own. Ending D states that last clause as the consequence of the dispersal.
questions.trap_note: Two endings in the list are true of the passage. Only one of them follows from a stem about dispersal.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the accumulated result of several dozen small transactions
paraphrase_link.note: A noun phrase naming the total becomes a verb phrase naming the spreading.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem gives a cause, so the ending must state what that dispersal makes possible. Endings about totals or about measurement describe the passage without completing this clause.

distractors.why_tempting: The idea that the premium goes unrecorded really is in the passage, and a reader who has skimmed the last paragraph reaches for it first.
distractors.why_wrong: That is about measurement after the fact; this stem is about why each individual charge looks reasonable.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph A does say the poorest buy less in total, so the ending feels like a direct lift from the same sentences.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the qualifier attached to a different claim, and it completes nothing about dispersal.

teaching.reusable_rule: An ending must follow from the stem's cause, not merely appear somewhere in the passage.

questions.prompt: Although the larger pack costs less per hundred grams,
questions.evidence_quote: a household with no freezer and no car cannot easily buy the large one
questions.explanation: Paragraph B grants that the large pack is cheaper by weight and then names the obstacle: a household with no freezer and no car cannot easily buy it. Ending A states that obstacle in general terms.
questions.trap_note: The concession clause is already granted by the stem, so any ending that repeats it is redundant rather than wrong-sounding.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: nowhere to store a large one
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: with no freezer and no car

title: The Land That Pays for the Road

passage_json.title: The Land That Pays for the Road

paragraphs.text: A city about to spread outwards meets the same obstacle everywhere. The ground beyond the last built street is rarely one large field in one pair of hands. It is a mosaic of narrow strips, some inherited and subdivided over generations until a single holding is thirty metres wide and four hundred long. Such a strip cannot be built on: it has no frontage onto a road and nowhere to put a drain, and its owner can create neither alone. The obvious remedy is for the authority to buy the area, lay out streets and sell serviced plots. Yet public purchase is slow, costly when a city has least money, and resented by owners who never wished to sell.

The method that emerged instead is usually called land readjustment, and its central idea is that owners surrender area rather than ownership. The parcels inside a defined boundary are treated, on paper, as a single pool. That pool is replanned as though the old field edges had never existed, and each owner receives a plot in the new layout in place of the strip they brought in. Nobody is bought out and nobody leaves with a cheque. What changes is the shape of the holding, its position by a few dozen metres, and above all its size. The ground needed for roads, drains and open space has to come from somewhere, and it comes from every owner at once.

The procedure is deliberately slow at the start. It opens when a proposal covering a defined area is put to the owners inside it. In most systems it can go no further until a stated majority of them, counted by number and by area, has agreed. Every parcel is then surveyed and valued in its existing state, and that figure becomes the basis of everything that follows. Only at this point do the planners draw the new layout of streets and services over the pooled ground. A deduction is calculated next, a percentage taken from every holding: part of it becomes public space and the rest is set aside as reserve plots, which the scheme sells on the open market. The receipts pay the contractors who build the roads. Owners take possession of their replacement plots when the works are finished, and only then is the register redrawn.

Why an owner agrees to hand over a third of a holding is a matter of arithmetic rather than generosity. Deductions in the schemes that work usually fall between a quarter and a half of the original area, and forty per cent is common where a district also needs a park. The plot that comes back is smaller, but it fronts onto a made road, it is connected to a drain, and it can be built on the week it is handed over. Land of that kind has sold for three or four times the price per square metre of the unserviced ground beside it. An owner who gives up two fifths of an area may still finish with a holding worth more than twice the old one. The catch is that the gain arrives at the end and the disturbance arrives at the beginning.

The difficult part is not the engineering but the allocation. Replacement plots are distributed by value rather than by area. An owner whose strip lay along the old road may therefore receive a smaller plot than a neighbour who brought in the same number of square metres from the back of the field. Most statutes also require that each owner be placed as close as possible to their original position. The rule reads well and constrains the planners severely, since it pulls against the first whenever the best position and the fair value differ. An objection period follows publication of the draft allocation, and disputes over valuation are heard before the scheme proceeds. Those who hold no registered title — tenant farmers, and families farming the same ground for decades without documents — are served worst, because the pool is a pool of registered claims and nothing else.

A scheme also needs two conditions outside its boundary, and both are often missing. The first is an accurate land register: where records are incomplete or contested, establishing who belongs in the pool takes longer than the construction, and schemes have collapsed at that stage without a spade being lifted. The second is a market. Reserve plots pay for roads only if somebody buys them at the price the budget assumed. A scheme launched into a falling market can finish its roads and still owe money for them. Its defenders point out that no other method delivers streets so cheaply; its critics answer that cheapness is easy to show if the failed schemes are left out.

The newest variants are smaller. Rather than a whole district, a scheme may cover four or five blocks, on the argument that a short project is easier to fund and to explain to the people inside it. Applying the method to ground already built on is much harder, since buildings as well as boundaries must move, and rehousing residents is a cost no sale of reserve land has ever comfortably covered. It has been suggested that the technique works best exactly once in the life of a place: at the moment a city reaches its farmland, and before it begins to rebuild itself.

difficulty_rationale.note: Ordinary vocabulary carrying several qualified claims per sentence, with the links between stages left for the reader to supply. Paragraph E states two rules and their conflict without a single connective of contrast.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It gives two allocation rules that pull against each other, then a third group who fall outside both, in four sentences.

texts.heading: Working alone: what the procedure asks of you

paragraphs.text: Kelmore Housing Trust employs about four hundred people, and roughly a third of them spend part of every week away from an office. If you visit a tenant's home, inspect an empty property, or carry out repairs outside normal hours, this procedure applies to you. Working alone is not forbidden and it is not, in itself, dangerous. What it removes is the help that is automatically there in a building full of colleagues: somebody who notices that you have not come back, and somebody who hears a raised voice through a wall. The procedure replaces that help with a routine, and a routine is only worth having if every visit follows it.

Every visit is planned before it is made. The address, the reason for the call and the expected finishing time go on the visit record, together with anything already known about the household: a previous incident, a dog, a relative who has been abusive to staff. Read that record before you set off, not in the car outside. Then look again when you arrive. A raised voice, a stranger in the hallway or the smell of alcohol changes the picture, and the judgement you made at your desk is worth less than the one you make on the doorstep. Nobody will second-guess a decision made there.

Each lone visit is covered by a nominated contact, normally your team coordinator. Send a short message when you go in and a second one when you come out; the second matters far more than the first. If no check-out message has arrived thirty minutes after your expected finishing time, the coordinator will telephone you. If two calls go unanswered the duty manager is informed, and the escalation set out in section nine begins. Coordinators are told not to wait until they are certain something is wrong. They act on silence, which is why an unreported delay causes as much disruption as a genuine incident, and why a courtesy text costs nothing.

You are entitled to leave. If a visit feels unsafe, end it, give a neutral reason and go; you do not need permission first and you will not be asked to justify the decision afterwards. Tell your coordinator once you are away from the property. A withdrawal is then written up on the same form as an incident, within one working day, and it is that record which allows the address to be marked for a paired visit next time. Staff who walk away and say nothing protect themselves for an afternoon and leave the next colleague with nothing.

texts.heading: The Halden fob and the response centre

paragraphs.text: Every lone worker is issued with a Halden fob, a small device worn on a lanyard or clipped to a belt. It is not a telephone. It does two things: it stores a short spoken message recorded before a visit, and it opens a listening line to the response centre when the top button is held down. The fob charges in a cradle at your desk and holds enough power for a full week of ordinary use, although cold weather shortens that noticeably. Fobs are issued by the facilities team on your first day and are signed for individually, so a fob is yours and is not to be lent to a colleague.

The spoken message is called the amber alert, and it is the step staff skip when they are running late. Before you go in, hold the side button and say where you are, who you are seeing and how long you expect to be. The fob keeps the recording with your location and starts a timer. Nothing is sent to anybody at this stage; the message stays on the device. Its value comes later: if you raise a red alert, the operator hears that recording first and knows where to send help without having to ask you a single question. An amber alert that is never followed by a red one is deleted automatically at midnight.

Holding the top button for three seconds raises a red alert. The centre does not speak to you and nothing sounds at your end; an operator simply begins listening and recording. If what the operator hears suggests a threat, they will call the emergency services themselves rather than wait for you to confirm anything, and they will pass on your amber recording and your location with the call. Operators must stay on the line until you cancel the alert with your personal code or a colleague reaches you. Pressing the top button a second time does not cancel anything, and that catches people out more often than any other part of the system.

Test your own fob on the first working day of each month by recording an amber alert and playing it back; facilities do not test it for you. Report a fault the same day. A replacement is normally available within twenty-four hours, and a loan fob is held at each area office for staff who cannot wait that long. A lost fob must be reported to the response centre before it is reported to your manager, because the centre can disable a missing fob remotely. There is no charge for a first loss. Fobs go back to facilities on your last working day.

difficulty_rationale.note: Everyday words carrying conditions: what must happen, when, and who is told first. The claims are short but each one is qualified, and the qualification usually sits in a subordinate clause.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: It describes a step that does nothing at the time and everything later, so a reader looking for an immediate effect finds the wrong sentence.

skim_plan.read_first: The two headings, then the first sentence of each paragraph. They tell you which document holds the procedure and which holds the equipment.
skim_plan.skip: The list of things that change on a doorstep in B, and the reason the centre disables a fob in H.
