questions.evidence_quote: Read that record before you set off, not in the car outside.
questions.explanation: The paragraph says the record, with everything already known about the household attached to it, is to be read before you set off, and adds that reading it in the car outside is too late.
questions.trap_note: 'In the car outside' is in the same sentence and is the thing the procedure rules out, not the thing it asks for.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Read that record before you
paraphrase_link.note: An imperative becomes a passive obligation, so the person doing the reading disappears from the sentence.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Before you' introduces a clause, so the gap takes a verb in its base form; only one verb in the paragraph occupies that slot.

distractors.why_tempting: The next sentence says 'when you arrive', and arriving is obviously later than reading.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage's own frame is 'before you set off'. 'Arrive' would make the instruction permit exactly what the sentence forbids.

distractors.why_tempting: Instructions are often written with -ing forms, and the learner supplies the form the note seems to want.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Before you' takes a finite verb, and the passage writes 'set off'.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a sentence names both the right moment and the wrong one, check which side of the comma your gap sits on.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'before you' wants a verb in its base form, and the passage's is two words.

questions.prompt: If no check-out message arrives {{gap}} after the expected finish, the coordinator telephones you.
questions.evidence_quote: If no check-out message has arrived thirty minutes after your expected finishing time, the coordinator will telephone you.
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives the delay that starts the coordinator's response: thirty minutes after the expected finishing time. Only after two unanswered calls does the duty manager become involved.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: your expected finishing time
paraphrase_link.note: Three words become two: the note drops the possessive and the head noun and keeps the meaning.

teaching.decision_rule: The gap sits between a verb and 'after', so it must be a measured interval, and the paragraph names exactly one.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the next quantity in the paragraph and it also triggers an action.
distractors.why_wrong: Two unanswered calls bring in the duty manager. The gap asks what happens before the first call is made.

distractors.why_tempting: Figures are quicker to write than words and the meaning is identical.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage writes the number in words. A completion answer is copied in the form the text uses.

teaching.reusable_rule: Copy a quantity in the form the text prints it. Converting words to figures is a rewrite, and a rewrite can be marked wrong.
teaching.grammar_cue: The gap is a length of time before 'after', so a number and its unit.

questions.prompt: A withdrawal goes on an incident form within {{gap}} working day.
questions.evidence_quote: A withdrawal is then written up on the same form as an incident, within one working day
questions.explanation: Leaving a visit early is written up on the same form as an incident, and the deadline for doing so is one working day. That record is what allows the address to be marked for a paired visit.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: written up on the same form as an incident
paraphrase_link.note: 'the same form as an incident' is squeezed into the compound 'an incident form'.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Working day' is singular, so the gap takes a single unit; the paragraph gives one deadline and it is expressed in words.

distractors.why_tempting: A figure is faster to write and numbers are allowed under this word limit.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage writes 'one'. Numbers are allowed, but the answer still has to be the text's own span.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the phrase nearest the word 'form' in the passage, so a reader matching on 'form' lands on it.
distractors.why_wrong: It belongs to the form, not to the deadline, and it cannot precede 'working day'.

teaching.reusable_rule: A singular noun after the gap rules out every plural answer before you have read a word of the text.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'working day' after the gap is singular, so the gap is a single unit.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the equipment guide?

teaching.strategy: Mark the modal and the time word in each statement first. Three of these four turn on one such word, and the fourth turns on a penalty the documents never mention. Work down the equipment guide; nothing here comes from the procedure.
teaching.order_note: In passage order: question 10's answer sits below question 9's. Search that band of text, not both documents.
teaching.watch_out: One statement describes a punishment. The documents say what staff skip, never what happens to them for skipping it.

questions.prompt: A fob that is fully charged will normally last a week of ordinary use.
questions.evidence_quote: holds enough power for a full week of ordinary use, although cold weather shortens that noticeably
questions.explanation: The paragraph states that a charged fob holds enough power for a full week of ordinary use. The cold-weather clause narrows when that holds; it does not deny the normal case, and the statement is hedged with 'normally' in the same way.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: enough power for a full week
paraphrase_link.note: 'holds enough power for' becomes 'will last': capacity turned into duration.

teaching.decision_rule: The claim is stated and nothing narrows it below the statement's own hedge. 'Normally' is weaker than the text, so there is nothing left over for the passage to contradict.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Cold weather shortens that noticeably' arrives in the same sentence and reads like a correction of the week.
distractors.why_wrong: It is a qualification of the normal case, and the statement only claims the normal case.

distractors.why_tempting: The words 'fully charged' and 'last' appear nowhere, so a search for the statement's own vocabulary returns nothing.
distractors.why_wrong: The proposition is stated in full in different words: the fob charges in a cradle and holds power for a full week.

teaching.reusable_rule: A clause beginning with a concession word narrows a claim. It only makes a statement false when the statement denies the narrowing.

questions.prompt: Staff who fail to record an amber alert are given a written warning.
questions.evidence_quote: The spoken message is called the amber alert, and it is the step staff skip when they are running late.
questions.explanation: The guide says plainly that staff skip this step when they are late, but it never says what follows for them if they do. No sentence anywhere in either document mentions a warning, a note on file or any other consequence for the worker.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: the guide criticises the habit, so a reader hears disapproval and treats the absence of a penalty as a denial that one exists.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is raised and the specific claim, a penalty for the worker, is neither stated nor denied. That is the NOT GIVEN condition exactly: no support, and nothing to point at as a contradiction.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence names the failure and the tone is disapproving, so a reader supplies the consequence a staff handbook would normally attach to it.
distractors.why_wrong: Expecting a consequence is outside knowledge. Neither document names one, so the statement cannot be confirmed from the text.

distractors.why_tempting: The guide sounds tolerant about staff who skip the step, which reads as evidence that nothing happens to them.
distractors.why_wrong: Sounding tolerant is not stating a rule. No sentence says that no warning is given, so there is nothing to contradict the statement.

teaching.reusable_rule: Naming a mistake is not the same as naming its punishment. A document can criticise a habit and say nothing about what follows.
teaching.nearest_text: it is the step staff skip when they are running late

questions.prompt: The amber recording reaches the response centre as soon as it is made.
questions.evidence_quote: Nothing is sent to anybody at this stage; the message stays on the device.
questions.explanation: The guide says the fob keeps the recording and starts a timer, then states in the next sentence that nothing is sent to anybody at that point and the message stays on the device. The centre hears it only if a red alert follows.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial arrives one sentence after the recording is described, and it is worded with 'nothing' rather than with the word 'centre'.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Nothing is sent to anybody at this stage
paraphrase_link.note: 'anybody' is the category the response centre belongs to, and the passive with 'nothing' rules the whole category out.

teaching.decision_rule: The passage addresses the moment of recording and states an outcome the statement cannot be true alongside. A contradiction is present, so the answer is FALSE and not NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: The previous sentence says the fob keeps the recording with your location, which sounds like a transmission being made.
distractors.why_wrong: Keeping and sending are different acts, and the passage says which one happens. Half of the statement is supported; that is not enough.

distractors.why_tempting: The words 'response centre' do not appear in the sentence that decides it, so a search for them lands elsewhere.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Nothing is sent to anybody' covers the centre without naming it, and the next clause says where the message stays.

teaching.reusable_rule: A denial may use a negative quantifier instead of the noun you are hunting for. Read the sentence after the one you located.

questions.prompt: An operator is required to stay connected until the worker cancels the alert or a colleague arrives.
questions.evidence_quote: Operators must stay on the line until you cancel the alert with your personal code or a colleague reaches you.
questions.explanation: The guide states the operator's obligation with 'must', and gives the same two end points as the statement: the worker cancelling with a personal code, or a colleague getting to the worker. Nothing in the statement is stronger than the text.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: must stay on the line
paraphrase_link.note: 'must' and 'is required to' carry the same force, so the swap changes nothing and the statement holds.

teaching.decision_rule: Both the obligation and both of its end conditions are stated. TRUE needs all of the statement supported, and here every part of it is.

distractors.why_tempting: The last sentence says pressing the button again cancels nothing, which reads as though the worker cannot end the alert at all.
distractors.why_wrong: That sentence rules out one method of cancelling. The personal code is the method the same paragraph gives.

distractors.why_tempting: 'Required' and 'connected' appear nowhere in the guide, so a keyword search finds no matching sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: The obligation is stated with 'must' and the two end points are listed in the same sentence.

teaching.reusable_rule: Obligation words are a small closed set. Learn which ones are equal in strength, because a swap between equals never changes a verdict.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Answer the questions below using words from the equipment guide.

teaching.strategy: Let the question word fix the answer's shape before you search: two of these want a thing, one wants a period of time and one wants a body that has to be told. All four come from the equipment guide.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, and they run from the front of the equipment guide to its last paragraph. Never search backwards.
teaching.watch_out: Three words maximum. Copy the passage's noun phrase whole: dropping 'personal' from 'personal code', or answering with a verb, loses the mark.

questions.prompt: Which control must be held down to connect a worker to the response centre?
questions.evidence_quote: it opens a listening line to the response centre when the top button is held down
questions.explanation: The paragraph names the fob's two functions, and the second is that it opens a listening line to the response centre when the top button is held down. The side button, mentioned later, records the spoken message instead.
questions.trap_note: The fob has two named buttons and the guide describes them in separate paragraphs, so the first one you meet is not the one this question wants.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: to connect a worker to the response centre
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: opens a listening line to the response centre
paraphrase_link.note: 'opens a listening line' is glossed as 'connect', so the question does not reuse the phrase you would search for.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Which control' asks for a named part of the device, so the answer is the noun phrase that is the subject of 'is held down'.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other named button and it is also held rather than pressed, so a reader who has met it first stops there.
distractors.why_wrong: The side button records the amber message. It never opens a line to the centre.

distractors.why_tempting: The learner copies the whole action from the guide because the question mentions holding.
distractors.why_wrong: The question asks which control, so it wants a noun phrase. A verb phrase does not answer 'which'.

teaching.reusable_rule: A 'which' question wants a name, not an action. Decide the word class from the question word before you look.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Which control' wants a noun phrase naming a part, not a verb.

questions.prompt: What does a lone worker have to supply in order to end a red alert?
questions.evidence_quote: until you cancel the alert with your personal code or a colleague reaches you
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives two things that stop a red alert: the worker cancelling it with a personal code, or a colleague reaching the worker. Only the first is something the worker supplies, and pressing the button again is explicitly ruled out.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: cancel the alert
paraphrase_link.note: One verb swap, 'end' for 'cancel', is enough to defeat a search for the question's own wording.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Supply' takes a thing, not an action, so the answer is the noun phrase after 'with' in the clause that names the cancelling.

distractors.why_tempting: A learner copies the head noun only, because one word looks safest under a word limit.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage's span is 'personal code'. The bare noun is not what the text prints and the limit allows three words.

distractors.why_tempting: It raises the alert, so a reader assumes the same control also clears it.
distractors.why_wrong: The last sentence of the paragraph says pressing the top button a second time cancels nothing.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a limit allows three words, a one-word answer is a choice, not a default. Copy the modifier that makes the phrase specific.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Supply' wants a noun phrase: a thing the worker provides, not an action.

questions.prompt: How long does a worker usually wait for a replacement fob?
questions.evidence_quote: A replacement is normally available within twenty-four hours
questions.explanation: The paragraph gives the usual wait for a replacement fob as twenty-four hours, and adds that a loan fob is held at each area office for anyone who cannot wait that long.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: usually wait for a replacement fob
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A replacement is normally available within twenty-four hours
paraphrase_link.note: 'is available within' seen from the other side becomes 'wait for': one interval, described from the worker's end.

teaching.decision_rule: 'How long' asks for a measured period, so the answer is the interval the paragraph attaches to a replacement and not the deadline attached to reporting.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest time expression in the paragraph and it sits in the sentence immediately before.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the deadline for reporting a fault, not the wait for a replacement.

distractors.why_tempting: Writing the figure is quicker and this word limit allows numbers.
distractors.why_wrong: The guide writes the number in words. Numbers being allowed does not license rewriting the passage's form.

teaching.reusable_rule: Two periods of time in neighbouring sentences measure different things. Check which noun each one is attached to.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'How long' wants a period: a number and its unit, in the text's own form.

questions.prompt: Who must be informed about a lost fob before the worker's manager?
questions.evidence_quote: A lost fob must be reported to the response centre before it is reported to your manager
questions.explanation: The paragraph fixes the order of reporting: the response centre first, the manager second, because only the centre can disable a missing fob remotely.
questions.trap_note: Both parties are named in one sentence, so the answer depends entirely on reading 'before' rather than on finding the nouns.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: must be informed about a lost fob
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: A lost fob must be reported to
paraphrase_link.note: The guide makes the fob the subject; the question makes the person told the subject.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Who' asks for the party told first, and 'before' in the source sentence fixes which of the two named parties that is.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other party in the same sentence, and telling a manager first is what most workplaces expect.
distractors.why_wrong: 'Before it is reported to your manager' puts the manager second. The order is the whole point of the sentence.

distractors.why_tempting: Facilities issue the fobs and take them back, so they look like the owners of the problem.
distractors.why_wrong: Faults go to facilities; losses go to the centre first, because only the centre can disable the device.

teaching.reusable_rule: When one sentence names two parties and a sequence word, the sequence word carries the answer, not the nouns.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'Who' wants a person or a body, not an action.

texts.heading: Repairs and maintenance: a guide for tenants

paragraphs.text: Report a repair by telephone on the number on your rent card, through the tenant portal, or in person at the Cadeley Road office. You will be given a job reference beginning with the letter R, and you should quote it whenever you contact us about the same fault. The portal is the only one of the three that will accept a photograph, and a picture often decides which trade is sent.

Every job is placed in one of three bands when it is logged. An emergency is anything that puts safety or the building at immediate risk. An operative will attend within twenty-four hours to make the home safe, although the lasting repair may be booked for a later date. Urgent jobs are completed within five working days and routine jobs within twenty. Replacing a kitchen or a bathroom is not a repair at all, and is dealt with through the yearly improvement programme.

The Trust looks after the structure and outside of your home, the water, gas and electrical installations, and the heating system. You are responsible for whatever you have fitted yourself, for decorating inside, for light bulbs and for keeping sinks and gullies clear. Blockages caused by cooking fat or wet wipes are the commonest of these, and the plumber's visit is charged to you.

Work made necessary by damage, neglect or misuse is rechargeable, whether by you, by someone in your household or by a visitor. The recharge tenants meet most often is a lock change after keys have been lost. The second is a missed appointment: telephone before eight o'clock on the morning of a booked visit and it will be moved at no cost to you.

Except in an emergency, you will be given at least twenty-four hours' notice in writing before anyone enters your home, and callers carry photographic identification. The annual gas safety check is the one visit that cannot be put off, because the Trust is required by law to carry it out. Where two appointments are missed the file passes to the legal team. No tenant is asked to leave a key with a contractor.

Damp is the fault reported most often and the one most often misunderstood. Where water is coming through a wall or a roof, or a seal has failed, it is a repair and you should report it. The Trust's surveyors say that most of the reports they visit are condensation instead, which forms when moist air from cooking and washing meets a cold surface. Opening a window while you cook, and keeping a low background heat in cold weather, prevents more of it than any product sold for the purpose.

texts.heading: Ending your tenancy

paragraphs.text: To end your tenancy you must give four weeks' notice in writing, and the notice period has to finish on a Sunday. A form is available at the office and on the portal, but a signed letter will do provided it states the date you intend to leave. Rent is charged to the end of the notice period even if you hand the keys back earlier, so notice given on a Tuesday still costs you the days to the following Sunday.

An officer will arrange to visit within seven days of receiving your notice. The purpose of this visit is not to inspect your housekeeping but to list any work that will be recharged, and you are told what it is likely to cost at the time rather than afterwards. Tenants who use the visit to ask what may be left behind almost always pay less than those who guess.

The home should be handed back empty, clean and free of rubbish, with the garden cut and any shed cleared. Fittings you added, such as a shower, an aerial or a fitted wardrobe, may stay only if the officer agrees at the inspection. Otherwise you must take them out and make good the surfaces beneath. Anything left in the property after the tenancy ends is stored for fourteen days, and the cost of clearing it is added to your rent account.

Keys, including window keys, meter keys and any door fobs, are returned to the office by noon on the last day of the tenancy. Rent continues to be charged until the keys arrive, and posting them is at your own risk. The rent account is closed on the day the keys are received. A balance owing is pursued in the usual way, and a credit is refunded within twenty-eight days.

Leave a forwarding address, even if you are moving abroad. It is used for the closing statement and for any refund, and a former tenant who cannot be traced is recorded as having left with the account unsettled, which other social landlords are able to see. Ask for a tenancy reference at the same time. The reference is usually ready within ten working days and covers your rent record, the condition of the home and any reports of nuisance.

difficulty_rationale.note: Plain wording carrying a condition, a deadline or a charge in nearly every sentence, with the exceptions placed in subordinate clauses rather than signposted, so a reader who stops at the main clause is wrong.
difficulty_rationale.why_hardest: Three short sentences permit, forbid and impose a duty in turn, and the permission is cancelled by two words inside the first.

skim_plan.read_first: The two headings and the first sentence of each paragraph. One document sorts faults; the other is a sequence with deadlines.
skim_plan.skip: The list of things the Trust maintains in the third paragraph. No question turns on it, and it reads like an answer.

conditions using only if or unless
what is charged back to you
what has to be in writing

paraphrase_families.passage_form: give four weeks' notice in writing
rewordings: tell your landlord in advance, in writing
put your leaving date on paper

restore the wall to its former state

hinge_words.why_here: It is the condition that decides question 12.
It sets the contrast that question 8 has to complete.
It ranks two things in the damp paragraph and points question 3 there.
It fixes the boundary that makes question 13 false.
It hedges the ten-day figure that question 14 sits beside.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Which paragraph of the repairs guide contains the following information? NB You may use any letter more than once.

options.text: Paragraph A
Paragraph B
Paragraph C
Paragraph D
Paragraph E
Paragraph F

teaching.strategy: Each stem names a kind of information rather than a topic: a way of avoiding a charge, a legal duty, a piece of advice. Decide what shape of sentence would carry it, then sweep the six paragraphs for that shape.
teaching.order_note: Not in order, so nothing narrows the search. Read all six paragraphs once before you place anything.
teaching.watch_out: Two paragraphs are about who pays and two mention appointments. The stem's verb, not its nouns, tells you which is wanted.

questions.prompt: how to avoid paying for an appointment you cannot keep
questions.evidence_quote: telephone before eight o'clock on the morning of a booked visit and it will be moved at no cost to you
questions.explanation: Paragraph D names the missed appointment as the second commonest recharge and then gives the way out of it: ring before eight on the morning of the visit and the appointment is rebooked without charge.
questions.trap_note: Paragraph E also discusses appointments, but only ones the Trust arranges for access, and it says nothing about payment.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: at no cost to you
paraphrase_link.note: Not paying is expressed as a cost that does not exist, so no word for money appears.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for a method, so the sentence has to contain an instruction and a consequence. Only one sentence in the document pairs an action by the tenant with a charge that then disappears.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other paragraph about appointments, and missed ones are mentioned there too.
distractors.why_wrong: Those are access visits the Trust arranges, and the consequence named is legal, not financial.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader hunting for the word 'charged' finds it in the last line of paragraph C.
distractors.why_wrong: That line is about blocked sinks, and it says who pays rather than how to avoid paying.

teaching.reusable_rule: A stem asking how to avoid something wants the sentence that names an action and its result, not the rule it lets you escape.

questions.prompt: the only reporting channel that will take an image of the fault
questions.evidence_quote: The portal is the only one of the three that will accept a photograph
questions.explanation: Paragraph A lists three ways of reporting a repair and then separates one of them: the portal is the only channel that accepts a photograph, and the picture helps decide which trade is sent.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: accept a photograph
paraphrase_link.note: One noun and one verb are swapped, and the sentence becomes invisible to a keyword search.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem turns on exclusivity, so the sentence must set one member of a list apart from the others. Paragraph A is the only place where three channels are listed at all.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader who has taken 'fault' as the key word looks where faults have consequences, which is the recharging paragraph.
distractors.why_wrong: Paragraph D is about who pays for damage; no method of reporting appears in it.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph F tells you to report something, so it reads like a paragraph about reporting.
distractors.why_wrong: It names what to report, not the channels available for doing so.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a text lists several channels, one usually has a capability the others lack, and that difference is what a stem asks about.

questions.prompt: advice said to be more effective than anything on sale
questions.evidence_quote: prevents more of it than any product sold for the purpose
questions.explanation: Paragraph F separates damp with a building cause, which is a repair, from condensation, which is not, and ends by saying that ventilating while cooking and holding a low background heat prevent more condensation than any product sold for the job.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph also tells you to report water coming through a wall, which is an instruction rather than a comparison.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: more effective than anything on sale
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: prevents more of it than any product sold for the purpose
paraphrase_link.note: A verb with a comparative object becomes an adjective phrase, and 'sold' becomes 'on sale'.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem promises a ranking, so the target sentence must compare two remedies and put one above the other. Only the final sentence of the document's first half does that.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph C is the other place that tells tenants what to do about a household problem, and it also names a cause.
distractors.why_wrong: It allocates responsibility for blockages and never compares one remedy with another.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph B ranks things, which is the shape the stem asks for.
distractors.why_wrong: What it ranks is the urgency of jobs, not the effectiveness of remedies.

teaching.reusable_rule: A comparison is often a paragraph's point. Find the sentence that ranks one thing above another and read the stem against that.

questions.prompt: work that is not treated as a repair at all
questions.evidence_quote: Replacing a kitchen or a bathroom is not a repair at all, and is dealt with through the yearly improvement programme
questions.explanation: Paragraph B sets out the three repair bands and then excludes one class of work from the service altogether: replacing a kitchen or a bathroom is handled by the yearly improvement programme instead.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: is not a repair at all, and is dealt with through the yearly improvement programme
paraphrase_link.note: Two clauses about what it is not and where it goes instead compress into one participle phrase.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem asks for an exclusion, so the sentence must both deny a category and name the one that applies instead. Nothing else in the document performs that pair of moves.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph C is the document's other list of what the Trust does not do, and it also uses the word 'responsible'.
distractors.why_wrong: It divides duties between landlord and tenant; the work in it is still repair work.

distractors.why_tempting: Recharged work also sounds like work the service will not simply carry out.
distractors.why_wrong: Rechargeable jobs are still done as repairs; only the bill moves.

teaching.reusable_rule: A sentence that says what something is not, and then names the category it belongs to instead, answers a stem about exclusions.

questions.prompt: a visit that the law obliges the landlord to make
questions.evidence_quote: the Trust is required by law to carry it out
questions.explanation: Paragraph E sets out the notice given before anyone enters, then singles out the annual gas safety check as the visit that cannot be put off, because carrying it out is a legal requirement on the Trust.
questions.trap_note: The duty here falls on the landlord, not on the tenant, although the paragraph goes on to say what happens when the tenant blocks it.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the Trust is required by law
paraphrase_link.note: A passive with a by-phrase is turned active, so the agent moves to the front of the clause.

teaching.decision_rule: The stem needs a duty and a source for it. Only one sentence in the document names an obligation and attributes it to legislation rather than to policy.

distractors.why_tempting: Paragraph B is full of things that must happen inside fixed periods, which reads as obligation.
distractors.why_wrong: Those are the Trust's own service standards, not requirements imposed from outside.

distractors.why_tempting: A reader searching for 'visit' finds a booked visit in paragraph D.
distractors.why_wrong: That visit is an ordinary repair appointment, and nothing legal is said about it.

teaching.reusable_rule: An obligation on the organisation reads differently from an obligation on you. Check which side of the sentence the duty sits on.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Complete each sentence with words taken from the passage.

teaching.strategy: Every answer here comes from the second document and they run through it from top to bottom. Fix each gap's class from the word in front of it: a day, a stretch of time, an adverb, a point in the clock.
teaching.order_note: In passage order: question 9's answer sits below question 8's. Search that band, not the whole document.
teaching.watch_out: Two words maximum, copied exactly. The document offers four different periods counted in days, and three of them belong to other questions.

questions.prompt: Notice to leave must be in writing, and the notice period must end on a {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: the notice period has to finish on a Sunday
questions.explanation: Paragraph G gives two conditions on a notice: it has to be in writing, and the four-week period has to finish on a Sunday. The gap takes the day itself.
questions.trap_note: Tuesday appears in the same paragraph, but as the day notice might be given rather than the day the period ends.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: the notice period has to finish
paraphrase_link.note: 'Has to' and 'must' are the same obligation, and 'finish' and 'end' the same event.

teaching.decision_rule: The frame 'on a' before the gap admits only the name of a day, and the paragraph names two. One is where the period stops; the other is an example of when notice is served.

distractors.why_tempting: It is a day of the week in the same paragraph, and it sits in the sentence that repeats the deadline.
distractors.why_wrong: Tuesday is the illustration of when notice is given; the period itself has to finish on a Sunday.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's most memorable figure and the first thing the sentence says.
distractors.why_wrong: It answers how long the notice runs, not which day it must end on, and it will not follow 'on a'.

teaching.reusable_rule: The word in front of a gap fixes its class. 'On a' wants a named day, and only one of those can be the answer.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'on a' before the gap admits only the name of a single day.

questions.prompt: Rent is payable up to the end of the {{gap}}, even when the keys are handed in sooner.
questions.evidence_quote: Rent is charged to the end of the notice period even if you hand the keys back earlier
questions.explanation: Paragraph G states that rent runs to the end of the notice period whatever the tenant does with the keys, and then illustrates it with notice served on a Tuesday.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: even when the keys are handed in sooner
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: even if you hand the keys back earlier
paraphrase_link.note: An active clause with 'you' becomes a passive one, and the tenant disappears from the sentence.

teaching.decision_rule: 'The end of the' has to be followed by something with a duration, which rules out both a day and a date. Only one stretch of time is named in the paragraph.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the paragraph's other deadline and the more memorable of the two.
distractors.why_wrong: A day cannot be what the frame asks for: it is the point the stretch reaches, not the stretch.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the right length of time and it appears in the paragraph's first line.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage's own words in this frame are 'the notice period', and a completion answer is copied, not reworded.

teaching.reusable_rule: A frame that asks for a stretch of time wants its name, not the day on which it stops. Decide the class first.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'the end of the' wants a noun naming a period, not a date.

questions.prompt: The likely price of any rechargeable work is given to you during the visit rather than {{gap}}.
questions.evidence_quote: you are told what it is likely to cost at the time rather than afterwards
questions.explanation: Paragraph H says the officer lists the work that will be recharged and tells you what it is likely to cost at the time rather than afterwards, so the contrast in the gapped sentence is the passage's own.
questions.trap_note: The gap sits on the second half of a contrast, so the answer is the option the passage rejects, not the one it recommends.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: at the time
paraphrase_link.note: A vague time reference in the text is spelled out as the occasion it refers to.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Rather than' balances two expressions of the same class, and the left-hand side is a time. The gap therefore takes the time adverb the passage puts on the other side of the same phrase.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest matching span and it is the phrase the stem has just paraphrased.
distractors.why_wrong: It is the half of the contrast the sentence already carries; the gap wants the half that is rejected.

distractors.why_tempting: It means the same thing and it is the word most readers would supply from their own English.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage writes 'afterwards'. A completion answer is copied from the text, not invented to fit.

teaching.reusable_rule: A contrast phrase balances two items of the same class. Read what stands on the left of it and match the shape.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'rather than' balances the phrase before it, so the gap takes an adverb of time.

questions.prompt: Property left behind is kept for {{gap}} before it is cleared.
questions.evidence_quote: Anything left in the property after the tenancy ends is stored for fourteen days
questions.explanation: Paragraph I says anything left in the home once the tenancy ends is stored for fourteen days, and that the cost of clearing it is then added to the rent account.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: Anything left in the property after the tenancy ends is stored
paraphrase_link.note: A long subject shrinks to two words and 'stored' becomes 'kept', so nothing matches on sight.

teaching.decision_rule: 'Kept for' takes a length of time, so the answer is a number with its unit. The paragraph names only one period, and it belongs to the storing of goods.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the nearest period in the document and it also counts from a moment in the leaving process.
distractors.why_wrong: Seven days is the window for the officer's visit, which happens before the tenancy ends rather than after.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the other period tied to money changing hands at the end of a tenancy.
distractors.why_wrong: That is the limit for refunding a credit on the rent account, and it is in the following paragraph.

teaching.reusable_rule: A preposition of duration wants a number and its unit together. Two words can be one answer, not two.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'kept for' wants a length of time, so a number and its unit.

questions.prompt: All keys and fobs must reach the office by {{gap}} on the final day.
questions.evidence_quote: are returned to the office by noon on the last day of the tenancy
questions.explanation: Paragraph J requires every key and fob to be back at the office by noon on the last day of the tenancy, and adds that rent runs on until they arrive.
questions.trap_note: The paragraph carries a second deadline, twenty-eight days for a refund, which belongs to the rent account rather than to the keys.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: on the last day of the tenancy
paraphrase_link.note: 'Last' becomes 'final' and the possessor is dropped, which is enough to defeat a keyword search.

teaching.decision_rule: The gapped sentence already carries the date, so the frame 'by' can only be waiting for the time within that day. One word in the paragraph occupies that slot.

distractors.why_tempting: It follows 'by' in the passage and it is the phrase a reader lifts whole.
distractors.why_wrong: The stem already says 'on the final day', so repeating the date leaves the sentence without a time.

distractors.why_tempting: It is the document's only other clock time and it is also a deadline for telephoning.
distractors.why_wrong: That deadline belongs to cancelling a repair appointment in the first document.

teaching.reusable_rule: When a deadline names both a point in the clock and a date, take whichever half the gap has been left empty for.
teaching.grammar_cue: 'by' before the gap wants a point in the day, since the date is already given.

question_groups.instructions_extra: Do the following statements agree with the information given in the passage?

teaching.strategy: Three of these four turn on a small word: a condition, a negation, a boundary in time. Underline the modal and the time expression in each statement before you go to the document, then read the clause that follows the one you locate.
teaching.order_note: In passage order, and all four come from the second document as its paragraphs appear.
teaching.watch_out: One statement is about a charge the document never mentions. Silence about a plausible fee is not a denial of it.

questions.prompt: The visit that follows your notice is intended to judge how well you have kept the home.
questions.evidence_quote: The purpose of this visit is not to inspect your housekeeping but to list any work that will be recharged
questions.explanation: Paragraph H states the purpose of the visit in a 'not X but Y' sentence: it is not an inspection of your housekeeping, it is a list of the work that will be recharged. The statement gives the visit the purpose the passage explicitly denies.
questions.trap_note: Missed contradiction: the denial is one clause long and sits between two positive-sounding statements about the visit.

paraphrase_link.stem_phrase: judge how well you have kept the home
paraphrase_link.text_phrase: inspect your housekeeping
paraphrase_link.note: A single noun in the text is unpacked into the clause a reader would use to explain it.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the passage denies exactly the claim the statement makes. A denial in the text is the FALSE condition, not the silent one, so NOT GIVEN is unavailable.

distractors.why_tempting: An officer coming round before a tenant leaves looks like an inspection of standards, and the visit does end in charges.
distractors.why_wrong: The charges are for work, not for a verdict on the tenant. The passage rules out the housekeeping reading in so many words.

distractors.why_tempting: The statement's words, 'judge' and 'kept the home', appear nowhere, so a keyword search finds nothing to compare.
distractors.why_wrong: The contradiction is carried by 'not to inspect your housekeeping', which is a different wording of the same idea.

teaching.reusable_rule: A 'not X but Y' sentence denies X outright. Name the word doing the denying before you choose between the three verdicts.

questions.prompt: A wardrobe you have fitted yourself cannot be left in the property unless the officer allows it.
questions.evidence_quote: Fittings you added, such as a shower, an aerial or a fitted wardrobe, may stay only if the officer agrees at the inspection
questions.explanation: Paragraph I allows fittings a tenant has added to remain only where the officer agrees at the inspection, and requires them to be taken out otherwise. 'Only if' and 'cannot ... unless' state the same condition from opposite ends.
questions.trap_note: The statement is negative and the passage is positive, which makes them look opposed until the condition on each is read.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: only if the officer agrees at the inspection
paraphrase_link.note: The same condition, approached from the negative side; nothing is added and nothing is loosened.

teaching.decision_rule: Every part of the statement is supported once the two conditions are matched: permission is necessary in the text and its absence is prohibitive in the statement. Nothing is claimed beyond what the sentence licenses.

distractors.why_tempting: The passage says the fitting 'may stay' and the statement says it 'cannot be left', so the two verbs look like a straight contradiction.
distractors.why_wrong: Both are conditional. Reading either verb without the condition attached to it produces the wrong verdict.

distractors.why_tempting: Neither 'unless' nor 'allows' appears in the passage, and a reader hunting for them finds only a permission.
distractors.why_wrong: The proposition is stated in full through 'only if', which is what 'unless' means when the main clause is negative.

teaching.reusable_rule: A negative statement can match a positive rule when a condition hangs on both. Turn one into the other before deciding.

questions.prompt: Rent stops being charged on the day a tenant moves out of the property.
questions.evidence_quote: Rent continues to be charged until the keys arrive
questions.explanation: Paragraph J fixes the end of the rent liability at the moment the keys reach the office, not at the moment the tenant leaves, and warns that posting the keys carries the risk of the delay. The earlier paragraph makes the same point from the other direction.
questions.trap_note: Moving out and handing the keys in are two different events, and the passage charges rent between them.

paraphrase_link.text_phrase: continues to be charged until the keys arrive
paraphrase_link.note: The text names the event that ends the liability; the statement names a different one and drops the condition.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is addressed and the passage names a later end point than the statement does. Two incompatible end points is a contradiction, which forces FALSE rather than NOT GIVEN.

distractors.why_tempting: Leaving a home feels like the end of paying for it, and an earlier paragraph does tie rent to the notice period.
distractors.why_wrong: That paragraph sets a floor, and this one sets the true end point: the keys arriving, whenever that is.

distractors.why_tempting: The phrase 'moves out' is never used, so a reader searching for it sees no sentence about the moment of leaving.
distractors.why_wrong: The passage states when charging stops, and a stated end point rules out any other.

teaching.reusable_rule: A liability tied to a named event does not stop when a person assumes it has. Locate the event the text names.

questions.prompt: Tenants are charged a fee for a tenancy reference.
questions.evidence_quote: The reference is usually ready within ten working days and covers your rent record, the condition of the home and any reports of nuisance
questions.explanation: Paragraph K says how to ask for a reference, how long it usually takes and what it covers. It says nothing at all about paying for one, and no other paragraph mentions a charge for a document.
questions.trap_note: Phantom contradiction: a sentence that describes a service fully without mentioning money reads like a statement that the service is free.

teaching.decision_rule: The topic is raised and the specific claim, that a fee is charged, is neither stated nor denied. No sentence would have to be rewritten for the statement to be true, which is the NOT GIVEN condition.

distractors.why_tempting: The document recharges tenants for several things, so one more charge fits the pattern the reader has built.
distractors.why_wrong: The recharges are all for work done to the property. Nothing here extends them to paperwork.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence sets out timing and contents in detail, and a full description with no price reads like a denial that there is one.
distractors.why_wrong: A description that omits a fee does not deny it. Nothing in the paragraph could be quoted against the statement.

teaching.reusable_rule: A list of what a thing includes is not a list of what it costs. Silence about money is not a denial of it.
teaching.nearest_text: Ask for a tenancy reference at the same time
